1.key: The sites have fast links, so physical transport isn't needed — what's needed is to speed up the actual upload over the internet into a single bucket. S3 Transfer Acceleration routes data to the nearest edge location, from where it travels to the bucket over the AWS backbone, and multipart upload parallelizes the transfer of large files. This is configured with a single switch on the bucket — there's almost no operational complexity.

opts.B: The approach works, but it adds extra buckets, replication rules, and cleanup of the source objects: operational complexity is noticeably higher for the same result.
opts.C: Shipping Snowball devices daily contradicts the "as quickly as possible" requirement: delivery takes days, and the links are already fast.
opts.D: Instances, volumes, snapshots, and restoration in another Region are the most complex and expensive construction of the options listed, and the data still ends up having to be placed in S3 anyway.

2.key: The data is already in S3, and the queries are simple and run on demand. Amazon Athena reads objects directly from the bucket, understands the JSON format, and is billed by bytes scanned — no cluster, no data loading, and no changes to the architecture.

opts.A: Loading the entire volume into Redshift means a separate data store, a loading pipeline, and a permanently running cluster.
opts.B: The logs are already in S3, and moving them into CloudWatch Logs is an architecture change and more expensive storage.
opts.D: A Glue catalog plus a transient EMR cluster solve the task, but they require setup and paying for nodes where a single service is enough.

3.key: The company needs to admit anyone who belongs to the organization, without rewriting the policy every time a new account is added. That's exactly what the aws:PrincipalOrgID global condition key is for: the bucket policy specifies the organization ID (o-xxxx), and the request succeeds only if the calling principal belongs to an account within that organization. Add an account and access appears automatically; remove it and access disappears. Nothing needs to be enumerated or maintained, hence the LEAST operational overhead.

opts.B: aws:PrincipalOrgPaths restricts access to specific organizational units and requires enumerating OU paths and maintaining them through reorganizations. The task, however, is to admit the entire organization.
opts.C: Watching organization events and then updating the policy is a homegrown synchronization of the account list: code, delay, and risk of error where a ready-made condition already exists.
opts.D: Tags on users mean someone has to apply and remove those tags in every account. Organization membership is checked automatically.

4.key: Private connectivity to S3 from a VPC is provided by a gateway endpoint: a route to the service's prefix list is added to the subnet's route table, and requests to the bucket travel within the AWS network without going out to the internet. There's no charge for the endpoint itself.

opts.B: Streaming to CloudWatch Logs and then exporting is a rework of how logs are handled, not a networking solution, and accessing S3 will still require a route.
opts.C: An instance profile grants access permissions, but the route stays the same: without an endpoint, traffic will still go over the internet.
opts.D: There's no such thing as private access to S3 through API Gateway: that's not how this mechanism works.

5.key: The symptom has a simple explanation: an EBS volume attaches to a single instance, so each machine has its own set of documents, and the load balancer shows one set or the other depending on where the request lands. What's needed is shared storage accessible to both machines at the same time — Amazon EFS mounts over NFS on all instances across all Availability Zones simultaneously. The existing files are copied to EFS, the application starts writing there, and the user sees the full list regardless of which instance the request reaches.

opts.A: A one-time copy synchronizes the volumes only at the moment of copying: the very next uploaded document will again end up on just one machine.
opts.B: Pinning a user to "their" server doesn't help: a single user's documents are already split across two volumes, and if that server fails, access to its files disappears.
opts.D: The load balancer sends a request to exactly one target. It can't split a request and stitch together the responses.

6.key: Two constraints apply: migrate as quickly as possible and use as little network bandwidth as possible. The second one directly rules out any network transfer, so the 70 TB travels offline — on an AWS Snowball Edge device (about 80 TB of usable capacity, i.e., a single order). Data is copied to the device locally, the device is shipped back to AWS, and the data lands in S3. A useful rule of thumb: 1 Gbps ≈ 10 TB per day, so 70 TB over the network would take a week with a fully free gigabit link, which isn't the case here.

opts.A: Copying via the CLI goes over the company's internet connection: the requirement to minimize bandwidth use is violated completely.
opts.C: S3 File Gateway is designed for ongoing hybrid access, not a one-time migration, and it still transfers data over that same network.
opts.D: Direct Connect takes months to set up and still transfers data over the link. It doesn't fit a one-time "as quickly as possible" transfer of 70 TB.

7.key: Dozens of independent applications consume the messages, and each needs its own copy. An SNS topic fans the message out to all subscribers, while an SQS queue for each consumer smooths out spikes up to a hundred thousand messages per second and lets each consumer process at its own pace. This is the classic fan-out pattern.

opts.A: Kinesis Data Analytics processes streams with queries; it doesn't store messages for dozens of independent consumers.
opts.B: Scaling instances based on CPU load doesn't decouple the producer from the consumers and can't keep up with sudden spikes.
opts.C: A single Kinesis shard is limited to roughly a thousand records per second — far short of a hundred thousand — and the intermediate table adds complexity without benefit.

8.key: The job coordinator is a bottleneck and a single point of failure. Jobs are placed into an SQS queue, and the compute nodes run in an Auto Scaling group whose size is driven by the queue length. This way the system reacts to the actual amount of work and survives the failure of any node.

opts.A: Scheduled scaling doesn't respond to the variable load stated directly in the requirements.
opts.C: CloudTrail records API calls and can't act as a destination for jobs, and keeping the primary server leaves a single point of failure.
opts.D: EventBridge routes events but doesn't hold a job queue, and the primary server remains in the design.

9.key: There are three requirements: add storage space, keep low latency for recently accessed files, and get lifecycle management. Amazon S3 File Gateway presents an SMB share to local clients, stores the data in S3, and keeps recently used files in a local cache — hence the low latency for fresh data. A lifecycle rule transitions objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after seven days, which addresses the growth in cost and volume.

opts.A: DataSync copies data but doesn't leave local applications with transparent SMB access to what has already moved, and it doesn't manage lifecycle itself.
opts.C: FSx for Windows File Server provides space and the SMB protocol, but it's fully paid file storage with no automatic transition to cheaper archive storage classes.
opts.D: A utility on every user's computer means changing workflows and giving up the familiar network share, and S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval is more expensive than Deep Archive for the same requirements.

10.key: Only an SQS FIFO queue guarantees the order in which orders are processed: it preserves sequence within a message group and guarantees exactly-once processing. API Gateway puts the order into such a queue, and a Lambda function reads it and processes orders in order.

opts.A: SNS doesn't guarantee delivery order: messages can reach a subscriber in any sequence.
opts.C: Blocking all requests while one order is being processed would destroy the application's throughput.
opts.D: A standard SQS queue works on a best-effort ordering basis, but reordering is allowed: it doesn't provide strict sequencing.

11.key: The password sits in a file on the instance, which means someone has to distribute it, change it on every machine, and make sure it doesn't leak along with the image. AWS Secrets Manager removes all of that: the secret is stored encrypted with a KMS key, the application retrieves it via API under the instance role's identity, and built-in rotation changes the password in both the Aurora database and the secret itself, using a ready-made function for supported databases. No code needs to be written — hence "minimize the operational overhead". The key difference from Parameter Store: only Secrets Manager has rotation built in out of the box.

opts.B: Parameter Store can store the password as a SecureString, but it has no built-in automatic rotation — it can't be turned on with a checkbox; you'd have to write and maintain your own function.
opts.C: A file in an encrypted bucket is still the same file: the password in the database and in the object would still have to be changed manually or with your own code.
opts.D: An encrypted EBS volume protects data at rest but doesn't solve anything in credential management: there's no rotation, and now the file exists on every instance.

12.key: The same service accelerates both static and dynamic content: CloudFront can have multiple origins and route requests by path-based behaviors — static files are served from the S3 bucket, dynamic requests are proxied to the load balancer. Dynamic content benefits not from caching but from TLS being terminated at the nearest edge location, after which the request travels over the AWS backbone. Route 53 points the company's domain at the distribution with an alias record.

opts.B: Global Accelerator doesn't support S3 as an endpoint: it works with ALB, NLB, EC2, and Elastic IP addresses. This design doesn't work.
opts.C: Putting an accelerator in front of CloudFront makes no sense: both services already provide a global network, and the design becomes more complex with no benefit.
opts.D: Two separate domains for static and dynamic content complicate the application, and S3 still can't be a Global Accelerator endpoint.

13.key: Two requirements: the same credentials are needed in multiple Regions, and they must change on a schedule, with a minimum of manual work. Secrets Manager has exactly both mechanisms: multi-Region secret replication keeps replicas of the secret in the required Regions and updates them automatically whenever the primary changes, and built-in rotation for RDS changes the password on a schedule using a ready-made AWS function. The application in each Region reads the local replica, with no latency from cross-Region calls.

opts.B: Systems Manager Parameter Store has neither cross-Region parameter replication nor built-in rotation. Both mechanisms would have to be built from scratch.
opts.C: A file in a bucket plus a custom EventBridge-triggered function means writing your own code for what Secrets Manager does with a configuration setting, and there's no cross-Region replication out of the box.
opts.D: The design with multi-Region KMS keys, a DynamoDB global table, and a custom rotation function works, but it's three services and a hand-built process instead of a single configuration.

14.key: Reads significantly outnumber writes, the load is unpredictable, and high availability is required. Aurora MySQL is compatible with the existing database, deploys across multiple Availability Zones, and can automatically add and remove read replicas based on load through Aurora Auto Scaling. The application switches to the reader endpoint without rewriting any queries.

opts.A: Redshift is an analytical data warehouse for complex queries over large datasets, not a transactional database for an online store, and a single node provides no high availability.
opts.B: A Single-AZ configuration contradicts the high-availability requirement, and RDS read replicas aren't added automatically based on load.
opts.D: Memcached is a cache with no data persistence and no replication; it isn't a database, and Spot Instances are unacceptable for a data store.

15.key: The on-premises inspection server did two things: examined traffic and filtered it. In AWS, that maps to AWS Network Firewall — a managed, stateful VPC-level firewall with Suricata-compatible rules, domain filtering, and deep protocol inspection. It's deployed in a dedicated subnet, and VPC traffic is routed through its endpoint. Distinction: Network Firewall filters traffic, WAF protects HTTP applications, Firewall Manager centrally manages policies, and GuardDuty only detects.

opts.A: GuardDuty analyzes logs and reports suspicious activity. It doesn't block anything and doesn't filter traffic.
opts.B: Traffic Mirroring copies traffic to an analyzer, but on its own it doesn't filter or block anything — it's an observability tool.
opts.D: Firewall Manager manages WAF, Shield, and Network Firewall policies across many accounts, but it doesn't perform inspection itself: it needs an underlying service, which is Network Firewall.

16.key: What's needed is visualization across multiple sources (S3 and RDS) with access segmentation: full access for management, limited access for everyone else. Amazon QuickSight connects to S3 through Athena and to RDS directly, and published dashboards are shared with QuickSight's own users and groups — the service has its own user and group model. This is exactly what distinguishes the correct option from the similar one: a dashboard can't be shared with an IAM role.

opts.A: QuickSight dashboards are published to QuickSight users and groups, not to IAM roles. Roles control the service's own access to data sources, not the visibility of a dashboard.
opts.C: Glue jobs produce report files, but that's not interactive visualization, and access control through bucket policies is coarser than dashboard-level permissions.
opts.D: Athena Federated Query solves the data-access problem, but it still produces tables and files rather than visualizations. The requirement for dashboards isn't met.

17.key: An EC2 instance can be granted permissions only one way — through an IAM role attached to the instance (technically, via an instance profile). The application obtains temporary credentials from the instance metadata, they refresh automatically, and no keys ever end up in files or environment variables. Policies, meanwhile, attach to the role, not to the instance; groups exist only for users.

opts.B: A policy can't be attached to an instance: policies attach to users, groups, and roles. The instance gets a role, and the role in turn carries the policy.
opts.C: An IAM group is a container for users. An instance can't be attached to one.
opts.D: An IAM user is long-lived credentials for a person or an external system. A user can't be attached to an instance, and placing its keys on disk is an anti-pattern.

18.key: Durable, stateless components are required. The S3 notification on upload places a message in an SQS queue, so the file details are stored reliably and survive a failure (A). The queue serves as the invocation source for the Lambda function, and the message is deleted after successful processing; on failure it returns to the queue and is retried (B).

opts.C: A text file in the function's memory is state that disappears along with the execution environment, and the function has no built-in way to poll the bucket itself.
opts.D: An EC2 instance with a log file adds both state and infrastructure to maintain.
opts.E: An email to the application owner is a notification to a person, not automated image processing.

19.key: The third-party inspection appliance accepts packets at the IP level — AWS has a purpose-built service for exactly this scenario. Gateway Load Balancer is deployed in the inspection VPC in front of the appliances, and a Gateway Load Balancer endpoint is created in the application's VPC: traffic is routed to the endpoint, passes transparently to the appliance over GENEVE, and returns the same way. Source addresses are preserved, and the load balancer takes care of scaling and health checks for the appliances — minimal operational overhead.

opts.A: A Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4 and changes the connection's destination: it doesn't provide transparent inspection of the full flow, and the return path for packets would have to be built manually.
opts.B: An Application Load Balancer parses HTTP and terminates the connection itself, whereas the appliance expects raw IP packets.
opts.C: A transit gateway connects networks, but on its own it doesn't forward traffic to an inspection appliance or load-balance across multiple appliance instances. Routes would have to be maintained by hand.

20.key: A volume restored from a snapshot is typically slow until blocks are lazily loaded from S3 on first access. Fast snapshot restore removes this behavior: volumes created from a snapshot with the feature enabled deliver full performance immediately. So the sequence is: take a snapshot, enable the feature, create new volumes from it, and attach them to the test instances — the copy is independent, and high performance is available from the first second.

opts.A: A snapshot cannot be restored to an instance store: an instance's local disks are not created from EBS snapshots.
opts.B: Multi-Attach connects the same volume to multiple instances, meaning the test environment would be writing to production data — a direct violation of the requirement.
opts.C: Manually initializing a volume by reading every block takes a long time, and time is exactly what needs to be minimized. The wording also reorders the steps.

21.key: Millions of requests per hour, millisecond-level response times, and minimal operational overhead point to a serverless architecture. Static content lives in S3 and is served through CloudFront with caching at edge locations, dynamic calls are handled by API Gateway and Lambda, and order data is stored in DynamoDB with single-digit-millisecond response times. Everything scales automatically, and there are no servers to manage.

opts.A: A fully static site can't handle purchases, and storing order data in S3 won't work: transactions and fast key-based access are needed.
opts.B: A fleet of instances, two load balancers, and an RDS database represent the most operational overhead and require manually configuring scaling for the peak.
opts.C: An EKS cluster means managing nodes and autoscaling settings, and RDS remains a bottleneck at peak load.

22.key: Two requirements work together here. "Resilient to the loss of an Availability Zone" rules out anything that lives in a single zone, i.e., One Zone-IA. "Unpredictable pattern" rules out classes that charge retrieval fees: if you don't know when a file will be needed, every unguessed access to an IA class costs money. That leaves S3 Intelligent-Tiering: it automatically moves objects between tiers based on actual access, charges no retrieval fee, and stores copies across three zones. Exam rule of thumb: "unpredictable access" almost always points to Intelligent-Tiering.

opts.A: S3 Standard does survive the loss of a zone, but it doesn't solve the other half of the problem: you pay the full rate for rarely accessed files. The requirement to minimize costs isn't met.
opts.C: Standard-IA is cheaper to store, but it charges a fee for every gigabyte retrieved and bills a minimum 30-day storage period. With unpredictable access, these fees easily eat up the savings.
opts.D: One Zone-IA stores data in a single Availability Zone. The very first requirement — surviving the loss of a zone — isn't met.

23.key: The access pattern here is known precisely: one month of active use, after which the files are never read again but must be kept forever. When the pattern is known, an explicit Lifecycle rule is the cheapest option, and the target class is chosen based on the required retrieval speed — which isn't specified in the question at all. So the cheapest archive tier, S3 Glacier Deep Archive, is the pick: roughly a dollar per terabyte per month against twenty-three for Standard. Compare with {{q:126}}, where part of the data must remain instantly accessible, and the answer changes.

opts.A: Intelligent-Tiering charges a per-object monthly monitoring fee and moves data based on actual access. When the schedule is already known, that's extra cost and extra uncertainty compared with a straightforward Lifecycle rule.
opts.C: Standard-IA costs roughly an order of magnitude more than Deep Archive. It's used when data is still read and instant access is needed, but here the files aren't accessed at all after the first month.
opts.D: One Zone-IA is cheaper than Standard-IA but still far more expensive than Deep Archive, and it also stores only a single copy in one Availability Zone — a poor trade-off for indefinite backups.

24.key: A two-month graph and root-cause analysis are needed with minimal effort. Cost Explorer provides both out of the box: ready-made graphs by period, filtering and grouping by service, instance type, tag, account, and Region, plus daily and hourly granularity. Nothing needs to be exported or built. Service boundaries: Cost Explorer is for interactive cost analysis, Budgets is for thresholds and alerts, CUR is raw data for custom analytics.

opts.A: AWS Budgets tracks thresholds and notifies when they're exceeded. It isn't a tool for analyzing why costs increased.
opts.C: The Billing dashboard shows summary totals without flexible filtering by instance type and without period-over-period comparison at the needed level of detail.
opts.D: The combination of CUR, S3, and QuickSight offers maximum flexibility, but it requires setting up the export, a catalog, and a dashboard. For a one-off analysis, that's unnecessary work.

25.key: The problem is that during a traffic spike, the number of concurrent function invocations hits the quota, and the database can't keep up with the writes. The right fix is to decouple ingestion from writing using a queue: one function receives the data and places a message in SQS, and another function reads the queue and writes to the database at a controlled rate. The queue absorbs the spikes, nothing is lost, and there's almost nothing to configure.

opts.A: Rewriting to Tomcat on EC2 instances is both a large amount of work and a step back to managing servers.
opts.B: Switching the database to DynamoDB with a DAX cluster means reworking the data model and every query, and the phrase about "existing DynamoDB API calls" contradicts the requirement, since the database here is Aurora.
opts.C: SNS delivers messages to subscribers immediately and does not buffer them: during a spike, the second function would hit the exact same overload, and failed deliveries would be lost.

26.key: The task is to detect unauthorized configuration changes on the buckets. That's a job for AWS Config: it captures a resource's configuration on every change, keeps a history, and evaluates it against managed rules (s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited, s3-bucket-versioning-enabled, s3-bucket-ssl-requests-only, and others). On noncompliance, it can notify or auto-remediate. Distinguish: Config is state and compliance, CloudTrail is who called which API, GuardDuty is threats.

opts.B: Trusted Advisor gives periodic recommendations across a limited set of checks. It doesn't provide continuous configuration monitoring or a change history.
opts.C: Amazon Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities; it doesn't check bucket configuration.
opts.D: Object access logs show data access, not changes to bucket settings.

27.key: The person has no AWS account, and creating one just to view a single dashboard isn't necessary: CloudWatch can share a dashboard externally. In the console you choose "Share dashboard," enter the email address, and the service creates separate credentials scoped to viewing just that dashboard and sends a link. Access is limited to a single resource and read-only — this is least privilege in its purest form.

opts.B: An IAM user with the CloudWatchReadOnlyAccess policy opens up every metric, log, and dashboard in the account, not just the one needed. It also creates long-lived credentials for an outside person.
opts.C: ViewOnlyAccess grants read access to resources across every service in the account — that's even broader and far from least privilege.
opts.D: A bastion host with cached credentials in the browser is both insecure and labor-intensive: the server has to be stood up, torn down, and access to it granted over RDP.

28.key: Users and groups stay in the on-premises Active Directory, and sign-in is needed across every account in the organization. The standard setup: turn on IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO), deploy AWS Managed Microsoft AD, and establish a trust with the on-premises forest. The requirement being tested here: this integration needs a two-way forest trust — Identity Center must both find users and authenticate them, and a one-way trust won't achieve that. A trust-free alternative would be AD Connector or an external SAML provider, but neither appears among the options.

opts.A: A one-way trust isn't enough to integrate Identity Center with a self-managed Active Directory: the documentation specifically requires a two-way forest trust.
opts.C: Directory Service on its own provides a directory, but not single sign-on into the organization's accounts — assigning account access is Identity Center's job.
opts.D: Deploying an on-premises identity provider of your own is possible, but the requirement is to keep managing users in the existing Active Directory, not build a new sign-in system.

29.key: UDP traffic rules out both CloudFront and Application Load Balancer — both work over HTTP. That leaves a Network Load Balancer in each Region, fronted by AWS Global Accelerator: it provides static anycast IP addresses, routes users to the Region with the lowest latency over the AWS backbone, and automatically shifts traffic if a regional endpoint group fails. The failover happens within seconds and doesn't depend on client-side DNS caching — an important advantage over Route 53-based routing.

opts.B: An Application Load Balancer only handles HTTP and HTTPS, but the service runs over UDP.
opts.C: CloudFront doesn't support UDP and can't use a Route 53 record as an origin for that kind of traffic. DNS-based failover also depends on TTL and resolver caching.
opts.D: Both the load balancer choice is wrong, and weighted routing doesn't select the Region with the lowest latency — and CloudFront is again inapplicable to UDP.

30.key: The database is needed for 48 hours a month, and the instance class can't be changed. The key detail: a stopped RDS instance restarts automatically after seven days, so simply "stopping it" for a month won't work. It's cheaper to take a snapshot, delete the instance, and restore from the snapshot before the next round of tests — you only pay for snapshot storage.

opts.A: Stopping only helps for seven days: after that AWS starts the instance back up on its own, and billing resumes.
opts.B: RDS has no automatic scaling for compute, and storage only scales upward.
opts.D: Downsizing the instance class is explicitly forbidden by the requirement: the compute attributes must not be touched.

31.key: Checking that all resources carry the required tags should be the job of a managed service, not custom code. The AWS Config required-tags rule specifies which tag keys are mandatory and for which resource types, evaluates them on every change, and keeps a compliance history. If desired, the rule can trigger automatic remediation through SSM Automation. Setup takes minutes and runs on its own after that.

opts.B: Cost Explorer shows spending and can group by tag, but it isn't an inventory tool for untagged resources, and manually tagging resources afterward doesn't scale.
opts.C: Custom code on an always-running instance means both development work and an extra machine to operate.
opts.D: A scheduled function removes the instance, but the code is still yours to maintain: pagination, new resource types, error handling. A ready-made Config rule does this without any development.

32.key: The content is entirely static: HTML, CSS, client-side JavaScript, and images. A site like this can be hosted directly in an S3 bucket with static website hosting enabled — you pay only for storage and requests, there are no servers at all, and the service itself handles scaling.

opts.A: Containers on Fargate are billed for task run time around the clock, even though there's nothing for them to do.
opts.C: A web server on an EC2 instance means a constant hourly charge plus patching and monitoring.
opts.D: A load balancer with a Lambda function to serve static content means both an hourly charge for the load balancer and charges per invocation, where a bucket alone would suffice.

33.key: Scalable, near-real-time ingestion is required, along with removing sensitive data and distributing it to several internal applications. Kinesis Data Streams ingests the transactions and retains them, a Lambda function strips the sensitive fields and writes the result to DynamoDB for fast access, and other applications read the same stream independently, each at its own position.

opts.A: DynamoDB has no rules that transform data on write, and table streams aren't designed for dozens of independent consumers of historical data.
opts.B: Firehose delivers data with tens of seconds of buffering and doesn't let multiple applications read the stream concurrently from their own positions.
opts.D: Batch-writing files to S3 isn't near-real-time, and rewriting files introduces a risk of inconsistency.

34.key: Two different questions call for two different services. AWS Config tracks configuration changes on resources: it keeps a history of state and lets you see what changed and when. AWS CloudTrail keeps a history of API calls: who performed which action, and from where.

opts.A: The services are swapped: CloudTrail doesn't keep a configuration history, and Config doesn't log API calls.
opts.C: Config is the right choice, but CloudWatch collects metrics and logs, not a history of API calls.
opts.D: Both halves here are wrong.

35.key: AWS provides two tiers of protection against large-scale DDoS attacks. Shield Standard is enabled for everyone at no cost and mitigates common network- and transport-layer attacks. Shield Advanced is a paid subscription that adds protection against sophisticated attacks, 24/7 support from the DDoS Response Team, cost protection for scaling during an attack, and detailed attack diagnostics; the resources to protect (here, the load balancer) must be explicitly added to the subscription. Since DNS is handled by a third-party provider, Route 53 is not part of this architecture — it is the load balancer that needs to be protected.

opts.A: GuardDuty detects suspicious activity from logs, but it does not absorb or mitigate DDoS traffic.
opts.B: Inspector scans instances for vulnerabilities. It has nothing to do with protecting against availability attacks.
opts.C: Route 53 is not in use here — DNS is served by a third-party service, so it is the ELB that needs protection. Also, Shield Standard is already enabled by default and does not require assigning any resources to it.

36.key: The requirement that rules everything else out is: "both S3 buckets must be encrypted and decrypted with the same KMS key," and the key must physically exist in both Regions. A regular KMS key is scoped to its own Region, and an object replicated to another Region is re-encrypted there with a different key. The only mechanism that provides the same key (same key ID and key material) across multiple Regions is a multi-Region KMS key. Of the options given, only B uses one. The ideal solution would combine a multi-Region key with SSE-KMS, but that option isn't offered, so we pick the one that satisfies the core requirement.

opts.A: SSE-S3 encrypts with keys that S3 itself manages. The requirement to use a customer managed KMS key is not met at all.
opts.C: A KMS key is created, but the buckets are configured for SSE-S3, so the created key is never actually used. The option contradicts itself.
opts.D: SSE-KMS is configured correctly, but there are two separate keys — one per Region. During cross-Region replication the object is decrypted with the source key and re-encrypted with the destination key, while the requirement calls for the same key throughout.

37.key: The company needs a repeatable, secure way to administer instances using native AWS services. AWS Systems Manager Session Manager delivers exactly that: the agent on the instance makes an outbound connection to the service, so no open ports, bastion host, or SSH keys are needed; access is granted through IAM policies, and the entire session is logged and can be streamed to CloudWatch Logs or S3. The instance just needs a role with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy attached — that's the "appropriate IAM role" the answer refers to.

opts.A: The EC2 serial console is an emergency tool for troubleshooting boot issues, not a day-to-day way to administer a fleet.
opts.C: A bastion host with a shared SSH key means an open port to the internet, key management overhead, and yet another server to operate. The Well-Architected Framework explicitly recommends moving away from this pattern.
opts.D: A VPN to every administrator plus direct SSH connections means building infrastructure and distributing keys instead of managing access through IAM policies.

38.key: The site is static and hosted in S3, so it's enough to put CloudFront in front of the bucket: content is cached at edge locations worldwide, latency drops, and data transfer out of CloudFront is cheaper than serving directly from S3. A Route 53 alias record points the domain at the distribution. This is the standard, and cheapest, pattern for delivering static content globally.

opts.A: Copies of the bucket in every Region mean paying for storage multiple times over plus constant synchronization, and geolocation routing doesn't guarantee proximity.
opts.B: Global Accelerator doesn't support S3 as an endpoint and is designed to accelerate TCP and UDP applications, not to serve static content.
opts.D: Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploading objects into the bucket through edge locations — it doesn't serve the site to end users, and it adds extra charges.

39.key: The bottleneck is stated directly: storage performance under heavy write load. At this data volume, a General Purpose SSD volume runs into its I/O limit, whereas Provisioned IOPS SSD storage lets you specify a guaranteed number of IOPS independent of volume size and delivers consistently low latency.

opts.B: More memory helps with read caching, but inserts are bottlenecked on disk, not memory.
opts.C: A burstable instance class delivers even less sustained performance — once the burst credits run out, things only get worse.
opts.D: Read replicas offload read queries, but the problem is with insert operations on the primary instance.

40.key: One terabyte of small alerts per day, no infrastructure of its own to manage, and minimal cost. Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose ingests the stream, scales automatically, and delivers the data to S3 without a single server to run, while an S3 Lifecycle rule transitions objects to Glacier after 14 days. Data from the last two weeks stays available for immediate analysis directly in S3.

opts.B: A fleet of instances behind a load balancer running custom scripts is exactly the extra infrastructure the requirements rule out.
opts.C: An OpenSearch cluster has to be administered and paid for continuously, and taking manual snapshots every day is manual work.
opts.D: An SQS queue isn't a storage layer for analysis, and having consumers check message age and act on it is both awkward and unreliable.

41.key: The instances are doing three jobs at once: pulling data from external SaaS sources, uploading it to S3, and sending notifications. Amazon AppFlow is a managed integration service for SaaS sources: it pulls the data and delivers it to the bucket without a single server involved. The completion notification comes from a native S3 event sent to an SNS topic. The instances disappear entirely.

opts.A: An Auto Scaling group speeds things up, but the instances and their upkeep remain — the operational burden isn't reduced.
opts.C: EventBridge can't write data directly into an S3 bucket as a rule target, and it doesn't handle ingesting data from arbitrary SaaS sources.
opts.D: Containers are still a compute environment you have to manage yourself, and Container Insights collects metrics — it doesn't notify on S3 upload completion.

42.key: As long as traffic to S3 flows through the NAT gateway, the company pays twice: for every gigabyte the gateway processes and for the hours it runs. A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 eliminates both charges: it adds a route to the S3 prefix directly in the route tables, traffic travels over the AWS internal network, and there's no charge for the endpoint itself or for the data passing through it. Traffic to S3 in the same Region via the endpoint isn't billed as data transfer at all. The same technique appears in {{q:91,497,612}}.

opts.A: A NAT gateway in every AZ eliminates cross-AZ transfer but keeps the main cost drivers — hourly charges per gateway and per-gigabyte processing charges. More gateways means more cost, not less.
opts.B: A NAT instance replaces the managed gateway with a regular machine: you pay for the instance and its traffic, and you're now responsible for its fault tolerance and throughput yourself.
opts.D: A Dedicated Host is a physical server reserved for your instances — a licensing and isolation concern. It has nothing to do with data transfer cost.

43.key: Complaints about internal users' internet bandwidth mean backup traffic and office traffic are competing for the same connection. The long-term fix is a dedicated AWS Direct Connect connection carrying only backup traffic: bandwidth becomes predictable, latency stays stable, and the internet connection is freed up for people. It also lowers the cost of outbound data transfer.

opts.A: A VPN still runs over the same internet connection: bandwidth doesn't increase, and encryption adds overhead. A gateway endpoint is also reachable only from inside the VPC.
opts.C: Shipping Snowball devices daily doesn't fit with data being described as time-sensitive — delivery takes days.
opts.D: There's no S3 limit at play here; the bottleneck is the company's own connection. A support ticket won't change that.

44.key: Protection against accidental deletion in S3 is built from two layers. Versioning (A) makes deletion reversible: instead of erasing the object, a delete marker is created and the prior version stays in place. MFA Delete (B) adds a second factor to irreversible operations — permanently deleting an object version and disabling versioning — so that not even the root owner can do this by mistake, and a compromised credential can't do it either. Versioning has to come first: MFA Delete can only be enabled on a versioned bucket.

opts.C: A bucket policy controls who is allowed to call which API actions. It doesn't protect against a mistake by someone who legitimately has delete permission, and it can't restore something already deleted.
opts.D: Default encryption protects the content from unauthorized eyes. It has nothing to do with the likelihood of an object being deleted.
opts.E: A lifecycle rule deletes objects on a schedule automatically — the exact opposite of what's needed here.

45.key: An SNS topic delivers a message immediately and, after a few failed delivery attempts, drops it. To make sure nothing is lost, an SQS queue is placed between SNS and the function: it subscribes to the topic (B), and the function reads from the queue instead (E). A message stays in the queue until it's successfully processed, and repeated failures route it to a dead-letter queue.

opts.A: Lambda functions already run across multiple Availability Zones by default — no configuration is needed, and this has nothing to do with lost messages.
opts.C: More CPU and memory speed up execution, but a message is still lost when a network failure occurs.
opts.D: Provisioned concurrency reserves pre-warmed execution environments and doesn't add anything to delivery reliability.

46.key: The requirement is to find personally identifiable information in uploaded files without writing custom detection code. Amazon Macie is purpose-built to find PII in S3 objects: it classifies the data, reports findings with the type and location of the PII, and publishes them to EventBridge, from which it's easy to trigger an SNS notification or automated remediation. There's no need to build custom search logic — hence the LEAST development effort.

opts.A: Inspector looks for vulnerabilities in workloads and doesn't analyze object content. A Lifecycle rule also can't delete objects based on a scan result.
opts.C: Writing a custom algorithm to detect PII in a function is the most labor-intensive part of this task — exactly what Macie already handles as a managed service.
opts.D: The same custom detection algorithm, plus trying to delete objects with a Lifecycle rule, which acts on age and prefix, not on content.

47.key: Guaranteed EC2 capacity is what an On-Demand Capacity Reservation provides, and a reservation is always made for a specific Availability Zone. So the company creates a reservation in each of the three required zones: the capacity is held for the entire duration of the event regardless of overall Regional demand.

opts.A: Reserved Instances are a financial commitment made in exchange for a discount; they don't guarantee capacity unless tied to a specific zone.
opts.B: A Capacity Reservation can't be created "for a Region" — it always applies to a specific Availability Zone.
opts.C: Even zonal Reserved Instances are meant for a long-term commitment of one or three years, which is disproportionate to a one-week event.

48.key: An instance store is ephemeral storage: the data disappears when the instance stops, so there is no durability at all. The catalog needs to move to storage that survives an instance failure and is accessible from multiple machines at once — that's Amazon EFS: the file system replicates across Availability Zones and can be mounted on all the web servers.

opts.A: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache. It is not durable storage: restarting the cluster without persistence enabled loses the data.
opts.B: A larger instance just means more ephemeral space — the problem isn't capacity, it's that the data disappears along with the instance.
opts.C: Glacier Deep Archive is an archive with a retrieval time measured in hours. A site catalog that's read on every request can't live there.

49.key: For the first year files are read irregularly, after that almost never, and both cost and fast access to recent files matter. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between tiers based on actual access patterns with no retrieval fee, and after a year a lifecycle rule moves them to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, where the retrieval delay is acceptable. Querying recent data is handled by Athena, and archived data by S3 Glacier Select.

opts.A: Glacier Instant Retrieval costs more to store than archival tiers, and searching by tags isn't a mechanism for querying content.
opts.C: S3 Standard storage costs more than Intelligent-Tiering throughout the first year given irregular access, and metadata stored in the same S3 bucket doesn't provide convenient search.
opts.D: Deep Archive takes hours to retrieve objects, and a separate RDS database just for metadata adds unnecessary cost and operational overhead.

50.key: The software is third-party, so standard baseline patch sets won't cover it — a custom command needs to be run instead. AWS Systems Manager Run Command executes it immediately across all selected instances with no SSH connection and no third-party agents required, which is exactly what's needed to close a vulnerability quickly.

opts.A: A Lambda function doesn't execute anything on the instances itself — it would still need a mechanism like Run Command.
opts.B: Patch Manager works with operating system updates and supported packages, not arbitrary third-party software.
opts.C: A maintenance window defers execution to a scheduled time, but the vulnerability needs to be closed as quickly as possible.

51.key: The task comes down to two steps. A scheduled EventBridge rule invokes a Lambda function once a day, and the function calls the application's API to retrieve the data (D). The function then formats the data as an HTML report and sends it to multiple recipients through Amazon SES (B).

opts.A: Firehose delivers streaming data into storage destinations and has nothing to do with generating a daily report.
opts.C: AWS Glue is an ETL service for processing datasets, not a tool for calling an application's REST API.
opts.E: SNS sends notifications as plain text, not HTML-formatted email, and an S3 event isn't tied to a daily schedule.

52.key: The defining requirement is a "standard file system structure" plus automatic scaling and high availability with minimal operations. Amazon EFS grows and shrinks automatically, stores data across multiple Availability Zones, and mounts over NFS to every instance in the Auto Scaling group. Volumes ranging from tens of gigabytes to hundreds of terabytes are not a problem for it.

opts.A: S3 is object storage: it lacks the familiar directory hierarchy and file operations, so the application would have to be rewritten.
opts.B: An EBS volume attaches to a single Availability Zone and, typically, to a single instance: there is no shared access and no automatic growth to hundreds of terabytes.
opts.D: The same problem as the previous option: EBS volumes are not shared between instances in the group and do not grow automatically.

53.key: Break this down by three requirements. First, one year of immediate access followed by nine years of archival: that calls for a Lifecycle rule moving objects from Standard for the first year to Glacier Deep Archive after that. Second, no one can delete the records, including administrators and root: only S3 Object Lock in compliance mode guarantees this, because governance mode can normally be bypassed by anyone holding the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission. Third, maximum resiliency: that means storage classes that keep copies across three Availability Zones, which rules out One Zone-IA. Meeting all three conditions points to option C.

opts.A: Storing everything in Glacier for the full period violates the requirement for immediate access in the first year, and an access policy is not real protection: whoever wrote it can also rewrite it.
opts.B: An administrator or root user can change an IAM policy at any time, so "no one can delete" is not actually guaranteed. Intelligent-Tiering by itself does not prohibit deletion either.
opts.D: Governance mode can be bypassed by a user with the bypass permission, and One Zone-IA stores a single copy in a single Availability Zone — both requirements are violated.

54.key: The key phrase is "preserves how users currently access the files": users work with Windows file shares over SMB, with NTFS permissions and typically Active Directory. Only Amazon FSx for Windows File Server preserves this access method, and a Multi-AZ configuration adds a synchronous replica in a second Availability Zone with automatic failover. The custom-built synchronization between the two instances goes away along with the instances themselves once they're retired.

opts.A: S3 is object storage accessed through an API: users would have to change how they work with files, and the familiar file shares would disappear.
opts.B: S3 File Gateway presents an SMB interface, but behind it are objects, not a Windows file system: lock semantics and NTFS permissions are lost. The instances and their maintenance also remain in place.
opts.D: EFS is a file system that uses the NFS protocol for Linux. Windows clients do not natively work with it.

55.key: The principle of least privilege is implemented here through security groups: the inbound rule on the database allows only the security group assigned to instances in the private subnets. The rule references a security group rather than addresses, so it keeps working regardless of how the fleet's membership changes, and nothing but those instances can connect to the database.

opts.A: Removing the route to the public subnets' CIDR blocks accomplishes nothing: routing between subnets within a VPC always works through the local route, which cannot be deleted.
opts.B: Security groups do not support deny rules — they can only allow traffic. A rule like this cannot be created.
opts.D: Peering connections are created between VPCs, not between subnets within the same VPC: connectivity within the VPC already exists.

56.key: For the API to respond on the company's own domain over HTTPS, three things are needed: a custom domain name in API Gateway, a certificate for it, and a DNS record. The key detail is the certificate's Region: for a Regional endpoint, the ACM certificate must be issued in the same Region as the API (here, ca-central-1) — only for an edge-optimized endpoint does it need to be issued in us-east-1. Once the certificate is attached, a Route 53 alias record points the domain to the Regional API Gateway endpoint.

opts.A: Stage variables pass values into integrations and do not change the URL at which the API is reachable. A custom domain is configured as its own custom domain name resource.
opts.B: For a Regional endpoint, the certificate must be issued in the same Region, not in us-east-1, and without a configured custom domain there's nothing for an alias record to point to.
opts.D: The same mistake with the certificate's Region, plus the A record should point to the API Gateway endpoint, not "to the company's domain name."

57.key: The task is to identify inappropriate content in images with minimal development effort. Amazon Rekognition has a built-in content moderation feature, so there's nothing to train, and Amazon Augmented AI plugs in human review for low-confidence predictions.

opts.A: Comprehend analyzes text, not images.
opts.C: SageMaker means developing and training a custom model — the direct opposite of the requirement for minimal effort.
opts.D: A custom model on Fargate means even more development plus managing the underlying infrastructure.

58.key: The company wants to focus on its applications, not the infrastructure underneath the containers. ECS with the Fargate launch type removes the nodes entirely: you describe the task and the resources it needs, and AWS handles the compute, patching, and scaling.

opts.A: Instances with Docker installed manually — maximum maintenance.
opts.B: EC2 worker nodes in an ECS cluster still need to be patched, scaled, and monitored for health.
opts.D: An ECS-optimized AMI simplifies setup, but the instances themselves remain the company's responsibility to maintain.

59.key: Thirty terabytes of clickstream data a day calls for streaming ingestion followed by analytics. Kinesis Data Streams ingests the stream, Kinesis Data Firehose delivers it to a data lake on S3 with no administration required, and Redshift loads the data for analytical queries. It's a standard pattern that scales with volume.

opts.A: AWS Data Pipeline is a legacy batch orchestrator, and an EMR cluster has to be provisioned and paid for — both more complex and more expensive.
opts.B: A custom fleet of instances to ingest the stream requires manual scaling, monitoring, and failure handling.
opts.C: CloudFront delivers content to users and is not a mechanism for ingesting clickstream data, and processing each object with a Lambda function is no substitute for a streaming pipeline.

60.key: The Application Load Balancer can perform the redirect itself: on the listener at port 80 you create a rule with a redirect action to HTTPS, typically using a 301 status code. No application changes are needed, and all traffic ends up arriving over the secured protocol.

opts.A: A network ACL would simply drop HTTP traffic: users would get an error instead of a redirect.
opts.B: A rule that "replaces HTTP with HTTPS in the URL" describes the same redirect but without saying where it's configured; the standard mechanism for this is called a listener rule.
opts.D: A Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4 and does not perform HTTP redirects.

61.key: The requirements read almost like a literal description of Secrets Manager: don't hardcode the password in the code, and rotate it automatically on a schedule. The secret is stored encrypted, the instance retrieves it through its role (no keys embedded in the application), and rotation for RDS is handled by a built-in AWS function that updates the password in both the database and the secret. Note the architectural detail: access is granted to the EC2 role, not to a user, so the credentials retrieved are temporary.

opts.A: Instance metadata is accessible to any process on the machine and isn't meant for secrets, and you'd have to write the synchronous password update in RDS and in metadata yourself.
opts.B: A configuration file in a bucket plus a custom rotation function means code, a schedule, and error handling instead of a single setting. Versioning only lets you roll back to previous values — it doesn't eliminate the development work.
opts.D: Parameter Store holds encrypted parameters, but it has no "turn on automatic rotation" switch: rotation has to be written yourself.

62.key: The certificate is issued by an external certificate authority, so ACM can only import it. ACM does not automatically renew imported certificates — that's the owner's responsibility. So the certificate is imported and attached to the load balancer, and an EventBridge rule triggered by the approaching-expiration event sends a notification so the certificate can be replaced manually.

opts.A: Managed renewal only works for certificates issued by ACM itself, and the requirement calls for a certificate from an external CA.
opts.B: You can't import "key material" into a certificate already issued by ACM: a certificate is either issued by ACM or imported in its entirety.
opts.C: A private certificate authority issues certificates that browsers don't trust: a public-facing web application would not work.

63.key: The workload is event-driven and uneven: a file gets uploaded, then gets converted. The most cost-effective option is to store both the originals and the results in S3, with an S3 PUT event triggering a Lambda function that performs the conversion. You pay only for the actual milliseconds of compute and for storage, there are no idle instances, and scaling as the user base grows happens automatically.

opts.B: DynamoDB isn't meant for storing files: the item size limit is 400 KB, while the average PDF is 5 MB. This design doesn't work.
opts.C: A fleet of instances with EBS storage is billed around the clock regardless of load, and EBS costs far more than S3 as the volume of files grows.
opts.D: The same problem: constantly running instances plus file storage cost more than the S3-and-Lambda combination, and the wording is even self-contradictory — it proposes storing the files in both EFS and EBS.

64.key: Three constraints apply at once: access from both the cloud and on premises with minimal latency, minimal administration, and "no significant changes to the existing file access patterns." That last one is decisive: the Windows workloads use SMB with NTFS permissions and Active Directory, so the target storage has to be FSx for Windows File Server, not object storage like S3. FSx File Gateway removes the on-premises latency over the VPN: it's deployed on site, caches hot files, and serves them over SMB, while the full copy lives in FSx in the cloud. That gives the pairing: FSx for Windows File Server in the cloud for cloud workloads, and FSx File Gateway on premises for on-premises workloads.

opts.A: FSx alone, with no gateway, means on-premises users reach the files over the Site-to-Site VPN. The requirement for minimal on-premises latency isn't met.
opts.B: S3 File Gateway presents an SMB interface, but behind it is object storage, not a Windows file system: NTFS ACLs, Active Directory integration, and lock semantics are lost. For Windows workloads that need to move without changes, that's a significant rework.
opts.C: Some workloads are moved to direct S3 access, meaning a rewrite to the object API. The requirement explicitly forbids significant changes to how files are accessed.

65.key: Reports arrive as PDF and JPEG files, so the text must first be extracted and then scanned for protected health information. Amazon Textract recognizes text in documents and images, and Amazon Comprehend Medical has a built-in PHI detection feature. Nothing needs training — it's just two calls from the same function.

opts.A: Custom libraries mean developing and maintaining your own text extraction and detection logic — maximum effort.
opts.B: SageMaker would require training a custom model, whereas a managed service already knows how to find PHI.
opts.D: Rekognition recognizes text in images but doesn't parse multi-page PDF documents: those require Textract.

66.key: Break this down by requirement. "Immediate accessibility is always required" rules out Glacier Flexible Retrieval, where retrieval takes minutes to hours. "Not easy to reproduce" means the data can't be lost, which calls for a storage class that keeps copies across three Availability Zones — ruling out One Zone-IA. "Frequently accessed in the first 30 days, rarely after" is exactly the pattern a Lifecycle rule is built for: Standard for the first 30 days, then Standard-IA. And company policy requires deleting the files after 4 years, so the rule needs an expiration action too. Be sure to compare this with question {{q:890}}: the same scenario, but Glacier Instant Retrieval appears among the options there — and the correct answer changes to that.

opts.A: S3 Glacier (Flexible Retrieval) returns an object in minutes with expedited retrieval and in hours with standard retrieval. The requirement for constant, immediate accessibility is violated.
opts.B: One Zone-IA keeps a single copy in a single Availability Zone. For critical data that's hard to reproduce, that's an unacceptable risk, and the savings over Standard-IA are only about 20%.
opts.D: This rule moves the files to Glacier in year four instead of deleting them. Company policy allows deletion after 4 years, but here you'd keep paying for storage indefinitely.

67.key: Duplicates in the database with no duplicates in the queue mean a message takes longer to process than the visibility timeout lasts: the message becomes visible again and gets picked up by another worker while the first one is still processing it. The fix is to increase the visibility timeout by calling ChangeMessageVisibility to a value greater than the processing time.

opts.A: A new queue doesn't change the underlying cause: the visibility timeout would stay the same.
opts.B: Permissions have nothing to do with duplicate processing.
opts.C: Long polling reduces the number of empty responses and the cost of requests, but it doesn't prevent a message from being redelivered.

68.key: The requirements are consistently low latency, high availability, and minimized cost, with slower traffic being acceptable if the primary connection fails. That points to Direct Connect as the primary link, with its predictable latency, and a VPN over the internet as the backup: it spins up quickly, costs very little, and only kicks in during an outage.

opts.B: VPN runs over the public internet, where latency is unpredictable, and the requirement calls for consistently low latency.
opts.C: A second Direct Connect connection is more reliable, but it doubles the port cost, while the requirement explicitly allows a slower backup.
opts.D: There is no such thing as a failover attribute for Direct Connect that automatically creates a backup connection.

69.key: High availability with minimum downtime and minimum data loss is required, at the least operational effort. For the application, that means spreading the Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones; for the database, deploying Aurora with a standby replica in another zone (Multi-AZ), where failover happens automatically within seconds and no data is lost. RDS Proxy rounds out the design: it maintains a connection pool and speeds up the application's recovery after failover. All of this is configuration, not a ground-up architecture.

opts.A: A multi-Region setup with Route 53 health checks is noticeably more work and cost, and DNS-based failover is slower and depends on resolver caching. For a 'least operational effort' requirement, this is overkill.
opts.C: A single Availability Zone with hourly snapshots means downtime during recovery and data loss of up to an hour.
opts.D: Writing data to S3 and then loading it into the database via a function means rewriting the application, with noticeably worse consistency as a result.

70.key: A Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 and knows nothing about HTTP response codes: its health check passes as long as the TCP connection opens. An Application Load Balancer can check a specific URL and expected response code, and an Auto Scaling group using the load balancer's health checks automatically replaces unhealthy instances — without a single line of custom code.

opts.A: The NLB does support HTTP health checks, but the requirement also calls for automatic instance replacement, which the NLB itself does not trigger; besides, an application-layer app is more naturally served behind an ALB.
opts.B: A cron job that restarts the app is exactly the kind of custom script the requirement rules out.
opts.D: The unhealthy host count alarm fires only once a Layer 4 health check declares an instance dead — it never sees HTTP errors.

71.key: This is about data corruption, not a Region failure, and losing up to fifteen minutes of data is acceptable. DynamoDB point-in-time recovery keeps continuous backups for the last 35 days and lets you restore the table to any second, accurate to the minute — enough to satisfy both the recovery point and the recovery time requirement.

opts.A: Global tables replicate data, including corrupted data: failing over to another Region would just return the same corrupted record.
opts.C: A daily export gives a recovery point of one day, far worse than the required fifteen minutes, and importing from the archive would take hours.
opts.D: DynamoDB is a managed service with no EBS volumes: there is no table volume to snapshot.

72.key: The data transfer charges arise because traffic to S3 travels through an internet gateway or a NAT gateway. An S3 gateway endpoint adds a route to the service's prefix, so traffic stays inside the AWS network and isn't charged, while the endpoint policy restricts access to the required buckets. Since the buckets are in the same Region, there's no cross-Region charge either.

opts.A: API Gateway isn't a networking device that requests to S3 can be routed through: there's no route table entry that could point to it.
opts.B: A NAT gateway charges for every gigabyte it processes — that would increase costs rather than reduce them, and it has no endpoint policies.
opts.C: A public subnet and internet gateway keep the same paid path over the internet and weaken security.

73.key: Access comes from the corporate network over the internet, so the bastion must accept connections from the company's external IP range — that's what the inbound rule specifies (C). The application instances in the private subnet should accept SSH only from the bastion, and the bastion reaches them over its private address, so the rule references the bastion's private address (D).

opts.A: Allowing the bastion to accept inbound connections from the application instances makes no sense: the direction of the connection is reversed.
opts.B: The company's internal IP range gets translated on the way out to the internet: what reaches the bastion is the external address, so this rule would never match.
opts.E: The bastion reaches the private instances inside the VPC using its private address; its public address plays no part in that traffic.

74.key: The web tier is public-facing, so its security group accepts inbound traffic on port 443 from the internet (A). The SQL Server database accepts connections only from the web tier, so its inbound rule allows port 1433 referencing the web tier's security group (C).

opts.B: Security group outbound rules allow everything by default, and restricting the web tier's outbound traffic has nothing to do with this requirement.
opts.D: Security groups are stateful: the database's response traffic is allowed automatically, so no separate outbound rule is needed.
opts.E: The database doesn't need port 443 inbound: connections to SQL Server go over port 1433, and adding an unnecessary allowance violates the principle of least privilege.

75.key: Transactions are dropped whenever one tier becomes overloaded, so the tiers need to be decoupled with a buffer and freed from server management. API Gateway accepts requests, Lambda functions run the logic and scale automatically, and SQS queues between the services hold messages during spikes, so nothing gets lost.

opts.B: Sizing instances for peak load isn't modernization, it just postpones the problem, and you end up paying for peak capacity even during idle periods.
opts.C: SNS delivers messages immediately and doesn't form a queue: there's no buffering, and the topic simply has no queue-length metric.
opts.D: The queue choice is correct, but the EC2 instances still have to be managed, and scaling on 'detected communication failures' reacts only after data has already been lost.

76.key: What needs to move is files (JSON on a SAN), and it has to happen reliably and securely. AWS DataSync is a service built specifically for file transfer: it verifies integrity, automatically retries failed transfers, encrypts data in transit, and can run on a schedule. Running it over Direct Connect is more reliable and predictable than over the internet, and for 10 TB a day, consistent bandwidth is critical.

opts.A: The same DataSync, but over the public internet: bandwidth is shared with other traffic, latency fluctuates, and reliability is lower.
opts.C: DMS migrates databases, not files on network-attached storage. It's the wrong tool for JSON files.
opts.D: A dedicated connection doesn't fix the underlying problem: DMS still isn't designed to copy files from a SAN to S3.

77.key: What's needed is an API, on-the-fly data transformation, and storage — with minimal operational overhead. API Gateway accepts requests and writes directly into a Kinesis data stream, Firehose reads the stream, invokes a Lambda function to transform the data, and delivers the result to S3. There isn't a single server anywhere in this design.

opts.A: An EC2 instance acting as the API is a machine that has to be maintained and scaled.
opts.B: Again a self-managed instance, and Glue is a batch ETL service, not built to ingest a real-time stream.
opts.D: AWS Glue is not a destination for streaming data from API Gateway: no such integration exists.

78.key: Keeping copies of the table for seven years is easiest to manage centrally. AWS Backup supports DynamoDB, lets you set a schedule and retention period through policy, stores copies in its own managed storage, and shows job status — no scripts and no manual steps.

opts.A: Point-in-time recovery retains data for at most 35 days: the seven-year requirement isn't met.
opts.C: An on-demand backup created from the console is a manual action, and it isn't exported to a bucket as a file that lifecycle rules can manage.
opts.D: A custom scheduled function is code and maintenance in place of a ready-made service.

79.key: The table sits idle for long stretches, and evening traffic is unpredictable and spikes very quickly. On-demand capacity mode adjusts throughput instantly and is billed on actual requests, so there's no charge for idle time and a spike doesn't run into a pre-set capacity ceiling.

opts.B: A secondary index solves the problem of accessing data by a different key and has nothing to do with cost under uneven load.
opts.C: Provisioned capacity auto scaling reacts on the order of minutes: during very sharp spikes, requests would be throttled with a throughput-exceeded error.
opts.D: A global table is meant for multi-Region operation and simply doubles the cost, and provisioned mode still can't keep up with the spikes.

80.key: The image is encrypted with a KMS key, so sharing it is really two separate operations. First: allow the other account to launch the image — add its account ID to the AMI's launchPermission (which also grants access to the underlying EBS snapshots). Second: allow that same account to use the key the volumes are encrypted with — an edit to the KMS key policy. Without the second step, the partner would see the image but wouldn't be able to decrypt the volumes. The 'MOST secure' requirement means granting access to that specific account, not publishing the image.

opts.A: Making the encrypted AMI public exposes the image to the entire world. Even if the key itself is granted only to the partner, this grossly violates the requirement for maximum security.
opts.C: A key policy can't 'trust another key': the snapshots are encrypted with your key, and only that key can decrypt them. The partner can re-encrypt a copy with their own key only after they've already been granted access to yours.
opts.D: Exporting the AMI to a bucket in the other account is a roundabout, labor-intensive path, and exporting a virtual machine doesn't even work for images encrypted with a KMS key.

81.key: Jobs need to be stored durably, the processors need to be stateless, and scaling should track the amount of work. An SQS queue holds the jobs, an AMI containing the processor application is used in the launch template, and the Auto Scaling group grows and shrinks based on the number of messages in the queue — that is, on the actual amount of work.

opts.A: SNS doesn't store messages: if no consumer is available at the moment, the job is lost, and scaling on CPU usage doesn't reflect the size of the queue.
opts.B: The queue choice is correct, but scaling on network usage is only loosely related to the number of pending jobs.
opts.D: SNS again fails to provide durable storage for jobs, and the number of published messages doesn't show how much work remains.

82.key: ACM has a managed AWS Config rule called acm-certificate-expiration-check: it flags certificates — including imported ones — as noncompliant when they're due to expire within a set window. EventBridge picks up the noncompliance event and sends a notification to the security team's SNS topic.

opts.A: ACM itself has no mechanism for rules that publish arbitrary messages to SNS on a schedule.
opts.C: Trusted Advisor only partially tracks load balancer certificates and requires a Business-level support plan or higher; the managed Config rule is the standard, more precise path.
opts.D: ACM does generate an expiration event, but by default 45 days out, and an EventBridge rule can't be configured with an arbitrary 30-day threshold — that's exactly what the Config rule is for.

83.key: The backend has to stay in the company's own data center, and what needs speeding up is European users, within just a few days. CloudFront supports an arbitrary custom origin, including a server outside AWS: requests land at the nearest edge location, static content gets cached, and dynamic content travels to the origin over the AWS backbone with an already-established TLS connection. No migration is involved, and setup takes hours.

opts.A: Moving the site to an instance in the US doesn't speed things up for European users: the distance stays the same, and migration takes time.
opts.B: The site is dynamic, so it can't be hosted on S3, and cross-Region replication would only solve the problem for static content.
opts.D: Geoproximity only chooses which origin to send a user to, but there's only one origin here — the same servers in the US. Latency wouldn't change.

84.key: Production instances run around the clock and predictably — they're most cost-effectively covered by Reserved Instances, with savings of up to 72 percent. The development and test instances run for a few hours and will be stopped by automation, so On-Demand pricing suits them: committing for a year to intermittent workloads isn't worthwhile.

opts.A: Interruptible instances are risky for production: AWS can reclaim the capacity at any time, and reserving irregular environments isn't cost-effective.
opts.C: Spot blocks (pre-paid blocks of Spot capacity for a fixed duration) are no longer offered to new customers, and that kind of capacity isn't suited to round-the-clock production anyway.
opts.D: Full-price production is overpaying, and interruptible capacity for development environments risks losing the instance mid-task.

85.key: 'Cannot be modified or deleted after they are stored' describes WORM storage, and in S3 that's handled by Object Lock. It works on top of versioning: the object is stored as an immutable version, and a retention period or legal hold prevents that version from being deleted or overwritten. That's why both are enabled together — versioning as the foundation and Object Lock as the actual restriction. The mode is chosen based on how strict the requirement is: compliance mode, when no one can bypass it, or governance mode, when a privileged user is allowed to.

opts.B: A Lifecycle rule changes the storage class. It doesn't prevent an object from being overwritten or deleted.
opts.C: Versioning makes deletion reversible, but doesn't prevent it, and an ACL is a legacy permissions mechanism that doesn't stop the owner or an administrator from deleting the object.
opts.D: Mounting EFS as read-only is a client-side setting: the same file system can be mounted for writing from another machine. That's not data immutability.

86.key: The requirement to "rotate user credentials frequently" combined with secure password retrieval by the web servers points to Secrets Manager. The password is stored encrypted with a KMS key, the servers retrieve it by calling GetSecretValue under the instance role, and rotation for RDS MySQL is handled by a managed, scheduled function. A useful operational detail: during rotation, Secrets Manager keeps secret versions labeled AWSCURRENT and AWSPREVIOUS, so a request that arrives right as the password changes does not break.

opts.B: OpsCenter in Systems Manager is a workspace for triaging operational incidents (OpsItems). It is not a secrets store.
opts.C: A password in an S3 object does not rotate itself: rotation would have to be built with custom code, and access would have to be restricted manually.
opts.D: Files on each web server's file system mean a copy of the secret on every machine, plus manual redistribution of the new password on every rotation.

87.key: During the upgrade the database is unavailable, and records that arrive during that window are lost. A buffer solves the problem: the function invoked from API Gateway places the customer data on an SQS FIFO queue, and a separate function polls the queue and writes to the database. While the database is upgrading, messages simply accumulate in the queue and are processed once it comes back; ordering is preserved throughout.

opts.A: RDS Proxy smooths over failovers and manages the connection pool, but during a version upgrade the database is still unavailable, so there is nowhere to write the data.
opts.B: Retries inside the function run into the function's execution time limit: the upgrade takes longer than that, so the data is lost anyway.
opts.C: A function's local storage is ephemeral and belongs to a specific execution environment instance: another function invocation won't see it, and it disappears once that instance is gone.

88.key: The bucket owner pays for outbound data transfer from S3, and that's exactly what needs to change. Requester Pays shifts the cost of requests and outbound transfer to whoever downloads the data: the marketing firm accesses the bucket with its own credentials and pays for its own downloads. The owner continues to pay only for storage. One limitation worth remembering: with Requester Pays enabled, anonymous access is not possible — every request must be signed and include a header confirming acceptance of the charges. The same answer applies in {{q:960}}.

opts.B: Cross-Region Replication would make the company pay for both cross-region transfer of every object and storage of the second copy. Costs would go up, not down.
opts.C: Granting cross-account access solves the permissions problem, but the bill for outbound transfer would still go to the bucket owner.
opts.D: Storage class has no effect on outbound transfer pricing, and syncing to someone else's bucket is still a transfer paid for by the company.

89.key: The concern is specific — accidental deletion of documents, not a data leak. That calls for reversibility and a second factor: versioning preserves prior versions on deletion and overwrite (a delete creates a delete marker), and MFA Delete requires a one-time code for irreversible operations — deleting a specific version and disabling versioning. Encryption and permission tweaks don't address this problem: whoever has delete permission can delete the encrypted object just as easily.

opts.B: MFA on console sign-in protects the account itself. It does not stop a DeleteObject call made with that account's access keys — that's exactly what MFA Delete on the bucket is for.
opts.C: Lifecycle rules apply to objects in a bucket, not to "IAM accounts," and they can only transition or expire objects. They can't enforce a deny.
opts.D: Blocking the audit team's access to the key means they can no longer read their own documents. It does nothing to prevent the object from being deleted.

90.key: The script's queries are interfering with the developers' work. A read replica removes that load from the primary instance: the script queries only the replica, while development continues to work against the primary database. It's set up with a single operation, and no code needs to change.

opts.A: The standby instance in a Multi-AZ configuration is not available for reads: the load would remain on the primary.
opts.C: A manual daily export is manual work, and the data goes stale.
opts.D: The queries run at random times and count new records: the cache would miss constantly, and the application would still have to be modified.

91.key: The requirement is categorical: none of the application's traffic may travel over the internet. S3 is a regional service with public endpoints, so "putting the bucket in a private subnet" isn't possible — what gets hidden is the path to it, not the bucket itself.
