A gateway endpoint adds a route to the VPC's route table pointing to the S3 prefix over the AWS network itself: packets never leave to the internet, and the instances don't need public addresses. Access can be further restricted with an aws:SourceVpce condition in the bucket policy, so the bucket only accepts requests through that endpoint.

opts.B: S3 buckets don't live inside VPC subnets: it's a regional service with its own namespace. That configuration simply doesn't exist.
opts.C: Being in the same Region only avoids cross-region transfer. The path still goes through the public S3 endpoint.
opts.D: A NAT gateway exists precisely to send traffic out to the internet. That's a direct violation of the requirement.

92.key: Two independent layers of protection. Network layer: a gateway endpoint for S3 (A) routes traffic from the VPC to the bucket over the internal AWS network, without going out to the internet. Authorization layer: a bucket policy (C) that permits access only to requests coming from this VPC or through this endpoint (using the aws:SourceVpc or aws:SourceVpce conditions) and only to the application tier's role. Together they provide both a private path and a denial of access from anywhere else. The instances operate under a role rather than stored keys throughout.

opts.B: Making a bucket with sensitive data publicly accessible is the direct opposite of the requirement.
opts.D: Copying an IAM user's keys onto the instance creates a long-lived secret sitting on disk. The proper approach is an instance role with temporary credentials.
opts.E: A NAT instance sends traffic out to the internet and adds a node that has to be maintained. The endpoint solves the same problem privately and without a server.

93.key: The problem is the full export every four hours: it loads the production database and locks the staging environment for a long time. Aurora can create a database clone almost instantly using storage-level copy-on-write, so the clone appears within minutes, doesn't physically copy the data, and doesn't add load to the source cluster. Developers get a fresh copy on demand.

opts.A: A mysqldump export is exactly the operation causing the load and the delay. The problem remains.
opts.C: The standby instance in a Multi-AZ configuration isn't available for reads or writes: it can't be used as a staging environment.
opts.D: Again a full export and restore: both the load on production and the long wait for developers remain.

94.key: The files are small, processing is simple and one-time, and demand is spiky. An S3 notification places an event on an SQS queue, a Lambda function reads the queue and processes the file, and the resulting JSON is stored in DynamoDB. Everything is serverless: it scales itself, costs nothing when idle, and requires almost no operational work. The queue also provides retries on failure.

opts.A: An EMR cluster is billed for node uptime and requires configuration — disproportionate for processing small files one at a time.
opts.B: EC2 instances reading the queue need to be scaled, patched, and monitored: more operational overhead than a function.
opts.D: EventBridge and Kinesis add an extra layer where an S3 notification is already enough, and Aurora is overkill for storing individual JSON documents.

95.key: Read and write traffic need to be split quickly, without sacrificing performance. Read replicas take on the SELECT queries while the primary instance remains responsible for writes. Important detail: the replica must have the same compute and storage resources as the source, otherwise it will start to lag and become a bottleneck itself.

opts.A: A Multi-AZ configuration doesn't split load: reads against the primary instance continue at the same volume.
opts.B: The Multi-AZ standby instance doesn't accept requests at all — reading from it isn't possible.
opts.C: A replica with half the source's resources can't keep up with the stream of changes; replication lag will grow, and the data will end up stale.

96.key: The policy has two statements, and they must be read together. The first allows ec2:TerminateInstances, but only if the request comes from an IP address within the 10.100.100.0/24 range. The second denies all EC2 actions if the Region is not us-east-1, and an explicit Deny overrides any Allow. The intersection of these conditions gives the answer: instances can only be terminated in us-east-1, and only from an address in that subnet; 10.100.100.254 falls within it. General IAM rule: an explicit deny is evaluated first, then whether an allow exists, and everything else is denied by default.

opts.A: The second statement denies EC2 actions in every Region except us-east-1. That is exactly the opposite of what the option states.
opts.B: The IpAddress condition checks the source IP of the request (aws:SourceIp), not the IP address of the instance itself. It's about where the API call came from.
opts.D: 10.100.100.254 falls within 10.100.100.0/24, so the allow applies — it isn't blocked.

97.key: SharePoint requires a Windows shared resource over the SMB protocol with Active Directory authentication — that is exactly the profile of Amazon FSx for Windows File Server. The file system joins the AD domain, supports Windows access control lists and shadow copies, and deploys in a Multi-AZ configuration for high availability.

opts.A: EFS is an NFS file system for Linux; it doesn't work with SMB and doesn't integrate with an Active Directory domain in the required way.
opts.B: A file gateway is a hybrid gateway for accessing S3 from an on-premises network, not a full-fledged shared storage solution for a workload that has moved entirely into AWS.
opts.C: There's no built-in way to mount an S3 bucket as a Windows volume, and it wouldn't provide the file-system semantics with locking that SharePoint needs.

98.key: Repeated emails mean a message is becoming visible in the queue again before the function finishes processing it. The visibility timeout needs to be set higher than the sum of the function's timeout and the batch window timeout — then the message won't be handed to a second instance of the function.

opts.A: Long polling reduces the number of empty responses and their cost, but it has no effect on message redelivery.
opts.B: A FIFO queue would solve the problem, but switching to it changes the queue type, limits throughput, and requires changes — while the problem can be fixed with a single setting.
opts.D: Deleting the message before processing it leads to data loss on any function failure.

99.key: The key phrase is Lustre clients. The only fully managed AWS service with that protocol is Amazon FSx for Lustre: it delivers very high throughput and low latency, is reachable from an on-premises network over Direct Connect or VPN, and is fully managed by AWS.

opts.A: Storage Gateway serves shares over NFS and SMB; it has no Lustre protocol.
opts.B: A self-managed Windows server is neither Lustre nor a managed service: it would have to be maintained in-house.
opts.C: EFS has no Lustre support mode: it's an NFS file system. That configuration doesn't exist.

100.key: The requirement is to encrypt and decrypt certificates in near real time, store the result in highly available storage, and avoid operational overhead. KMS turns cryptography into a managed service: the EC2 role is granted permission to use the key, the application encrypts the data (in practice via envelope encryption using GenerateDataKey) and puts the ciphertext in S3, which stores objects across three Availability Zones. No custom libraries and no key servers to run.

opts.A: Secrets Manager is designed for secrets, not arbitrary certificate files, and the option explicitly calls for manual updates — which is exactly the operational overhead the requirement asks to avoid.
opts.B: A custom function with a cryptography library means you're responsible for the algorithms, the keys, and their storage yourself. "Store the function in an S3 bucket" also isn't a way to run it.
opts.D: Encrypting via KMS is the right choice, but an EBS volume is tied to a single Availability Zone and a single instance. The requirement for highly available storage is met by S3, not EBS.

101.key: The private subnets need outbound internet access, and the solution has to be fault tolerant. A NAT gateway is a zonal resource, so one is created in the public subnet of each Availability Zone, and each zone's private route table sends all non-VPC-bound traffic to its "own" gateway. A zone failure doesn't affect the others, and no cross-zone data transfer charges apply.

opts.B: NAT instances need to sit in the public subnets, not the private ones, and they require manual maintenance and scaling.
opts.C: A VPC can have only one internet gateway, and a subnet with a route to it is, by definition, public.
opts.D: An egress-only internet gateway works only with IPv6, while the scenario uses IPv4 blocks.

102.key: The task is to automate moving the data from the on-premises server into EFS. AWS DataSync does this natively: an agent is installed in the company's data center (B) and gets access to the SFTP server's NFS file system, after which a location is configured in DataSync pointing at that source (E). The transfer task then runs on a schedule, verifies integrity, and works incrementally.

opts.A: The EFS file system is reachable from every Availability Zone through its mount targets, so there's no need to co-locate the zone with the instance, and it has nothing to do with automating the transfer.
opts.C: An extra EBS volume contradicts the requirement: the data has to end up in EFS.
opts.D: Manually copying with an operating-system command is the exact opposite of the automation being asked for.

103.key: AWS Glue keeps a marker of where the previous successful run left off — this is a job bookmark. With bookmarks enabled, the next run picks up only the S3 objects that appeared after the last run and leaves already-processed objects alone. Nothing needs to be deleted or rewritten; the service tracks the state itself. It's also worth remembering the flip side: if the job needs to reprocess all the data from scratch, the bookmark can be reset (job bookmark reset).

opts.B: Deleting the source data after processing solves the symptom at the cost of losing raw data that is usually needed for reprocessing and auditing. This is not an incremental-processing mechanism, it's destruction of the source.
opts.C: NumberOfWorkers sets the number of workers, which controls run speed and cost. It does not change the volume of data read.
opts.D: FindMatches is an ML transform for finding duplicate records. It has nothing to do with choosing to read only new files.

104.key: Two complementary measures address a distributed attack from thousands of addresses. Shield Advanced (A) provides protection against large-scale attacks, automatic mitigations, access to the DDoS response team, and cost protection against scaling triggered by the attack. CloudFront (C) moves the entry point onto a global network of edge locations that absorbs volumetric attacks and stops them far from your instances, with all content — including dynamic content — passing through it. Together this is the standard combination for a requirement where "downtime is not acceptable."

opts.B: GuardDuty detects and reports threats but does not automatically block traffic.
opts.D: A custom solution that adds addresses to network ACLs does not scale: ACLs have a hard limit on the number of rules, while an attack involves thousands of addresses that keep changing.
opts.E: Scaling based on CPU utilization only pays for the attack with more compute capacity, and Spot Instances can also be reclaimed at any moment.

105.key: Permission for an external service to invoke the function is granted through a resource-based policy on the function itself, not through the execution role: the execution role describes what the function is allowed to do, not who is allowed to invoke it. Least privilege here means the action lambda:InvokeFunction and the principal events.amazonaws.com — only the EventBridge service, and only permission to invoke.

opts.A: The execution role grants permissions to the function itself, and a wildcard as the principal opens up invocation to anyone.
opts.B: This is again an execution role instead of a resource-based policy, and the principal is wrong: it should be the EventBridge service invoking the function, not the Lambda service itself.
opts.C: The resource-based policy is the right choice, but the action lambda:* grants far more than a single invocation — the least privilege principle is violated.

106.key: The three requirements are addressed one by one. Encryption at rest is provided by every option. "Encryption key usage must be logged for auditing" rules out SSE-S3 and SSE-C: key access is visible in CloudTrail only for KMS keys, where every Decrypt and GenerateDataKey call is logged along with who accessed which object. "Keys must be rotated every year" combined with "MOST operationally efficient" rules out manual rotation: a KMS key has built-in automatic rotation once every 365 days, turned on with a single setting. That leaves SSE-KMS with automatic rotation.

opts.A: With SSE-C, the key is held by you and sent with every request. AWS neither logs nor rotates it, and all management falls on the application — the opposite of operational efficiency.
opts.B: SSE-S3 provides neither a log of key access nor control over the rotation schedule: the service manages the keys, and these operations are not visible in CloudTrail.
opts.C: Manual rotation satisfies the requirement but requires a human action every year and oversight to make sure it isn't forgotten. Automatic rotation does the same thing without intervention.

107.key: Location data points must be ingested and served through a REST API with minimal infrastructure. API Gateway provides the REST interface itself, while Lambda functions store and return the data. The combination is serverless, scales to handle peak operating hours, and integrates easily with the existing analytics platform.

opts.A: Athena runs queries against data in S3, but it is not a REST interface for an application.
opts.C: QuickSight and Redshift are a dashboard and an analytical data warehouse, not a way to ingest and serve data points through an API.
opts.D: Kinesis Data Analytics processes streams with queries but does not serve data to an application through a REST interface.

108.key: The sale event needs to reach several independent systems. RDS publishes an event notification to an SNS topic, and several SQS queues are subscribed to that topic — one per receiving system. Each system then gets its own copy, can process it at its own pace, and survives temporary unavailability. Lambda functions read the queues and update the target systems.

opts.A: A Lambda function is not invoked by a row change in an RDS database — no such trigger exists.
opts.B: Same nonexistent-trigger problem, and a FIFO queue does not solve fan-out to multiple recipients.
opts.C: The direction is reversed: fan-out to multiple recipients is done by a topic, while a queue is a single-consumer destination.

109.key: Pay attention to the wording: objects must remain unchangeable for a nonspecific amount of time, meaning the duration is not known in advance and the company will remove the protection manually. A retention period does not describe this — it is always defined by a date or a number of days. This scenario matches a legal hold: it holds indefinitely until removed by someone with the s3:PutObjectLegalHold permission. That's also where the second half of the answer comes from: this is exactly the permission granted to the few people allowed to remove the hold and delete the objects.

opts.A: Vault Lock in S3 Glacier is a mechanism of the older archival service, applied to an entire vault and immutable once locked. It does not support flexibly lifting protection at the company's discretion.
opts.B: A 100-year period is a fixed duration, not "until the company decides." Governance mode can also be bypassed by anyone with the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission.
opts.C: CloudTrail and restoring from backups are an after-the-fact reaction. The requirement is that the object cannot be changed in the first place.

110.key: Two separate bottlenecks are resolved individually. Uploads are slow because the bytes travel through the web server: a presigned URL gives the browser the ability to put the file directly into the bucket (C), removing EC2 as the middleman. Resizing is decoupled through an event: an S3 Event Notification invokes Lambda after the object has already been written (D), so the user doesn't wait for processing.

opts.A: S3 Glacier is an archival storage class: uploading there does not speed up the request, and reads take minutes to hours. It has nothing to do with decoupling components.
opts.B: The web server still receives the file and forwards it to S3 — the bytes still flow through the instance, so the slow upload remains.
opts.E: A schedule in EventBridge means batch resizing every N minutes: the image appears with a delay, and the upload event itself is ignored. An event-driven model here is both simpler and faster.

111.key: The question is about the highest availability with the least operational complexity, so every tier needs to move to a managed, cross-AZ redundant service: Amazon MQ in active/standby mode instead of self-managed ActiveMQ, Amazon RDS for MySQL with Multi-AZ instead of a database on an instance, and — the key difference from option C — an Auto Scaling group for the consumers across two Availability Zones, which replaces a failed instance automatically.

opts.A: All three tiers remain self-managed on EC2: nobody recovers a failed instance, and MySQL replication has to be maintained manually.
opts.B: The queue and consumers are made redundant, but the database is still on EC2 with manual replication — the weakest link.
opts.C: The right combination of managed services, but the second consumer is added statically: if that instance fails, nothing replaces it. The Auto Scaling group in option D does this automatically.

112.key: The application is already containerized, the code cannot change, and operations must be minimized. ECS on Fargate runs the existing images without managing a single server, service Auto Scaling grows the number of tasks with load, and an Application Load Balancer distributes incoming requests.

opts.B: Two machines is fixed capacity with no automatic growth, plus the burden of maintaining the instances.
opts.C: Rewriting for Lambda contradicts the requirement of minimal code changes.
opts.D: ParallelCluster is designed for high-performance computing workloads, not for handling web requests.

113.key: There is no available bandwidth for transfer at all, so any network-based transfer is off the table and an offline device is required. 50 TB fits only on a Snowball Edge (about 80 TB of usable capacity); Snowcone provides 8 TB on HDD or 14 TB on SSD. The second requirement is that the transformation job must keep running once it's in the cloud. The key picks Glue: it's a managed service with no infrastructure underneath it, and that's usually how the exam interprets "least operational overhead." The disputed part is that option D keeps the existing application as-is and doesn't require rewriting it for Glue, but it hands you EC2 administration in return. Practical rule: when a question says "least operational overhead" and pits a managed service against your own server, the exam picks the managed service.

opts.A: DataSync transfers data over the network, and the scenario states plainly that there is no free bandwidth in the data center. The first half of the answer alone is impossible.
opts.B: Snowcone holds 8 TB (HDD) or 14 TB (SSD) — 50 TB physically will not fit. Also, an application running on the device does not move the transformation job into the cloud, which is exactly what's required.
opts.D: A strong alternative: the application moves over without a rewrite. But you end up with an EC2 instance that you must patch, monitor, and scale yourself — more operational overhead than a serverless Glue job.

114.key: The number of users fluctuates sharply throughout the day, so an architecture that scales itself is needed. Lambda handles image processing, invoked on each upload, the images themselves are stored in S3 (object storage that grows without limits and is cheap), and the metadata stays in DynamoDB. There isn't a single instance that has to be scaled manually.

opts.A: Images cannot be stored in DynamoDB: the item size limit is 400 KB, and photos are noticeably larger.
opts.B: Firehose delivers streaming records into storage destinations, but it does not process images and is not suitable as image storage.
opts.D: Three instances is fixed capacity that does not adapt to daily fluctuations, and EBS volumes provide neither shared access nor scaling for a growing volume of photos.

115.key: The requirement is that traffic to S3 must not go over the internet. The instances are moved to private subnets, and a gateway endpoint is created for S3, with a route to it added in the route table of those subnets. Traffic stays inside the AWS network, there's no charge for the endpoint, and the instances need no other network access, which matches the stated condition exactly.

opts.A: A NAT gateway is a path out to the internet: this directly violates the requirement, and it also adds a charge for processed traffic.
opts.B: A prefix list in the security group restricts where traffic can go, but the route itself stays the same — through the internet gateway.
opts.D: Direct Connect links the company's own premises to AWS. The instances are already inside AWS, so building a dedicated connection for them makes no sense.

116.key: The site is updated four times a year and has no dynamic content, so there's no reason to run servers at all. A static site in an S3 bucket (D) eliminates patching and maintenance, scales automatically, and costs pennies. CloudFront in front of it (A) adds HTTPS with a custom domain (certificate from ACM), caching close to the user, and the ability to attach WAF, while the bucket is locked down from direct access via an OAC. That's the least operational overhead with high scalability.

opts.B: AWS WAF filters requests, but it does not provide HTTPS and is not a TLS termination point. The option is factually wrong.
opts.C: A Lambda function for serving static content is extra code and extra invocations where S3 can serve the files directly.
opts.E: A fleet of instances behind a load balancer brings back exactly the operational burden the company is trying to escape: patching, scaling, updates.

117.key: CloudWatch Logs has a built-in subscription for delivering log data to OpenSearch Service: it's configured in the console and streams records in near-real time without any custom code or intermediate services.

opts.B: A custom Lambda function means delivery code, error handling, and retries that you have to maintain.
opts.C: A log group cannot be a source for a Firehose delivery stream directly: a subscription is still required, making the stream an unnecessary extra layer.
opts.D: Installing agents on every application server is the most labor-intensive path, especially since the logs are already collected in CloudWatch Logs.

118.key: 900 TB of text documents, accessed from a web application, with spikes in demand and an explicit cost requirement. S3 scales without any configuration, costs noticeably less per gigabyte than file or block storage, handles any number of concurrent requests, and requires no capacity planning. The application retrieves documents by key — file semantics aren't needed here.

opts.A: EBS volumes are tied to an Availability Zone and to an instance, are limited in size, and cost far more than S3. The option doesn't work for 900 TB.
opts.B: EFS solves the problem technically but costs considerably more per gigabyte than S3, and cost is stated as the deciding factor.
opts.C: OpenSearch is a search engine, not storage: keeping 900 TB of documents in it would be impractical and very expensive.

119.key: SQL injection and cross-site scripting are filtered by AWS WAF, but the question asks about the least administrative effort across multiple accounts and Regions. AWS Firewall Manager lets you define a WAF policy once in the organization's admin account and have it applied automatically to all matching resources across every account, including newly created ones. The web ACLs themselves remain Regional, but they're managed centrally. Note: Firewall Manager requires AWS Organizations and delegated administration to be enabled.

opts.A: Configuring WAF manually in each Region and account is possible, but the rules then have to be maintained separately in every location — exactly the extra administrative effort being avoided.
opts.C: AWS Shield protects against DDoS and does not filter SQL injection or XSS. WAF is needed for that.
opts.D: Same mistake of using Shield, plus protecting only one Region leaves the other unfiltered.

120.key: The DNS service runs over UDP and sits behind a Network Load Balancer, so CloudFront cannot be used. What's needed is AWS Global Accelerator: it provides a pair of static anycast IP addresses, accepts traffic at the edge location closest to the user, and delivers it over the AWS backbone to the nearest healthy group of endpoints — in this case, either us-west-2 or eu-west-1. If a Region fails, traffic switches over automatically, without waiting for DNS record TTLs to expire.

opts.A: CloudFront does not serve UDP traffic and cannot use a DNS record as an origin for this kind of service.
opts.C: The scheme with Elastic IP addresses on six instances removes the load balancers and shifts fault tolerance onto DNS records, and CloudFront is still not applicable.
opts.D: Replacing the NLBs with ALBs won't work for DNS: an ALB only handles HTTP and HTTPS.

121.key: The key thing to remember about RDS: you cannot turn on encryption for an existing unencrypted instance. There is only one path — take a snapshot, copy it with encryption enabled (specifying a KMS key at copy time), and restore a new instance from the encrypted copy, then cut the application over to it. All subsequent snapshots of the new instance inherit encryption automatically. The reverse is also impossible: an encrypted instance cannot be decrypted, only have its data exported.

opts.B: EBS volumes have nothing to do with RDS storage — the service manages it itself. And turning on encryption for an existing instance, as this option suggests, isn't possible.
opts.C: Restoring a snapshot always creates a new database instance. RDS has no way to restore a snapshot "into an existing instance."
opts.D: A copy of the snapshot in an encrypted bucket protects only that copy. The database itself and its regular snapshots remain unencrypted.

122.key: The task is to give developers a managed key infrastructure without building it themselves. AWS KMS is built exactly for this: keys are stored in hardware modules, never leave the service in plaintext, access is described by the key policy and IAM policies, every use is logged to CloudTrail, and automatic rotation is a checkbox away. Applications work through envelope encryption: they request a data key, encrypt locally with it, and store an encrypted copy of that key alongside the data.

opts.A: Multi-factor authentication protects account sign-in. It is not a key management infrastructure and does not solve the problem of applications encrypting data.
opts.C: ACM issues and maintains TLS certificates for load balancers, CloudFront, and API Gateway. It does not handle keys for encrypting data inside applications.
opts.D: An IAM policy restricts access, but by itself it does not create, store, or rotate keys. It complements KMS rather than replacing it.

123.key: The bottleneck is encryption on the web servers themselves. It can be offloaded by moving TLS termination to the Application Load Balancer: the company's own certificate is imported into ACM, and the HTTPS listener uses it. The load balancer decrypts traffic using its own resources, while the instances receive plain HTTP and free up CPU.

opts.A: Certificates issued by ACM cannot be exported and installed on instances, and more importantly, the encryption work would still stay on the servers.
opts.B: S3 is object storage; it plays no part in TLS termination. No such setup exists.
opts.C: A separate proxy instance would indeed take the load off, but it's a machine of its own — its own patching, scaling, and a new single point of failure in place of a managed service.

124.key: The job is stateless, can be stopped and resumed at any time without consequences, and runs for over an hour. That's the ideal profile for interruptible instances: up to a 90 percent discount, and capacity reclamation causes no harm because the work can simply start over.

opts.B: Reserved Instances imply steady consumption over a one- or three-year term, and the workload is described as highly variable.
opts.C: On-Demand pricing is noticeably more expensive when interruptions are acceptable anyway.
opts.D: The job runs for more than an hour, while the Lambda function execution limit is fifteen minutes.

125.key: The instances and the database must not be exposed to the internet, but the instances need outbound access to the payment service, and everything must survive an Availability Zone failure. So the Auto Scaling group launches instances in private subnets, and the RDS database in a Multi-AZ configuration also sits in private subnets (A). The network is built from two public subnets for the load balancer, two private subnets for the workload, and two NAT gateways — one per zone (E).

opts.B: An Application Load Balancer that's reachable from the internet must sit in public subnets: in private subnets it can't accept user traffic.
opts.C: Instances in public subnets are exposed to the internet — a direct violation of the requirement.
opts.D: One public and one private subnet mean a single Availability Zone for each tier: the load balancer needs subnets in at least two zones, so there's no high availability.

126.key: The requirement splits along a timeline: the most recent two years need high availability and instant retrieval, while everything older just needs to survive 25 years as cheaply as possible. That's literally a description of a Lifecycle rule transitioning to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 2 years: recent data stays in Standard, and old data costs about a dollar per terabyte per month. Deep Archive returns an object within 12 hours under standard retrieval, but no speed requirement was set for data older than two years.

opts.A: Moving to Deep Archive immediately violates the core requirement: data from the last two years must be available instantly, and Deep Archive returns an object only after hours.
opts.C: Intelligent-Tiering moves objects to archive tiers based on lack of access (after 90 and 180 days), not on a fixed two-year age. An unused but recent object would be archived ahead of schedule, plus you'd pay monitoring charges per object for 25 years.
opts.D: S3 One Zone-IA stores data in a single Availability Zone, while recent data is required to be highly available. The intermediate transition is also pointless here: it saves pennies at the cost of reduced fault tolerance.

127.key: Three requirements, three different storage types. Maximum I/O performance for video processing calls for the instance's local NVMe disks (instance store), which outperform any network-attached volume; data loss risk isn't a concern here because it's just a processing scratch space. Durable storage for 300 TB of media content is S3, with eleven nines of durability. The 900 TB archive of content that's no longer accessed is S3 Glacier.

opts.A: EBS volumes are fast, but they fall short of the instance's local NVMe disks in performance, and the requirement calls for the maximum.
opts.B: Same performance shortfall here, plus EFS as durable storage for media content is noticeably more expensive than S3.
opts.C: Using EFS for 300 TB is more expensive than S3, and plain S3 for a 900 TB archive is more expensive than Glacier: both substitutions make the solution worse.

128.key: The applications are stateless and tolerate disruptions, so interruptible instances fit — up to a 90 percent discount. Among the container options, an EKS managed node group takes node provisioning and patching off the team's plate and itself handles Spot interruption notices, replacing nodes as needed.

opts.A: An Auto Scaling group on Spot Instances is cheap, but the team would have to build container orchestration themselves — more operational overhead.
opts.C: On-Demand Instances are noticeably more expensive, while the requirement explicitly allows for interruptions.
opts.D: Managed node handling is convenient, but On-Demand pricing does not minimize cost.

129.key: The problem is stated directly: infrastructure operations and capacity planning are holding back growth. So server management needs to go away. The containers move to AWS Fargate running on ECS — no nodes to manage at all (E) — and the PostgreSQL database moves to Aurora, where storage scales itself and AWS handles availability and backups (A).

opts.B: EC2 instances are the same servers with patching and capacity planning, just in the cloud: the original problem remains.
opts.C: CloudFront speeds up content delivery but does not remove the operational burden.
opts.D: A cache can help performance, but it does not solve the stated problem of infrastructure and capacity management.

130.key: The requirement sets a target value for a metric — roughly 40 percent CPU utilization. A target tracking policy is built exactly for this: it calculates on its own how many instances to add or remove to keep the average utilization at the specified level.

opts.A: A simple scaling policy fires on a threshold and adds a fixed number of instances rather than aiming to hold a specific value, and it requires a cooldown period between actions.
opts.C: A custom function that changes the desired capacity is code in place of a ready-made mechanism.
opts.D: A schedule does not react to actual load: it cannot hold utilization at 40 percent.

131.key: The goal is to close off direct access to the bucket and leave a single door through CloudFront. To do that, the distribution is given a special identity: an origin access identity (in modern deployments, origin access control), which is specified as the principal in the bucket policy, after which only it is granted read access. Public access to the bucket is turned off entirely, and the direct S3 URL for the object stops working. Signed URLs can then be layered on top, as in {{q:542,313}}.

opts.A: "Individual policies for each bucket" doesn't describe a mechanism: what matters is not the number of policies but which principal they name. Without an OAI or OAC, there's nothing to name in the policy.
opts.B: An IAM user is not assigned to a CloudFront distribution: the service does not act on behalf of an IAM user. No such construct exists.
opts.C: A distribution ID is not an IAM principal and cannot be placed in the Principal field. The principal is the OAI, or for OAC, the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service with a condition on the distribution's ARN.

132.key: The reports are static files that users download from around the world. Storing them in S3 requires no servers at all and costs cents per gigabyte, while CloudFront caches the files at edge locations, delivering the fastest possible response time and lowering the cost of outbound traffic. The requirements to avoid provisioning infrastructure, keep costs low, and respond as fast as possible are all met at once.

opts.B: Lambda and DynamoDB are for dynamic logic and data, whereas here ready-made files are being served: extra calls and extra cost for nothing.
opts.C: A fleet of instances behind a load balancer means provisioning resources and paying for them continuously, which the requirement asks to avoid.
opts.D: Internal load balancers aren't reachable from the internet and don't solve the problem of serving files globally.

133.key: The key constraint is that access to the database's underlying operating system is required, which standard RDS does not provide. Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle keeps the managed benefits (patching, backups, replicas) while also opening up access to the underlying system. For disaster recovery, a read replica is created in another Region and promoted to primary if a disaster occurs.

opts.A: A database on an EC2 instance provides OS access, but all maintenance and replication setup then falls on the company.
opts.B: Standard RDS gives no OS access, and cross-Region automated backups yield a far larger recovery time than a replica does.
opts.D: There's still no OS access, and a standby instance in another Availability Zone is not a plan for a Region-level failure.

134.key: There are three requirements: serverless SQL analysis of data in S3, encryption, and cross-Region replication. Amazon Athena is the only one of the given options that runs SQL directly against S3 objects in a serverless way, so the options with RDS drop out immediately. Next comes the choice of encryption scheme: replicating objects encrypted with a KMS key to another Region requires a key that's usable there too, and a multi-Region key solves this without re-encryption and without a second policy — one key with identical key material in both Regions. That leads to the combination "SSE-KMS with a multi-Region key plus CRR plus Athena."

opts.B: Amazon RDS is a database server that data has to be loaded into, while the requirement calls for a serverless solution over objects already sitting in S3.
opts.C: Athena is the right choice, but SSE-S3 means keys fully managed by the service, separately in each Region: there's no way to confirm or control the key used for the replica. When encryption and cross-Region replication appear together in the requirements, the exam expects multi-Region KMS keys.
opts.D: Two problems at once: RDS instead of a serverless analysis solution, and SSE-S3 instead of company-managed keys.

135.key: The connection must be private, restricted to a single target service, and initiated only from the company's side — that is exactly what AWS PrivateLink describes. The provider publishes its service as an endpoint service behind a Network Load Balancer, the company creates an interface endpoint in its own VPC, and reaches it over a private address. Only that one service is visible, not the provider's whole network, and connections cannot be initiated in the reverse direction.

opts.A: VPC peering connects entire networks: the route opens access to the provider's whole address space, and connections can go in either direction. The requirement to restrict access to a single service isn't met.
opts.B: A virtual private gateway is a VPN or Direct Connect attachment point; it has nothing to do with PrivateLink.
opts.C: A NAT gateway sends traffic out to the internet, meaning the connection stops being private.

136.key: Both the source and target are PostgreSQL, so there's no need to convert the schema. It's enough to stand up an AWS DMS replication server (C) and create a task with ongoing (continuous) replication (A): DMS first migrates the existing data, then reads the transaction log and applies the changes, so the source database stays available and both databases remain in sync.

opts.B: Restoring from a backup gives a point-in-time snapshot and doesn't keep the databases in sync, which would also require stopping the database.
opts.D: The Schema Conversion Tool is needed when the engine changes, for example Oracle to PostgreSQL. Here it's the same engine on both sides.
opts.E: An EventBridge rule is monitoring. It doesn't migrate or synchronize anything.

137.key: Two parts to the requirement. Notifications must not be missed, which means each account's root address should not be a personal inbox but a distribution list that several administrators read (one person goes on vacation, the list remains). Notifications must reach only administrators, so the distribution list must be narrow, not company-wide. The second part is covered by alternate contacts: each account can have separate addresses for billing, operations, and security, and AWS sends category-specific notifications to those addresses directly. Related question — {{q:878}}.

opts.A: Forwarding root notifications to every employee in the organization is the opposite of the requirement to limit recipients to administrators.
opts.C: A single person as the sole recipient just recreates the original problem — that person is the one who missed the notification. Plus it adds manual forwarding to groups.
opts.D: Using the same root email address for every account means administrators of one business unit see notifications for other accounts, and accounts can no longer be separated by ownership.

138.key: Each component is replaced with a managed equivalent and stretched across two Availability Zones. The RabbitMQ queue moves to Amazon MQ in an active/standby broker configuration, the application runs in a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group, and the PostgreSQL database becomes an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance in a Multi-AZ deployment. This gives the least operational overhead and the highest availability.

opts.A: Running PostgreSQL in an EC2 Auto Scaling group doesn't work — the instances would have no shared data.
opts.C: Self-managed RabbitMQ brokers in an Auto Scaling group require manual cluster configuration and ongoing maintenance.
opts.D: This option has both a homegrown broker cluster and a database in an Auto Scaling group — both are either non-functional or high-effort.

139.key: Copying between buckets is handled by native S3 replication — no custom function is needed for that. To have a single event fan out to two destinations at once (the Lambda function and the SageMaker Pipelines pipeline), notifications are routed through EventBridge: an ObjectCreated rule supports multiple targets, while a plain S3 event notification can only deliver an event to one destination per event type.

opts.A: A custom copy function is unnecessary code, and an S3 event notification can't send a single event to two different targets of this kind.
opts.B: EventBridge is the right choice here, but a custom copy function is redundant when replication already handles it.
opts.C: Replication is the right choice here, but plain S3 notifications can't target both a Lambda function and a SageMaker pipeline at the same time.

140.key: Different layers call for different purchasing models. Data ingestion on EC2 instances is sporadic, unpredictable, and interruption-tolerant, which points to Spot Instances with up to a 90 percent discount (A). The Fargate front end and the Lambda API layer are predictable a year out, and the only way to cover both under a single commitment is a Compute Savings Plan, which applies across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda (C).

opts.B: On-Demand Instances for interruption-tolerant workloads is a significant overpay.
opts.D: Reserved Instances assume steady, ongoing usage, but data ingestion is described as sporadic and unpredictable.
opts.E: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan covers only EC2 instances and does not apply to Fargate or Lambda.

141.key: CloudFront speeds up more than just cacheable static content. For personalized dynamic content, the gain comes from the user establishing their TLS connection with the nearest edge location, after which the request travels to the origin over AWS's optimized backbone with connections already warmed up — noticeably faster than crossing the public internet to a distant Region. So a single deployment plus CloudFront routing every path through the distribution delivers the lowest latency without duplicating the stack.

opts.B: Two copies of the stack in different Regions doubles both cost and complexity, and latency-based routing still sends the user across the public internet to reach the Region.
opts.C: Serving dynamic content directly from the load balancer leaves distant users without the AWS backbone speedup — and dynamic content is exactly what suffers most.
opts.D: A user's geographic location doesn't equal the lowest latency, and duplicating the stack again doubles the cost.

142.key: The three requirements point unambiguously to one service. UDP traffic rules out ALB and CloudFront. Static IP addresses for the entry point are provided only by AWS Global Accelerator (a pair of anycast addresses). Accepting traffic at the nearest edge location and carrying it over the AWS backbone delivers low latency. Behind the accelerator sits a Network Load Balancer, which operates at layer 4, plus an Auto Scaling group of instances, since the application needs a modified Linux kernel, which rules out any serverless option.

opts.A: ALB doesn't support UDP, and Lambda can't run an application with a modified kernel.
opts.B: CloudFront doesn't serve UDP traffic and doesn't provide static IP addresses, and Lambda again doesn't fit the modified-kernel requirement.
opts.D: API Gateway works with HTTP and WebSocket, not arbitrary UDP, and it doesn't provide static addresses.

143.key: The monolith needs to be split into several applications while keeping as much of the existing code as possible, and the result needs to scale with minimal operational overhead. Containers fit best here: the code carries over with almost no changes, each piece becomes its own ECS service owned by its own team, and an Application Load Balancer routes requests to the right service by path or header.

opts.A: Porting the monolith to Lambda requires substantial code rework and doesn't naturally support splitting the work across teams.
opts.B: Amplify is built for the front end, and pairing it with API Gateway and Lambda again means rewriting the backend.
opts.C: Instances behind a load balancer keep the monolith intact as a single unit and leave the company responsible for managing the servers.

144.key: The reports create a heavy read load that interferes with the main application. The cheapest fix is to offload reporting to an Aurora Replica: it reads from the same shared storage, lags by milliseconds, and can be added with a single action. The primary instance is freed up, and the only added cost is one extra reader instance.

opts.A: Moving reporting to Redshift means a separate data store, a loading pipeline, and an always-on cluster — noticeably more expensive and more complex.
opts.C: Scaling the primary instance up to a larger class raises cost around the clock even though the spike only happens once a month, and it doesn't separate the workloads.
opts.D: Aurora has no Provisioned IOPS setting — its storage is shared and managed by the service itself.

145.key: The application is bottlenecked on a single instance hosting both the web server and the database. The cheapest fix is to separate the layers and make compute elastic: the database moves to a managed Aurora MySQL instance, the application image becomes a launch template, an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer adds and removes instances with load, and using Spot capacity within a fleet cuts compute cost by a large factor. For a stateless web tier, Spot interruptions are absorbed simply by replacing the instance.

opts.A: Two fixed-size On-Demand instances don't scale with peaks and cost more than an elastic Spot-backed group.
opts.B: DNS weighted routing doesn't check target health as responsively as a load balancer, and it doesn't scale capacity.
opts.C: Changing the instance type from a function triggered by an alarm is vertical scaling with a restart and downtime, not seamless scaling.

146.key: The load consists of a steady baseline (moderate overnight, high during the day) plus a variable overlay. The baseline is most cost-effective covered with discounted Reserved Instances, while the extra capacity during peaks is covered with Spot Instances: the application is stateless, so reclaiming some instances doesn't affect availability.

opts.A: Fully Spot capacity puts the baseline service level at risk — a mass interruption would leave the application unavailable.
opts.C: Paying full price for the baseline is an overpay when usage is predictable a year in advance.
opts.D: Dedicated Instances cost the most and are only needed for hardware isolation requirements, which aren't part of this scenario.

147.key: More than 10 TB of logs a month, kept for ten years: the cheapest approach is to store them as S3 objects and use a lifecycle rule to move anything older than a month into S3 Glacier Deep Archive, the cheapest storage class. The most recent month stays instantly accessible.

opts.A: AWS Backup doesn't manage storage classes for S3 objects — transitions between classes are handled by a lifecycle rule.
opts.C: Storing logs in CloudWatch Logs is noticeably more expensive than S3, and AWS Backup doesn't apply to CloudWatch Logs.
opts.D: S3 lifecycle rules don't act on logs sitting in CloudWatch Logs — they'd first need to be exported.

148.key: Network failures cause the function invocation to fail, and the notification is lost. For asynchronous invocations, Lambda has a configurable destination for failures: an SQS queue is set as the on-failure destination, events that couldn't be processed land there, and the function picks them up later. Nothing gets lost.

opts.A: Lambda functions already run across multiple Availability Zones — there's nothing to configure there, and it doesn't protect against network failures.
opts.B: More memory and CPU don't affect events being lost during a connectivity failure.
opts.C: Increasing SNS retries lowers the chance of loss but doesn't guarantee it — once retries are exhausted, the message is still lost.

149.key: Processing order must be preserved, and operational overhead must be minimal. An SQS FIFO queue preserves order within a message group and guarantees exactly-once processing, and a Lambda function reads from it as an event source — no servers involved.

opts.B: SNS doesn't guarantee delivery order to subscribers.
opts.C: A standard queue can reorder messages, so strict ordering isn't guaranteed.
opts.D: A topic with a plain queue subscriber also doesn't preserve order, and the scenario doesn't even describe a processor for it.

150.key: Action is only needed when two conditions hold at the same time — high CPU utilization and high disk read IOPS. A CloudWatch composite alarm combines multiple alarms with a logical expression and fires only when they coincide, which is exactly what eliminates false alarms from short spikes.

opts.B: Dashboards are useful for eyeballing metrics but don't create automatic notifications.
opts.C: Synthetics canaries check application endpoint availability from the outside and have nothing to do with instance metrics.
opts.D: A regular CloudWatch alarm tracks a single metric — you can't set a condition spanning two different metrics in one.

151.key: There are two requirements: operate only in ap-northeast-3, and prevent VPCs from reaching the internet, and both must hold for everyone, including administrators. Both are met by preventive, organization-level guardrails. AWS Control Tower offers ready-made data residency guardrails that deny both resource creation in other Regions and attaching internet gateways (A). The same outcome can be built manually with service control policies (SCPs) in AWS Organizations — using the aws:RequestedRegion condition and denying creation of internet gateways and NAT (C). The key point: the requirement that "administrators are not permitted" is only satisfied by SCPs, because an administrator can rewrite an IAM policy on themselves.

opts.B: AWS WAF filters HTTP requests to applications and doesn't control VPC internet access. There's also no "deny Regions account-wide" setting.
opts.D: A network ACL can be changed back, and an administrator can rewrite an IAM policy on themselves. Neither is a preventive restriction that can't be bypassed from inside the account.
opts.E: AWS Config detects and alerts after the fact. The requirement is to prevent these resources from being created, not to find out about them afterward.

152.key: The application is only accessed for 12 hours a day, so the database shouldn't be billed for the other 12. A stopped RDS instance isn't charged for compute (only storage and snapshots continue to accrue), and the question is really about what stops and starts it. The standard pairing is an EventBridge scheduled rule invoking a Lambda function that calls Stop and Start. Keep in mind RDS's limit: a stopped instance restarts automatically after 7 days, so the schedule needs to stop it regularly, which is exactly what happens here.

opts.A: Session Manager provides access to servers, not scheduling. The role and trust policy have nothing to do with stopping the database.
opts.B: A Redis cache doesn't replace the database — writes and ad hoc queries still need somewhere to go. It also adds another always-on service, increasing cost.
opts.C: A dedicated EC2 instance with cron just to make two API calls is a machine that still needs to be paid for and maintained. The serverless pairing is cheaper and more reliable.

153.key: The access pattern is known and tied to object age: heavily downloaded for the first 90 days, rarely after. A known pattern like this is most cheaply described with a Lifecycle rule, and the requirement to keep "the most accessed files readily available" means the target class must still serve files instantly — that's Standard-IA. The file size is mentioned for a reason: Standard-IA has a minimum billable object size of 128 KB, and the "at least 128 KB" condition confirms there's no small-object overcharge.

opts.A: Putting objects straight into Standard-IA is a bad deal — for the first 90 days they're downloaded heavily, and Standard-IA charges per gigabyte retrieved. There's also a 30-day minimum storage duration.
opts.B: Intelligent-Tiering moves objects after 30 days without access and its threshold can't be set to 90 days. Across millions of files it also adds a monthly monitoring charge per object.
opts.C: S3 Inventory is a CSV or Parquet report of bucket contents. It doesn't move anything itself — moving objects would still require a Lifecycle rule or Batch Operations.

154.key: Three requirements are handled by different mechanisms, but the decisive one is "no users can have the ability to modify or delete any files," with a minimum retention of one year from the creation date. The only guarantee that neither an administrator nor root can bypass is S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a 365-day retention period. Write access for a few scientists and read-only access for everyone else is granted through an ordinary bucket policy — that part of the requirement is orthogonal and doesn't affect the choice of option. Also note the distinction: the retention period is tied to the object version's creation date, while a legal hold has no expiration date and is removed manually via a separate permission.

opts.A: Governance mode can routinely be bypassed with the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission, and "a legal hold for one year" isn't a real construct: a legal hold has no duration and stays in place until it is removed.
opts.C: The role and bucket policy control who is allowed to do what. Whoever writes these policies can also rewrite them, so they don't provide immutability.
opts.D: A hash computed by the Lambda function only records that an object was changed, after the fact. The requirement is to prevent modification, not to detect it after it happens.

155.key: The goal is to deliver files quickly to users worldwide while keeping the content confidential. CloudFront caches objects at edge locations, so requests are served close to the user, and access to the bucket is locked down with origin access control: no one can reach S3 directly — files are served only through the distribution, where signed URLs or signed cookies can be enabled.

opts.A: DataSync copies data between storage systems and isn't a tool for delivering content to end users.
opts.B: Global Accelerator optimizes the network path to applications, but it doesn't cache objects and doesn't work with S3 as a content origin.
opts.D: SQS is a message queue and has nothing to do with delivering media files.

156.key: Data arrives both as batches from databases and as streams from sensors, and it all needs to land in one place with minimal effort. Blueprints in AWS Lake Formation describe common ingestion scenarios, and AWS Glue jobs crawl the sources and land the data in S3 in Apache Parquet format (E). One-time queries against that data are run with Athena, and QuickSight builds the KPI dashboards (A).

opts.B: Kinesis Data Analytics processes streams in real time — it doesn't run one-time queries against data already staged in S3.
opts.C: Custom functions for moving individual records mean code to write and maintain, and Redshift is overkill here.
opts.D: JSON loses to Parquet on query cost, and multiple OpenSearch clusters are unnecessary, expensive infrastructure.

157.key: There are two requirements. Storing data for five years and then deleting it: Aurora's automated backups are capped at 35 days, so AWS Backup is needed, with a plan and a five-year retention period (E). Indefinite audit logs of actions performed within the database: enable a CloudWatch Logs export for the cluster, where the log group's retention can be set to never expire (D).

opts.A: A manual snapshot is a single point-in-time capture, not a continuous five-year retention strategy.
opts.B: Aurora's automated backups have no lifecycle policy — their retention is capped at 35 days.
opts.C: Automated backups can't be configured with a five-year retention period — the limit is 35 days.

158.key: CloudFront speeds up both the live stream and the on-demand playback: video segments (HLS or DASH) are cached at edge locations, so thousands of viewers in a region get them locally instead of from the origin. For a live event this also protects the origin from a flood of requests for the same segments. The other services solve different problems: Global Accelerator speeds up TCP and UDP applications, Route 53 handles DNS routing, and S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads into S3.

opts.B: Global Accelerator optimizes the path to application endpoints, but it doesn't cache content, and caching is exactly what pays off when streaming video at scale.
opts.C: Route 53 only routes the client to the right resource and doesn't change the performance of the delivery itself.
opts.D: Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploading files into a bucket, not delivering video to viewers.

159.key: The goal is to block requests from unauthorized parties at the entry point, before they reach Lambda, using two complementary controls. A usage plan with an API key (A) separates legitimate users from everyone else: without a key, API Gateway itself rejects the request, and this also enables quotas and throttling. AWS WAF (C) filters everything that arrives, whether it carries a key or not: rules based on IP address, geography, rate-based rules against botnets, and managed rule groups. Both options stop traffic before the function is invoked, so the Lambda bill doesn't grow either.

opts.B: Filtering inside the function means you've already paid for a Lambda invocation and consumed its concurrency for every fraudulent request. Filtering needs to happen at the entry point.
opts.D: A private API is reachable only from inside a VPC — the public application would stop working for legitimate users.
opts.E: An IAM role for every visitor to a public application isn't feasible: visitors don't have AWS accounts.

160.key: The volume is tiny — 300 MB a month — the data must be kept for 30 days, and access must be in milliseconds. The S3 Standard storage class gives instant access and costs only cents at this volume, while the minimum storage durations and retrieval fees of the archival classes make them uneconomical over a one-month horizon.

opts.A: OpenSearch is a search cluster billed for continuously running nodes: disproportionately expensive for a backup.
opts.B: Glacier is cheaper to store in, but retrieval takes minutes to hours, while the requirement is milliseconds.
opts.D: An RDS for PostgreSQL database is billed hourly and is designed for queries, not for storing JSON file backups.

161.key: The application is small, runs thousands of times a day, and is triggered by each document's arrival. A Lambda function invoked by an S3 event notification delivers high availability, scalability, and near-zero operational overhead all at once: you pay only for actual execution time. The results are written into a managed Aurora DB cluster.

opts.A: A fleet of instances is billed around the clock, has to be patched and scaled, and is a poor fit for thousands of short invocations a day.
opts.C: EBS Multi-Attach is limited to a single Availability Zone and requires a cluster-aware file system: this is the most complex and least scalable of the options.
opts.D: An ECS cluster on the EC2 launch type still means managing compute nodes, while the workload is a perfect fit for serverless, event-driven execution.

162.key: Two related things are needed: a high-performance file system for hundreds of instances, and persistent storage where the results land long-term. Amazon FSx for Lustre integrates directly with S3: a bucket is linked to the file system, its objects appear as files, and job output is exported back to S3. This is the standard pattern for HPC workloads on interruptible instances — the file system lives independently of the ephemeral fleet.

opts.B: FSx for Windows File Server uses the SMB protocol and is built for Windows workloads, while the computations run on Linux and need Lustre-level performance.
opts.C: Glacier is an archive with retrieval measured in minutes to hours, so it can't serve as working storage for computations, and EBS volumes can't be shared across hundreds of instances.
opts.D: S3 by itself isn't a file system, and a gp2 EBS volume attaches to a single instance: hundreds of machines can't work with it at the same time.

163.key: What's needed is image storage, orchestration without managing nodes, and automatic scaling. Container images are stored in Amazon ECR, an ECS cluster with the AWS Fargate launch type runs the containers without a single instance to manage, and a target tracking policy scales automatically with demand. High availability comes from spreading tasks across multiple Availability Zones.

opts.B: The Amazon EC2 launch type brings node management back: patching, scaling, and monitoring fall on the team.
opts.C: A self-hosted registry on an EC2 instance and manually launching new instances as needed is maximum operational effort and risk.
opts.D: Packing the container image into an AMI and scaling EC2 instances manually means giving up container orchestration entirely.

164.key: About a thousand messages an hour, processing that can take up to two days, and a requirement to keep failed messages from affecting the rest — this is the classic use case for an Amazon SQS queue. Its message retention period goes up to 14 days, comfortably covering the two-day processing window, and a dead-letter queue collects the messages that failed to process without blocking the remaining messages.

opts.A: A self-managed Redis instance is a machine you have to operate, plus store/process/delete logic you'd have to build yourself.
opts.B: Kinesis is built for streaming processing in sequence; it has no built-in way to isolate and separately retain individual failed records, and integrating the KCL requires writing your own consumer code.
opts.D: SNS delivers a notification immediately and doesn't hold it for two days: if the subscriber is unavailable, the message is lost.

165.key: For all website traffic to actually pass through WAF inspection, two conditions must hold. First, WAF is enabled on the CloudFront distribution itself (a web ACL) — this way every request is inspected at the edge location. Second, direct access to the bucket must be blocked, otherwise requests could bypass CloudFront and WAF entirely; this is done with an origin access identity (today, origin access control), with the bucket policy allowing reads only from it.

opts.A: AWS WAF has no ARN principal that can be referenced in a bucket policy: it never talks to the origin. It's CloudFront that makes the requests to S3.
opts.B: CloudFront doesn't "forward requests to WAF": a web ACL is associated with the distribution and inspects requests on the spot, before the origin is contacted.
opts.C: Security groups don't apply to Amazon S3 — it's a service with a public API. Restricting access to CloudFront's IP addresses isn't built that way.

166.key: Millions of views of the same static pages is the classic use case for a CDN. CloudFront with the S3 bucket as its origin caches the pages at edge locations, so the vast majority of requests never reach the bucket: latency drops, outbound data transfer cost drops, and load on the origin drops. The bucket is also locked down from direct access via origin access control.

opts.A: A presigned URL is a mechanism for temporary access to private objects. It doesn't speed up delivery and doesn't fit public pages.
opts.B: Cross-Region replication to every Region means paying for many copies of storage and manually managing routing, while a CDN cache achieves the same result more cheaply.
opts.C: The geoproximity feature of Route 53 distributes users across multiple origins, but here there's only one origin, and this routing policy provides no caching.

167.key: The application must keep processing without any downtime, and traffic is unpredictable and often intermittent. The steady baseline is covered by discounted Reserved Instances, and spikes are handled by On-Demand Instances, which can't be reclaimed. Interruptible capacity doesn't fit here: the "no downtime" requirement is incompatible with instances that can be reclaimed at any time.

opts.A: Spot Instances for the entire maximum capacity risk a simultaneous reclaim that halts processing.
opts.B: Reserving the entire maximum capacity year-round means overpaying for capacity that's only needed some of the time.
opts.C: Cheaper, but Spot Instances again conflict with the requirement to process messages continuously without downtime.

168.key: The goal is to restrict a set of services and actions across every account in the organization, from a single point, in a way a local administrator can't undo. That's exactly what a service control policy does: an SCP is attached to the organization's root (or an OU) and sets a permissions ceiling for every principal in every member account, including that account's root user. The key mechanic to understand: an SCP never grants anything — it only restricts. Effective permissions are the intersection of the SCP and the IAM policies.

opts.A: An ACL in AWS refers to network subnet access control lists, plus a legacy S3 access mechanism. Neither can manage service-level permissions across every account.
opts.B: A security group filters network traffic to instances. It has nothing to do with permissions for API calls.
opts.C: Cross-account roles would have to be created and maintained in every single account, and they don't stop local administrators from acting directly. There's no single point of control.

169.key: The requirement is direct: reduce the risk of DDoS attacks against the application behind the ALB. AWS Shield Advanced is subscribed to the resources you want protected (ALB, CloudFront, Global Accelerator, Route 53, Elastic IP), and it provides automatic mitigations at the network and application layers, access to the DDoS Response Team, and cost protection against a billing spike during an attack. Shield Standard is already active regardless, but without these advanced capabilities.

opts.A: Amazon Inspector scans instances and images for vulnerabilities; it has no "agent" that attaches to a load balancer and provides no protection against attacks.
opts.B: Amazon Macie looks for sensitive data in S3. It has nothing to do with DDoS protection.
opts.D: GuardDuty detects suspicious activity, but it doesn't absorb attack traffic.

170.key: Restricting access to one specific country is an application-layer rule, because the country is determined from the source IP address using a geolocation database. AWS WAF has exactly this capability: a geo match statement blocks or allows requests from selected countries, and the web ACL is attached to the Application Load Balancer. Security groups and network ACLs operate on address ranges and ports and know nothing about countries — manually maintaining the subnet list for an entire country isn't realistic.

opts.A: The EC2 instances' security group receives traffic from the load balancer, not from clients, and it works with CIDR ranges, not countries.
opts.B: The load balancer's security group also operates on address ranges: listing every subnet for a country in it is not feasible.
opts.D: A network ACL is an address-and-port filter at the subnet level with a hard limit on the number of rules. Geo-blocking can't be built with it.

171.key: Load spikes sharply during the holiday season and is nearly nonexistent the rest of the time. API Gateway with Lambda functions scales instantly and is billed only for actual invocations: no capacity planning and no idle servers.

opts.A: A single instance doesn't scale at all and becomes a bottleneck during the season.
opts.C: Two machines behind a load balancer represent fixed capacity that either can't handle the peak or sits idle the rest of the year.
opts.D: Putting API Gateway in front of the instance only adds a layer: computation is still bottlenecked on a single machine.

172.key: HTTPS only protects data in transit: at the load balancer and onward through the stack, it's decrypted again. CloudFront field-level encryption encrypts specific form fields with a public key right at the edge location, so sensitive values stay encrypted throughout the entire path, and only the application holding the matching private key can decrypt them.

opts.A: A signed URL restricts access to the distribution's content but does nothing to protect the data the user submits.
opts.B: Signed cookies solve the same content-access-restriction problem and have nothing to do with field-level encryption.
opts.D: Protocol settings only provide encryption in transit — the same layer that's already present in the scenario and already deemed insufficient.

173.key: The files are the same for every user, the audience is global, load on the origin must be reduced, and cost matters. CloudFront in front of the bucket caches objects at edge locations, so the vast majority of requests never reach S3: both the load and the outbound-traffic cost drop, since traffic served from CloudFront is cheaper than traffic served directly from S3.

opts.A: Global Accelerator optimizes the network path but doesn't cache objects: the load on the origin stays the same.
opts.C: Redis caches data in memory within a single Region and isn't built to serve large media files to a global audience.
opts.D: Memcached has the same drawback: it's a regional in-memory cache, not a content delivery network.

174.key: The single weakness is that all six machines sit in one Availability Zone. It's enough to spread the Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones, three instances in each: the load balancer already works across multiple zones, the application doesn't need to change, and a zone failure leaves half the capacity running.

opts.A: Multiple Regions solve a different problem and require rebuilding routing and data replication — more than what's needed, and it touches the application.
opts.C: A template for quickly creating instances in another Region is a recovery plan, not high availability.
opts.D: The Application Load Balancer already distributes requests; the distribution algorithm doesn't help when the single zone fails.

175.key: The diagnosis is given right in the scenario: too many open connections to the database. During a spike, Lambda spins up hundreds of concurrent instances, each opening its own connection, and Aurora chokes. RDS Proxy maintains a pool of persistent connections and reuses them across function invocations — the change amounts to swapping the endpoint address used by the function.

opts.A: Provisioned concurrency speeds up cold starts but doesn't reduce the number of connections, and a global database solves an entirely different problem — cross-Region disaster recovery.
opts.C: A read replica won't help: the problem is connections, including for writes, and routing by query string parameters in API Gateway means reworking the application.
opts.D: Moving to DynamoDB means rewriting the data model and every query, which directly conflicts with the requirement for minimal changes.

176.key: Private access to DynamoDB comes from a gateway endpoint: a route to the service prefix is added to the private subnets' route table, traffic never leaves the AWS network, and the endpoint policy restricts access to the required tables. There's no charge for the endpoint itself.

opts.B: A NAT gateway sends traffic out to the internet — that violates the requirement to stay within the AWS network, and it adds a charge for processed data.
opts.C: A NAT instance sits in a public subnet and still routes traffic out to the internet; it doesn't even work from a private subnet.
opts.D: An internet gateway is a direct path to the internet — the opposite of the requirement.

177.key: The application can't be rewritten, the workload is read-heavy, and latency needs to go away without adding operational overhead. DynamoDB Accelerator is a cache built directly into the service: it's API-compatible with DynamoDB, so pointing to the cluster endpoint is enough, and reads start being served in microseconds.

opts.A: Redis would require rewriting the data-access logic and managing cache invalidation yourself.
opts.C: Global tables solve multi-Region operation, not read latency within a single Region.
opts.D: Memcached also requires application changes and managing the cache yourself.

178.key: Copies are needed in another Region for two different services with minimal operations. AWS Backup supports both EC2 and RDS, defines a single plan with a cross-Region copy rule, and shows the status of every job in one place. No scripts and no separate mechanism per service.

opts.B: Amazon DLM manages EBS snapshots and AMIs, but RDS backups are outside its scope.
opts.C: Manually copying AMIs plus a cross-Region read replica means a database instance running continuously and manual steps — more work and more cost.
opts.D: Four different mechanisms (snapshots, copying, export, bucket replication) instead of one plan — maximum operational load.

179.key: This tests understanding of how a compute resource gets permissions. An instance is assigned an IAM role (through the instance profile), and a policy is attached to that role — a policy can't be assigned directly to an instance. The second nuance: a SecureString parameter is encrypted with a KMS key, so ssm:GetParameter alone isn't enough — the role also needs kms:Decrypt on that key, otherwise the read fails with an access error. That exact pair of permissions is what the correct option describes.

opts.B: An IAM policy can't be "assigned to an instance": policies attach to users, groups, and roles, and an instance is granted a role. The wording describes an operation that doesn't exist.
opts.C: A trust relationship is set up between a role and the principal that assumes it. "Trust between a parameter and an instance," with RDS named as the principal, is a construct that doesn't exist in IAM.
opts.D: Same mistake: a role's trust policy doesn't link a database instance to an application instance, and Systems Manager isn't a principal that assumes a role here.

180.key: Protection is needed on two different fronts. SQL injection and XSS are HTTP-layer attacks, and AWS WAF filters those — a web ACL can be attached to API Gateway (C), since WAF doesn't attach to a Network Load Balancer. Large, sophisticated DDoS attacks call for Shield Advanced, which does support NLB and Elastic IP addresses (B), providing automatic mitigations and support from the DDoS Response Team. That gives the pair "WAF on API Gateway plus Shield Advanced on the NLB."

opts.A: AWS WAF doesn't support Network Load Balancer: the list of supported resources is limited to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync, Cognito, and a few others.
opts.D: GuardDuty only detects, and Shield Standard is enabled by default and doesn't provide the protection against sophisticated attacks that the scenario requires.
opts.E: Shield Standard operates automatically and isn't a separately configurable solution, and it provides no protection against injection attacks at all.

181.key: Data is processed sequentially, but the order of results doesn't matter, and there will be many consumers. An SQS queue fits exactly this: producers place messages, consumers pull them independently and scale with the queue length, each message is processed once, and a failure puts it back on the queue.

opts.B: SNS delivers a copy of the message to every subscriber: that doesn't work for distributing work across consumers, and there's no buffering.
opts.C: A function acting as a go-between for services adds a synchronous dependency and a point of failure instead of decoupling.
opts.D: DynamoDB Streams could be adapted, but that means an extra table, extra cost, and noticeably more complex logic than a queue.

182.key: The requirement that "every transaction is stored on at least two nodes" means synchronous replication. RDS for MySQL's Multi-AZ configuration synchronously writes every transaction to a standby instance in another Availability Zone and fails over automatically.

opts.A: RDS has no synchronous three-node, three-zone replication mode for MySQL: that configuration doesn't exist.
opts.C: Cross-Region read replicas replicate asynchronously: the word "synchronously" in this option is wrong.
opts.D: Homegrown replication through a Lambda function is never synchronous and adds both complexity and points of failure.

183.key: Minimal server maintenance is required, along with the fastest possible scaling of both read and write capacity. This is a fully serverless stack: static content in S3, dynamic content through API Gateway and Lambda, data in DynamoDB in on-demand mode, delivery through CloudFront. On-demand mode adjusts both writes and reads instantly, with no capacity planning.

opts.B: Aurora Auto Scaling adds read replicas, but writes remain on a single primary instance and don't scale up quickly.
opts.C: EC2 instances require maintenance and patching, and DynamoDB provisioned write capacity doesn't adjust instantly.
opts.D: This has both servers to maintain and Aurora's write-scaling limitation.

184.key: By default, a Lambda function has no access to private networks — it runs inside the AWS-managed service network. To reach the database in the data center, the function must be connected to the VPC: subnets and a security group are specified, and a network interface is then created in those subnets.
