From there, the existing routing takes over — all traffic leaving the VPC goes to the virtual private gateway and through Direct Connect to the data center.

opts.B: The Direct Connect links already exist, and a function outside the VPC couldn't use a new VPN either: the problem isn't a missing link, it's that the function isn't connected to the network.
opts.C: The VPC route tables already send all non-VPC traffic to the virtual private gateway. As long as the function isn't in the VPC, those routes don't apply to it.
opts.D: An Elastic IP address is a public address, and the phrase "without a network interface" describes a capability that doesn't exist: Lambda's access to a private network comes specifically from an interface in the VPC.

185.key: An ECS task has two distinct roles, and this question checks that you can tell them apart. The task execution role is used by the agent: to pull the image from ECR and write logs to CloudWatch. The task role is the role of the application itself running in the container, and it's the one specified as taskRoleArn in the task definition; the container obtains temporary credentials through it and calls S3. Keys never end up in the image, and rotation happens automatically.

opts.A: "Update the S3 role to allow access from Amazon ECS" describes a construct that doesn't exist: the service doesn't call the bucket on its own behalf — permissions belong to the task role.
opts.C: A security group controls network traffic, not permissions for S3 API calls. Access would still be denied on permissions grounds.
opts.D: An IAM user and launching instances "under that account" isn't the right mechanism: the container gets its permissions from the task role, and long-lived keys aren't needed in this model.

186.key: A shared Windows file share for instances across multiple Availability Zones is Amazon FSx for Windows File Server. It speaks the SMB protocol, supports Windows ACLs and Active Directory integration, deploys in a Multi-AZ configuration, and mounts on every instance as an ordinary network drive.

opts.A: Volume Gateway serves block volumes over iSCSI and is meant for hybrid scenarios, not shared file access for multiple instances in the cloud.
opts.C: EFS speaks NFS: that's not the native access method for Windows applications and instances, and it has no support for Windows ACLs.
opts.D: An EBS volume generally attaches to a single instance, and a file system on it isn't designed for simultaneous writes from multiple machines, let alone from different Availability Zones.

187.key: Both tiers need to be highly available with as little manual intervention as possible. The database — RDS in Multi-AZ configuration, with synchronous replication and automatic failover (A). The containers — an ECS cluster with the Fargate launch type, where there are no nodes to maintain and tasks are spread across Availability Zones (D).

opts.B: Read replicas don't fail over automatically and are meant to offload reads, not to provide fault tolerance.
opts.C: A self-managed Docker cluster on instances means nodes that have to be maintained and scaled manually.
opts.E: The EC2 launch type works, but it requires managing nodes, while the scenario calls for minimal manual intervention.

188.key: The partner needs the SFTP protocol, and the solution must be highly available with minimal operations. AWS Transfer Family is a managed service: it stands up an SFTP endpoint, provides availability across multiple zones on its own, and drops files straight into the data lake bucket. No servers, no scripts.

opts.B: S3 File Gateway isn't an SFTP server: it serves resources over NFS and SMB and is meant for local-network use.
opts.C: A single instance is a single point of failure, plus a self-managed SFTP server, a VPN, and a scheduled script that has to be maintained.
opts.D: A fleet of instances behind a load balancer adds availability, but all the operational burden of the SFTP servers and the upload scripts still falls on the company.

189.key: There are two requirements here, and they're met by two different mechanisms. Five-year immutability comes from S3 Object Lock in compliance mode (B): in this mode, no one — including the root user — can delete or overwrite an object version before the retention period ends. Encryption with automatic yearly key rotation comes from a customer managed key in KMS with automatic rotation enabled (D): AWS generates new cryptographic material once a year on its own, while retaining the old material so previously written objects can still be decrypted. That's exactly why rotation doesn't break access to older documents.

opts.A: Governance mode can be bypassed by anyone holding the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission. That's not enough for a legal requirement that documents "cannot be overwritten or deleted."
opts.C: With SSE-S3, rotation is managed entirely by the service — the customer can't configure or confirm a yearly period. The requirement to "rotate automatically every year" isn't verifiably met.
opts.E: Automatic rotation isn't supported for keys with imported material: new material has to be imported manually. That's both not automatic and the highest possible operational cost.

190.key: The Java-and-PHP application moves over as-is, frequent testing of new features is needed, and operations must stay minimal. AWS Elastic Beanstalk deploys applications like this on a managed platform with a load balancer and Auto Scaling, and swapping URLs between two environments gives instant switching between the current and the tested version, with an equally instant rollback.

opts.A: PHP is a server-side language, S3 static hosting can't execute it, and moving all the logic to Lambda means a rewrite.
opts.C: Self-managed instances configured with Java and PHP still need patching and updates — that's not a managed solution.
opts.D: Containers on EC2 instances again leave nodes to maintain, and the AWS Load Balancer Controller belongs to Kubernetes, not to instances running containers directly.

191.key: The reporting queries are interfering with order processing. A read replica takes on those queries, freeing the primary instance for transactions. Employees keep running their queries, and the timeouts during order placement go away.

opts.B: Routing the ordering application to the replica too doesn't work: writes to a replica aren't possible, and reads from it may return stale data.
opts.C: Moving to DynamoDB means rewriting the application, and ad hoc reporting queries are awkward there.
opts.D: Moving the queries to off-peak hours takes away employees' ability to work with reports during the day, which the scenario doesn't allow.

192.key: The documents are scanned, so the text needs to be recognized. A Lambda function triggered on upload calls Amazon Textract to extract the text and Amazon Comprehend Medical to find the medical information (E). The result lands in S3, and SQL queries against it run through Amazon Athena (B) — no servers, and pay only for data scanned.

opts.A: A MySQL database on an EC2 instance requires maintenance and scales poorly with hundreds of documents a day.
opts.C: A custom application on a fleet of instances is maximum development and operational effort where ready-made services already exist.
opts.D: Rekognition doesn't parse multi-page documents, and Transcribe Medical works with speech, not text.

193.key: There are two requirements: cut database read load and preserve high availability, without rewriting the application. RDS read replicas solve both: SELECT queries route to the replica, the primary instance is offloaded, and the replica can be promoted to primary if needed. A cache also offloads reads, but it requires application changes (cache-aside logic and invalidation) and by itself adds nothing to the database's availability.

opts.B: ElastiCache for Redis does offload reads, but it requires rewriting the data-access code and doesn't improve the database's own availability.
opts.C: DNS caching relates to name resolution and has no effect at all on the number of database queries.
opts.D: Memcached doesn't support replication or data persistence, so it's even weaker on availability, and the application would still need to change.

194.key: The scenario specifically requires using EC2 for the database, so managed services are off the table. Fault tolerance has to be built by hand: two instances in different Availability Zones within the same Region, the database installed on both, a cluster and replication configured — when one zone fails, the role transfers to the second node automatically.

opts.B: Recovering from an image after a disaster is a manual or delayed action with noticeable downtime, not an automatic failover.
opts.C: Two Regions complicate replication and add latency; two zones within one Region are enough for fault tolerance.
opts.D: EC2 automatic recovery restarts the same machine and doesn't help if the entire Availability Zone fails.

195.key: Orders get lost because the request is handled by the same instance that can fail. An SQS queue holds the order until processing is confirmed: if the instance goes down, the message becomes visible again and another instance picks it up. Meanwhile, the instances sit in an Auto Scaling group and scale with the queue length.

opts.A: EventBridge routes events but doesn't store them and doesn't guarantee reprocessing after a failure.
opts.B: A load balancer distributes requests, but if an instance fails partway through processing, the order is still lost.
opts.D: SNS doesn't store messages, and dispatching commands through Run Command is an awkward and fragile way to process orders.

196.key: DynamoDB has a built-in item-expiration mechanism: an attribute holding a timestamp up to which the item is valid is added to each item, and the table is configured to use that attribute as the TTL attribute. The service deletes expired items on its own, with no write-capacity cost and no cleanup code at all.

opts.A: Recreating the stack every 30 days means losing all the data at once, including the recent data.
opts.B: An instance running a third-party application plus a deletion script is maximum cost and maintenance.
opts.C: A function that deletes old items consumes write capacity and requires code, whereas TTL does the same thing for free.

197.key: The requirement is minimal code changes and high availability. The .NET-on-Windows application moves over as-is into Elastic Beanstalk on the .NET platform in a Multi-AZ deployment (B), and the Oracle database migrates through AWS DMS into Oracle on Amazon RDS in a Multi-AZ deployment (E). The database engine stays the same, so the queries and schema don't change.

opts.A: Rewriting for Lambda is exactly the kind of major application rework the scenario asks to avoid.
opts.C: Moving the Windows .NET application to the Amazon Linux AMI requires code changes and compatibility testing.
opts.D: DynamoDB is a non-relational store: every SQL query would have to be rewritten.

198.key: Neither the code nor the deployment method can change, which means keeping Kubernetes and MongoDB. So EKS preserves the familiar manifests and tooling, the Fargate mode removes node management, and Amazon DocumentDB is MongoDB-compatible, so the application's drivers and queries stay the same.

opts.A: ECS is a different orchestration system: the Kubernetes manifests would need to be rewritten, and MongoDB on instances still needs maintenance.
opts.B: Both the orchestration is different and DynamoDB is incompatible with MongoDB: the code would have to change.
opts.C: Kubernetes is preserved, but the EC2 worker nodes still need maintenance, and moving to DynamoDB requires code changes.

199.key: Recognizing multiple speakers and transcribing calls is Amazon Transcribe with speaker diarization enabled. The finished transcripts land in S3, where they can be kept for as long as seven years, and Amazon Athena runs queries against them using plain SQL, billed by data scanned.

opts.A: Rekognition analyzes images and video, not speech.
opts.C: Translate translates text between languages and doesn't distinguish speakers.
opts.D: Again, Rekognition isn't for speech, and Textract extracts text from documents rather than analyzing finished transcripts.

200.key: The users already live in a Cognito user pool, so their token should be validated by a built-in mechanism, not by custom code. API Gateway lets you configure a Cognito user pool authorizer: the client sends a JWT in the Authorization header, and the gateway itself validates the signature, the expiration, and, if desired, groups and scopes. Zero development. A custom Lambda authorizer is only needed when the authorization logic is more complex than checking a token.

opts.A: A Lambda authorizer is code that has to be written and maintained. With a Cognito user pool already in place, the built-in authorizer does the same thing for free.
opts.B: API keys are meant for usage plans and throttling, not for authenticating users. Plus, again, a custom validation function.
opts.C: Sending the email address in a header just takes the client's word for it: forging such a header is trivial.

201.key: Two-way SMS messaging is needed, with responses stored and later analyzed. Amazon Pinpoint supports two-way SMS and messaging journeys, and events — including incoming replies — are sent to a Kinesis data stream for archiving and analysis.

opts.A: Amazon Connect is built for contact centers and voice scenarios, not bulk SMS messaging with response analysis.
opts.C: SQS is an internal message queue; it can't send SMS messages to users.
opts.D: SNS can send SMS, but it doesn't support receiving replies from users, and FIFO topics can't be used with SMS.

202.key: This question is worded the same way as {{q:825}}, but the two carry different answer keys — a contradiction within the dump itself, which is why the question is flagged as disputed. Resolving it comes down to weighing two phrases in the scenario. "Automatically rotated every year" is precisely and documentably satisfied only by a customer managed key in KMS: automatic rotation happens every 365 days, and the fact of rotation is visible in the console and in CloudTrail. "LEAST operational overhead" points toward SSE-S3, where the service fully manages the keys and there's nothing to configure. Practical takeaway: if the scenario stresses a verifiable yearly period, go with KMS and automatic rotation; if the emphasis is only on "we don't care how, as long as it happens on its own," go with SSE-S3.

opts.A: A strong alternative, and the answer key for {{q:825}}: SSE-S3 really does rotate keys through the service and requires no configuration at all. Its weak point is that the rotation period isn't documented as yearly and can't be confirmed to an auditor.
opts.C: Manual rotation once a year satisfies the requirement in substance, but it requires a human action every year. With an "automatic rotation" option available, that's unnecessary operational cost.
opts.D: Importing your own key material is the most labor-intensive path, and automatic rotation in KMS isn't supported for imported material. The option contradicts itself.

203.key: The invitations are arriving late because the instances reading the queue can't keep up with the growing number of messages. The right fix is to put those instances into an Auto Scaling group and scale it based on the depth of the SQS queue: the more messages pile up, the more processing instances get launched.

opts.A: DAX speeds up reads from DynamoDB, but the bottleneck is in sending invitations, not in reading data.
opts.B: Putting API Gateway in front of intake doesn't affect how fast requests get processed afterward: requests are already being accepted successfully.
opts.C: CloudFront caches content for readers and does nothing to speed up background processing of messages from the queue.

204.key: Data lives in two places — S3 and RDS — and access needs fine-grained control with minimal operations. AWS Lake Formation builds a data lake on top of S3, connects to RDS through a JDBC connection in AWS Glue, and lets you grant permissions at the database, table, column, and row level from a single place.

opts.A: Moving all the purchase data into a relational database means both higher cost and lost scalability, and it doesn't give RDS fine-grained column-level control.
opts.B: Custom copy functions and bucket policies only provide coarse, object-level access control and require ongoing maintenance.
opts.D: A Redshift cluster is billed continuously, and copying data with Lambda functions is unnecessary extra development.

205.key: The site is static, updates infrequently, and needs a cost-effective and resilient origin for CloudFront. A private S3 bucket satisfies both conditions: you pay only for storage and requests, durability is eleven nines, and there are no servers at all. Access to the bucket is opened only to the distribution through an origin access identity, and content is uploaded with the AWS CLI.

opts.A: The Lightsail instance is billed around the clock and remains a single point of failure that has to be maintained.
opts.B: An Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer is the most expensive setup for a static site that's updated about once a month.
opts.D: A public bucket plus an always-on AWS Transfer Family endpoint means both unnecessary cost and open access to the content that bypasses CloudFront.

206.key: EventBridge receives API call events from CloudTrail directly: you create a rule that matches the CreateImage event and set an SNS topic as the target. No code, no querying logs — the alert arrives right after the call is made.

opts.A: Periodically parsing logs with a function means both delay and code that has to be maintained.
opts.B: A notification when new log files arrive, plus queries in Athena, means a delay of minutes and requires manual work.
opts.D: CloudTrail does not send logs to an SQS queue as a destination — no such integration exists.

207.key: The table's throughput has already been provisioned to the budget's maximum, and requests are still being lost. That calls for a buffer: one function places the request on an SQS queue, and another function reads the queue and writes to DynamoDB at a controlled rate. Spikes are smoothed out, nothing is lost, and existing users notice no change.

opts.A: Rate limiting in API Gateway drops some requests — that is, it turns data loss into policy and affects users.
opts.B: DAX speeds up reads and does not buffer writes: the write problem remains.
opts.C: A secondary index adds another consumer of write throughput and will only make things worse.

208.key: Neither API calls nor data may travel public routes, and only this instance is allowed to upload. The first requirement is met by a VPC endpoint, the second by a bucket policy that allows access only to the instance's role (and, if desired, only through that endpoint). Here the key selects the interface endpoint: it is created in a specific subnet, gets a private IP address, and is protected by a security group. The difference from a gateway endpoint matters: a gateway endpoint works through routes in the route table, has neither an IP address nor security groups, and is not reachable from on premises — compare with {{q:667,471}}.

opts.B: The description doesn't match the mechanism: a gateway endpoint isn't placed in an Availability Zone and doesn't support security groups — it's a route in the VPC route table.
opts.C: S3 has no "private bucket IP address" that can be looked up with nslookup and set as a route. A private address only appears together with an interface endpoint.
opts.D: The ip-ranges.json file contains AWS's public IP ranges. A route to them does nothing to make the traffic private.

209.key: Instances are frequently added and removed, so session state can't be kept on them. ElastiCache moves sessions out to an external in-memory store: any instance reads and writes the same data, response time is measured in fractions of a millisecond, and code changes are allowed under the stated condition.

opts.B: Session affinity keeps a user pinned to a specific instance, and when that instance is removed from the group the session is lost.
opts.C: Session Manager from Systems Manager is administrator access to an instance's shell — it has nothing to do with application user sessions.
opts.D: GetSessionToken issues temporary AWS credentials — it doesn't store web application sessions.

210.key: Order collection is fast, fulfillment is slow — so the stages need to be decoupled with two queues and each scaled to its own load. The right metric for a queue is backlog per instance: the number of messages in the queue divided by the number of consumers, with the Auto Scaling group holding that value steady. That way capacity tracks the actual volume of work, and no data is lost during scaling.

opts.A: Permanently keeping peak minimum capacity is overpaying, and CPU utilization is a poor reflection of the volume of accumulated orders.
opts.B: Creating new Auto Scaling groups on a signal is an unworkable, unmanageable design.
opts.C: The queues are chosen correctly, but SQS doesn't send notifications you can scale on — you need a metric based on message count.

211.key: Resources are tagged and scattered across multiple Regions and services. Tag Editor in AWS Resource Groups searches by tag across all Regions and resource types at once and produces a ready list — this is the fastest path, with no code required.

opts.A: CloudTrail shows API calls, not a current inventory of resources with a given tag.
opts.B: Polling every service in every Region via the CLI is slow and labor-intensive.
opts.C: CloudWatch Logs Insights works with logs, not with resource inventory.

212.key: The key phrases are "variable and changes rapidly" and "must not increase retrieval time." The first means the access class can't be guessed manually; the second rules out anything that doesn't return the object instantly or that charges for retrieval. Intelligent-Tiering satisfies both: objects move between the frequent and infrequent tiers automatically, there's no retrieval fee, and access time is the same on both tiers. At 2–5 GB, the objects are large enough that the monitoring fee is negligible.

opts.B: Glacier Instant Retrieval returns the object instantly, but charges a noticeable retrieval fee and requires a minimum 90-day storage duration. The data lives up to three months and is read unpredictably often — both conditions work against it.
opts.C: S3 Standard doesn't optimize anything: during periods when nobody reads the export, you pay the full rate.
opts.D: Standard-IA is designed for infrequent access. With a rapidly changing pattern, the retrieval fee and the 30-day minimum storage duration make it more expensive than Intelligent-Tiering.

213.key: Cross-site scripting and SQL injection are application-layer attacks, and AWS WAF is what filters them: a web ACL is attached to the load balancer, AWS managed rule groups are enabled (including the Core rule set and the SQL database rule set), and traffic is inspected before it reaches the application. AWS itself updates the managed rules, so a team with no dedicated administrators doesn't maintain signatures by hand — this directly answers the requirement to reduce its share of the responsibility.

opts.B: Public hosting of static content in S3 has nothing to do with filtering attacks and doesn't fit an application sitting behind a load balancer.
opts.C: Shield Advanced protects against DDoS but doesn't inspect the content of HTTP requests for injection attempts.
opts.D: A third-party firewall on an instance is a server that has to be patched and maintained — the opposite of the requirement.

214.key: Converting formats with minimal development is what AWS Glue is for. A crawler determines the structure of the CSV files and creates a table in the data catalog, and an ETL job with built-in transforms writes the result in Parquet format to the target bucket. There's almost no code and no infrastructure to manage.

opts.A: An EMR cluster and a Spark application mean both development work and cluster management.
opts.C: A Bash script to convert to Parquet would have to be written from scratch, and AWS Batch adds environment configuration on top.
opts.D: A Lambda function would need its own conversion code, and large files might not fit within its time and memory limits.

215.key: Start by checking the timing: 700 TB at 500 Mbps takes roughly four months of continuous transfer, while the deadline is one month. That rules out the network link, so the data travels physically, on Snowball devices. Storing rarely requested copies for seven years is cheapest in S3 Glacier Deep Archive, which a lifecycle rule transitions the objects into.

opts.B: A VPN runs over the same internet connection: the deadline can't be met.
opts.C: A 500 Mbps Direct Connect connection gives the same speed as the existing internet link, plus the lead time to physically provision it — usually weeks. That won't fit in a month.
opts.D: DataSync is a good tool, but it's limited by the same bandwidth, and it can't upload directly into the Glacier storage class: data lands in S3 first.

216.key: The task splits in two: new objects and the millions already sitting there. For new objects, it's enough to turn on default encryption on the bucket — after that S3 encrypts everything that arrives. The existing objects need a bulk rewrite: S3 Inventory builds a report listing the objects and their encryption status, and S3 Batch Operations runs a copy operation against that report, which rewrites each object already encrypted. All of this is managed tooling — no downloading, no custom code.

opts.A: Downloading and re-uploading millions of objects through local storage means traffic in both directions, time, and a high risk of error — exactly what the "LEAST amount of effort" wording asks you to avoid.
opts.C: Turning on default encryption only affects new objects, and versioning has nothing to do with encryption. The millions of objects already uploaded stay unencrypted.
opts.D: There's no console operation for bulk-applying encryption to selected objects, and going through millions of objects by hand is physically impossible.

217.key: Up to 30 minutes of downtime and some data loss are acceptable, and the standby site doesn't need to handle the load — this describes a pilot light or warm standby design with active-passive failover. A minimal-size infrastructure is deployed in the standby Region, data is kept current with a cross-Region Aurora replica (which can be promoted to primary), and Route 53 with health checks fails traffic over when the primary site goes down. The design is cheaper than active-active and fits within the stated RTO and RPO.

opts.B: An active-active configuration means the standby site is constantly serving part of the traffic, and the requirement explicitly says that's not needed. That's unnecessary cost.
opts.C: A full copy of the infrastructure running active-active costs even more, and restoring the database from the latest snapshot gives a worse RPO than a replica.
opts.D: Provisioning infrastructure from backups only after a disaster won't fit in 30 minutes, and a "second Aurora primary instance" in another Region describes a global database, not what's asked for here.

218.key: Two layers of filtering are involved. A security group is stateful, so a single inbound rule for port 443 from any source is enough (A). A network ACL is stateless, so it needs two rules: inbound on port 443 and outbound to the ephemeral port range 32768–65535, where responses to the client go out (E).

opts.B: An outbound security group rule isn't needed for inbound connections: the response leaves automatically.
opts.C: An inbound-only rule in the network ACL isn't enough: responses would be blocked on the way out.
opts.D: Allowing port 443 outbound makes no sense: the web server's responses leave from ephemeral ports, not from port 443.

219.key: The application performs in-memory tasks, so the bottleneck is RAM, and the general-purpose M5 family doesn't fit that profile. The instances are swapped for R5, which is memory-optimized, and the change is made in the CloudFormation template that deploys the infrastructure. For future capacity planning, the CloudWatch agent is installed to collect custom application latency metrics — EC2 has no built-in memory or latency metrics.

opts.A: T3 instances are burstable with a limited performance budget: they're worse for sustained memory-heavy work, and changes made outside the template would cause configuration drift.
opts.B: Manually resizing capacity isn't operational efficiency, and the instance type is still wrong for the workload.
opts.C: The instance type is chosen correctly, but EC2 has no built-in memory metrics — only the agent provides them.

220.key: Requests arrive rarely and unevenly, and processing takes seconds. A Lambda function is billed only for actual execution time, so nothing is paid for during idle hours, and it scales instantly. This is the cheapest way to serve this traffic profile.

opts.A: An AWS Glue job is built for batch data processing, starts with noticeable delay, and is billed in minimum-duration increments.
opts.C: An EKS cluster is billed continuously, including a control plane fee, even when there are no requests.
opts.D: EC2 instances behind ECS run and are billed around the clock regardless of request volume.

221.key: Logs must be kept for seven years and read concurrently by a reporting tool. S3 is cheaper per gigabyte than any block or file storage, allows any number of simultaneous reads, and lifecycle rules let you move older logs into even cheaper storage classes. The instances simply upload the files to the bucket.

opts.A: An EBS volume is tied to an Availability Zone and to an instance, costs more per gigabyte, and doesn't give the reporting tool concurrent access.
opts.B: EFS does provide concurrent access, but it's significantly more expensive per gigabyte of storage than S3, and for a seven-year archive that's the deciding factor.
opts.C: Instance store data disappears along with the instance: a seven-year retention requirement is impossible to meet with it in the first place.

222.key: An external vendor doesn't need credentials in your account — it needs the ability to act as your role. You create a role in your account with the required policies, and its trust policy allows a principal from the vendor's account to assume it. The vendor's tool calls AssumeRole and receives temporary credentials. A good practice on top of this is an external ID in the trust policy condition: it protects against the confused deputy problem, when the vendor serves many clients.

opts.B: An IAM user with a password is long-lived credentials inside your account handed out externally — and you'd have to revoke them manually.
opts.C: A user from a different account can't be added to an IAM group: groups only work within their own account.
opts.D: There's no "AWS account" identity provider type in IAM: what's configured there is SAML and OIDC. Cross-account access is done with a role and a trust policy.

223.key: There are two separate requirements — permissions and routing. Permissions: the EKS pod is given a role through IRSA (the role is linked to a service account via the cluster's OIDC provider), after which the application runs on temporary credentials (A). Routing: to keep calls to DynamoDB from going out to the internet, a VPC endpoint is created — for DynamoDB that's a free gateway endpoint (D). No keys in code, no NAT gateway anywhere in the design.

opts.B: An IAM user isn't "attached" to a pod: that's long-lived credentials, whereas pods get permissions through a role.
opts.C: A network ACL allows or denies traffic, but without an endpoint the path to DynamoDB would still go out through an internet gateway or a NAT gateway.
opts.E: Access keys in code are a direct anti-pattern: the secret ends up in the image and the repository and never gets rotated.

224.key: There are two separate requirements here. Fault tolerance across zones: instances are split evenly between two Availability Zones, so the loss of one zone doesn't cut capacity unevenly in half — hence four instances, two in each zone (E). Random distribution of requests across all running instances: the multivalue answer policy in Route 53 returns up to eight records with associated health checks, the client picks one of them, and unhealthy addresses are excluded from the answer (C).

opts.A: Failover sends traffic to a standby resource only when the primary fails — that's not random distribution across all instances.
opts.B: Weighted routing distributes traffic in set proportions, while the requirement is random distribution across all healthy targets.
opts.D: Three instances split two plus one is uneven: if the zone with two instances fails, only a third of capacity remains.

225.key: High availability, growing volume, and on-demand SQL queries are all required with minimal operational overhead. Kinesis Data Firehose ingests the stream without shard management and delivers the data straight to a Redshift cluster, where SQL queries can run immediately, including against historical data.

opts.A: Data sitting in an S3 bucket doesn't give you SQL queries by itself: you'd still need a catalog and a query engine, and a Kinesis data stream requires shard management.
opts.C: Custom processing functions triggered on file arrival mean code and maintenance, and the design contains no query engine at all.
opts.D: A custom ingestion service on instances plus a relational RDS database scale poorly to petabytes and require full operational management.

226.key: Millions of devices, a raw data stream, and a requirement for minimal operations mean ingestion has to be serverless and elastic. API Gateway accepts the devices' HTTP requests and puts records onto a Kinesis Data Streams stream, and Firehose buffers them and drops them into S3 with no servers involved (E). The transformation the instance used to do is handled by managed ETL — AWS Glue, working directly on the data already in S3 (A). No instances remain in the design at all.

opts.B: Route 53 distributes requests across instances, but the instances don't go anywhere: the operational burden remains.
opts.C: Adding more instances is exactly the manual scaling the requirement asks you to avoid.
opts.D: An SQS queue with processing on instances flattens spikes but still leaves a fleet of machines to operate, and Kinesis is the more natural fit for streaming data.

227.key: The symptom is described precisely: no new logs have been added, yet the object count keeps rising — meaning stale versions are piling up. On a versioned bucket, a lifecycle rule with an Expiration action only removes the current version, turning it into a delete marker, while the earlier versions remain and keep being billed. The fix is to add NoncurrentVersionExpiration to the rule (and clean up expired delete markers while at it). This is a configuration change, not code, which is why it's also the cheapest.

opts.A: The CloudTrail trail itself has no setting for how long objects are retained in the bucket: object lifecycle is managed by S3.
opts.C: A function that enumerates objects and versions means code, and paying for invocations plus LIST and DELETE requests. A lifecycle rule does the same thing for free.
opts.D: Object ownership affects access permissions to the objects, not how many versions are kept or what that costs.

228.key: Two requirements: reduce the number of connections to the database and don't lose data during traffic spikes. An SQS queue accepts records instantly and holds onto them, and a Lambda function reads the queue in batches and writes to the database with limited concurrency — so there are few connections, and a spike just makes the queue longer.

opts.A: More memory doesn't increase the number of allowed connections and won't prevent data loss during a spike.
opts.B: The standby instance in a Multi-AZ configuration doesn't accept writes: writing "to all active instances" isn't possible.
opts.D: SNS delivers messages immediately and doesn't buffer them: if the subscriber is unavailable, the data is lost.

229.key: The company is manually handling replication and scaling for MySQL on instances. Aurora Serverless for Aurora MySQL removes that entirely: the engine is MySQL-compatible, so the application doesn't need to change, capacity adjusts automatically, storage grows on its own, and data is stored in six copies across three Availability Zones.

opts.B: The PostgreSQL option requires switching engines and rewriting queries, whereas the company runs MySQL.
opts.C: Combining the databases onto larger instances is manual vertical scaling — exactly the work they want to move away from.
opts.D: A relational database can't be scaled with an EC2 Auto Scaling group: new instances won't share the same data.

230.key: High availability, fault tolerance, and automatic scaling are all required. A NAT gateway is a managed service that scales on its own up to tens of gigabits and is maintained by AWS. Placing one gateway in each Availability Zone keeps the zones independent if one of them fails.

opts.A: Both gateways in the same Availability Zone means that zone's failure knocks internet access out for every subnet.
opts.B: NAT instances in an Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer is a homegrown design: a default route can't point at a load balancer.
opts.D: Spot Instances can be reclaimed at any time, and routing outbound traffic through a load balancer doesn't work.

231.key: Both networks belong to the same account and are inside AWS, so they should be connected privately. VPC peering creates a direct route between the networks over AWS's internal infrastructure: traffic never goes out to the internet, the database stays without a public address, and access is further narrowed with security groups.

opts.A: Allowing by public IP address means the traffic travels over the internet, and the rule itself is easily bypassed if the address changes.
opts.C: Public access to the database is a blunt violation of basic security practice: it becomes visible to the entire internet.
opts.D: A proxy on a separate instance adds a point of failure, cost, and maintenance where ordinary peering would be enough.

232.key: A signal is needed the moment someone connects to an environment over RDP or SSH. The standard way to see the connection itself is VPC flow logs: they record accepted connections with destination ports 3389 and 22, are sent to CloudWatch Logs, a metric filter there turns them into a metric, and an alarm sends the notification. Everything is built from managed components and works the same way across all the isolated VPCs.

opts.A: CloudWatch Application Insights monitors application health and metrics, not the fact of an SSH or RDP login.
opts.B: A role with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy lets you manage the instance through Systems Manager, but on its own it doesn't notify anyone of anything.
opts.D: EC2 Instance State-change events report an instance starting, stopping, and terminating. A user connecting isn't one of those events.

233.key: The root user account can't be restricted with IAM policies — it always has full permissions in the account. So protecting root comes down to making sign-in harder: a strong, unique password (A) and multi-factor authentication (B), ideally on a hardware or virtual device kept separately. On top of that, AWS recommends never creating access keys for root at all, and doing day-to-day work under IAM roles instead.

opts.C: Root shouldn't have access keys to begin with — then there's nothing to store. An encrypted bucket doesn't change the fact that leaking such a key means full control of the account.
opts.D: Root isn't subject to IAM policies: adding it to a group with administrative permissions does nothing and restricts nothing.
opts.E: You can't attach an inline policy to the root user. Its actions can only be limited by an SCP policy from the AWS Organizations management account, and even then not completely.

234.key: This question tests which service is responsible for what. Encryption at rest in AWS is KMS: EBS volumes and the Aurora cluster's storage have encryption turned on with a specified KMS key. Encryption in transit to the user is a TLS certificate on the load balancer, and certificates are issued and managed by ACM, free of charge and with automatic renewal. That exact pair — KMS for data on disk, ACM for traffic — is what the correct option describes.

opts.A: The services' roles are swapped: KMS doesn't issue TLS certificates for a load balancer, and ACM doesn't encrypt EBS volumes or database storage.
opts.B: There's no global "turn on encryption for everything in the account" switch, and doing everyday work under the root account contradicts basic security guidance.
opts.D: BitLocker is a Windows mechanism you maintain yourself, instead of managed volume encryption. And you can't attach a KMS key to a load balancer in place of an ACM certificate.

235.key: Moving from Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL is an engine change, so the AWS Schema Conversion Tool converts the schema and stored code. DMS then runs a full load plus change data capture task across all tables: it migrates the data first, then continuously applies changes, so the databases stay in sync throughout the months of staged application migration. Given the high volume of reads and writes, a memory-optimized replication instance is used — DMS keeps its change cache in memory.

opts.A: DataSync moves files, not database contents, and a CDC-only task with no initial load would leave the target database empty.
opts.B: The same mistake, with DataSync cast as the tool for the initial database migration.
opts.D: A compute-optimized instance is worse suited to CDC with a high volume of changes, and selecting only the largest tables would leave the rest out of sync.

236.key: Scalability and high availability are required with the least change to the application. Elastic Beanstalk takes the existing code as-is and deploys it into environments with a load balancer and multiple Availability Zones, the database moves to RDS in a Multi-AZ configuration, and user images are moved out to S3, taking the load off the instances.

opts.A: Moving to Lambda and DynamoDB means rewriting the application, which the requirement asks to avoid.
opts.B: Read replicas don't provide automatic failover, and storing images in a relational database is inefficient.
opts.C: A larger database instance solves neither the availability requirement nor image storage.

237.key: Private connectivity is needed between networks in different accounts, with no single point of failure and no bandwidth limits. VPC peering satisfies all of this: it's a managed capability of the AWS network itself, has no intermediate devices that could fail, and has none of the bandwidth limits typical of tunnels.

opts.B: A gateway endpoint gives access to services like S3 and DynamoDB, not to instances in someone else's VPC.
opts.C: A virtual private gateway is the attachment point for a VPN or Direct Connect connection to your own site — it isn't used to connect two VPCs.
opts.D: A private virtual interface belongs to Direct Connect and is created for a connection from a data center, not between two VPCs.

238.key: A notification is needed when EC2 usage for a given month crosses a threshold, and as cheaply as possible. AWS Budgets is built exactly for this: a budget with a monthly period, filtered to the EC2 service, with an alert threshold, sends its notification to an SNS topic. The first two budgets in an account are free, and beyond that it costs cents per day. Cost Explorer and CUR are analysis tools — they don't send threshold notifications.

opts.A: Cost Explorer builds reports but can't send notifications when a threshold is exceeded — that's what Budgets is for.
opts.B: Same mistake: a Cost Explorer report isn't a notification mechanism.
opts.D: The combination of CUR, Athena, and scheduled queries works, but it's several services, custom queries, and paying for scans where a budget alone would do.

239.key: A single HTTPS endpoint for a single function with IAM authentication is needed. That is exactly what a Lambda function URL with the AWS_IAM authentication type (B) provides: no additional service, and the endpoint is created together with the function.

opts.A: IAM authorization on API Gateway technically works, but it adds a service that must be configured, versioned, and paid for. The requirements do not call for routing, API keys, or throttling — so this is an unnecessary layer.
opts.C: Lambda@Edge requires a CloudFront distribution, and the authentication logic would have to be written by hand — the most work of all the options.
opts.D: CloudFront Functions fail on two counts: they are lightweight JavaScript functions for editing headers with no network access, and they have no AWS_IAM authentication type.

240.key: Charges apply only to traffic leaving AWS. If the visualization tool runs in the same Region as the data warehouse, the 50 MB query results never leave AWS at all — only the 500 KB web pages go out, a hundred times less data. On top of that, this egress traffic is routed over Direct Connect, where the per-gigabyte rate is noticeably lower than the internet rate.

opts.A: The on-premises tool pulls the full 50 MB result of every query out of AWS, and at the most expensive internet rate on top of that. The worst option.
opts.B: The location is right and the outbound volume is small, but internet traffic costs more than traffic over Direct Connect.
opts.C: The connection is cheaper than the internet, but the full query results still go out — a hundred times more data than the pages.

241.key: The data must remain available online across multiple Regions at all times, with minimal operational overhead. An RDS read replica in another Region is created with a single operation, continuously receives changes, is available for queries, and can be promoted to a standalone database if needed.

opts.A: A self-managed PostgreSQL cluster on instances is the heaviest amount of maintenance.
opts.B: Multi-AZ operates within a single Region: there will be no data in other Regions.
opts.D: Copying snapshots to another Region does not provide online access: a database still has to be restored from them first.

242.key: The requirement is to return the addresses of all healthy instances in the DNS response. That's what the multivalue answer routing policy does: Route 53 returns up to eight records, each tied to its own health check, and unhealthy ones are excluded from the response.

opts.A: The simple routing policy returns records as-is and does not support health checks.
opts.B: The latency routing policy picks a single Region with the lowest latency, rather than returning the whole list.
opts.D: Geolocation picks a response based on the client's location and does not return a list of all healthy addresses.

243.key: The clinics need file-based access to data stored in S3, with minimum latency locally. A file gateway is deployed as a virtual machine at each clinic: it presents local applications with a familiar NFS or SMB share backed by the S3 bucket, and caches frequently read files locally. Applications don't change, and latency is governed by the local cache.

opts.B: DataSync is a tool for one-time or periodic transfers, not ongoing file access. Copying the entire dataset to every clinic is wasteful and doesn't provide a single source of truth.
opts.C: A volume gateway presents block volumes over iSCSI, while the clinics' applications work with files.
opts.D: An EFS file system cannot be mounted on arbitrary on-premises servers over the internet: that requires private connectivity to the VPC, and latency in that case would be governed by the link, not by a local cache.

244.key: The layers need to be separated, fault tolerance across zones is required, and scaling is needed. The database moves to Aurora with a read replica in another Availability Zone, an AMI is created from the existing instance, and the web layer becomes an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer across two Availability Zones. A zone failure stops neither the application nor the database.

opts.A: Both machines and the load balancer sit in a single Availability Zone: a zone failure takes down the whole site, and manually launching instances provides no scaling.
opts.B: The replica and the second machine are again in the same Availability Zone — there is no resilience to its failure.
opts.D: A database on a separate instance with copies in S3 remains a single point of failure with a long recovery time, whereas a managed database solves this natively.

245.key: The cost of the development environment is determined by how many instances are actually running, not by how the load balancer distributes requests. The key reads option A as 'keep one instance in dev instead of two' — cutting the spend in half. This is a genuinely disputed question: literally 'reconfiguring the target group' does not change the desired capacity of the Auto Scaling group, and the group would bring the second instance back. Part of the community therefore picks D. The counterargument to D: maximum is only a ceiling; if dev holds a desired capacity of 2 and never scales up, lowering the maximum saves nothing.

opts.B: The balancing algorithm distributes requests among instances that are already running. Their count — and the bill — doesn't change at all.
opts.C: Reducing the instance size also affects production, which is expected to see periods of high traffic. The question asks to reduce cost only for dev, and this option risks the performance of the production environment.
opts.D: A strong alternative if you assume dev actually scales up. But maximum only caps the peak: with a steady two instances, lowering the maximum saves nothing, whereas reducing the actual number of targets does.

246.key: An internet-facing load balancer must sit in public subnets: without them it has nowhere to receive traffic. So public subnets are created in each Availability Zone, assigned to the load balancer, and traffic to the instances in the private subnets travels over the VPC's internal routing.

opts.A: Changing the load balancer type doesn't help, and a NAT gateway handles outbound connections, not inbound.
opts.B: Moving the instances into public subnets exposes them to the internet unnecessarily and doesn't fix the load balancer's configuration.
opts.C: A route to the internet gateway from the private subnets makes them public and requires the instances to have public addresses.

247.key: A read replica for RDS for MySQL is built on the binary log, which is only kept when automated backups are enabled: the retention period must be greater than zero (E). In addition, long-running transactions on the source should be allowed to finish before creating the replica, otherwise replica creation will stall or fail (C).

opts.A: Binary log replication doesn't need to be enabled separately: it is activated by automated backups.
opts.B: Failover priority relates to Multi-AZ configuration and has nothing to do with read replicas.
opts.D: Global tables are a DynamoDB feature, not an RDS for MySQL feature.

248.key: The instances are running at 100% CPU and some requests are being lost — so both the requests need to be held onto and processing needs to scale. An SQS queue accepts requests instantly and holds them until they're processed, while an Auto Scaling group grows based on queue length, i.e., exactly in line with actual user load.

opts.A: A load balancer distributes requests, but if both machines are overloaded, requests will still be lost, and there's no scaling.
opts.B: An S3 endpoint changes the network path and cost, but doesn't reduce CPU load.
opts.C: A more powerful instance is a one-time vertical scale-up with downtime, and it will hit its limit again as load grows.

249.key: The defining words are SMB clients and 'fully managed solution.' That's Amazon FSx for Windows File Server: it natively speaks SMB, supports Windows access control lists and Active Directory integration, and AWS handles maintenance, backups, and fault tolerance.

opts.A: A volume gateway presents block volumes over iSCSI, not file shares over SMB, and is intended for hybrid scenarios.
opts.B: A tape gateway emulates a tape library for backup systems — it has nothing to do with shared file access for an application.
opts.C: A self-managed Windows server with a file server role is a machine you'd have to patch, scale, and back up yourself — not a managed solution.

250.key: The flow logs are needed frequently for the first 90 days, then only occasionally afterward — a classic use case for S3 with a lifecycle rule. Logs are written straight to the bucket, and after 90 days the objects transition to the Standard-Infrequent Access class, where storage costs roughly half as much at the same instant availability.

opts.A: A retention period can be set in CloudWatch Logs, but after 90 days the logs would simply be deleted, while the requirement is to keep them for occasional access; storage in CloudWatch is also more expensive.
opts.B: Kinesis is a transport for streaming data, not long-term storage, and a stream's maximum retention period is limited.
opts.C: CloudTrail records API calls and cannot serve as a destination for VPC flow logs.

251.key: The instance in the private subnet needs to be able to initiate outbound connections while remaining unreachable from outside. A NAT gateway is created in a public subnet, and the private subnet's route table sends all outbound traffic to it. Updates get downloaded, and inbound connections from the internet remain impossible.

opts.A: A route to the internet gateway turns the subnet public and requires the instances to have public addresses — violating the privacy requirement.
opts.C: A NAT instance must sit in a public subnet: placed in the same private subnet, it can't reach the internet itself either.
opts.D: Two mechanisms are mixed here: the route points to the internet gateway, and the NAT instance is placed incorrectly — the setup doesn't work.

252.key: The files must be accessible simultaneously from multiple instances, the volume is growing, and built-in redundancy is required. Amazon EFS satisfies all three: it mounts over NFS to any number of instances, grows automatically, and in Standard mode stores data across multiple Availability Zones.

opts.B: An EBS volume normally attaches to a single instance and lives in a single Availability Zone: there's no simultaneous access by multiple servers and no built-in cross-zone redundancy.
opts.C: Glacier Deep Archive is an archive with retrieval times measured in hours. Working files that applications need to access can't be kept there.
opts.D: AWS Backup is a backup service, not a store that applications read files from directly.

253.key: The effective permissions are the union of all Allow statements minus all Deny statements. Policy1 grants full access to EC2 (ec2:*) and Directory Service (ds:*), but only read access (Get and List) for IAM, and also only read access (Get and Describe) for CloudWatch Logs. Policy2 explicitly denies ds:Delete*. So deleting EC2 instances is allowed, deleting directories is not because of the explicit Deny, and deleting IAM users or logs is not allowed simply because those permissions were never granted. The evaluation rule: look for an explicit Deny first, then Allow, and everything else is denied by default.

opts.A: Only iam:Get* and iam:List* are granted for IAM, i.e. read access. There is no delete action among them.
opts.B: Policy1 allows ds:*, but Policy2's explicit Deny takes away ds:Delete*, and an explicit deny always overrides an allow.
opts.D: Only logs:Get* and logs:Describe* are granted for CloudWatch Logs — again read-only access; deleting logs is not permitted.

254.key: Least privilege between application tiers is implemented by referencing security groups: the inbound rule specifies the ID of the neighboring tier's security group. The permission automatically extends to exactly the instances that belong to that group and keeps working as they're replaced or scaled.

opts.A: An instance ID cannot be specified as a source in a security group rule: that kind of source doesn't exist.
opts.C: The entire VPC's CIDR block grants access to every resource on the network — the opposite of least privilege.
opts.D: A subnet CIDR block is broader than needed: any resource in the subnet would get access, not just the neighboring application tier.

255.key: Duplicates arise because the form gets resubmitted after a timeout. The order is stored in the database, and its order number is sent to an SQS FIFO queue: it guarantees exactly-once processing and preserves order, so the payment service processes each order exactly once even if the message arrives twice.

opts.A: Firehose delivers streams to storage destinations and is not an exactly-once queue for a payment service.
opts.B: CloudTrail records calls to AWS APIs, not requests inside the application, and it has no rules of this kind.
opts.C: SNS doesn't guarantee exactly-once delivery and doesn't support polling by a subscriber: messages would be duplicated.

256.key: The requirements are subtle: protect against accidental deletion, keep all versions of the documents available, while still letting users download, modify, and upload documents. Versioning (B) provides both a version history and reversibility of deletion. MFA Delete (D) adds a second factor to irreversible operations — deleting a specific version and disabling versioning. Neither one interferes with normal document workflows, unlike options that simply block writes.

opts.A: A read-only ACL would strip users of the ability to upload and modify documents — a direct requirement of the task.
opts.C: A bucket policy, not an 'IAM policy,' is attached to a bucket, and no policy preserves previous versions of documents. The versioning requirement remains unmet.
opts.E: Encryption with a KMS key protects the content from being read by unauthorized parties. It has nothing to do with accidental deletion or version history.

257.key: Scaling status needs to be collected serverlessly and without affecting the speed of instance launches. A CloudWatch metric stream continuously exports metrics to Kinesis Data Firehose, which then lands them in S3 in near real time. No agents on machines, no launch delays.

opts.B: An EMR cluster is not a serverless solution and requires managing nodes.
opts.C: Running a function on a schedule introduces delay and is not near-real-time streaming delivery.
opts.D: Installing an agent at instance launch lengthens the boot process, which the requirement explicitly forbids.

258.key: Hundreds of 1 GB files an hour is a job for a ready-made ETL tool. An AWS Glue job performs the CSV-to-Parquet conversion without custom processing code, and a Lambda function triggered on the PUT event simply starts it. No clusters and no conversion logic to write.

opts.A: A gigabyte-sized file doesn't fit well within a function's memory and time limits, and conversion code would have to be written and maintained.
opts.B: A custom Spark application means both development work and cluster management.
opts.C: Periodic queries through Athena followed by an export is a complex, delayed chain, whereas an ETL job does this directly.

259.key: Daily consistent backups retained for two years with restore capability are required. AWS Backup provides all of this in one place: a backup vault, a plan with a daily schedule and a two-year retention period, and RDS instances assigned to the plan. Backups are created as consistent snapshots by the RDS service itself, and centralized reporting and retention policies remove the manual work.

opts.B: RDS automated backups are limited to a 35-day retention period, and Amazon DLM manages EBS snapshots, not RDS.
opts.C: Transaction logs in CloudWatch Logs are not a restorable database backup: you cannot restore an instance from them.
opts.D: DMS with a CDC task streams a stream of changes into S3 — that's not a consistent backup and not a means of restoring an instance.

260.key: FSx for Windows File Server has no identity system of its own: permissions on folders and files are governed by Windows ACLs, and identities come from the Active Directory domain. So the only step that actually works is joining the file system to the domain (the self-managed Active Directory, via its domain controllers). After that, the familiar domain groups continue to control access exactly as they did on premises. IAM roles and policies are irrelevant here: they govern access to the AWS API, not the contents of an SMB share.

opts.A: AD Connector is a proxy to your directory for services like WorkSpaces and Identity Center. There is no mapping of domain groups to IAM groups, and file permissions aren't granted that way.
opts.B: Tags are labels for tracking resources. They have nothing to do with access permissions on folders and files inside the file system.
opts.C: A service-linked role lets the FSx service itself perform actions in your account. It does not restrict users' access to files.

261.key: The task is to serve different content versions to different devices. CloudFront with a Lambda@Edge function parses the User-Agent header and returns the appropriate object variant (C), while the distribution itself is configured to cache multiple versions of the same path — by including device type in the cache key (A). Together this gives both correct version selection and caching of each variant.

opts.B: A Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4 and does not see HTTP headers: Host-based routing is impossible for it.
opts.D: Global Accelerator speeds up the traffic path but doesn't select content by device, and the NLB again cannot parse headers.
opts.E: Same mistake: path-based routing is a feature of an application-layer load balancer, not an NLB, and device type cannot be inferred from the path.

262.key: Both networks are in the same Region, and connecting them needs to be cheap. VPC peering has no hourly charge and no processing charge: only the transferred traffic is billed. Routes are added to both route tables, plus an inbound security group rule on the cache cluster referencing the application instances' security group — this works over peering within a single Region.

opts.B: A transit VPC adds its own appliances or gateway with hourly charges — noticeably more expensive than peering for two networks.
opts.C: Peering has no security group of its own: the rule is created on the resource itself, i.e., on the cache cluster.
opts.D: Here there's both an unnecessary transit VPC and a nonexistent security group for the transit network.

263.key: No additional infrastructure is allowed, and maintenance and scaling must be minimized. An ECS cluster is created (A), and the service is launched with the Fargate launch type and a desired task count of at least two (D): there are no nodes at all, tasks are spread across Availability Zones, and scaling is configured through a service policy.

opts.B: A Kubernetes control plane on your own instances is exactly the infrastructure that must be avoided.
opts.C: The EC2 launch type requires managing the cluster's nodes.
opts.E: Kubernetes worker nodes on EC2 instances again means your own infrastructure.

264.key: The problem is that DNS is returning addresses of unhealthy instances. The correct fix is architectural: put an Application Load Balancer with health checks in front of the instances and point Route 53 to it with an alias record. The load balancer stops sending requests to an unhealthy target instantly, whereas routing through DNS always depends on TTL and the client resolver's cache — even with health checks, some users would keep getting the old address.

opts.A: The simple routing policy doesn't support health checks at all: it returns records as-is.
opts.B: The failover routing policy is designed for a primary/secondary pair of resources, not a dozen equally weighted instances, and it still runs into DNS caching.
opts.C: CloudFront speeds up delivery but doesn't solve the problem of removing unhealthy instances from rotation: it too needs a load balancer with health checks.

265.key: The most secure of the workable designs: the instances sit in private subnets and are not reachable directly from the internet, a public Application Load Balancer sits in front of them, and CloudFront uses that load balancer as its origin, delivering HTTPS content from the edge location closest to the user. The load balancer's security group can also be restricted to accept traffic only from CloudFront.

opts.A: Instances in public subnets are directly reachable from the internet — an unnecessary attack surface for the same result.
opts.B: Making the instances the origin for CloudFront, bypassing the load balancer, means either exposing them publicly or ending up with a setup that doesn't work; fault tolerance is also lost.
opts.D: Both weaknesses are present here at once: public subnets and going straight to the instances instead of through the load balancer.

266.key: The application is deployed in every Region, is latency-sensitive, and needs health monitoring plus traffic redirection away from failed sites. Global Accelerator creates a listener on the required port, an endpoint group is attached to each Region, and the load balancer serves as the endpoint. The accelerator continuously checks target health, routes each player to the nearest healthy Region, and shifts traffic within seconds, independent of DNS caching.

opts.B: CloudFront is optimized for content caching, while gaming traffic is dynamic; it doesn't provide health checks or fast cross-Region failover.
opts.C: An S3 bucket can't serve as the origin for a gaming application: there's no logic and no session state there.
opts.D: DynamoDB and DAX are about data storage and have nothing to do with routing traffic to healthy Regions.

267.key: Ingesting a stream, encrypting it, writing it in Parquet format, and analyzing it in near real time are all required with the least operational overhead. Kinesis Data Firehose does all of this itself: it encrypts the data, converts records to Parquet, and lands them in S3 without shard management, while Kinesis Data Analytics runs the stream analysis using SQL queries.

opts.A: A Kinesis Data Streams stream doesn't write to S3 by itself and requires shard management, and an intermediary function complicates the design.
opts.B: An EMR cluster has to be provisioned and paid for, and the stream still doesn't deliver data to S3 on its own.
opts.C: Firehose is chosen correctly, but using an EMR cluster for analysis means managing nodes instead of using a managed service.

268.key: The constraint in the wording is 'minimizing changes to the application's architecture.' RDS Proxy sits between the application and the database transparently: only the connection string changes, and there's no need to touch the code. It removes the main cause of the 'long delays and interruptions' during spikes — exhaustion and re-establishment of connections to MySQL. The disputed part is that Proxy doesn't add read capacity, and the question says 'database read performance,' which leads part of the community to pick ElastiCache. The exam rule of thumb: complaints about connections and interruptions point to Proxy; complaints about heavy repeated reads, with no restriction on changing code, point to a cache or a read replica.

opts.A: A strong alternative on the merits: a cache genuinely offloads reads. But a cache doesn't work on its own — cache-aside logic has to be added to the application: read from the cache, fall through to the database on a miss, invalidate on write. That's an application change, which the question asks to avoid.
opts.C: Moving to Lambda changes the compute layer, but the database is what's slow. The read problem stays exactly the same, while the architecture changes the most of any option.
opts.D: Migrating to DynamoDB means rewriting the data model and every query. The maximum architectural change for a requirement of minimal change.

269.key: The cause of the degradation is read-only queries from the analysts. A read replica takes them off the primary: the application keeps working with the primary instance, the analysts connect to the replica, and code changes are minimal.

opts.A: DynamoDB requires rewriting the queries and is a poor fit for ad hoc analytics.
opts.B: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache; arbitrary SQL analytics queries can't be run against it.
opts.D: Redshift would require a separate load pipeline and a constantly running cluster: significantly more change and cost.

270.key: The distinguishing detail is a single word: the data must be encrypted 'before the data is uploaded.' Any server-side encryption (SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, SSE-C) happens only after S3 has already received the object, meaning the data is still in plaintext along the way for anything sitting between the application and S3. Only client-side encryption meets the requirement: the application encrypts the object itself, and only ciphertext arrives at S3. Encryption in transit is provided by TLS, which S3 supports by default and which can be enforced with the aws:SecureTransport condition in a bucket policy.

opts.B: Server-side encryption is performed by the service after it receives the object. The 'encrypt before upload' requirement is not met by definition.
opts.C: A bucket policy only forces the client to request SSE-S3 — the same server-side encryption, just made mandatory. The point at which encryption happens doesn't change.
opts.D: Default bucket encryption with a KMS key is again a server-side scheme: the object is encrypted after it's received.

271.key: The peak is known in advance: the jobs always start at 1 AM, and the required capacity is the same every night. Scheduled scaling raises the needed number of instances ahead of that time, so the hour-long wait disappears, and after the jobs finish the group scales back down through its normal policy.

opts.A: A permanently raised minimum capacity means paying for idle instances around the clock.
opts.B: Maximum capacity only sets a ceiling and has no effect on how fast scaling ramps up.
opts.D: A larger step size speeds up growth, but scaling would still only begin after load appears and is detected.

272.key: The architecture can't be duplicated, so the existing entry point is what needs to be sped up. CloudFront with the load balancer as its origin reduces latency even for dynamic content: TLS terminates at the nearest edge location, and the request travels to the Region over the AWS backbone. Language versions are served correctly once the Accept-Language header is included in the cache key in the cache behavior settings — a separate cached copy is then kept for each language.

opts.A: The site is dynamic, and fully moving it into an S3 bucket would mean rewriting the application — the requirement doesn't call for that.
opts.C: API Gateway with stage-level caching is an extra layer in front of the load balancer that provides neither a global edge network nor a latency benefit for users on other continents.
opts.D: Custom cache servers in every Region are infrastructure that would have to be deployed and maintained — exactly the multi-Region setup the company doesn't want.

273.key: The requirements are: the database in the second Region must be as up to date as possible, and recovery time must be minimized while the infrastructure there runs at reduced capacity but is already up. An Aurora global database replicates data at the storage layer with typically sub-second lag, and a warm standby deployment means everything in the second Region is already running in a scaled-down state and only needs to scale up. This is faster than standing up an environment from scratch.

opts.A: A pilot light deployment implies a shut-down or minimal compute layer that must be deployed during a disaster, giving a higher recovery time than a warm standby.
opts.C: A Multi-AZ configuration operates within a single Region and provides no copy of the data in another Region at all.
opts.D: The same mistake: Multi-AZ is not a cross-Region solution, regardless of the standby mode chosen.

274.key: An RTO of under four hours allows the DR site to stay offline rather than running, and resource usage during normal operations must be minimal. The AMIs are copied to a secondary Region, and the entire infrastructure is described in an AWS CloudFormation template: during a disaster the stack is deployed in a single operation, using a standard mechanism with no custom scripts to maintain.

opts.A: Custom functions and deployment scripts are code that has to be written, tested, and maintained.
opts.C: Instances that run continuously in the second Region directly violate the requirement to minimize resource usage.
opts.D: A second Availability Zone does not protect against a Region-level failure, and it also means machines running continuously.

275.key: The morning slowdown happens because the group only reacts after the load has already appeared. A target tracking policy with a lower CPU utilization threshold starts adding capacity earlier, and a shorter cooldown period lets instances be added more frequently. Costs rise only during the actual period of increased load.

opts.A: Setting the desired capacity to 20 in advance means paying for the peak configuration even when it isn't needed yet.
opts.B: Step scaling would also work, but it adds fixed increments of instances and doesn't hold the target level as precisely as target tracking does.
opts.D: Hard-coding the minimum to 20 instances prevents the group from ever scaling down and makes the solution the most expensive one.

276.key: There are two separate problems here, each solved independently. The database is running out of storage, which is fixed by enabling storage Auto Scaling on the RDS instance so the volume grows as it fills up with no downtime (A). The instances are overloaded, and the Auto Scaling group has no metric configured at all, so a scaling policy based on average CPU utilization is set up so the fleet grows along with traffic (D).

opts.B: Migrating to Aurora would require giving up the Oracle-specific PL/SQL functions that the scenario explicitly states are in use.
opts.C: A low-free-storage-space alarm only notifies about the problem; it doesn't add any storage itself.
opts.E: Free memory isn't a default CloudWatch metric — it would need to be collected via an agent — and as a primary signal of web-tier overload it's a weaker indicator than CPU utilization.

277.key: Video files are write-once, read-during-processing objects, so keeping them in a file system like EFS is expensive. It's cheaper to store the source files and results in S3 and copy just the file being processed onto an EBS volume attached to the instance for the duration of transcoding. This eliminates the ongoing cost of persistent file storage, and S3 costs a fraction of EFS per gigabyte.

opts.A: File Gateway is a hybrid gateway for accessing S3 from an on-premises network. Placing it between cloud instances and a bucket is pointless — it's just an extra layer and extra cost.
opts.B: Volume Gateway solves the same hybrid problem for block volumes and is equally out of place here.
opts.C: Storage still stays in EFS, so the main cost driver doesn't change, and moving the results onto EBS only adds to it.

278.key: Two independent requirements. Storing hierarchical employee data with minimum latency under heavy load points to DynamoDB (B): a partition key and sort key map naturally onto a hierarchy, latency stays in the single-digit milliseconds, and a monthly export to S3 provides material for auditing. Detecting financial information and sending a monthly notification points to Amazon Macie (E): it classifies sensitive data in S3, publishes findings to EventBridge, and from there the notification goes out to subscribers of an SNS topic.

opts.A: Redshift is an analytical warehouse built for complex queries over large volumes, not a source for high-traffic, low-latency point lookups.
opts.C: Sending events to a Lambda function means the email sending and subscription logic would have to be built from scratch. An SNS topic does this with no code.
opts.D: Athena and QuickSight provide analytics and dashboards, but they solve neither the fast-application-query requirement nor the financial-data-detection requirement.

279.key: AWS Backup covers the entire set of requirements with a single plan: a monthly schedule, a lifecycle policy that moves the backup to cold storage after six months, and a seven-year retention period. No scripts and no manual operations.

opts.B: DynamoDB backups cannot be moved into an S3 bucket and managed with lifecycle rules — they are internal objects of the service.
opts.C: Two custom scheduled scripts is the most development and maintenance overhead possible where a ready-made managed service already exists.
opts.D: The on-demand backup command doesn't accept parameters for transitioning to cold storage or for a deletion schedule — that is defined by an AWS Backup plan.

280.key: The CloudFront logs already sit in S3, so the most convenient way to query them is with standard SQL in Amazon Athena, paying only for the bytes scanned. Amazon QuickSight builds the visualizations — it connects to Athena as a data source and lets you assemble dashboards and reports without any infrastructure of your own.

opts.A: AWS Glue is an ETL and data catalog service, not a visualization tool.
opts.C: DynamoDB cannot run SQL queries against objects in S3 — it's a non-relational store with its own API.
opts.D: The same mistake with DynamoDB as the query engine, even though the visualization choice is correct.

281.key: An RPO of under one second means essentially zero data loss, which only synchronous replication can provide. RDS Multi-AZ synchronously writes every transaction to the standby instance in another Availability Zone, so a failover happens with no loss of committed transactions.

opts.B: There is no such thing as automatic instance scaling for an RDS database instance, and a single Availability Zone doesn't protect against that zone failing.
opts.C: Read replicas replicate asynchronously — the lag is measured in seconds and can't guarantee the required recovery point.
opts.D: DMS CDC tasks are also asynchronous and are designed for migration, not for database fault tolerance.

282.key: The requirement is to accept traffic only from the load balancer and from no one else. This is done by referencing a security group: the instances' inbound rule allows traffic only from the ALB's security group. No other source, inside or outside the subnet, can connect.

opts.A: A route from the internet to the instances' private addresses can't be created, and even if it could, it would expose them to the entire world.
opts.C: Moving the instances into the public subnet with Elastic IP addresses does exactly the opposite — it puts them on the internet.
opts.D: Allowing any TCP traffic on any port for the load balancer doesn't restrict access to the instances themselves and weakens the security posture.
