283.key: The root cause is two different protocols: the Linux simulation writes over NFS, the Windows visualization reads over SMB, and the company is stuck maintaining two synchronized copies. Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP is the only AWS file service that serves the same data simultaneously over both NFS and SMB. The applications move to EC2 instances with no code changes, and the duplication goes away.

opts.A: Lambda isn't suited to a long-running simulation or a Windows desktop application, and moving to S3 means rewriting both applications, which the requirements rule out.
opts.B: FSx File Gateway is a hybrid gateway for accessing FSx from an on-premises network, not shared storage with dual-protocol access for workloads inside AWS.
opts.C: SQS passes messages, it doesn't provide a file resource — the applications would have to be rewritten to work with a queue.

284.key: What's needed is a breakdown of costs by consumer for department budget planning, and it needs to be quick. Cost Explorer lets you build a report grouped by cost allocation tags (for example, by owner or department), by linked account, and by service, view it on a chart, and export it to CSV. This is the shortest path — no exports, no SQL, no storage to set up.

opts.A: Athena queries a Cost and Usage Report export, which first has to be enabled, generated, and connected. That's extra steps for a ready-made report.
opts.C: The bill from the billing console dashboard shows totals by service, without the needed grouping by owner and without flexible filtering.
opts.D: AWS Budgets sends alerts when thresholds are crossed and is not a tool for building cost-structure reports.

285.key: With fewer than 100 visits a month, paying for a server that runs continuously makes no sense. The form is handled by a call to API Gateway, backed by a Lambda function that sends the email through Amazon SES. This combination costs nothing while idle, and at a hundred requests a month it stays within the free tier.

opts.A: ECS tasks are billed for time running around the clock, even though there's almost no traffic.
opts.C: A Lightsail instance is a fixed monthly fee, and WorkMail is billed per mailbox.
opts.D: A continuously running instance with a LAMP stack also needs to be maintained — the most expensive and labor-intensive option offered.

286.key: Deployments succeed and the files in the bucket are updated, but users still see the old version — meaning CloudFront is serving from cache. Objects are held at edge locations until their TTL expires, so an invalidation is needed after each deployment, and it's best to build that into the same delivery pipeline.

opts.A: A load balancer distributes traffic across instances, but the site is static and lives in a bucket — that has nothing to do with a stale cache.
opts.B: A cache in front of the database speeds up queries, but it isn't what's serving the stale files — the content delivery network is.
opts.D: Certificate validation is about TLS and has no bearing on content freshness.

287.key: The scenario names SQL Server features that a managed service doesn't offer: native engine backups and Data Quality Services. So the database has to stay on an EC2 instance. Shared file exchange between tiers in a Windows environment is provided by Amazon FSx for Windows File Server — an SMB share with Windows ACLs, accessible from all three tiers.

opts.A: FSx File Gateway is meant for accessing FSx file systems from an on-premises network, but all the tiers are already in AWS — it would just be an unnecessary intermediary.
opts.C: RDS for SQL Server supports neither native backups the way the company uses them nor Data Quality Services — a direct violation of the requirements.
opts.D: Same problem with RDS, plus an EBS volume isn't a shared file resource that multiple instances can use.

288.key: Shared file access for a group of Linux servers with no application changes is Amazon EFS. The file system is mounted over NFS on all the web servers across all Availability Zones, the application keeps working with ordinary paths and files, and the storage scales itself.

opts.A: S3 is object storage, accessed through an API. To use it, the application would have to be rewritten, which the requirements rule out.
opts.B: CloudFront in front of S3 speeds up delivery of static content, but it still doesn't give the servers a shared file system.
opts.D: An EBS volume attaches within a single Availability Zone, and a regular file system on it isn't designed for simultaneous writes from multiple servers.

289.key: The correct way to grant permissions to any compute resource in AWS is a role. The Lambda function gets an execution role, and an IAM policy attached to that role grants s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket on the specific bucket and, if needed, a specific prefix. The credentials involved are temporary: they're issued by STS, refresh automatically, and are never stored anywhere. The key phrase in the question is 'MOST secure manner' — between a role scoped to one bucket and a role scoped to all buckets, the former is chosen because least privilege applies even within a single account.

opts.A: A bucket policy describes who is allowed to access the resource, but the function still needs its own identity and permissions. Within a single account this is normally handled with a role, not by opening up the bucket.
opts.C: An access key embedded in the function's code is a long-lived secret sitting in the repository and the deployment package, and it can't be rotated automatically. The worst option offered.
opts.D: The role is the right approach, but the permissions are granted on every bucket in the account. That violates least privilege, and the question asks for the most secure option.

290.key: The company doesn't want a long-term commitment, so Reserved Instances and Savings Plans are out. That leaves a mixed group: a baseline on On-Demand Instances to guarantee availability, plus additional capacity for spikes on interruptible Spot Instances at up to a 90 percent discount.

opts.A: Dedicated Instances are the most expensive option and are only needed when there's a hardware-isolation requirement.
opts.B: On-Demand Instances alone don't provide any savings beyond the base price.
opts.D: Reserved Instances are exactly the one- or three-year commitment the company wants to avoid.

291.key: The scenario hides two separate user constraints, and each is solved by its own CloudFront mechanism. A client that doesn't support cookies can't work with signed cookies — for that user, a signed URL fits, since the signature lives in the link itself. Users whose URL is hardcoded and can't be changed can't switch to a signed URL — for them, signed cookies fit instead, because the address stays the same while the signature arrives in the Cookie header. So both mechanisms belong in the answer: each serves its own group with the least impact on users.

opts.C: AWS AppSync is a managed GraphQL API service. It has nothing to do with restricting access to content in CloudFront.
opts.D: A JWT by itself isn't an authorization mechanism in CloudFront — validating such a token would require writing a Lambda@Edge function. That's development work, not 'least impact.'
opts.E: Secrets Manager stores application secrets. It doesn't manage viewer access to video files.

292.key: Three things are required: ingesting streaming data, transforming it before it's written, and being able to query the result with SQL. Both working combinations end in S3 and Athena. The first: Kinesis Data Streams ingests the stream, Kinesis Data Analytics transforms it on the fly, and Firehose delivers the result to S3 (A). The second: Amazon MSK ingests the stream, and AWS Glue performs the transformation and writes to S3 (B).

opts.C: DMS migrates data out of databases — it doesn't ingest real-time streams from multiple sources.
opts.D: Data in S3 cannot be queried through the Amazon RDS query editor — that tool works against the database itself.
opts.E: The same mistake with the RDS query editor, which cannot reach objects in S3.

293.key: The key requirement is preserving local access to all the data, not just part of it. That's exactly what Storage Gateway does in stored volume mode: the complete dataset stays on local disks, while snapshots go up to S3 asynchronously and encrypted. Backup becomes automatic, and access latency stays local.

opts.A: Snowball is a one-time transport device — it has no persistent S3 endpoint to mount and doesn't provide automatic, ongoing uploads.
opts.B: Snowball Edge is also meant for a one-time transfer and isn't a persistent backup solution.
opts.C: Cached volume mode keeps only a portion of the data locally, but the requirement calls for local access to the entire volume.

294.key: There's one requirement: traffic must not cross the internet. For S3, that's a gateway VPC endpoint — a route to the service prefix is added to the VPC's route tables, traffic stays within the AWS network, and there's no charge for the endpoint itself. On top of that, the bucket can be locked down with an aws:SourceVpce condition so it only accepts requests through this endpoint. The same technique is covered in {{q:91,480,710}}.

opts.A: A Route 53 private hosted zone handles name resolution within the VPC and has no effect on the route to S3.
opts.C: A NAT gateway is a path out to the internet — it directly violates the requirement, and it also charges for processed traffic.
opts.D: A Site-to-Site VPN connects a VPC to an external network, not to the S3 service — no such construct exists.

295.key: It's the same data, but different applications need different views of it. S3 Object Lambda lets you attach a function to an access point: it transforms the object on the fly as it's returned, so two applications get a version with the personal data removed while the third gets the original. No extra copies of the data appear, and all the logic fits in a single function.

opts.A: A custom proxy layer is an application that has to be written, scaled, and maintained.
opts.C: Three copies of terabytes of data mean triple the storage cost and constant synchronization.
opts.D: The same idea, but in DynamoDB, where storing terabytes is even more expensive and requires rewriting how the data is accessed.

296.key: Two constraints apply. Peered VPC address ranges must not overlap, so 192.168.0.0/24 and anything within it are out. And the smallest allowed VPC block size is /28, so a /32 mask is never valid at all. Of the options given, only 10.0.1.0/24 is left.

opts.A: A /32 mask designates a single address — a VPC can't be created with that block; the minimum is /28.
opts.B: This block matches the existing network's block exactly, and overlapping address ranges make peering impossible.
opts.C: Again a /32 mask, which is invalid for a VPC, and the address also falls within the neighboring network's range.

297.key: The instances already exist and the load balancer and target group are already configured — what's needed is automatic scaling without overpaying. An Auto Scaling group is created that uses the same load balancer and the same target group, with a target tracking policy based on average CPU utilization: capacity grows during a spike up to 65 percent and shrinks back down to the minimum during quiet periods.

opts.A: A custom function that terminates instances on a signal can't scale up and bypasses the standard scaling mechanisms.
opts.C: A group with no scaling policy simply holds a fixed instance count and doesn't react to spikes.
opts.D: Manually changing the instance count after receiving an email isn't automation — and automation is what's required.

298.key: A subnet in AWS always belongs to exactly one Availability Zone, so there's no such thing as a subnet that 'spans' multiple zones. The correct approach: one subnet per Availability Zone, the Auto Scaling group spreads the instances across both, and the database is switched to a Multi-AZ deployment with synchronous replication and automatic failover.

opts.A: The subnets are set up correctly, but the database still stays in a single zone — 'connections to each network' doesn't add fault tolerance to it.
opts.B: A subnet cannot span two Availability Zones, and the database again remains a single point of failure.
opts.D: The same spanning-subnet mistake, even though the database is configured correctly.

299.key: Hard numbers are specified: sub-millisecond latency and at least 6 GBps of throughput while hundreds of Linux instances are working. That profile matches Amazon FSx for Lustre on persistent SSD storage — it's the only option that delivers those numbers. The source data lives in S3 and is linked to the file system through import/export, which is convenient both for loading data and for saving results.

opts.A: FSx for NetApp ONTAP is a general-purpose file service — it isn't built for gigabyte-per-second throughput to hundreds of clients, and its tiering policy would also push data down to a slower storage tier.
opts.C: Persistent storage on HDD disks can't deliver sub-millisecond latency: mechanical disks are inherently slower.
opts.D: Turning off tiering removes one problem, but ONTAP's performance still doesn't reach the required numbers.

300.key: The application runs continuously around the clock, and the database storage keeps growing over time. For steady, constant load, Reserved Instances are the cheapest option — a discount of up to three-quarters off the On-Demand price. Aurora also expands its storage automatically, so the growing volume needs no manual intervention, and Aurora Reserved Instances lower the cost of the data layer as well.

opts.A: AWS can reclaim Spot Instances at any time — unacceptable for an application that must run around the clock — and S3 doesn't replace a relational database.
opts.B: On-Demand RDS instances are billed at the full rate, even though the load is constant and predictable.
opts.D: Here it's the opposite: the discount applies to the database, but the largest layer — the application — is billed at the full rate.

301.key: Thirty terabytes over a gigabit link takes roughly three days at full utilization, so hitting the five-day window is possible as long as the link isn't fully occupied by other traffic. The main requirement is controlling the bandwidth used, and that's exactly what AWS DataSync provides: a task can have a bandwidth limit set on it, and it transfers data over parallel streams with integrity checks and can write directly into FSx for Windows File Server.

opts.A: Snowcone only holds a few terabytes — 30 TB would require multiple devices, and shipping time would eat into the deadline.
opts.B: FSx File Gateway provides ongoing access to a file system from an on-premises network, but it isn't a one-time migration tool with bandwidth control.
opts.D: AWS Transfer Family provides SFTP, FTPS, and FTP over S3 and EFS — it offers neither bulk migration with bandwidth limiting nor writes into FSx.

302.key: There are two separate problems, each solved on its own. The files are too large in their raw form — they need to be transcoded into formats and bitrates suited to mobile devices, which is what the managed Amazon Elastic Transcoder does (C). Latency and buffering for users around the world are addressed with edge caching, meaning a CloudFront distribution placed in front of the bucket (A).

opts.B: Copying files to buckets in other Regions increases storage costs and requires its own routing logic, while a CDN cache achieves the same effect more cheaply.
opts.D: A custom fleet of instances in Local Zones for content delivery is infrastructure that has to be maintained, instead of using a ready-made delivery network.
opts.E: Transcoding on self-managed instances means managing a fleet and queues instead of using a managed transcoding service.

303.key: The tasks run on Fargate, so there are no instances to scale at all. The number of service tasks is controlled by AWS Application Auto Scaling: a target tracking policy holds a set CPU or memory utilization level, adding tasks at the peak and removing them during a lull — automatically cutting costs.

opts.A: EC2 Auto Scaling manages instances, which don't exist with the Fargate launch type, and scaling based on past patterns doesn't respond to actual load.
opts.B: A custom function that resizes the service based on signals is code that has to be written and maintained, whereas a built-in policy does the same thing.
opts.C: Again, scaling EC2 instances, which don't exist in this architecture.

304.key: Periodic, bidirectional transfer of large volumes between NFS file systems in two Regions is a textbook AWS DataSync task. It works between storage locations within AWS, runs on a schedule, transfers only the changes, verifies integrity, and requires no servers or scripts.

opts.B: Snowball devices are meant for a one-time transfer over a weak link, not for regular synchronization between AWS Regions.
opts.C: A self-managed SFTP server on an instance is a machine and scripts that would have to be maintained.
opts.D: DMS migrates database data, not file system contents.

305.key: The requirements are simple and specific: SMB access and a fully managed solution. That's Amazon FSx for Windows File Server — a file system with native SMB, Windows ACL support, and Active Directory integration, all managed by AWS. For the exam: SMB maps to FSx for Windows, NFS maps to EFS, object access via API maps to S3, and a self-managed file server on EC2 violates the 'fully managed' requirement.

opts.A: DataSync moves data between storage locations and doesn't provide a mountable file system.
opts.B: A file server on a Windows instance would have to be patched, backed up, and scaled manually. The managed-service requirement is violated.
opts.D: S3 is object storage and doesn't support SMB. A bucket can only be mounted with third-party tools, and without full file semantics.

306.key: The goal is maximum network throughput, minimum latency, and minimum data transfer charges. All of this comes from placing the instances in a single Availability Zone within a cluster placement group: the machines end up close together on the same network segment, and traffic within a zone between private addresses isn't charged.

opts.B: Different Availability Zones mean cross-AZ data transfer charges and higher latency, and the partition strategy is designed for spreading instances across racks for fault tolerance.
opts.C: Spreading across zones again introduces cross-AZ traffic, and scaling based on network utilization doesn't address the latency requirement.
opts.D: The same cross-AZ charge problem, and step scaling has nothing to do with network performance.

307.key: Two words determine the answer. iSCSI means block-level access, so a Volume Gateway is needed: S3 File Gateway serves files over NFS and SMB, and Tape Gateway emulates a tape library. "Only its recently accessed data to remain stored locally" points to the volume mode: in cached volumes, the primary dataset lives in AWS while the on-premises side keeps a cache of the hot blocks, so there's no need to grow local capacity. Stored volumes work the opposite way — the full copy is kept locally, and only snapshots go to AWS.

opts.A: S3 File Gateway provides file access over NFS and SMB. It does not suit an application that works over iSCSI.
opts.B: Tape Gateway is a virtual tape library for backups. It is not storage for an application's day-to-day operation.
opts.C: Stored volumes keep a full copy of the data on premises, so the need for local capacity stays the same. The requirement to "minimize the need to scale local storage" is not met.

308.key: The instances run continuously for 90 days, so the savings come from moving to Reserved Instances, which is exactly what the Trusted Advisor "Amazon RDS Reserved Instance Optimization" check flags (C). You need to view it in the consolidated billing account (B): RI recommendations are calculated across the whole organization at once, not per individual account.

opts.A: Recommendations from the account where the instances run would have to be collected account by account, and purchasing RIs that way wouldn't account for the organization's combined usage.
opts.D: The "Idle DB Instances" check looks for databases with no connections over the past several days. The question explicitly states the instances are active, so this check won't flag them. This was the error in the dump's answer key.
opts.E: The Redshift Reserved Node check applies to a different service and has nothing to do with RDS.

309.key: S3 Storage Lens is a built-in storage analytics dashboard: it shows size and object count across all buckets, and — with advanced activity metrics turned on — access frequency as well. Nothing needs to be configured or analyzed manually.

opts.B: The standard S3 console shows bucket contents, but not summarized access statistics.
opts.C: The bucket size metric reflects volume, not access frequency, and requires its own analysis.
opts.D: Enabling object-level event logging in CloudTrail sharply increases log volume and requires writing your own queries — considerably more operational overhead.

310.key: The cost comes from data transferred out of S3 to customers in North America and Europe. Putting CloudFront in front of the bucket reduces cost (CloudFront's data transfer out rate is lower than S3's direct rate) while also bringing the files closer to users. Access control then shifts to CloudFront signed URLs — S3 signed URLs don't apply once requests go through the distribution.

opts.A: Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads into the bucket and is billed as an add-on: costs would increase, not decrease.
opts.C: A second bucket with Cross-Region Replication doubles the storage cost for these large datasets and adds a charge for the replication itself.
opts.D: Proxying the data through the company's own application loads the instances, keeps the same amount of outbound traffic, and adds development work.

311.key: Requests must be separated by type, must never be lost, and must be handled within 24 hours with minimal operational overhead. A single SNS topic with message filtering routes each message to its own SQS queue based on the type attribute, and each group of backend servers reads only its own queue. The queue retains messages for up to 14 days, so nothing gets lost.

opts.A: Multiple Kinesis streams require managing shards and writing custom code on top of the KCL — more operational overhead.
opts.B: An SNS topic with a subscriber function doesn't store messages: if processing fails, the request is lost.
opts.D: Firehose and an OpenSearch cluster form an analytics pipeline, not a task queue; searching an index for messages as a way to process them is highly impractical.

312.key: Both the instance configuration and the data on every attached volume need to be backed up, and recovery needs to happen in a different Region. AWS Backup can treat an EC2 instance as a single resource: the backup includes the machine image plus all attached volumes. A plan with a nightly schedule and a cross-Region copy rule is configured once.

opts.A: A custom snapshot function means code, schedules, and error handling that you have to maintain, and it still doesn't preserve the instance configuration.
opts.C: If only the volumes are added to the plan, the instance configuration isn't backed up: you won't be able to restore the machine as a whole.
opts.D: Copying to a different Availability Zone doesn't protect against a Region-level failure, and a custom function again means extra operational overhead.

313.key: Millions of mobile users plus the requirement to allow only authorized users points to CloudFront with signed URLs. After verifying the user's entitlement, the application issues a signed URL with a limited lifetime (optionally tied to an IP address), content is served from the nearest edge location, and the bucket is locked down to direct access using origin access control. Scaling then becomes the CDN's job, not yours.

opts.A: A public bucket means access for everyone, which contradicts the "authorized users" requirement. KMS keys, moreover, don't "stream" anything — that's an encryption key management service.
opts.B: An IPsec VPN to a mobile app running on millions of devices is infeasible both technically and organizationally, and it doesn't solve the problem of delivering video.
opts.D: Client VPN is designed for connecting employees to a corporate network, not for publicly delivering content to millions of viewers. Its cost and complexity are out of proportion to the task.

314.key: The key phrase is "without selecting a particular instance type." That's exactly what Aurora Serverless for MySQL provides: capacity is defined as a range of ACUs and scales automatically, including as new users arrive. Access is infrequent, so you pay little during quiet periods, and MySQL compatibility keeps the application unchanged.

opts.A: A standard Aurora cluster requires choosing an instance class — a direct contradiction of the requirement.
opts.C: Redshift Spectrum reads data in S3 for analytics and is not a transactional MySQL database.
opts.D: RDS for MySQL also requires choosing an instance class and manual resizing as load grows.

315.key: The requirement is active scanning for vulnerabilities on the instances plus a report of the findings — that's Amazon Inspector. It runs continuous scanning through the SSM agent, matches installed packages against the CVE database, assesses network reachability of each vulnerability, and produces prioritized findings that can be exported and distributed. The distinction to remember: Inspector finds vulnerabilities, GuardDuty finds signs of compromise, Macie finds sensitive data, and Shield defends against DDoS.

opts.A: AWS Shield protects against availability attacks and performs no scanning at all.
opts.B: Macie looks for sensitive data in S3, not vulnerabilities in instance software.
opts.C: GuardDuty detects suspicious activity and signs of compromise, but it doesn't produce a list of vulnerable packages.

316.key: The script only polls the queue and processes messages, yet the instance is billed around the clock. A Lambda function with SQS as its event source runs only when messages arrive, scales automatically as their number grows, and is billed only for execution time.

opts.A: A larger instance speeds up processing, but costs would go up, not down.
opts.B: Turning the instance off on a schedule leaves messages unprocessed during that window and requires its own automation.
opts.D: Run Command runs the script on demand, but the instance still has to exist and be paid for.

317.key: The application can only work with Redshift and S3, but the data arrives as CSV. A scheduled AWS Glue job reads the files, transforms them, and loads them into Redshift — a ready-made ETL tool with no custom code and no cluster management.

opts.B: A custom script on EC2 instances means development and maintenance, and .sql files still wouldn't suit the application anyway.
opts.C: DynamoDB isn't among the data sources the application understands: it can't run SQL queries against it.
opts.D: A weekly EMR cluster means both added latency and node management, plus higher cost.

318.key: There are two separate requirements, met by two separate services. AWS CloudTrail records who called which API and when — for example, who launched an oversized instance or changed a security group rule (A). AWS Config tracks the configuration history of resources and lets you define compliance rules that flag violations — for example, disallowed instance types or overly permissive rules (D).

opts.B: Data lifecycle policies manage snapshots and images, not change auditing.
opts.C: Trusted Advisor gives general recommendations about account configuration, but it doesn't keep a change history or enforce compliance rules.
opts.E: CloudFormation can deploy infrastructure, but it isn't a tool for auditing or rolling back arbitrary changes.

319.key: Shared SSH keys need to be removed while access is preserved. Session Manager achieves this without a single key and without open ports: an agent on the instance initiates an outbound connection to the service, permissions are described through IAM policies, actions are attributed to individual users, and sessions are logged to CloudWatch Logs or S3. The instance just needs a role with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore. Administrative overhead is minimal: no bastions, no key distribution, no address lists.

opts.B: STS issues temporary AWS credentials, not SSH keys. No such mechanism exists.
opts.C: Bastions with shared keys don't solve the problem: shared keys remain, there are just fewer of them.
opts.D: Combining Cognito with a custom key-generation function is a homegrown system built around keys — the very thing the company asked to eliminate.

320.key: The problem is that data is lost the moment the instance reboots, because it lives only in the instance's memory and on its disk. Kinesis Data Streams accepts records and stores them in the stream independently of consumer state, so a restart loses nothing, and Kinesis Data Analytics lets you query the data in near real time.

opts.B: Firehose buffers data and delivers it to Redshift with a delay of tens of seconds or more: that's no longer near-real time, and the buffer itself can also be lost if the source fails.
opts.C: Storing ingested data in an instance store keeps the original problem intact: everything disappears when the instance reboots.
opts.D: An EBS volume and a Redis channel form a homegrown setup with no delivery guarantees and no convenient way to query the ingested data.

321.key: You need to guarantee that an unencrypted object simply never lands in the bucket, rather than fix things after the fact. That's done with a bucket policy that explicitly denies s3:PutObject when the request lacks the x-amz-server-side-encryption header (or when its value isn't the one required — for example, not aws:kms). This Deny fires before the write: the client gets AccessDenied and must retry the request with encryption. Also remember the distinction: default encryption encrypts everything that arrives, while a Deny policy specifically forces the client to request encryption explicitly.

opts.A: The x-amz-acl header sets the object's access control list. It has nothing to do with encryption.
opts.B: Same issue: a value of private restricts who can see the object, but the object could still be written unencrypted.
opts.C: The aws:SecureTransport condition requires TLS, i.e., encryption in transit. Data would arrive over a secure connection and still be written to disk unencrypted — the question is about encryption at rest.

322.key: The user needs an immediate response, while thumbnail generation can take up to a minute. An SQS queue solves this: the application places a message about the new image and immediately confirms the upload, while processors generate the thumbnail asynchronously, at their own pace, with a guarantee that the task won't be lost.

opts.A: A function that both generates the thumbnail and notifies the user leaves a sixty-second wait on the response path.
opts.B: Step Functions orchestrates the steps, but the user notification is still tied to the completion of generation, and the design is more complex.
opts.D: SNS doesn't store messages: if a subscriber fails, the thumbnail-generation task is lost.

323.key: The readers send messages over HTTPS, so a managed HTTPS endpoint and a serverless processor are needed. API Gateway accepts the requests and invokes a Lambda function, which parses the message and writes the result to DynamoDB — all three components are highly available by default, scale on their own, and require no administration. The data in DynamoDB is available to the security team for analysis, if needed via export to S3 and Athena.

opts.A: A single EC2 instance is a single point of failure that requires patching, scaling, and monitoring. The high-availability requirement isn't met.
opts.C: Route 53 doesn't invoke Lambda functions: it's a DNS service. An HTTP endpoint, such as API Gateway, is needed between the client and the function.
opts.D: The readers send HTTPS requests, not files written to a bucket, and building a VPN to the building for this purpose is overkill.

324.key: End users must retain immediate access to all file types without latency, and changes to existing infrastructure must be minimal. Volume Gateway in stored volumes mode connects to the existing file server over the same iSCSI protocol, the full dataset stays on local disks, and scheduled snapshots go to AWS. In a disaster, a snapshot is restored to an EBS volume and attached to an instance.

opts.A: This involves both switching the protocol to NFS and modifying applications — a direct violation of the minimal-change requirement.
opts.B: Tape Gateway is designed for backup to a virtual tape library and doesn't provide immediate local access to files.
opts.C: Cached volumes mode keeps only 10 TB of cache locally out of hundreds of terabytes: access to the rest of the data would go to the cloud with noticeable latency.

325.key: A Cognito token by itself doesn't grant any AWS permissions. The flow works like this: the user authenticates in the user pool and receives a JWT, that token is then exchanged in the identity pool for temporary IAM role credentials, and it's that role that grants s3:GetObject on the protected bucket. An access error means the identity pool's role for authenticated users isn't configured (or is configured incorrectly). Keep the distinction in mind: the user pool handles "who this is," and the identity pool handles "what AWS permissions to give them."

opts.B: ACLs are a legacy S3 mechanism and can't grant permissions based on Cognito authentication results. The modern approach is a bucket policy plus a user role.
opts.C: S3 has long provided strong read-after-write consistency, and consistency has nothing to do with access errors.
opts.D: Custom attribute mapping helps pass along user information, but by itself it doesn't grant any AWS permissions: permissions come from the role that the identity pool issues.

326.key: There are two independent cost items here. The first is the objects themselves: after 30 days access becomes rare but "inconsistent," i.e. unpredictable, which calls for Intelligent-Tiering (A) rather than a class that bills for retrieval. The second is incomplete multipart uploads (B): with parallel multipart uploads, parts of aborted operations remain in the bucket, aren't visible in the object listing, and are still billed as storage until a Lifecycle rule ("AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload") removes them. For large assets this invisible line item can sometimes account for a noticeable share of the bill.

opts.C: Cleaning up expired delete markers matters in a versioned bucket. The scenario describes overwriting objects, and a delete marker itself takes up zero storage — there's no savings here.
opts.D: Standard-IA charges a retrieval fee, and access after 30 days is described as inconsistent. Every unexpected access costs money, so Intelligent-Tiering is more cost-effective here.
opts.E: One Zone-IA stores a single copy in one Availability Zone, and the question requires maintaining high availability and fault tolerance.

327.key: The restriction is stated in terms of domain names ("the third party's URL"), and security groups and network ACLs only work with addresses and ports. AWS Network Firewall can distinguish domains: a stateful rule with a domain list allows traffic to the listed names and blocks everything else, and the private subnet's traffic is routed through the firewall endpoint via the route table. This is the standard way to build a domain-based egress filter.

opts.B: AWS WAF protects inbound HTTP requests to your applications and doesn't filter outbound instance traffic.
opts.C: Security group rules can't specify a URL or domain name — only CIDR blocks, prefix lists, and other security groups.
opts.D: A load balancer distributes inbound requests to your targets. Outbound internet traffic isn't routed through it.

328.key: A sharp, sudden surge is expected, and every order must be processed. CloudFront takes the static content off the instances, and purchase requests are accepted into an SQS queue: the queue accepts them instantly and holds them until the processors work through them. This way no request is lost, even if the instances temporarily can't keep up.

opts.A: Manually adding instances can't keep up with a sudden spike, and caching dynamic content through CloudFront provides little benefit.
opts.B: An Auto Scaling group based on network traffic takes minutes to grow, and requests that arrived earlier would still be dropped during the overload.
opts.C: A cache in front of the load balancer doesn't help with writing orders, and CloudFront for dynamic content doesn't solve the problem of preserving them.

329.key: There are two requirements here, met by two different services. Vulnerability scanning is Amazon Inspector: continuous scanning of packages on the instances via the SSM agent, with prioritized findings. Regularly applying updates and reporting patch status is Patch Manager, part of Systems Manager: patch baselines, maintenance windows, and a compliance report per instance. Both parts are managed, with no custom code required.

opts.A: Macie analyzes data in S3, and a cron job on every instance is a manual scheme with no reporting or compliance tracking.
opts.B: GuardDuty doesn't scan packages for vulnerabilities, and Session Manager provides access to an instance but doesn't manage patching.
opts.C: Amazon Detective helps investigate incidents from logs rather than find vulnerabilities, and an EventBridge schedule by itself doesn't apply any patches.

330.key: Encryption at rest in RDS is turned on when the instance is created (or when restoring from an encrypted snapshot copy) and relies on a KMS key — either your own customer managed key or the AWS default key. This simultaneously encrypts the data on disk, automated backups, snapshots, and read replicas. Don't confuse this with encryption in transit — that's handled by a TLS connection to the database, which is a separate matter.

opts.B: Secrets Manager stores secrets, such as database passwords. It doesn't provide keys for encrypting RDS storage — that's KMS's job.
opts.C: A certificate from ACM provides encryption for the connection, i.e., protection of data in transit. It doesn't encrypt the data on disk.
opts.D: Same issue, plus the IAM certificate store is a legacy mechanism that has since been replaced by ACM.

331.key: This is solved with arithmetic. The available bandwidth is 70% of 15 Mbps, or about 10.5 Mbps, which works out to roughly 113 GB per day. At that rate, twenty terabytes would take about 180 days, but the deadline is 30. Any online method fails on time regardless of how convenient it is, so what's left is offline delivery: Snowball. Keep this rule of thumb in mind: 100 Mbps ≈ 1 TB per day, 1 Gbps ≈ 10 TB per day — enough to rule out online options in ten seconds.

opts.B: DataSync transfers data over the same link. It speeds up and verifies the transfer, but it doesn't change the underlying physics of 10.5 Mbps.
opts.C: A VPN is the same link plus the overhead of encryption. The deadline is even less achievable.
opts.D: Transfer Acceleration optimizes the route from an edge location to the bucket, but the bottleneck here is the data center's own uplink, which the acceleration can't reach.

332.key: The files sit on a Windows share with domain-based permissions, space is running out, and employees work remotely. Migrating to FSx for Windows File Server preserves the familiar SMB protocol and NTFS permissions, integrating with the existing Active Directory preserves the same authorization, and Client VPN gives remote employees a secure channel into the VPC where the file system lives. Downloads then go over the encrypted tunnel rather than the open internet.

opts.A: A file server in a public subnet with an IP-based filter for employees means SMB exposed to the internet and manually maintaining an address list. It's both insecure and inconvenient for remote work.
opts.C: A private endpoint is reachable only from inside the VPC, and employees work from outside it, so they wouldn't be able to reach it. Moving to object storage also changes how people are used to working with files.
opts.D: A "public VPC endpoint" doesn't exist. And signing in through Identity Center doesn't solve the problem of securely delivering files to devices.

333.key: The spike is known in advance: midnight on the first of every month. That means the instances need to be scaled up before it starts, not reactively. A scheduled scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group ramps up capacity ahead of the known time and scales back down afterward, so CPU utilization never gets pinned at a hundred percent.

opts.A: CloudFront caches content for users, while the load is generated by a batch calculation inside the application.
opts.B: A simple CPU-based scaling policy triggers only after utilization has already hit a hundred percent: the application will be unavailable for the few minutes it takes new instances to launch.
opts.D: A cache offloads read traffic, but the peak load here comes from a computational task, not from data requests.

334.key: There's an SFTP client that can't be changed, and a local Active Directory where the users live. AWS Transfer Family provides a managed SFTP endpoint directly on top of an S3 bucket and can authenticate users against an external directory, including Active Directory via AWS Managed Microsoft AD or a custom identity provider. The application keeps working over SFTP, with no infrastructure to run underneath it.

opts.B: AWS DMS migrates databases. It provides neither SFTP nor file synchronization.
opts.C: DataSync copies data on a schedule, but it doesn't give the client an SFTP endpoint for downloading files.
opts.D: A custom SFTP server on a Windows instance is a machine that has to be maintained, patched, and scaled. A managed service does the same thing without a server.

335.key: Startup latency when launching an instance from an image happens because the root volume's blocks are pulled from the snapshot on first access. Fast snapshot restore eliminates exactly that: volumes created from a snapshot with the feature enabled run at full performance immediately. An AMI is created from such a snapshot, and the Auto Scaling group is switched over to it.

opts.A: Registering an image from a snapshot by itself doesn't speed up initialization, and Step Functions only orchestrates the steps.
opts.C: Amazon DLM automates scheduled image creation, but it doesn't affect how fast the first launch is.
opts.D: AWS Backup manages backups, and Auto Scaling group capacity limits aren't an EventBridge event source.

336.key: The requirement is to encrypt database credentials and rotate them every 14 days with the least operational effort. Secrets Manager does both through configuration: the secret is encrypted with a KMS key, associated with the Aurora cluster, and the rotation schedule is set to any number of days — 14 is set as a custom period. AWS itself provides the rotation function for supported databases, so there's no need to write one. Every other option proposes building the same result out of custom code.

opts.B: Parameter Store stores the password encrypted, but rotation would have to be implemented and maintained in a Lambda function yourself. That's noticeably more work than setting a rotation period in Secrets Manager.
opts.C: A file on a shared file system plus a custom rotation function adds development effort, file access permissions to manage, and the risk of the database and file getting out of sync.
opts.D: Downloading the password file from the bucket "regularly" means there's a window in which the application uses a stale password, and again, custom rotation code.

337.key: Replica lag in RDS for MySQL grows under load because replication goes through the binary log and is applied on each replica independently. Aurora works differently: replicas read from the same shared storage, so lag is measured in milliseconds and is almost independent of load. Aurora Auto Scaling adds replicas as traffic grows, and stored procedures are replaced with native Aurora MySQL functions — the application changes minimally.

opts.B: A cache in front of the database requires reworking the application's logic and doesn't reduce lag on the replicas themselves.
opts.C: Self-managed MySQL instances mean the most operational overhead, while the replication mechanism stays the same, with the same lag.
opts.D: DynamoDB means rewriting the data model and the queries, and DynamoDB streams don't replace stored procedures.

338.key: This is a disputed question. The dump's answer key is option D: an Aurora global database replicates data to the second Region at the storage level with about a one-second lag, and at least one instance is kept there so the Region is ready to take on load. A strong alternative is option B, a headless configuration: AWS explicitly documents a secondary cluster with no instances, which is cheaper because you only pay for storage and replication. Read literally, "most cost-effective" favors B; read as "the disaster recovery plan must be ready to work immediately," D wins.

opts.A: MySQL binary log replication as a way to replicate Aurora across Regions is slower and requires manual upkeep, whereas a global database does this at the storage level.
opts.B: Technically this configuration is valid and cheaper than the key's answer, which is why the question is flagged as disputed: the only objection to it is that a Region with no instance won't accept traffic immediately after a disaster.
opts.C: DMS is a migration tool, not Aurora's standard mechanism for ongoing cross-Region replication: an extra component that can itself fail.

339.key: The constraint in the wording is "with the least amount of programming effort." Secrets Manager for RDS MySQL supports rotation out of the box: you turn on a schedule, and AWS provides the function that changes the password in the database and updates the secret. The application is left with a single GetSecretValue call instead of hardcoded credentials. This is exactly what distinguishes the correct option from the similar one where you're asked to write that same rotation yourself.

opts.A: KMS manages encryption keys, not database credentials. You can't load a username and password from it.
opts.B: The design is valid, but writing a custom rotation function is exactly the programming effort the question asked to avoid: it has to be written, tested, and maintained.
opts.D: Parameter Store has no built-in rotation mechanism, so "setting up a rotation schedule through Parameter Store" isn't possible.

340.key: SQL injection is an attack at the HTTP request level, and it's filtered by AWS WAF in front of the application. A web ACL is attached to the Application Load Balancer, managed rule groups are enabled (in particular the SQL database rule set), and malicious requests are blocked before they reach the instances. This is a compensating control: in parallel, the code should be fixed to use parameterized queries, but the question's requirement is satisfied specifically by WAF.

opts.B: An ALB listener rule routes by path, host, headers, and method, but it doesn't inspect the request content for signs of injection.
opts.C: Shield Advanced defends against availability attacks and doesn't parse SQL injection.
opts.D: Inspector finds vulnerabilities and reports on them, but it doesn't filter traffic or block anything.

341.key: The key requirement is column-level access control with the least operational overhead. Lake Formation does exactly this: it maintains a catalog, grants permissions at the table, column, and row level, and propagates them to the engines that query it — primarily Athena. So data from Aurora is ingested into the lake through a Lake Formation blueprint, column-level permissions are configured there, and QuickSight connects through Athena and automatically sees only the permitted columns. No bucket policies, no separate datasets per team.

opts.A: EMR for data ingestion is heavy machinery, and it doesn't provide column-level access control — you would have to manually prepare separate extracts.
opts.B: An IAM policy can't restrict access to individual columns within S3 files — its granularity is objects and prefixes.
opts.C: A bucket policy is even less able to distinguish columns within objects. On top of that, Glue Elastic Views is a service that never reached general availability.

342.key: The jobs run weekly, the baseline load is known (at least 60 percent), and there is no one to analyze the patterns manually. Predictive scaling does this automatically: it builds a forecast from the metric's history and pre-launches instances ahead of time, with the pre-launch lead time set explicitly — here, 30 minutes before the jobs start.

opts.A: A dynamic scaling policy reacts only after the load appears: it can't give you 30 minutes of lead time.
opts.B: Scheduled scaling works, but it requires someone to determine and maintain the required capacity manually, and the scenario states there are no resources for that analysis.
opts.D: A custom function triggered by an alarm is both extra code and a reaction after the fact, not proactive scale-out.

343.key: The disaster recovery design must span multiple AWS Regions with the least operational overhead. Aurora Global Database does this natively: the primary DB cluster runs in the primary Region, the secondary cluster runs in the DR Region, replication happens at the storage layer with typically sub-second lag, and promoting the secondary cluster is a single operation. The self-managed MySQL setup, along with all its operational burden, goes away entirely.

opts.A: Self-managed instances with manually configured replication mean the most work and the most risk, and failover is manual too.
opts.B: Multi-AZ configuration and read replicas in different Availability Zones operate within a single Region: the multi-Region requirement isn't met.
opts.D: Restoring from a backup stored in a bucket takes hours and requires manual steps, and the data lags by the interval between backups.

344.key: The 256 KB limit is a hard limit of the SQS service itself and can't be changed. The standard workaround is the Amazon SQS Extended Client Library for Java: the body of a large message is stored in S3, and only a reference to the object goes through the queue, with the library handling this transparently. The application code changes minimally — you just swap in the extended client.

opts.B: EventBridge has its own 256 KB event size limit, so it doesn't solve the problem, and it would mean changing the entire messaging model.
opts.C: The 256 KB limit is a hard service limit that can't be raised through configuration or a support request.
opts.D: Referencing files stored in EFS could work in principle, but you would have to write all the logic for writing, reading, and cleaning up files yourself, whereas the ready-made library does this for you.

345.key: Fewer than 100 users, a serverless architecture, global content delivery, and the lowest possible login latency. Cognito handles authentication (essentially free at this user count), CloudFront serves the application from edge locations, and token validation runs in Lambda@Edge — that is, at the same edge location the user connected to, without a round trip to the origin Region. That's exactly what minimizes login latency.

opts.B: AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a directory service billed hourly, overkill for a hundred users, and an ALB doesn't serve content globally.
opts.C: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads into a bucket, not the serving of a website, and a regular Lambda function runs in a single Region, which adds latency.
opts.D: The AD directory is again overkill and expensive, and Elastic Beanstalk means servers — a step away from a serverless architecture.

346.key: Client workstations need to keep the same look and feel, and the data must move to S3 and fall under lifecycle rules. That's Amazon S3 File Gateway: it exposes NFS and SMB shares while storing each file as an object in a bucket, so lifecycle rules apply normally, frequently accessed data is cached locally, and the workstations notice no difference.

opts.A: Volume Gateway presents block volumes over iSCSI and stores data as snapshots rather than individual objects: lifecycle rules can't be applied to user files this way, and the workstations would lose their familiar shares.
opts.B: Tape Gateway emulates a virtual tape library for backup software; it has nothing to do with the workstations' network shares.
opts.C: FSx File Gateway caches access to FSx file systems, not S3, so there are no S3 lifecycle rules in this setup.

347.key: The commitment runs for three years, but the instance family and size may change within six months. A Compute Savings Plan gives up to a 66 percent discount and isn't tied to instance family, size, Region, or even service — the discount carries over when you move to different instances, Fargate, or Lambda.

opts.B: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan is tied to a specific instance family in a specific Region: changing the family voids the discount.
opts.C: Zonal Reserved Instances lock in a fixed instance type and Availability Zone.
opts.D: Standard Reserved Instances give the biggest discount but don't allow changing the instance family.

348.key: The workload is constant and predictable, and the budget needs to stay in check. Provisioned mode with defined read and write capacity units costs less than on-demand mode under a steady workload and produces a predictable bill: you pay for provisioned capacity rather than per request.

opts.A: The Standard-IA table class lowers storage cost but raises the cost of requests — not cost-effective under a steady workload — and "reserving capacity" is described imprecisely here anyway.
opts.C: On-demand mode doesn't let you set capacity units at all, and under a steady workload it costs more than provisioned mode.
opts.D: On-demand mode is incompatible with both specifying capacity units and reserving capacity — no such configuration exists.

349.key: The snapshot is encrypted with a KMS key, so sharing it again takes two steps: allow the other account to use the key (update the key policy, and a grant if needed) and explicitly share the snapshot itself with that account. The receiving side typically makes its own copy of the snapshot right away, re-encrypting it with its own key so it isn't dependent on yours. An important restriction that shows up often in exam questions: a snapshot encrypted with the default AWS-managed key (aws/rds) can't be shared at all — only one encrypted with a key you manage.

opts.A: You can't copy an encrypted snapshot into an unencrypted one in RDS — there's no way to decrypt the data that way. And for confidential data, that would also be a step down in protection.
opts.C: You can't share a snapshot encrypted with an AWS managed key, and a key alias is just a convenient name — it doesn't grant access to anyone.
opts.D: You can't download an RDS snapshot to disk — the service doesn't offer that option. The workaround through an S3 upload is more complex and less secure than sharing the snapshot directly.

350.key: There are two requirements here. High availability with automatic recovery means converting the instance to a Multi-AZ deployment with synchronous replication and automatic failover (A). Speeding up reports without affecting transactions means a read replica in a different Availability Zone, with all report queries directed to it (C).

opts.B: Restoring from a snapshot creates an independent copy that starts going stale immediately, and it provides no automatic failover.
opts.D: RDS Custom is for cases where you need access to the underlying operating system; it has nothing to do with availability or reporting.
opts.E: RDS Proxy manages a connection pool and can't defer queries until a maintenance window.

351.key: The requirement is an event-driven, distributed architecture built on serverless components with the least operational overhead. AWS Step Functions describes the workflow as a state machine, invokes Lambda functions at each step, and handles errors, retries, and branching — all without a single server and without custom orchestration code.

opts.A: AWS Glue is an ETL service for processing data, not an orchestrator for arbitrary workflows.
opts.B: EC2 instances in the workflow steps bring back infrastructure that has to be maintained.
opts.C: EventBridge on a schedule means periodic invocation, not an event-driven workflow with state and branching.

352.key: UDP across eight Regions, with the requirement to minimize latency and packet loss. Global Accelerator creates UDP listeners and endpoint groups in each Region: the player enters the AWS network at the nearest edge location and then travels over the AWS backbone, where loss and jitter are significantly lower than on the public internet. The anycast IP addresses stay static, and a failed Region is pulled out of rotation within seconds.

opts.A: Transit Gateway and inter-Region peering connect AWS networks to each other. They have no effect on the path from the player to the nearest Region.
opts.C: CloudFront has no UDP support: it serves HTTP and HTTPS only.
opts.D: VPC peering provides connectivity within AWS, not improved access for outside users. There is no such thing as "turning on UDP" for peering.

353.key: Peak traffic of 1,000 IOPS with headroom for double that, so 2,000. A 1 TB gp2 volume delivers 3,000 IOPS based on the three-IOPS-per-GB formula, which covers that with margin, and it costs noticeably less than io2. The database also moves to managed RDS for MySQL in a Multi-AZ configuration, which provides fault tolerance and removes the administrative burden.

opts.A: io2 Block Express is built for tens of thousands of operations per second and is expensive: paying for it when you only need 2,000 IOPS is wasteful.
opts.C: S3 is object storage — it cannot serve as a database.
opts.D: Two large instances in active-passive mode is still a self-managed database, and the requirement calls for a fully managed solution.

354.key: The errors stem from connections being exhausted: during a traffic spike, Lambda spins up many concurrent instances, and each one opens its own database connection. RDS Proxy maintains a connection pool and reuses connections, and the only code change needed is pointing to the proxy endpoint instead of the database endpoint.

opts.A: Lowering the function's allowed concurrency would limit the application's throughput and cause a different kind of failure.
opts.C: A larger instance class raises the connection limit, but the problem returns with unpredictable spikes, and you'd be paying for it continuously.
opts.D: Migrating to DynamoDB means rewriting the data model and the queries — the maximum possible amount of code change.

355.key: The job needs 64 vCPUs and 512 GiB of memory and runs for 15 minutes — well beyond Lambda's limits and too large for a typical Fargate task. AWS Batch on EC2 automatically picks an instance type that fits the job's requirements, launches it, runs the computation, and tears the capacity down afterward — the service handles queuing and scheduling for you.

opts.A: A Lambda function is capped at roughly 10 GB of memory and 15 minutes of execution time — the requirements don't fit.
opts.B: Fargate's maximum task size is far below 64 vCPUs and 512 GiB of memory.
opts.C: Lightsail offers small, fixed configurations and isn't built for this kind of workload.

356.key: The phrase "the same high availability and resiliency" fixes the choice to three Availability Zones and immediate access, so the decision comes down to Standard versus Standard-IA. Age then decides it: 75% of the data is rarely read after 30 days, and Standard-IA is roughly 45% cheaper for storage at the same durability and the same retrieval speed. Hence a lifecycle rule that transitions objects on day 30.

opts.A: S3 Glacier Deep Archive returns an object after hours. That breaks the requirement to keep the data immediately accessible.
opts.C: S3 One Zone-IA keeps data in a single Availability Zone: 99.5% availability versus 99.9% for Standard-IA, and losing the zone means losing the data. That fails the "same resiliency" requirement.
opts.D: The same single-zone problem applies here, plus moving everything immediately also hits the 25% of data that is still read frequently, which would then incur retrieval charges.

357.key: The application splits into two parts, and each needs its own storage. The static files go into S3 and are served through CloudFront with caching at edge locations (A). The server-side code has to be shared across all the instances, and those instances run Windows Server — which calls for an SMB share, meaning Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, mounted on each instance (D).

opts.B: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache within a Region; it doesn't cache objects at edge locations and doesn't serve static files.
opts.C: EFS speaks the NFS protocol and is built for Linux — it isn't a native access method for Windows instances.
opts.E: A gp2 volume attaches within a single Availability Zone and isn't designed to be mounted by multiple instances at once: no shared access and no high availability.

358.key: Resizing images and switching formats on the fly, at a rate of thousands of requests per second, is best done at the edge. A Lambda@Edge function with an image-processing library attaches to the CloudFront cache behavior that serves the images: it receives the request, generates the needed variant, and returns it, with the result then cached. No servers of your own to run.

opts.A: A library running on an EC2 instance means a fleet you'd have to scale to thousands of requests per second and operate.
opts.B: An origin request policy controls which headers and parameters are forwarded to the origin. It doesn't transform images.
opts.D: A response headers policy adds headers to the response and doesn't change the content either.

359.key: The requirements break down into three parts. "Encrypted in transit" means enforcing HTTPS with an aws:SecureTransport condition in the bucket policy (otherwise TLS is available but not mandatory). "Encrypted at rest" means default encryption on the bucket. "The compliance team must administer the encryption key" is the deciding detail — only a KMS key can be administered, since it has a key policy, rotation, a usage log, and revocable access. SSE-S3 offers none of that: the service manages those keys itself.

opts.A: An ACM certificate can't be attached to S3: the service serves data over HTTPS using its own certificate. There's also no mechanism here to enforce TLS.
opts.B: SSE-S3 doesn't let anyone "administer keys": they aren't visible, carry no policy, and can't be revoked. The compliance team's requirement isn't met.
opts.D: Macie discovers and classifies sensitive data but doesn't encrypt it. The requirement for encryption at rest is left unaddressed.

360.key: A private API in API Gateway is reachable from inside a VPC only through an interface endpoint: it creates a network interface with a private address and a DNS record, so one service calling another travels over the private network. No code changes are needed — the API's name just needs to resolve to the private address.

opts.A: An API key relates to authorization and has no effect on the network path.
opts.C: A gateway endpoint exists only for S3 and DynamoDB; there is no such endpoint type for API Gateway.
opts.D: A queue between the services changes the interaction model from synchronous to asynchronous, which means rewriting code, and it doesn't fix the network path anyway.

361.key: The requirements call for sub-millisecond reads and one-time queries on historical data, with the least operational overhead. DynamoDB with a DAX cache delivers microsecond-level response times for frequently accessed data, the built-in table export moves data to S3 without writing a single line of code, and Athena runs the one-time queries against the exported data.

opts.A: RDS cannot deliver sub-millisecond response times, and a custom export script adds extra code to write and maintain.
opts.B: Reading directly from S3 takes tens of milliseconds, and retrieving from S3 Glacier Deep Archive takes hours — the requirement is not met.
opts.D: The Kinesis Data Streams and Kinesis Data Firehose combination works, but it adds extra components compared with the built-in export, and without a cache it won't deliver sub-millisecond response times.

362.key: Order must be preserved within a single payment ID. Both correct options use this ID as the partitioning key: an SQS FIFO queue with the payment ID as the message group ID preserves order within the group and processes each message exactly once (E), while a Kinesis data stream using the same value as the partition key places all records for a given payment into a single shard, where order is guaranteed (B).

opts.A: A DynamoDB table stores data, but it is not a message queue with guaranteed processing order.
opts.C: Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached is an in-memory cache with no data persistence and no ordering guarantees.
opts.D: A standard SQS queue can deliver messages out of order, and a message attribute has no effect on ordering.

363.key: Events must fan out to multiple recipients while preserving order. SNS FIFO topics do both: they deliver to multiple subscribers while preserving the sequence within a message group and preventing duplicates.

opts.A: An EventBridge event bus fans events out to multiple targets, but it does not guarantee delivery order.
opts.C: A standard SNS topic likewise does not preserve message order.
opts.D: An SQS FIFO queue preserves order, but each queue has a single consumer, so it can't fan out concurrently to three services.

364.key: Data flows through both SNS and SQS, so both links need to be protected, not just one. Server-side encryption is turned on for each using an AWS KMS customer managed key — only this key type lets you edit the key policy and restrict which principals are allowed to encrypt and decrypt messages. On top of that, the queue policy (and the topic policy) gets an aws:SecureTransport condition so that only TLS connections are accepted. The key nuance: access to a KMS key is governed primarily by the key's own policy — without a grant there, no IAM policy can provide access on its own.

opts.A: The phrase "default key policy" refers to an AWS managed key, whose policy cannot be edited. This makes it impossible to restrict the set of principals, and there's no TLS requirement here either.
opts.C: The same problem applies to the default key policy for SNS: it can't be changed, so restricting access this way isn't achievable.
opts.E: This gets the mechanism wrong: access to a KMS key is granted by the key policy, and an IAM policy only supplements it. Restricting access "through an IAM policy alone" does not protect the key from other principals in the account.

365.key: Restoring to any point within the last 30 days, accurate to within a few minutes, is provided by RDS automated backups: they continuously capture transaction logs, and the retention period can be configured for up to 35 days.

opts.A: Read replicas replicate every change, including erroneous ones, so the corrupted data ends up there too.
opts.B: Manual snapshots are discrete points in time; they don't let you restore to "five minutes before an arbitrary change."
opts.D: A Multi-AZ deployment protects against infrastructure failure, but it also replicates erroneous changes.

366.key: Subscribers need to be separated from everyone else at the entry point, without rewriting the business logic. API Gateway offers a ready-made mechanism for this: a usage plan with API keys — a key is issued to each subscriber and tied to a plan with quotas and throttling limits, and a request without a valid key is rejected by the gateway itself. No changes to the Lambda function or the DynamoDB table are needed. If access needed to be differentiated based on Cognito user attributes instead, the next step would be a Lambda authorizer, but that means writing code.

opts.A: API caching and throttling manage load and cost, but they don't distinguish a subscriber from a regular user.
opts.B: AWS WAF filters on request properties — IP addresses, headers, patterns. It has no knowledge of whether a user has paid for a subscription.
opts.C: Fine-grained IAM permissions on DynamoDB items apply when a client accesses the table directly using its own credentials. Here, a Lambda function running under its own role sits between the user and the table.

367.key: The application stays in the company's own data centers, runs over UDP, and both performance and availability need to improve. AWS Global Accelerator takes in traffic at the edge location closest to each user, routes it over the AWS global network backbone, and can direct it to the on-premises sites when they're registered as IP-address targets through a Network Load Balancer in each Region. An NLB is chosen because the traffic is UDP, and an ALB only handles HTTP. Failover away from a failed site happens at the accelerator level, without waiting for DNS record TTLs to expire.

opts.B: An Application Load Balancer does not support UDP, so it cannot serve this application.
opts.C: CloudFront does not work with UDP traffic and cannot use a Route 53 record as an origin for it.
opts.D: This has two errors at once: an ALB doesn't support UDP, and CloudFront isn't applicable to this type of traffic.

368.key: In IAM, a password policy is set once for the entire account: minimum length, required character types, reuse prevention, and password expiration. There is no such thing as an individual password policy per user. The setting applies to all IAM users in the account, including new ones, which is exactly what the requirement calls for.

opts.B: IAM has no per-user password policy: there is a single policy that applies to the whole account.
opts.C: Third-party software does not govern IAM user password requirements — that's handled by the service itself.
opts.D: Reacting to the user-creation event means writing code and a delay — the password already exists by then. The built-in setting solves this proactively instead.

369.key: The tasks are written in different languages, run for an hour each, and need to run in parallel. AWS Batch runs them as jobs in containers, automatically provisions and tears down compute capacity, manages the job queue and retries, and EventBridge handles the scheduling. The languages and runtime environments can stay whatever they already are.

opts.B: AWS App Runner is designed for web services and APIs, not for scheduled batch jobs.
opts.C: The tasks run for an hour, but the maximum Lambda function execution time is fifteen minutes; on top of that, not every language is supported.
opts.D: Running multiple copies of the same machine image doesn't solve the problem of running different jobs in parallel, and it still leaves the instances to be maintained.

370.key: A managed path to the internet is needed for the private subnets. A NAT gateway is created in a public subnet, and the private subnets' route tables send all outbound traffic to it. It's a managed resource: AWS handles its availability and scales it up to tens of gigabits per second on its own.

opts.A: A NAT instance works, but it's an ordinary EC2 instance: patching, monitoring, scaling, and fault tolerance all fall on the company.
opts.B: A NAT instance in a private subnet has no internet access and simply cannot work.
opts.D: A NAT gateway must be located in a public subnet: placed in a private one, it would have no way to send traffic outbound.

371.key: EBS volumes for an EKS node group are created automatically as the group scales, so encryption has to be set up in advance rather than volume by volume. Enabling EBS encryption by default in the Region with the customer managed key selected as the default key means that every new volume, including those created by EKS, is encrypted with that key with no action required on your part (C). The second piece is granting access to the key to whatever creates volumes on your behalf: an IAM role with permissions on the KMS key is associated with the cluster, otherwise the nodes simply fail to come up because they can't access the key (D). The key insight: you cannot turn on encryption for an existing EBS volume — it can only be created encrypted from the start.

opts.A: A Kubernetes plugin that performs the encryption is an extra component you have to install, update, and troubleshoot yourself. That violates the LEAST operational overhead requirement.
opts.B: You cannot enable encryption on an EBS volume that already exists — encryption is set at creation time. You would have to take a snapshot, copy it with encryption enabled, and recreate the volumes.
opts.E: A KMS key cannot be "stored as a Kubernetes secret" — the key material never leaves the service. You work with the key through its API, not by copying it around.

372.key: Both reasonable options share the same core idea: high-resolution images don't belong in database rows. They get moved out to S3, leaving only the geographic code and a reference in the database. The key picks D — the metadata stays in a relational table in Oracle on RDS Multi-AZ: migration effort is minimal, the application keeps working against the familiar schema, and Multi-AZ provides high availability. The dispute is a fair one: B (S3 plus DynamoDB) is cheaper and handles a burst of tens of thousands of updates per minute better, because DynamoDB scales horizontally while a single RDS instance does not. The counterargument for D: the Oracle license and schema are preserved, and "a single image per geographic code" doesn't necessarily mean the whole data model reduces to a simple key-value lookup.

opts.A: Storing the images themselves as rows in Oracle on RDS is the most expensive option: you pay for premium database storage, and the update burst runs into the IOPS limit of a single instance.
opts.B: A strong alternative on both cost and scalability. The key doesn't pick it because of the migration: DynamoDB would require rewriting how the data is accessed, and the question describes migrating an existing Oracle schema.
opts.C: A DynamoDB item is capped at 400 KB — high-resolution images don't fit. DAX also accelerates reads, while the workload described here is write-heavy.

373.key: The access pattern here is known in advance, not random: the last 30 days of data are read every morning, then accessed four more times over the course of the year, and after a year the data is kept only for archival purposes. A known pattern is described most cheaply by an explicit Lifecycle chain: S3 Standard for the first 30 days, then Standard-IA up to a year, then Glacier Deep Archive. Scale matters separately here: trillions of objects make Intelligent-Tiering expensive, since its monitoring fee is charged per object.

opts.A: Intelligent-Tiering across trillions of objects means a huge monitoring fee, with no benefit to show for it — the access pattern is known ahead of time and can be described with a simple rule.
opts.B: On top of the monitoring fee, the mechanics here are wrong too: Intelligent-Tiering moves objects into archive tiers based on lack of access, not on a calendar year, and the archive tiers have to be enabled separately.
opts.C: Standard-IA from day one hits the busiest period hardest: the data is read every morning for the first 30 days, and every one of those reads is billed as an IA retrieval.

374.key: There are two requirements: connectivity between the three VPCs, and steady delivery of hundreds of gigabytes a day to a latency-sensitive on-premises site. The cheapest way to get both is a single Direct Connect connection plus a transit gateway: every VPC attaches to the gateway and gets connectivity to the others, and the connection attaches to the same gateway through a Direct Connect gateway. One physical connection instead of three, and no mesh of peerings to manage.

opts.A: Three Site-to-Site VPN connections run over the internet, so latency is unpredictable and hundreds of gigabytes a day will run into the tunnels' bandwidth limits. They also don't provide connectivity between the VPCs.
opts.B: Running your own virtual appliances in every VPC means licensing, maintenance, and scaling it all yourself — and it still runs over the internet.
opts.C: Three separate Direct Connect connections cost three times as much, whereas one connection through a transit gateway serves all three VPCs.

375.key: This calls for orchestration with manual approvals, tying together Lambda functions and resources outside them — EC2 instances, containers, and on-premises servers. AWS Step Functions is built for exactly this: a state machine with branching, retries, and a wait-for-callback step for manual approval, with integrations that cover both Lambda and other services.

opts.B: AWS Glue is an ETL service, not a workflow orchestrator with manual approval steps.
opts.C: A queue passes messages along, but it doesn't describe a sequence of steps and has no built-in support for waiting on an approval.
opts.D: Functions tied together with events can work, but you'd have to build all the state tracking, retry logic, and approval-waiting yourself.

376.key: Connection-rejected errors during spikes from serverless applications are a classic sign of connection exhaustion. RDS Proxy maintains a connection pool and reuses connections, smoothing out swings in the number of clients, while the application only needs to point at a different endpoint.

opts.B: ElastiCache for Memcached caches reads and has no effect on the number of database connections, and the application would still need to be changed.
opts.C: A larger instance class raises the connection limit, but it costs more and doesn't address the underlying cause during sharp spikes.
opts.D: Multi-AZ improves availability; the standby instance doesn't accept connections, so there's nothing for the application to switch between.

377.key: The report has to go out at the exact moment an instance launches and terminates. EC2 Auto Scaling groups have lifecycle hooks for exactly this: the instance is held in a pending launch or terminate state, the required action runs, and only then does the transition complete. It's the only way to reliably send the data before the instance is removed.

opts.A: A scheduled function isn't tied to the moment of launch or termination, and a terminated instance can no longer be polled.
opts.C: User data runs only on first boot — it doesn't fire on instance termination.
opts.D: An Auto Scaling group doesn't invoke scripts inside the operating system — that's exactly what lifecycle hooks exist for.

378.key: The two requirements map to two separate services. UDP traffic with sharp spikes calls for a Network Load Balancer in front of the Auto Scaling group: it operates at layer 4, supports UDP, and handles millions of connections without warm-up. Non-relational data (player scores, profiles) that scales without manual intervention calls for DynamoDB in on-demand mode: capacity adjusts automatically, with no capacity planning needed.
