opts.A: Route 53 distributes requests via DNS with no awareness of connection state and with resolver-cache delays, and Aurora Serverless is a relational database, while the data described here is non-relational.
opts.C: The load balancer choice is right, but Aurora Global Database is again a relational store built for cross-Region replication, not for non-relational data with automatic scaling.
opts.D: Application Load Balancer doesn't support UDP, and DynamoDB global tables are meant for multi-Region writes, which the requirements don't call for.

379.key: The latency comes from a cold start: the function loads a large number of libraries every time. Provisioned concurrency keeps the required number of instances pre-initialized, so a request lands in an environment that's already warmed up. It changes neither the code nor the architecture — it's just a setting on the function.

opts.A: Connecting the frontend directly to the database and bypassing the API breaks the architecture and requires exposing the database publicly — that's both a redesign and a security hole.
opts.C: Caching results in S3 only helps for repeated, identical queries and does nothing to address the library-loading delay.
opts.D: A larger database raises the connection limit, but the function's initialization time stays the same.

380.key: This comes down to starting and stopping resources on a schedule. A Lambda function calls the necessary APIs, and EventBridge invokes it on a schedule: there are no servers to run, you pay only for the seconds the function executes, and maintenance amounts to a few lines of code.

opts.A: Elastic resize is an Amazon Redshift feature, and RDS instances cannot be scaled down to zero.
opts.B: A third-party Marketplace solution means extra cost and vendor dependency for something two native services already handle.
opts.C: A separate instance running crontab is a machine that runs around the clock and has to be patched and monitored — more expensive and more maintenance.

381.key: Reports run relational queries that take several hours, and they must not interfere with writes of new documents. Aurora PostgreSQL is compatible with the current database, so it requires minimal code changes, and the Aurora Replica reads from the same shared storage with millisecond-level lag. Reports go to the replica while writes continue on the primary instance.

opts.A: DocumentDB is compatible with MongoDB: the relational queries would have to be rewritten entirely.
opts.C: The standby instance in an RDS Multi-AZ configuration is not available for reads — reports cannot be directed to it.
opts.D: DynamoDB does not run relational queries, and moving the documents there would mean rewriting the application.

382.key: The requirement is specific — improve the security of data in transit, not defend against attacks or protect data at rest. A Network Load Balancer can terminate TLS: you create a listener on a TLS port, install a server certificate (typically from ACM) on the load balancer, and traffic from devices to the NLB is encrypted. The segment to the instances can be encrypted further if needed. Keep the distinction clear: TLS protects data in transit, KMS protects data at rest, and WAF and Shield protect against attacks.

opts.B: Shield Advanced and WAF protect against DDoS and common web attacks, but they encrypt nothing. In addition, WAF cannot be attached to a Network Load Balancer.
opts.C: Replacing the load balancer with an ALB plus WAF again addresses protection against attacks, not encrypting the channel. Using an ALB by itself does not encrypt traffic.
opts.D: Encrypting EBS volumes protects data at rest on the instances' disks. Data in transit remains unprotected.

383.key: The licenses are tied to sockets and cores, which means access to the physical host is required — that's Dedicated Hosts, the only EC2 option that exposes and accounts for the server's physical configuration. The workload has predictable capacity and uptime, so reserving the host gives the biggest discount.

opts.B: Dedicated On-Demand Hosts satisfy the licensing requirement, but paying the full on-demand rate for a predictable, round-the-clock workload is not cost-effective.
opts.C: Dedicated Instances only guarantee that no other tenants share the underlying hardware — they don't expose the host's sockets and cores, so the license cannot be mapped to them.
opts.D: The same licensing limitation, plus no reservation discount.

384.key: A POSIX-compliant file system is required, shared across instances in different Availability Zones, with maximum durability and lower costs for infrequently read data. That's EFS in the Standard storage class, which stores data across multiple Availability Zones, combined with a lifecycle policy that moves files older than 30 days to EFS Standard-Infrequent Access — the price per gigabyte drops by roughly a factor of ten while keeping the same file system semantics.

opts.A: S3 is not a POSIX-compliant file system, and Glacier does not provide instant access either.
opts.B: The S3 Standard-IA class is cheaper, but the underlying problem remains: object storage doesn't fit a use case where the application needs a POSIX file system.
opts.D: The One Zone class stores data in only a single Availability Zone, while the requirement calls for maximum durability.

385.key: Least access means each tier accepts traffic only from its neighboring tier. The web servers allow port 443 not from the whole internet but from the load balancer's security group, and the MySQL servers allow port 3306 from the web servers' security group. Referencing security groups instead of addresses keeps working as the fleet scales.

opts.A: Allowing port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 directly on the web servers is broader than necessary: they could then be reached by more than just the load balancer.
opts.B: Network ACLs work on addresses and subnets and cannot reference a security group — this kind of rule cannot be created.
opts.D: Same mistake: a network ACL cannot accept a security group as either a source or a destination.

386.key: The problem is that the same queries repeat frequently. An in-memory ElastiCache cache returns such a dataset in a fraction of a millisecond and removes the repeated load from the database — this is the standard solution for repeated, identical queries.

opts.A: SNS is a notification service; it cannot be used to store database queries.
opts.C: A read replica offloads the primary instance, but it is not a cache: every query still runs against the database in full.
opts.D: Firehose delivers streaming data into storage destinations and has nothing to do with speeding up reads.

387.key: Least privilege for an engineer working with CloudFormation is built from two parts. First: a dedicated IAM user in a group with a policy that allows only CloudFormation actions — the person themselves does not get permission to create resources directly (D). Second: a separate service role that the stack assumes during deployment, defining the specific permissions for the resources being created (E). This way, permissions on the resources belong to the stack, not the person, and can be scoped down to exactly what's needed.

opts.A: The root account should never be used for day-to-day operations at all: it cannot be restricted with policies and cannot be shared among people.
opts.B: PowerUsers grants nearly full access to all services except IAM management. That's disproportionately broader than what's needed for deploying stacks.
opts.C: AdministratorAccess is full access to the entire account — the maximum possible violation of least privilege.

388.key: All settings are at their default state: the network ACLs allow all traffic, the local route within the VPC already exists, but the default security group does not allow inbound connections from other security groups. So an inbound rule must be added to the database allowing traffic from the web tier's security group on the MySQL port.

opts.A: The default network ACL already allows all traffic: there's nothing to add a rule for.
opts.B: The route between subnets in the same VPC is created automatically by the local route entry and cannot be deleted.
opts.C: Splitting the tiers into separate VPCs and configuring peering is an excessive rebuild when a single rule is all that's missing.

389.key: Reporting queries need to be moved off the primary instance so they don't interfere with writes. An RDS read replica receives an asynchronous copy of the data and takes on the entire reporting load without affecting write operations on the primary database.

opts.B: A load balancer cannot distribute queries to a database and does not create additional copies of the data.
opts.C: A larger instance raises the overall ceiling, but heavy reports would still compete with writes for the same resources.
opts.D: The standby instance in a Multi-AZ configuration does not serve queries: it exists solely for failover.

390.key: There's one requirement: store session data durably, so that replacing an instance in the Auto Scaling group doesn't drop the customer's cart. A durable external session store means DynamoDB or ElastiCache for Redis. The dump key gives AD, and this is the most disputed spot: sticky sessions don't actually store anything — they only pin a client to the same instance, and the session is lost when that instance is replaced. A significant part of the community picks BD, and going strictly by the wording of the requirement — "store session data durably" — that is the stronger answer. Keep in mind: what matters in this question isn't the letter of the key, it's the underlying technique — moving state out of the instances.

opts.B: Formally this is the strongest of the options: DynamoDB is durable by definition, replicates data across three Availability Zones, and is the standard AWS session store. The dump key didn't pick it, and this is exactly where the dispute lies.
opts.C: Cognito manages user accounts and authentication tokens, not the cart or transaction state. That's a different layer of the problem.
opts.E: Systems Manager Application Manager is a console for operating application resources. It is not a user session store in any form.

391.key: The application is stateless and does not need temporary local storage, so taking snapshots of the instance volumes is pointless — it is enough to keep up-to-date AMIs, from which the Auto Scaling group can launch any number of instances. A two-hour recovery point for the data is covered by RDS automated backups with point-in-time recovery.

opts.A: Instance volume snapshots are unnecessary for a stateless application and just consume resources, and "database snapshots every two hours" duplicate RDS's built-in mechanism.
opts.B: An EBS snapshot lifecycle policy again backs up something that does not need backing up, and without point-in-time recovery the two-hour RPO is not guaranteed.
opts.D: This also snapshots unnecessary instance volumes, wasting resources, even though the second half of the option is correct.

392.key: Customers are located worldwide and have dynamic IP addresses, so listing their source addresses is impossible — the web tier must accept HTTPS from 0.0.0.0/0. The database, however, stays locked down: its security group allows port 3306 not from IP addresses but by referencing the web servers' security group, so access automatically applies to whatever instances currently belong to that group, and only to them.

opts.B: You cannot enumerate customer IP addresses since they are dynamic, and global users would simply lose the ability to reach the site.
opts.C: Same mistake with customer IP addresses, plus the database is opened up by a list of addresses instead of referencing the web servers' security group.
opts.D: Opening port 3306 to the entire internet is a direct violation of the security requirement.

393.key: Two operations are needed: transcribe the speech and strip out personal data. Amazon Transcribe does both in a single job — it has a built-in PII redaction feature for the transcript. A Lambda function triggered by the upload event starts the transcription job, and the output is stored in a separate bucket.

opts.A: Kinesis Video Streams handles streaming video, not already-recorded audio files, and it does not perform speech recognition.
opts.B: Textract extracts text from documents and images; it does not understand audio.
opts.D: Amazon Connect is a contact center for live calls, not a tool for batch-processing already-recorded files; a custom-built PII scanner is also unreliable.

394.key: The limit is specific: a single gp3 volume tops out at 16,000 IOPS, while the application is hitting 20,000. The fix is to spread the load across two gp3 volumes and combine them at the database or file system level — the combined limit doubles while the cost per gigabyte stays the same.

opts.A: A magnetic volume is tens of times slower, so performance would get noticeably worse.
opts.B: gp3 IOPS can only be raised up to 16,000, which is below the required 20,000, so the limit would still be hit.
opts.C: An io2 volume does deliver more IOPS, but it costs substantially more, whereas two gp3 volumes meet the requirement more cheaply.

395.key: The question of "who called which API and when" is always answered with AWS CloudTrail: it logs management-operation API calls along with the caller's identity, time, source address, and request parameters, and the AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress event shows exactly who changed the rules. It's worth remembering the split between services: CloudTrail tells you who did what, Config shows what a resource's configuration looked like and how it changed, GuardDuty flags signs of malicious activity, and Inspector finds vulnerabilities in workloads.

opts.A: GuardDuty looks for signs of compromise and suspicious behavior. It is not a log of user actions.
opts.B: Inspector scans instances and images for vulnerabilities and insecure configurations; it does not record who changed a resource.
opts.D: AWS Config will show that the security group's configuration changed and how, but the answer to "which user did this" lives in CloudTrail.

396.key: You need to protect the point where the traffic actually arrives — the static anycast addresses of Global Accelerator. AWS Shield Advanced supports the accelerator as a protected resource, so that's what you add to the subscription: the attack is absorbed at the edge of the AWS global network before it ever reaches the instances. Note that this is a DNS service running over UDP, so WAF is inapplicable in principle — it only filters HTTP.

opts.B: The instances sit behind the accelerator and don't receive traffic directly; the entry point is what needs protecting. Also, Shield Advanced protects an Elastic IP, not an instance as such.
opts.C: AWS WAF filters HTTP requests and cannot be attached to Global Accelerator: it is useless for DNS traffic.
opts.D: WAF cannot be attached to EC2 instances, and it's still inapplicable to DNS traffic.

397.key: The job runs for up to an hour, so Lambda's fifteen-minute limit rules it out. The CPU and memory requirements are known in advance and constant — a perfect fit for an ECS task on Fargate: a scheduled EventBridge rule launches it once a day, the task runs to completion, and there's no infrastructure to maintain.

opts.A: A Lambda function is capped at fifteen minutes of execution: an hour-long job would be cut off.
opts.B: Same execution limit, plus an unnecessary API Gateway layer; on top of that, a synchronous call through an HTTP API is constrained even more tightly.
opts.D: The EC2 launch type means a continuously running instance in the group that must be maintained, even though the job only runs once a day.

398.key: Do the math: 600 TB at 100 Mbps takes over a year to transfer, but the deadline is two weeks. Any option that relies on the existing link is ruled out arithmetically. That leaves physical devices: several Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices move the data in days, encrypt the contents with AWS KMS keys, and don't consume any internet bandwidth. See {{q:215}} for more on transferring data over a network link.

opts.A: Multipart upload speeds up a single object, but the overall bandwidth stays the same: the deadline still isn't met.
opts.B: A VPN still rides the same 100 Mbps link, just adding encryption overhead on top.
opts.D: A 10 Gbps Direct Connect connection would technically be fast enough, but provisioning the physical link usually takes weeks, and its cost is out of proportion to a one-time bulk transfer compared with renting the devices for a single trip.

399.key: An HTTP flood is a large volume of requests that are valid in form, and the way to cut them off is rate limiting. AWS WAF has a rate-based rule for exactly this: it counts requests from each address over a rolling five-minute window and blocks anyone who exceeds the threshold. A Regional web ACL attaches directly to the API Gateway stage, so no extra components are added to the architecture — hence the minimal operational overhead.

opts.A: CloudFront with a long TTL helps with repeated requests for cacheable content, but stock quotes are dynamic, and CloudFront by itself provides no rate limiting.
opts.C: The metric and alarm notify people about the problem, but they don't block any requests.
opts.D: A custom function that maintains per-address counters means development work and state that has to be maintained, instead of a ready-made WAF rule.

400.key: The alert needs to fire on every new record without affecting the existing application. DynamoDB Streams publishes a feed of table changes, a handler sends a message to a single SNS topic, and all four teams subscribe to that topic. The application itself doesn't change at all.

opts.A: DynamoDB transactions guarantee write atomicity and don't notify anyone.
opts.B: This requires modifying the application and setting up four topics instead of one — extra work and extra upkeep.
opts.D: Polling the table every minute for a flag means added latency, constant scanning, and a custom scheduler; on top of that, multiple teams can't all subscribe to a single SQS queue.

401.key: The single point of failure was the database, and that's the first thing to eliminate. RDS in a Multi-AZ configuration synchronously replicates data to another Availability Zone and fails over automatically, so a power outage in one zone does not result in data loss. The application layer sits in an Auto Scaling group spread across multiple Availability Zones, which provides both fault tolerance and the ability to scale with demand.

opts.B: A single Availability Zone still leaves a single point of failure in place, and EC2 Auto Recovery protects against neither a zone failure nor the loss of data on the instance's disk.
opts.C: A read replica operates asynchronously and requires manual promotion during an outage, which means both data loss is possible and recovery time is long.
opts.D: Multi-Attach works only within a single Availability Zone, so the described setup with databases in different zones is not possible.

402.key: The application pulls data only every other day, but a Kinesis stream retains records for 24 hours by default — anything older is dropped before the consumer arrives. Increasing the retention period (up to 7 days in standard mode, and longer with extended retention) is enough to stop the data loss.

opts.B: The Kinesis Producer Library improves write efficiency, but it has no effect on how long already-written data is retained.
opts.C: A shortage of shards shows up as write failures, but here writes succeed and the data is lost later, during the read.
opts.D: S3 Versioning preserves versions of objects that have already been uploaded to S3 and does nothing to save data that was already removed from the stream.

403.key: Lambda functions get their permissions through an execution role: the role is assigned to the function, and a policy with the required actions — for example, s3:PutObject on a specific bucket — is attached to that role. At runtime, the function automatically obtains temporary credentials for that role, so nothing needs to be stored in the code. The existing IAM user here is just a distractor: putting a person's keys inside a service's code is an anti-pattern. Don't confuse Lambda's two kinds of policies — the execution role defines what the function is allowed to do, while a resource-based policy defines who is allowed to invoke it.

opts.A: The function's resource policy defines which services and accounts are allowed to invoke it. It does not grant permission to write to S3.
opts.B: Signing requests with the existing user's keys means embedding a long-lived secret in the function's code. It would work, but it goes against accepted practice and doesn't solve the permissions-management problem.
opts.C: A new user and its keys are the same mistake: long-lived credentials in the code instead of temporary credentials from a role.

404.key: During a traffic spike, direct invocation from S3 runs into the function's concurrency limit, and the excess events are lost, since asynchronous invocations have a limited number of retries. An SQS queue accepts every event, holds it, and hands it to the function at exactly the pace the function can keep up with — no document gets dropped.

opts.A: A 15-minute runtime timeout doesn't help if the event never reaches the function in the first place.
opts.B: Replication copies objects into another bucket, but it doesn't perform any processing and doesn't preserve events.
opts.C: A second function doesn't raise the account's overall concurrency limit and doesn't provide buffering, and Lambda invocations can't be load balanced this way.

405.key: Load rises during business hours and disappears entirely on weekends. For the workday, a target tracking scaling policy based on average CPU utilization fits well — capacity follows actual demand (D). For weekends, scheduled scaling sets the Auto Scaling group's minimum, desired, and maximum capacity to zero, then restores the previous values at the start of the week (E).

opts.A: The Application Load Balancer scales automatically as a managed service; its capacity cannot and does not need to be configured.
opts.B: The internet gateway is a logical construct with no throughput limit, so there's nothing to scale.
opts.C: Deploying across multiple Regions addresses global availability, not intraday load fluctuations, and it costs considerably more.

406.key: The two-tier design is built on security groups: the web servers open port 443 to the whole internet, since a public site needs to accept visitors (C), and the database allows port 3306 by referencing the web servers' security group (D) — that way access is granted to exactly those instances, regardless of their addresses, and no one else.

opts.A: Network ACLs operate at the subnet level and aren't needed here; denying outbound traffic on port 3306 would break the web servers' connections to the database.
opts.B: Allowing traffic by the subnet's address range opens the database to any resource in that subnet, not just the web servers.
opts.E: Security groups have no deny rules — only what's explicitly allowed is permitted — so a rule like this cannot be created.

407.key: The defining phrase again is Lustre clients. There is exactly one managed file system in AWS that speaks this protocol: Amazon FSx for Lustre. It delivers sub-millisecond latency and throughput in the gigabytes per second, while AWS handles all the operational work. A similar walkthrough appears in {{q:99}}.

opts.A: DataSync moves data between storage systems and doesn't create a mountable file system.
opts.B: Storage Gateway serves resources over NFS and SMB; it has no Lustre protocol.
opts.C: EFS has no mode that supports Lustre — no such configuration exists.

408.key: UDP traffic, minimal latency, and rapid failover to another Region point to Global Accelerator with a Network Load Balancer in each Region. The accelerator ingests packets at the nearest edge location, routes them over the AWS global network backbone, and switches to a healthy Region within seconds, without depending on DNS caching. Serverless processing is provided by ECS on Fargate, registered as the load balancer's target. An ALB is out of the question here by definition — it doesn't support UDP.

opts.A: Failover through Route 53 is slower because of TTL and resolver caching, and a Network Load Balancer can't invoke a Lambda function as a target.
opts.C: The Application Load Balancer doesn't support UDP: the devices simply wouldn't be able to send their data.
opts.D: Neither is the ALB suitable for UDP, nor does DNS-based failover provide a fast, fault-tolerant transition.

409.key: The IIS application runs on Windows and accesses the network share over the SMB protocol. The most resilient and durable replacement is Amazon FSx for Windows File Server in a Multi-AZ configuration: data is replicated synchronously between Availability Zones, Windows ACLs and Active Directory are supported, and instances in every zone mount the same file share.

opts.A: RDS is a relational database; it cannot serve as a file share.
opts.B: Storage Gateway is designed for hybrid scenarios and relies on a local virtual machine, which itself becomes a single point of failure. For a workload fully migrated to AWS, it isn't needed.
opts.D: EFS uses the NFS protocol: for an IIS application on Windows this isn't a native access method, and Windows ACLs aren't supported there.

410.key: For EBS volumes, encryption is set at creation time and covers the data on disk, data in transit between the volume and the instance, snapshots, and volumes created from those snapshots. Encryption cannot be turned on for an existing unencrypted volume — instead you take a snapshot, copy it while specifying a KMS key, and create a new volume from the encrypted copy. So the right approach is to create the volumes as encrypted from the start; at the account level, this is conveniently enforced with the EC2 "EBS encryption by default" setting.

opts.A: An IAM role describes what a principal is allowed to do. It has no property that "encrypts volumes" and has no effect on how volumes are created.
opts.C: A tag is just a label for tracking and search. On its own it turns nothing on; at most you can build policies around it, but a volume doesn't get encrypted because of a tag.
opts.D: A KMS key policy defines who is allowed to use the key — it doesn't force encryption of volumes across the account. Enforcement is done through the default EBS encryption setting or an SCP policy with an ec2:Encrypted condition.

411.key: Load spikes unpredictably, the database can't be changed, and cost matters. MySQL-compatible Aurora Serverless is exactly right here: the application runs unmodified, and capacity scales automatically to handle the surges at the start of each month and week, then scales back down during quiet periods, so the company doesn't pay for peak capacity around the clock.

opts.A: DynamoDB is a non-relational store: the queries and data model would have to be rewritten.
opts.B: RDS for MySQL requires choosing an instance class sized for the peak and paying for it continuously, even when there's no load.
opts.D: A relational database can't be scaled with an EC2 Auto Scaling group: new instances don't share the underlying data.

412.key: The requirement is that no object in the entire account can ever become public, even if someone misconfigures a policy. The first layer is S3 Block Public Access at the account level: it overrides any public ACLs or bucket policies regardless of their content. The second layer is an SCP that denies the s3:PutAccountPublicAccessBlock action (and disabling the block on individual buckets), so the setting can't be turned off from inside the account. This is preventive protection, not after-the-fact detection.

opts.A: GuardDuty analyzes threats and suspicious activity, but it doesn't monitor bucket policies or roll them back.
opts.B: Trusted Advisor finds public buckets after the fact and sends a notification, while the fix stays manual. The data can end up exposed in the meantime.
opts.C: Resource Access Manager shares resources across accounts and has nothing to do with finding public buckets.

413.key: The problem is email delivery, and the company wants to stop dealing with its complexity. Amazon SES is a managed email service: sender reputation, delivery queues, bounces, and complaints are all handled by the service — the application just calls the API.

opts.A: A dedicated email tier of EC2 instances leaves all the delivery complexity on the company and adds more infrastructure.
opts.C: SNS delivers notifications to subscribers, but it isn't a full email-sending tool for customers: no templates, no reputation management.
opts.D: Same as option A, just with Auto Scaling added: operational overhead doesn't go down, it goes up.

414.key: The business system can only write to a network share, it can't be modified, and the data needs to reach the cloud in near-real time. S3 File Gateway presents exactly that kind of network share, but every file saved to it is asynchronously turned into an S3 object — essentially in real time and without writing a single line of automation. The system just points to the new share.

opts.A: A once-a-day task isn't near-real time: reports would sit and wait until the end of the day.
opts.C: A custom application calling the DataSync API is code that has to be written and maintained, while the gateway does the same job out of the box.
opts.D: A script that watches for new files and uploads them over SFTP is once again custom automation with its own failures and retries to manage.

415.key: The discriminator is "MOST operational efficiency" when access patterns are unknown. Intelligent-Tiering needs no analysis and no manual decisions: it monitors access to each object itself and moves it between tiers, with no retrieval fees. A single Lifecycle rule per bucket covers petabytes of data. Keep the caveat in mind: objects smaller than 128 KB never move to the archive tiers and are always billed at the frequent-access tier.

opts.B: Storage class analysis only produces a report. Moving petabytes of objects based on its results has to be done by hand, and repeated every time the access pattern changes — the most operational overhead of any option.
opts.C: Glacier Instant Retrieval gives instant access, but charges a noticeable retrieval fee and carries a 90-day minimum storage duration. Some of the petabytes are read frequently, and for those it ends up costing more than Standard.
opts.D: One Zone-IA reduces fault tolerance to a single zone and charges a retrieval fee — a poor choice for data with an unknown access pattern.

416.key: The slow page loads come from two sources. CloudFront speeds up the static content and part of the dynamic content: content is cached at edge locations, and requests travel to the Region over the AWS backbone (B). A read replica for RDS takes the load off the database, absorbing the read queries and freeing up the primary instance for transactions (D).

opts.A: Redshift is an analytics warehouse and has nothing to do with page-load speed on a transactional site.
opts.C: Dynamic content by definition can't be hosted in S3: it's generated by the application.
opts.E: A Multi-AZ configuration improves availability, but the standby instance doesn't serve requests, so it doesn't improve performance.

417.key: The company needs to save money on both the instances and the functions, and the functions need direct network access to the instances. A Compute Savings Plan covers EC2, Lambda, and Fargate together, giving a discount on all of the application's compute. Direct access comes from connecting the functions to the same private subnet where the instances run — traffic stays inside the VPC with minimal latency.

opts.A: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan only discounts instances: spending on the growing number of functions stays at full price.
opts.B: The same limited savings plan, and connecting the functions to a public subnet doesn't bring them any closer to the instances — it just complicates routing.
opts.D: Staying in the Lambda service VPC means the functions don't get direct network access to the instances in the private subnet.

418.key: Classic cross-account access isn't built by duplicating users — it's built on a role: the target account has a role with permissions on the bucket, and that role's trust policy lists who is allowed to assume it. The role in production already exists, so what's left is to add the development account as a principal in its trust policy (and let users assume the role via sts:AssumeRole on their side). Users keep living in a single account, temporary credentials are issued for the duration of the session, and permissions are limited to what the role's policy grants — that's least privilege.

opts.A: AdministratorAccess grants full access to the entire development account and does nothing to open up the bucket in production. A direct violation of least privilege.
opts.C: Turning off Block Public Access exposes the bucket to the outside world and has nothing to do with granting the team access. That's a security regression, not a solution.
opts.D: Separate users in production mean a second set of long-lived credentials per person that have to be created, rotated, and revoked. A role solves the same problem with temporary credentials.

419.key: This question is flagged as disputed because of how one option is worded. The intended solution is: a preventive ban on creating unencrypted volumes for everyone, including the root users of member accounts, can only come from an SCP with a condition on ec2:Encrypted equal to false (C) — an IAM policy can simply be rewritten by the account's own administrator, and a permission boundary can't be attached to an organizational unit anyway. The other half is making encryption transparent for employees: default EBS encryption means new volumes are encrypted automatically and nobody hits a denied request. The catch is that this setting is configured per account and per Region individually (option A), while option E, as worded in the answer key, describes it as a setting on the organization's management account, which doesn't exist.

opts.A: This is actually an accurate description of how default encryption is configured: an account attribute in the EC2 console plus a default KMS key. That's exactly why the pair A and C looks more correct than the dump's answer key.
opts.B: A permission boundary attaches to a user or a role and caps their maximum permissions. It cannot be attached to an organizational unit.
opts.D: IAM policies in each account can be changed by that account's own administrator, and they don't apply to the account's root user at all. That gives no preventive guarantee.

420.key: The key requirements are failover in under 40 seconds and offloading reads at the lowest possible cost. An RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster consists of one primary instance and two standby instances that are also readable at the same time: failover typically completes in around 35 seconds, and all the read traffic can go to the reader endpoint without adding a single extra instance.

opts.A: A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment takes up to one to two minutes to fail over, and a read replica is yet another instance you pay for.
opts.B: The cluster choice is right, but the two extra read replicas are redundant: the cluster's nodes are already readable, and the requirement is minimum cost.
opts.C: In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, the standby instance doesn't serve requests.

421.key: The requirements are a serverless service, high I/O performance, finely configurable security, and continued control over user permissions. AWS Transfer Family removes the need for self-managed instances, and the storage is an encrypted EFS file system with familiar POSIX permissions, while the endpoint is deployed inside a VPC with internet-facing access and elastic IP addresses so that a security group can be attached to allow only trusted addresses.

opts.A: An EBS volume cannot be attached to a Transfer Family service: only S3 and EFS are supported as storage. A public endpoint also does not let you apply a security group.
opts.C: S3 as the storage backend provides neither familiar POSIX permissions nor the same I/O performance profile, and a public endpoint removes the ability to finely control network access with security groups.
opts.D: An endpoint in a private subnet with no internet access blocks the trusted sources on the public internet that the scenario explicitly requires.

422.key: The workload pattern is extremely uneven: a model can sit idle for weeks and then suddenly receive thousands of requests at once. An SQS queue absorbs and holds everything, while the models run as ECS services that read from it; scaling based on queue length grows both the number of service copies and the cluster capacity. Containers are the right fit because each model loads about a gigabyte of data into memory at startup — in a container this happens once for the lifetime of the task.

opts.A: A Network Load Balancer cannot invoke Lambda functions as a target, and loading a gigabyte of data on every cold start of the function would devastate latency.
opts.B: A load balancer in front of services that read from a queue is unnecessary, and App Mesh is a service mesh for routing traffic — it does not handle cluster scaling.
opts.C: The number of vCPUs for a Lambda function is not adjustable through Auto Scaling (memory is set in the configuration), and a gigabyte-sized model held in memory does not fit well with the Lambda execution model.

423.key: This is a question about what an identity-based policy is. Such a policy describes what a principal is allowed to do and can be attached only to IAM principals: a user, a group, or a role. Of the options given, that means role and group. Resources (an EC2 instance, an ECS task, a bucket) cannot have a policy attached directly to them — they get a resource-based policy instead, and compute resources gain permissions through a role. An organization is not a principal either: SCPs are attached to it and its organizational units, but an SCP is a guardrail policy, not an identity-based policy.

opts.C: An organization in AWS Organizations is not an IAM principal. Service control policies are attached to it, and those set a permissions ceiling rather than grant permissions.
opts.D: An ECS resource cannot carry an IAM policy: a container gets permissions through the task role (taskRoleArn), as covered in {{q:185}}.
opts.E: An EC2 instance gets permissions through a role attached via an instance profile. A policy cannot be attached directly to an instance — see {{q:17}}.

424.key: Two distinct load profiles call for two different purchasing models. The frontend runs around the clock and is predictable, so Reserved Instances give the deepest discount. The backend spins up briefly, the number of machines varies throughout the day, and interruptions are acceptable — which points to Spot Instances, with discounts of up to 90 percent.

opts.A: Fargate for the backend nodes costs more than Spot Instances given the same tolerance for interruption.
opts.C: Spot Instances for an around-the-clock frontend are risky: AWS can reclaim that capacity at any time, and reserving capacity for a variable workload is not cost-effective.
opts.D: This combines a risky Spot-based frontend with a more expensive Fargate backend for the variable workload.

425.key: The key requirement is provisioning performance independently of storage capacity, at up to 15,000 IOPS peak. That is exactly the gp3 volume profile: a baseline of 3,000 IOPS is included in the price, and IOPS can be raised up to 16,000 independently of volume size. Per gigabyte, gp3 costs less than gp2 and far less than provisioned-IOPS volumes.

opts.A: gp2 performance is tightly coupled to size — three IOPS per gigabyte — so reaching 15,000 IOPS would require provisioning a 5 TB volume.
opts.B: io2 meets the requirement but costs considerably more, and it's justified only when you need tens of thousands of IOPS or higher volume durability.
opts.D: io1 is the previous generation of provisioned-IOPS volumes: it too costs more than gp3 and falls short of io2 on specifications.

426.key: The requirements are a secure migration of already-accumulated data and audit access at the level of the data itself. AWS DataSync encrypts the transfer, verifies data integrity, and moves the files into S3, while CloudTrail data event logging records every read and write of an object — exactly what the regulation calls for. Management events do not provide that level of detail.

opts.B: Snowcone is sized for a few terabytes and a one-time transfer, and a management event log does not capture access to the objects themselves.
opts.C: Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads but is not a tool for migrating an existing data set with integrity verification; the logging half of this option is otherwise correct.
opts.D: Storage Gateway is a persistent hybrid gateway, not a migration tool, and a management event log does not cover access to the data.

427.key: The Java application under Tomcat needs to be carried over as-is, with high availability. Elastic Beanstalk offers a ready-made Tomcat platform: it provisions a load balancer and a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group on its own and manages updates, and a rolling deployment policy rolls out new versions without downtime.

opts.A: Porting a complex Tomcat application to Lambda means rewriting it from scratch.
opts.C: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache and cannot replace a relational MySQL database.
opts.D: Running MySQL on the same instance as the application, inside an Auto Scaling group, produces diverging copies of the data and no real availability.

428.key: The most secure way to grant any AWS service permissions is a role, not long-lived keys. The role must trust the Lambda service (principal lambda.amazonaws.com in its trust policy), carry a policy with the needed actions such as dynamodb:GetItem and PutItem scoped to the specific table, and be assigned to the function as its execution role. The resulting credentials are temporary and rotate automatically, with no secrets in the code or environment variables.

opts.A: Access keys in environment variables are a long-lived secret, visible to anyone who can read the function's configuration, and rotation is left entirely up to you.
opts.C: Storing the same keys in Parameter Store only hides them: a compromised key is still valid, whereas a role would provide temporary credentials with no key storage needed at all.
opts.D: The role needs to trust the Lambda service, not DynamoDB: the trust policy defines who can assume the role. And a role cannot be attached from within the function's code either — it is set in the configuration.

429.key: Read the two statements together. The first allows any EC2 action, but only within the us-east-1 Region (the ec2:Region condition). The second is an explicit Deny that blocks StopInstances and TerminateInstances whenever the request lacks an MFA indicator (BoolIfExists on aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent — a construction that also matches when the key is absent). The net effect: within us-east-1 everything is allowed, but stopping or terminating an instance requires signing in with MFA. Outside that Region there is no permission at all, since the Allow is restricted by its condition.

opts.A: Policy statements are not "cut off" after the first Allow: all statements are evaluated, and an explicit Deny always overrides an Allow.
opts.B: The Deny applies only to two actions — stopping and terminating instances — not to all EC2 operations.
opts.C: The Allow applies only within us-east-1, so "in all Regions" is wrong: in other Regions the group has no permission whatsoever.

430.key: The images are needed right after upload — that calls for an event-driven Lambda function triggered when a file appears, with no polling and no idle machines (B). From there, lifecycle policy handles the rest: the images become useless after a month and are simply expired, while the source files are needed only twice a year for planned-in-advance training, so transitioning them to S3 Glacier after just one day gives the cheapest storage that still meets the acceptable retrieval time (C).

opts.A: An instance that downloads files once an hour violates the "as soon as possible" requirement and adds unnecessary infrastructure.
opts.D: S3 One Zone-IA costs more than Glacier and keeps data in a single Availability Zone — an unnecessary risk for the sole copy of the training data.
opts.E: S3 Standard-IA is noticeably more expensive than Glacier, and Reduced Redundancy Storage is deprecated and no longer recommended.

431.key: The requirements are a near-real-time leaderboard and score durability across a stop/restart of the game. ElastiCache for Redis satisfies both: sorted sets compute the top 10 in sub-millisecond time, and Redis's disk persistence and replication let the state be restored after a restart.

opts.A: Memcached has neither sorted data structures for ranking nor data persistence: the scores would be lost after a restart.
opts.C: CloudFront caches responses at edge locations, but the leaderboard changes constantly, and a distribution has no ability to compute it.
opts.D: A read replica would offload traffic, but recalculating the top 10 with a query against a relational database thousands of times per second would still be slow.

432.key: The requirements are both model training and dashboards, with minimal operations. Amazon SageMaker handles model building and hosting, while Amazon QuickSight is the business intelligence service that can call a SageMaker model and surface the enriched data directly in a dashboard.

opts.A: The AWS Glue ML transform only solves the narrow task of finding duplicate records, and OpenSearch Service is a search engine, not a reporting platform.
opts.C: A pre-built AMI from the Marketplace means managing your own instances, patching, and upkeep — the opposite of the requirement.
opts.D: QuickSight calculated fields are formulas; they cannot be used to train machine learning models.

433.key: The requirement is to preventively block modification of cost allocation tags across every account in the organization, except by specific trusted principals. Only an SCP can enforce that boundary: it applies to all principals in member accounts, including their root user, and cannot be bypassed by a local IAM policy. Typically this is written as a Deny on tag:* or on actions like ec2:CreateTags and ec2:DeleteTags, with a condition on the tag key and an exception via aws:PrincipalArn for the roles that are allowed to make the change.

opts.A: AWS Config compares configuration against a rule and reports noncompliance after the fact. It does not block the operation at call time.
opts.B: CloudTrail records who called what. It's a log, not an enforcement mechanism.
opts.D: CloudWatch Logs stores log records. It places no restrictions on what actions can be taken in AWS.

434.key: The key phrase is "minimal downtime." That means the infrastructure in the disaster recovery Region must already exist beforehand rather than being created after a failure: the Auto Scaling group and load balancer are already deployed, the DynamoDB global table continuously replicates data to both Regions, and a Route 53 record with a failover policy switches traffic based on health checks. Recovery time comes down to the DNS record's TTL.

opts.B: Deploying a CloudFormation stack only after the failure means minutes or tens of minutes of waiting, plus the DynamoDB table still has to be populated with data. The downtime is inherently longer.
opts.C: The data side is fine here (global table), but the compute layer is still created from a template at the moment of the disaster, so the failover is slower than the option with an Auto Scaling group already stood up.
opts.D: The infrastructure exists beforehand, but switching over via a CloudWatch alarm and a Lambda function that updates Route 53 records adds its own delay and extra logic instead of relying on a built-in failover policy with health checks.

435.key: Twenty terabytes in two weeks with minimal downtime is a classic pairing: the full data load travels on a Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device, while the changes accumulated during transit are caught up by AWS DMS's ongoing replication. Once the replication lag reaches zero, the application is cut over to the new database — the downtime window is measured in minutes. Storage Optimized is chosen because the task is purely about data volume.

opts.B: Snowmobile is a truck built for tens of petabytes. For 20 TB it is disproportionately expensive and slow to arrange.
opts.C: The GPU-accelerated device is meant for on-site computation (machine learning, video processing) and costs more. There's no computation needed here.
opts.D: A dedicated connection makes sense as permanent infrastructure, not as a one-time migration method: provisioning it typically takes longer than two weeks, and you'd be paying for months of port charges.

436.key: The condition explicitly rules out adding infrastructure, so the only way to grow is up: scale the existing instance larger. And to make that cost-effective, reserved DB instances are purchased for the steady workload — a discount of over 60% compared to on-demand pricing.

opts.B: Multi-AZ improves availability but adds no performance: the standby instance doesn't serve requests, yet you'd pay double.
opts.C: A second DB instance is exactly the kind of added infrastructure the condition rules out.
opts.D: On-demand pricing is the most expensive option and does nothing to handle the increased workload.

437.key: The offending IP addresses keep changing, so they can't be blocked by static lists — what's needed is a limit on request rate. An AWS WAF rate-based rule attached to the Application Load Balancer counts requests from each address and temporarily blocks anyone who exceeds the threshold, without affecting normal users. The rule can be scoped by path or headers so the limit only applies to the heavy endpoints.

opts.A: Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities and doesn't operate on load balancer traffic.
opts.C: Network ACLs apply at the subnet level, have a hard limit on the number of rules, and would require manually maintaining lists of addresses that keep changing.
opts.D: GuardDuty detects suspicious activity, but it has no rate-limiting capability at all.

438.key: The auditor needs its own copy of the database in its own account, and it has to be shared as securely as possible. The standard mechanism is an encrypted RDS snapshot: it's shared directly with the specified account, and to let the recipient read it, they're granted access to the KMS key that encrypted the snapshot. The auditor then restores the database on their own side. No exported files, no credentials handed over. Keep in mind the limitation: a snapshot encrypted with the AWS managed default key can't be shared — you need your own customer managed key, as in {{q:349}}.

opts.A: A read replica stays in your account and your VPC, but the auditor needs its own copy. "IAM standard database authentication" also isn't a real mechanism: what exists is IAM database authentication, and it doesn't solve the problem of handing over a copy.
opts.B: Exporting to text files loses the schema, indexes, and data types, and it means creating an IAM user for an outside party inside your own account. That's both more work and less secure.
opts.C: Handing an IAM user's access keys to an external party is a direct violation of basic security practice — those are long-lived credentials that belong inside your account.

439.key: You can add an additional IPv4 CIDR block to a running VPC — up to four secondary CIDRs on top of the primary. This is done in place, with no downtime and no need to move resources: new subnets are created in the new range, and new instances launch into them. Routing within the VPC across all the blocks works automatically.

opts.B: A second VPC with peering is a separate network with its own route tables, its own security groups, and ongoing maintenance. The problem can be solved by changing a single setting.
opts.C: Transit Gateway solves the same problem even more heavily, and at extra cost: attachment charges and per-GB data processing charges.
opts.D: A homegrown VPN on an EC2 instance between two VPCs is maximum complexity, an extra point of failure, and paying for instances that do nothing useful.

440.key: There are two backups of different kinds, and each is migrated its own way. The final RDS for MySQL snapshot can be restored directly into an Aurora MySQL-compatible cluster — this is a standard console operation (A). The dump taken with mysqldump is uploaded to an S3 bucket and imported into Aurora from there (C).

opts.B: RDS snapshots can't be exported to S3 as a file for later import: restoration happens directly from the snapshot.
opts.D: DMS works against a running database as its source, not an RDS snapshot: a snapshot isn't a supported DMS source.
opts.E: Likewise, a dump sitting in an S3 bucket isn't a source DMS can use — importing a dump into Aurora is done through Aurora's own standard procedure.

441.key: Instances get added because of the static content they serve — and that is the most expensive kind of work for a compute fleet. Move the static content into an S3 bucket and serve it through CloudFront: caching at edge locations absorbs the overwhelming majority of requests, the instances stop scaling in response to this traffic, and costs drop.

opts.A: Reserved Instances give a discount, but the fleet still grows under static-content load: you would still pay for the extra instances, just at a lower rate.
opts.B: Spot Instances are cheaper, but AWS can reclaim them at any time, and the root cause of the fleet growth is not addressed.
opts.D: A Lambda function behind API Gateway to serve static files is an awkward design that ends up noticeably more expensive than S3 and CloudFront.

442.key: The data lives across multiple accounts, and it needs to be shared selectively without manual work every time the shared data set changes. Lake Formation addresses this with tag-based access control (LF-TBAC): tags are attached to databases, tables, and columns, and permissions are granted not on specific objects but on tag combinations — including across accounts. When a new table appears with the right tag, engineers automatically get access without any grant changes. No data copies are created in the process.

opts.A: Copying data into a common account means duplicating petabytes, copies drifting out of sync, and extra storage costs.
opts.B: Manually granting permissions in each account for every object scales linearly with the number of tables — exactly what tag-based access control eliminates.
opts.C: AWS Data Exchange is designed for publishing data sets to external subscribers, not for internal access control within a data lake.

443.key: Users worldwide both upload and download unique files up to several gigabytes in size. Uniqueness matters here: there is nothing to cache, so the win comes not from a cache but from a shorter, more reliable path to the bucket. S3 Transfer Acceleration routes traffic to the nearest edge location and then over the AWS backbone, speeding up both uploads and downloads.

opts.B: Cache-control headers help with repeated requests for the same objects, but the data here is unique to each user.
opts.C: CloudFront is optimized for serving and caching content; it does not speed up uploads of unique multi-gigabyte files, and the instance fleet adds cost on top.
opts.D: An in-memory cache within a single Region has no bearing on transferring gigabyte-sized files or on global latency.

444.key: Reliability is failing on two fronts, and both need to be addressed. Database: switch to a Multi-AZ configuration plus deletion protection, so the manual-deletion incident cannot repeat. Web tier: put the instances behind a load balancer in an Auto Scaling group spanning multiple Availability Zones, so an instance failure or the loss of an entire zone does not take the application down.

opts.A: Keeping a single instance with termination protection is a step backward: the failure of that one machine or its zone still means downtime.
opts.C: Writing to two databases through a custom function is homegrown replication that has to be built and maintained, instead of using the built-in Multi-AZ configuration.
opts.D: The web tier is improved, but the database is still left without deletion protection or redundancy, so the original cause of the outage is not fixed; Spot Instances can also be reclaimed at any time.

445.key: Check whether the transfer fits the deadline: 700 TB over a 10 Gbps link takes roughly a week of continuous transfer, and the deadline is 90 days. So the link is sufficient, and physical devices are not needed. AWS DataSync, with an agent in the data center, moves data from the NAS to S3 incrementally, verifies integrity, automatically retries failed transfers, and does not get in the way of ongoing file access: files can still be accessed and updated during the transfer, and rerunning the task catches up on the difference.

opts.B: Snowball devices are for when the link is not big enough. Here the link is sufficient, and "mount a target S3 bucket on the on-premises file system" describes an operation that does not exist.
opts.C: rsync at this scale is slow and non-parallel, provides neither service-level integrity checking nor automatic retries, and the scripts would have to be maintained by hand.
opts.D: Tapes and shipping them are the slowest and least controllable path, and mounting a bucket as a file system still is not possible.

446.key: A legal requirement to retain data for 7 years means no one — including an administrator or root — should be able to delete an object. That is S3 Object Lock's compliance retention mode: while the retention period is in force, an object version cannot be deleted or overwritten, and the period itself cannot be shortened. Governance mode does not fit here: anyone with the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission can bypass it. The second half of the question concerns existing objects: Object Lock applies to new versions, and bringing millions of existing objects into compliance with the least effort is what S3 Batch Operations does — it applies retention settings in bulk from an S3 Inventory report.

opts.A: Versioning and MFA Delete make deletion harder, but do not prevent it: an administrator can still remove versions. The lifecycle rule that deletes data after 7 years is solving an unrelated problem here — it protects nothing.
opts.B: Governance mode can be removed by a user with the corresponding permission, so it does not satisfy the legal requirement. Plus it still requires manually recopying every object.
opts.C: The retention mode chosen is correct, but "recopy all existing objects" means rewriting the entire data set by hand — scripts, transfer traffic, error handling. S3 Batch Operations accomplishes the same thing as a managed job, so this option loses on the LEAST operational overhead criterion.

447.key: DNS distributes traffic across Regions: health checks in each Region combined with an active-active failover configuration in Route 53 (A) give both load balancing and automatic removal of a failed Region. This is the standard construct for public regional API Gateway endpoints.

opts.B: CloudFront does not have health checks in the sense needed here: an origin group fails over based on response error codes, not an independent health check of a Region, and you cannot build active-active distribution across Regions this way.
opts.C: Transit Gateway routes traffic between VPCs and on-premises networks. API Gateway is a public service endpoint — it cannot be attached to a Transit Gateway.
opts.D: An ALB cannot target an API Gateway hostname, and the load balancer itself lives in a single Region and becomes a single point of failure — the exact opposite of what is needed.

448.key: The single point of failure is stated right in the question: the VPN from the Management VPC runs through a single customer gateway device in the data center. The standard AWS fix is a second physical device and a second set of tunnels from it: each Site-to-Site connection already has two tunnels, but both terminate on the same hardware. A second router removes that dependency. Production already has redundancy — two Direct Connect connections.

opts.A: A VPN between the VPCs does not remove the dependency on the single device in the data center; it just adds a parallel path alongside what peering already covers.
opts.B: A VPC can have only one virtual private gateway, and the failed element here is not the gateway — it is the equipment on the company's side.
opts.D: A second peering connection between the same two VPCs cannot be created, and peering itself is a managed, redundant service, not a point of failure.

449.key: The application needs third-party database features that require privileged access — standard RDS does not grant that kind of access. Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle keeps managed backups and maintenance while still giving the administrator that access: it is cheaper and faster than managing the database on EC2.

opts.A: Replacing the third-party features with cloud services means reworking the application, but the company wants to migrate quickly and has limited resources.
opts.C: Oracle on EC2 gives full access, but it hands the company back all the administration and backup work it is trying to get away from.
opts.D: Moving to PostgreSQL and rewriting the code is the longest and most expensive path, and directly contradicts the requirement to migrate quickly.

450.key: The Well-Architected Framework calls for tier separation, fault tolerance, and least privilege. The application is split into three tiers, each in its own private subnet across two Availability Zones, with Auto Scaling groups for the web and application tiers (C). A load balancer sits in front of the web tier, and access between tiers is controlled through security groups that reference each other (E). The database is deployed as a Multi-AZ cluster in private subnets and accepts connections only from the application tier's security group (F).

opts.A: Keeping the original monolithic architecture on instances does not meet the best-practices requirement: the tiers are not separated, and there is no load balancer.
opts.B: A single database instance is a single point of failure, so the resiliency requirement is not met.
opts.D: The access rule is correct, but a single database without a Multi-AZ configuration is still a single point of failure.

451.key: This is a shared responsibility model question. The company's operational team retains what it configures itself: creating the RDS instance and setting the scheduled maintenance window (B), installing and configuring additional software inside ECS containers and on ECS hosts — monitoring, application patch management, log collection, and host intrusion detection (C), and encrypting data in transit over Direct Connect, since Direct Connect itself does not encrypt traffic (F).

opts.A: The infrastructure layer, operating system, and platform of the managed RDS database are handled by AWS — the customer simply has no access to them.
opts.D: AWS applies the database engine patches during the maintenance window. The customer only chooses the timing and decides when to apply version upgrades.
opts.E: Physical security of the data centers is AWS's responsibility — "security of the cloud" itself.

452.key: The job runs for ten seconds once an hour and needs one gigabyte of memory. A Lambda function with 1 GB of memory, triggered by an EventBridge scheduled rule, is billed only for those ten seconds — roughly two and a half minutes of runtime per day instead of an instance running around the clock.

opts.A: A Fargate task is billed with a minimum billing increment and includes container startup time, which is noticeably more expensive for a ten-second job.
opts.C: The instance stays running and is billed regardless of whether the container is actually doing work.
opts.D: Stopping and starting the instance every hour saves some cost, but the boot time is comparable to the job itself, and managing that cycle adds operational work.

453.key: The regulator requires that the copies cannot be altered or deleted before the retention period ends. AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode makes the lock irreversible: once the cooling-off period ends, no one can remove it, not even the account's root user.

opts.A: Governance mode also locks changes, but users with a special permission can remove the lock — that is not enough to satisfy a regulatory requirement.
opts.B: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager takes scheduled volume snapshots, but it does not guarantee immutability and does not cover S3 buckets.
opts.C: S3 File Gateway is a gateway for accessing S3 over file protocols, not a backup tool; lifecycle rules manage storage classes, not a prohibition on modification.

454.key: The requirement is not just to list resources but to build a map of the relationships between workloads across multiple accounts and Regions. The purpose-built Workload Discovery on AWS solution does exactly that: it collects data from the accounts and automatically draws architecture diagrams.

opts.A: Systems Manager Inventory collects software information from managed instances and does not show relationships between services.
opts.B: Step Functions is a process orchestrator; the data it gathers would still need to be diagrammed manually, making this the most labor-intensive path.
opts.D: X-Ray traces requests within an instrumented application and does not provide an overall map of account resources.

455.key: Both an alert and automatic prevention of resource provisioning are needed once the threshold is reached. In AWS Budgets this takes three steps. The budget is created in the billing console of the required account (B). For the budget to take action on your behalf, it needs an IAM role with the necessary permissions — a role, not a user, because the action is performed by the service itself (D). The budget action itself is to apply an SCP that denies resource creation once the threshold is crossed (F). An alert is configured alongside the action.

opts.A: Cost and Usage Reports is a detailed export of cost data, not where a budget is defined.
opts.C: Budget actions are performed by the service assuming a role. An IAM user with long-lived keys is not used for this.
opts.E: An AWS Config rule flags noncompliance but does not prevent resource creation. The budget action must apply an SCP or IAM policy, not a Config rule.

456.key: The requirement is cross-Region backups plus centralized management from a single account, all done cost-effectively. AWS Backup covers all of it: a backup plan with a copy rule to the second Region, a single console and reporting, and billing only for the storage of the copies. There is no need to keep any running instances in the second Region.

opts.A: A full fleet copy in the second Region is billed around the clock — the most expensive of these approaches.
opts.B: Manually copying volume snapshots is possible, but it means building your own automation, with no unified retention plan and no centralized management.
opts.D: Running instances in the second Region plus continuous synchronization via DataSync costs several times more than a backup plan.

457.key: In AWS, exactly one service supports the AS2 protocol — AWS Transfer Family (alongside SFTP, FTPS, and FTP). Authentication can still be performed by the company's own identity provider: Transfer Family can invoke a Lambda function as a custom identity provider, which validates the user against the external system and returns the permissions and home directory. No servers need to be stood up.

opts.A: DataSync moves files between storage systems and does not support the AS2 protocol.
opts.B: AppFlow integrates with SaaS applications through their APIs. AS2 is not among its connectors.
opts.D: Storage Gateway provides hybrid access to storage, not AS2 data exchange, and Cognito is not an authentication mechanism for this transfer protocol.

458.key: The workload needs roughly one gigabyte of memory for computation and a relational data store, with minimal administrative effort. AWS Lambda runs the logic behind API Gateway — no servers at all (B), while Amazon RDS stores the data as a managed relational database (C).

opts.A: EC2 instances require patching, scaling, and monitoring — the most administrative effort of the options.
opts.D: DynamoDB is not a relational database, and the requirement explicitly calls for a relational data format.
opts.E: An EKS cluster is the most operationally intensive option listed and is overkill for a single API function.

459.key: For costs to be broken down by department across every account, the tag must become a cost allocation tag. It can only be activated in the organization's management account, from the billing console, and since the company created the tag itself, it is a user-defined tag rather than one AWS applies automatically (which use the aws: prefix). Once activated, Cost Explorer can build a report grouped by that tag and filtered to EC2 — a single report covering the whole organization.

opts.B: AWS-defined tags are the ones the platform itself creates, using the aws: prefix. The department tag was created by the company, so it is a user-defined tag.
opts.C: Cost allocation tags cannot be activated from a member account: this must be done in the organization's management account.
opts.D: This option compounds two errors: the wrong account and the wrong tag type.

460.key: The task is to regularly and securely move data from Salesforce to S3, encrypting it with a customer-owned KMS key. Amazon AppFlow was built for exactly this: it has a ready-made Salesforce connector, transfers data over TLS, lets you configure the flow without code, and lets you specify a customer managed KMS key when writing to S3. AppFlow can also route traffic through PrivateLink so it never touches the public internet. Every other option involves building this connector yourself.

opts.A: Lambda functions mean writing your own integration code against the Salesforce API: authentication, pagination, retries, and handling schema changes. A managed connector does all of this for you.
opts.B: Step Functions orchestrates steps, but the actual Salesforce calls would still need to be written. An orchestrator does not replace a connector.
opts.D: A custom connector represents the most development and maintenance effort when a managed service already delivers the same result.

461.key: The traffic is both TCP and UDP, which means the load balancer must be a network-level one — an Application Load Balancer works with HTTP only. The lowest latency globally comes from Global Accelerator: the player enters the AWS network at the nearest edge location and then travels over the AWS backbone to the Region where the NLB sits with the Auto Scaling group's instances registered.

opts.A: ALB does not support UDP: part of the game traffic simply would not get through.
opts.C: CloudFront works only with HTTP and HTTPS, so it cannot serve TCP on a non-standard port or UDP.
opts.D: This has two errors at once: CloudFront is not applicable to this kind of traffic, and ALB does not support UDP.

462.key: During a traffic spike, orders arrive faster than a single instance can write them. An SQS queue accepts orders instantly and holds them until they're processed, so nothing is lost, and the Auto Scaling group reads from the queue and scales based on queue length — processing speeds up exactly when it's needed.

opts.A: Manually increasing instance size can't keep up with spikes, and subscribing the database endpoint to an SNS topic isn't possible: SNS can't write to a database.
opts.C: SNS delivers messages immediately and doesn't buffer them: it doesn't smooth out the spike, and subscribing the database to the topic is still not possible.
opts.D: Scheduled scaling doesn't react to unpredictable spikes, and switching to the queue only after a CPU threshold is reached means some orders are already lost.

463.key: The task is tiny: two megabytes of data, a gigabyte of memory, thirty seconds of runtime, triggered by an event. This is a textbook fit for a Lambda function: it fits within both the memory limit and the time limit, is billed per second, and starts immediately after the file is uploaded.

opts.A: An AWS Glue job is billed for a minimum of one DPU-hour and takes minutes to start — overkill and expensive for thirty seconds of processing.
opts.B: An EMR cluster running Spark for two megabytes of data is a mismatch of scale, plus it means constantly running infrastructure.
opts.D: The same Glue, just with PySpark: the same minimum billing rates and the same startup time.

464.key: The single point of failure is the Single-AZ instance, and it's eliminated by turning on Multi-AZ right in the settings of the existing instance. AWS creates a standby copy in another Availability Zone and replicates data synchronously; on failover the endpoint name stays the same, so the application code doesn't need to change. The switch happens in place, with no migration.

opts.B: A snapshot-based approach works, but it means extra downtime for the restore and a change of endpoint, and the result is the same as simply modifying the setting.
opts.C: A read replica is not a tool for write fault tolerance, and Route 53 weighted records would send part of the requests to a read-only replica: the application would break the moment it tries to write.
opts.D: RDS is a managed service — its instances are not placed in an EC2 Auto Scaling group. No such configuration exists.

465.key: Simultaneous writes from multiple instances to a single volume is the Multi-Attach feature, and it's supported only by Provisioned IOPS volumes: io1 and io2. Of the options given, io2 qualifies, and the instances must be Nitro-based and in the same Availability Zone, which the scenario already states.

opts.A: gp3 volumes don't support Multi-Attach: this configuration simply can't be created.
opts.B: st1 volumes, on magnetic disks, also don't support Multi-Attach.
opts.D: gp2 has no Multi-Attach support.

466.key: The only weak point here is the web tier: the database is already Multi-AZ, but the EC2 instances sit in a single Availability Zone. The application is stateless, so it's enough to stretch the Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones and put an Application Load Balancer in front of it — it distributes requests and excludes unhealthy targets, while the group restores the needed instance count if a zone fails.

opts.B: Snapshots to another Region are backup, not high availability: restoring from them takes time and manual action.
opts.C: Latency-based routing makes sense when there are multiple deployed locations. Here there's only one location, and this policy adds no redundancy at all.
opts.D: A load balancer operates across multiple Availability Zones by definition, but without an Auto Scaling group spread across those zones it has nowhere to route traffic if a zone fails.

467.key: In an organization with consolidated billing, discounts from Savings Plans and Reserved Instances are shared across all accounts by default: an unused commitment in one account automatically covers matching usage in other accounts. This is controlled by the discount sharing switch (RI/SP sharing), located in the billing settings of the organization's management account — a member account cannot change this setting. Turning on sharing is exactly how you put the purchased commitment to full use without migrating workloads.

opts.A: The discount sharing setting is available only in the organization's management account. There's no such switch in a member account.
opts.C: Migrating workloads between accounts is a project with downtime and risk, for something a single billing setting already solves.
opts.D: The Reserved Instance Marketplace only sells standard EC2 Reserved Instances. Savings Plans cannot be resold.

468.key: Users need a REST API, and the backend runs in containers in private subnets. A REST-type API Gateway connects to them through a private VPC link: a link is created to a Network Load Balancer in front of the ECS service, and traffic flows over the internal network with no public addresses.

opts.A: A WebSocket API is meant for persistent, bidirectional connections, and the requirement explicitly calls for REST.
opts.C: Both the API type is wrong, and a security group doesn't give API Gateway network access into a private subnet — a VPC link is required for that.
opts.D: The API type is correct, but you can't connect to a private subnet through a security group — a VPC link is specifically required.

469.key: The key phrase is "cannot predict or control the access pattern": the pattern is set by the customer, depending on the type of analytics they order. Anything that requires guessing an object's age or paying retrieval fees works against you here. Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between tiers on its own, based on actual access, and charges no retrieval fee, so an unexpected analytics request doesn't turn into a surprise bill.

opts.A: Replication copies objects into another bucket rather than changing the storage class of existing ones. With this setup you pay for two copies instead of saving.
opts.B: Transitioning to Standard-IA by age assumes that after N days the object really does stop being read. The requirement explicitly says this can't be predicted, and every access to IA will be charged.
opts.D: S3 Inventory is a report — it doesn't move objects; moving them would still be the job of a Lifecycle rule. On top of that, manually analyzing access patterns duplicates what Intelligent-Tiering already does automatically.

470.key: The addresses are IPv6, outbound connections are needed, inbound connections are prohibited. This is exactly what an egress-only internet gateway is for: it allows traffic initiated from inside and returns responses over the connection's state, but doesn't let anything be opened from outside.

opts.A: A NAT gateway works only with IPv4; it doesn't apply to IPv6.
opts.B: A regular internet gateway is bidirectional: external services would be able to initiate a connection to the instances.
opts.C: A virtual private gateway is the attachment point for VPN and Direct Connect — it has nothing to do with internet egress.

471.key: There are two requirements here: keep traffic off the public internet, and avoid unnecessary cost at 1 TB per day. A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 adds a route to the VPC's route tables, so traffic to S3 travels over the AWS internal network — and, crucially, the endpoint itself is free, with no charge for the gigabytes that pass through it. An interface endpoint is also private, but it is billed hourly per Availability Zone plus per gigabyte processed: at 1 TB a day that adds up to a meaningful sum. Remember the distinction: the gateway endpoint exists only for S3 and DynamoDB and costs nothing, while every other service is reached only through an interface endpoint.
