opts.A: A storage class changes storage cost, not the traffic path. The requirement to keep data off the internet is not met.
opts.B: Transfer Acceleration does the opposite: it routes traffic through the global network of edge locations and charges extra for it. That is both more expensive and not private.
opts.D: An interface endpoint does solve the privacy requirement, but it is billed hourly plus per gigabyte, so at 1 TB a day it loses to the free gateway endpoint. On top of that, an interface endpoint is created in subnets with security groups rather than being "associated with route tables" — that association is exactly how the gateway endpoint works.

472.key: The requirement is minimal read latency for new messages with minimal application changes. DAX is DynamoDB's built-in in-memory cache, serving data in microseconds; it's compatible with the same API, so the change amounts to swapping the endpoint address for the DAX cluster endpoint.

opts.B: DynamoDB has no read replicas: read scaling is done through capacity, global tables, or DAX.
opts.C: Doubling the read capacity units removes throttling, but response time stays in the millisecond range — there is no latency improvement.
opts.D: A Redis cache would deliver low latency, but it requires its own cache-loading and invalidation logic in the code, meaning substantial application changes.

473.key: The site serves static content and traffic is growing, so costs are being incurred both for data transfer out of the Region and for the instances handling repeated requests. CloudFront addresses both: files are cached at edge locations, so repeat requests never reach the load balancer or the instances, and data transfer out of CloudFront is cheaper than transferring directly out of EC2. It also reduces latency for users far from the origin.

opts.B: ElastiCache is a cache for application data (sessions, query results), not for serving files to clients. The load balancer has no way to serve content out of ElastiCache.
opts.C: AWS WAF filters requests and caches nothing — it has no such capability.
opts.D: A second load balancer in another Region means a second copy of the infrastructure, and it does not reduce the cost of serving static content.

474.key: There are multiple VPCs across Regions, all of them need connectivity to each other, and administrative overhead must be minimized. Transit Gateway acts as a central router within a Region: each VPC connects through a single attachment, and the number of connections grows linearly. Between Regions, the gateways connect through transit gateway peering. The number of objects to configure is minimal, and routing is managed in the gateway's route tables.

opts.A: A mesh of peering connections grows quadratically: for n networks you need n times (n minus one) divided by two connections, and every route table ends up with an entry for each partner. That's hard to administer, and peering does not support transitive routing.
opts.B: Direct Connect gateway is for connecting an on-premises location to a VPC — it does not provide VPC-to-VPC connectivity.
opts.D: PrivateLink publishes a single service through an endpoint and gives one-way access to it, not full network connectivity between all the VPCs.

475.key: There are three requirements: a file system with a mount target in every Availability Zone, high durability, and replication to another Region via AWS Backup with an RPO of 8 hours. Amazon EFS with the Standard storage class satisfies all of them: data is stored across multiple Availability Zones, mount targets are created in every zone, and AWS Backup can copy EFS backups to another Region on a schedule.

opts.A: FSx for Windows File Server uses the SMB protocol, and in a Multi-AZ deployment it has a single active endpoint rather than a mount target in every zone.
opts.B: FSx for NetApp ONTAP in a Multi-AZ deployment likewise has a single active endpoint for access, not a separate mount target in each Availability Zone.
opts.D: FSx for OpenZFS deploys in a single Availability Zone, so the availability requirement is not met.

476.key: Permissions in IAM are granted through policies, and groups exist precisely so a policy can be attached once for an entire department. A new hire joins the group and automatically picks up the right permission set, and a policy change applies to everyone at once. A role doesn't fit here: a role can't be attached to a group — it's assumed, not inherited through group membership. Least privilege comes from the content of the policy itself: only the actions needed on the resources needed.

opts.A: SCPs are an organization-level tool that caps the maximum permissions available in accounts. They don't grant anything, so new users would still end up with no permissions.
opts.B: A role cannot be attached to an IAM group: a role is assumed by a principal through AssumeRole, not inherited through group membership.
opts.D: A permissions boundary sets a ceiling on what a user or role can be granted, but it doesn't grant any permissions by itself. Without a policy, no permissions actually appear.

477.key: The mistake in the original policy is a classic one: actions on objects and actions on the bucket require different ARNs. s3:ListBucket applies to the bucket itself (arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name), while s3:DeleteObject applies to the objects inside it (arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name/*). The policy only specifies the bucket ARN, which is why deletion doesn't work. Exactly one permission needs to be added — s3:DeleteObject on arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name/* — and nothing beyond that, since the company follows least privilege.

opts.A: The s3:*Object wildcard grants GetObject, PutObject, RestoreObject, and other actions the group never asked for. The ARN is correct, but the permissions go beyond what's needed.
opts.B: s3:* is literally every S3 operation on the bucket's objects. Of the options given, this is the most severe violation of least privilege.
opts.C: The action is correct, but the ARN "arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name*" is still bucket-level scope (and, incidentally, covers every bucket whose name starts the same way). It doesn't cover the objects inside the bucket, so deletion still won't work.

478.key: The two requirements pull in opposite directions: the files must be publicly readable, yet unmodifiable until a set date. Public read access comes from a bucket policy granting s3:GetObject to anonymous requests (typically paired with static website hosting), while immutability comes from S3 Object Lock with a retention period set to the target date, layered on top of versioning. One key detail rules out half the options: anonymous readers' access is governed by a bucket policy, not IAM permissions — the public has no AWS accounts to grant anything to.

opts.A: IAM permissions apply only to AWS principals, and "the public" isn't one: the files would either stay inaccessible or become accessible through some other mechanism entirely. And there's no protection against modification here at all.
opts.C: A function that restores the object from a backup after it's been modified is a reaction after the fact. The requirement is that modification be impossible in the first place.
opts.D: Object Lock is enabled at the bucket level (and requires versioning) — you can't select a "folder" and protect just that. Plus it repeats the same IAM-permissions mistake for anonymous readers.

479.key: A manually built prototype needs to become a repeatable deployment. AWS CloudFormation describes the whole infrastructure as a template: the Auto Scaling group, the load balancer, and the database are all created in one operation, and identical development and production environments are deployed from the same template with different parameters.

opts.A: Systems Manager manages resources that already exist and does not describe infrastructure as code.
opts.C: AWS Config records configuration state and checks compliance, but it doesn't create anything.
opts.D: Elastic Beanstalk deploys applications using its own platform templates and cannot replicate arbitrary existing infrastructure.

480.key: The requirement is framed around the network path: traffic between EC2 and S3 must not travel over the public internet. Only a VPC endpoint changes that path — for S3 this is typically the free gateway endpoint, which adds a route to the route table pointing at the service's prefix inside the AWS network. Encryption, subnet type, and gateways to an on-premises network have no effect on this path. Access is also commonly further restricted using the aws:SourceVpce condition in the bucket policy.

opts.A: KMS encrypts the objects but doesn't change the packet's path: the encrypted data would still travel over S3's public endpoint.
opts.C: An instance in a private subnet without an endpoint reaches S3 through a NAT gateway — that is, over the internet. A private subnet by itself doesn't satisfy the requirement.
opts.D: A virtual private gateway is the connection point for a VPC to an on-premises network over VPN or Direct Connect. It has nothing to do with requests to S3.

481.key: The requirement is stated literally: data must land in the cache at the moment of writing, and the cache contents must always match the database. That's the write-through strategy — on every write, the application updates both the database and the cache, so stale values never occur.

opts.A: Lazy loading only puts data into the cache after a read miss, so between the write and the first read, the cache lags behind the database.
opts.C: A TTL limits how long a discrepancy can persist, but it doesn't eliminate it and doesn't update the cache when data is added.
opts.D: AWS AppConfig distributes application configuration parameters and is not a data caching strategy.

482.key: This question is flagged as disputed: both reasonable options satisfy the requirements, and everything hinges on how you read "least operational overhead." The math says the link is fast enough: 100 GB over a 100 Mbps connection takes roughly 2.5 hours, so an offline transfer isn't needed. In-transit encryption comes from TLS, which both approaches provide. The corrected key selects AWS DataSync: the agent splits the transfer into parallel streams, retries failed chunks, and verifies data integrity on its own. The case for aws s3 sync is that it's a single command with no deployed component at all, whereas DataSync means standing up and running an agent for a one-time job. The practical rule of thumb: reach for DataSync for recurring or large transfers that need verification, and for the CLI for a one-off copy of tens to hundreds of gigabytes.

opts.A: A strong alternative: the aws s3 sync command runs over HTTPS, uses multipart upload, and requires nothing to be deployed. Its weak point is that it lacks DataSync's built-in integrity checking and automatic retries.
opts.C: AWS Snowball is an offline transfer method for 100 GB of data that would move over the network in a couple of hours anyway. Ordering, waiting for, copying to, and shipping back a device is disproportionate effort.
opts.D: An IPsec VPN adds a second layer of encryption on top of the already-secured TLS connection to S3 and requires setting up and maintaining a tunnel. It's an extra component with no payoff.

483.key: The job is short, runs every ten minutes, and is packaged as a Windows container. Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate supports Windows containers and lets you create a scheduled task: the container spins up, runs for one to three minutes, and terminates, so you pay only for that runtime and there are no servers to manage.

opts.A: AWS Lambda cannot run Windows containers: only Linux-based images are supported.
opts.B: AWS Batch on Fargate resources does not support Windows containers, so the job would not run.
opts.D: Windows Task Scheduler runs inside the operating system, and with the Fargate launch type there's simply no underlying machine for it to live on.

484.key: This is a two-part task. First, move to a multi-account architecture: create an organization in AWS Organizations with all features enabled so SCPs and centralized management become available, and create the new accounts inside it (A). Second, provide single sign-on through the existing corporate directory: that's AWS IAM Identity Center, connected to the company's directory as the identity source, with permission sets assigned to accounts (E). Users sign in with their corporate credentials and receive temporary roles in the appropriate accounts.

opts.B: Amazon Cognito is meant for application end users, not employees. IAM Identity Center does not accept Cognito as a corporate identity source.
opts.C: An SCP governs restrictions, not authentication, and "add IAM Identity Center to AWS Directory Service" gets the order backwards: the directory is connected to Identity Center as its identity source, not the other way around.
opts.D: The organization itself has no authentication mechanism: sign-in is configured in IAM Identity Center, while Organizations is responsible for account structure and policies.

485.key: Two numbers settle this: access is rare, and the retrieval time cannot exceed five minutes. Instant-access classes (IA) satisfy the timing requirement but are expensive for data that sits idle for years, while S3 Glacier Deep Archive can't meet a five-minute window. That leaves S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval with Expedited retrievals: an expedited retrieval returns the archive in 1–5 minutes, versus 3–5 hours for a standard retrieval. You pay the expedited retrieval cost only when you actually need the data, while storage the rest of the time is billed at the archive rate.

opts.B: A Standard retrieval from S3 Glacier takes 3–5 hours, which violates the "maximum of five minutes" requirement.
opts.C: S3 Standard-IA returns objects instantly, but its storage cost is roughly three times that of S3 Glacier. Given the requirement to minimize cost and the rarity of restores, that's paying a premium for speed needed maybe once a year.
opts.D: S3 One Zone-IA is cheaper than S3 Standard-IA, but its storage cost is still higher than S3 Glacier's, and it keeps only a single copy in one Availability Zone — a questionable trade-off for a news footage archive.

486.key: The requirements are simple deployment and low operational costs. S3 hosts the static content with no servers involved at all; ECS on Fargate runs the logic tier's containers without any nodes to manage; a managed RDS cluster stores the data. Every tier is chosen so there's no infrastructure left to maintain.

opts.B: CloudFront doesn't store content by itself — it needs an origin — and running ECS on EC2 instances brings node management back into the picture.
opts.C: Amazon EKS requires managing a Kubernetes cluster and costs more than ECS for the same workload — added complexity with no upside.
opts.D: Hosting static content on Reserved Instances is the most expensive and labor-intensive of these options.

487.key: Gathering the requirements: a file system that can be mounted with native tools both from AWS and from the on-premises network over the already-configured VPN, with no minimum size, that's scalable and highly available. That's Amazon EFS with mount targets in multiple Availability Zones: each mount target serves clients in its own zone, and the on-premises Linux servers mount the file system over NFS through the tunnel.

opts.A: The Amazon FSx family is built for SMB, Lustre, ONTAP, or OpenZFS, and as described it doesn't satisfy the requirement to mount natively from Linux instances with no minimum size.
opts.B: Amazon EBS Multi-Attach attaches a volume to multiple instances only within a single Availability Zone and requires a cluster-aware file system, and such a volume isn't reachable from the on-premises network at all.
opts.D: A single mount target means clients in other zones all route through that one target, turning its zone into a single point of failure. Access points manage permissions, but they don't replace mount targets.

488.key: This is a strict requirement: billing information must be inaccessible to anyone in member accounts, including their root user. IAM policies are powerless here — they have no effect on an account's root user. The only mechanism that can constrain a member account's root user is a service control policy attached to the organization's root or the relevant OU: it sets a permissions ceiling for every principal in the account. The SCP would deny actions such as aws-portal:* (or account:GetAccountInformation and related billing operations).

opts.A: The AWS managed Billing policy grants access, and the requirement is the opposite — to block it. It also has no effect on member accounts' root users.
opts.B: An identity-based policy does not apply to the root user: only an SCP from the organization can restrict root.
opts.D: Switching to the consolidated billing feature set strips the organization of SCPs and other governance tools, making the situation worse rather than solving the problem.

489.key: Undelivered SNS messages are routed to a dead-letter queue — and that target is always an SQS queue attached to the subscription. SQS's retention period can be set up to 14 days, giving plenty of time to analyze the messages afterward. No code needs to be written at all — it's just a subscription setting.

opts.A: An SNS dead-letter queue target can only be an SQS queue; a Kinesis Data Stream is not supported in that role.
opts.B: A queue placed in front of the topic doesn't help: the messages are lost between SNS and the on-premises endpoint, which is downstream of the topic.
opts.D: A DynamoDB table also cannot serve as the target of an SNS dead-letter queue.

490.key: DynamoDB has a built-in table export to S3 that runs on top of continuous backups, so it requires point-in-time recovery to be turned on. The export reads from the backup, not from the live table, so it consumes no read capacity units and has no effect on application availability. No code is required.

opts.A: An Amazon EMR cluster running a Hive job reads the table itself, consuming read capacity units, and adds infrastructure to manage.
opts.C: Streams plus a Lambda function mean writing and maintaining custom processing code, whereas the built-in export accomplishes the same thing with a single setting.
opts.D: A periodic export via a Lambda function means both code and reading the table, and it's not a continuous backup but a scheduled snapshot.

491.key: Three requirements: asynchronous processing, "at least once" delivery, and minimal cost with proper protection. "At least once" is exactly the guarantee that standard SQS queues provide, and standard queues are cheaper than FIFO queues and aren't limited by FIFO's throughput; FIFO is needed when strict ordering and exactly-once processing matter, and this scenario doesn't require that. Encrypting the card data with a KMS key the company manages makes sense here. Finally, the kms:Decrypt permission is granted to the function's execution role — the role, not the "function," is the IAM principal.

opts.B: A FIFO queue is more expensive than a standard queue and isn't needed here: the requirement is at-least-once delivery, not strict ordering. An SQS managed key also doesn't give the company control over the key, which is usually required for payment data.
opts.C: The encryption choice is correct, but FIFO again imposes unnecessary guarantees and extra cost compared with a standard queue.
opts.D: The queue type and encryption are correct, but the permissions are described incorrectly: the permission to use the KMS key (kms:Decrypt) is granted to the Lambda execution role, not to the "function" itself.

492.key: The restriction needs to apply centrally across multiple accounts without requiring development work. That calls for an SCP: the development accounts are grouped into a separate OU, and a policy with a Deny on ec2:RunInstances is attached, conditioned on the instance type not being in the allowed list (the ec2:InstanceType condition). The deny applies to every principal in the accounts, including root, and can't be bypassed with local policies. There's no code or product catalog to maintain.

opts.A: Systems Manager templates describe a process but don't prohibit anything: staff can still launch an instance outside the template.
opts.C: Reacting with a function after an instance has already been created means writing code and paying for the time a large instance ran before being caught. There's no preventive block.
opts.D: Service Catalog provides a convenient catalog of approved configurations, but it requires preparing products and doesn't stop instances from being created directly unless permissions are restricted separately.

493.key: The pipeline is built from three managed services, each handling one step. Amazon Transcribe converts the call recordings into text in any supported language (D). Amazon Translate translates that text into English (E). Amazon Comprehend performs the sentiment analysis and produces the material for the reports (F). No custom machine learning models need to be maintained at any step.

opts.A: Comprehend analyzes text — it can neither translate nor transcribe audio.
opts.B: Amazon Lex builds conversational bots, not sentiment analysis reports.
opts.C: Amazon Polly works in the opposite direction — it turns text into speech.

494.key: The policy contains two statements: an Allow for ec2:TerminateInstances and an explicit Deny on the same action with a NotIpAddress condition on aws:SourceIp. It reads as "deny everyone whose source IP address is not in 192.0.2.0/24 or 203.0.113.0/24." The administrator is calling the API from a network that isn't on that list, so the Deny fires and a 403 is returned. This is a common pattern: allow an action, then deny it unless the source matches a condition — used to restrict operations to a corporate network or VPN.

opts.A: The EC2 instance has no resource-based policy — those exist on buckets, queues, topics, and KMS keys. The denial comes from the condition in this same IAM policy.
opts.B: An identity-based policy never specifies a Principal element — the principal is whoever the policy is attached to. Its absence is not an error.
opts.C: The action is specified correctly: ec2:TerminateInstances is exactly what's needed to terminate the instance, and it's granted by the first statement.

495.key: The task is to find personal and financial data inside S3 objects: passport numbers, card numbers. That's exactly what Amazon Macie with managed data identifiers is for: it runs a discovery job, scans the objects (including sampling, so you don't pay to scan everything), and returns findings with the data type and location. There's no need to write custom rules or regular expressions.

opts.A: Audit Manager collects evidence of compliance against frameworks, but it doesn't analyze object contents.
opts.B: S3 Inventory lists objects and their metadata. It doesn't know what's inside the files.
opts.D: S3 Select runs a query against the content of a single object with a known structure. It's not a tool for searching a bucket for sensitive data.

496.key: The applications use two different kinds of storage, and they can't be rewritten. So the replacement has to match by protocol: a file gateway replaces the NFS storage, serving data from S3 with local caching (B), and a volume gateway replaces the block storage, serving volumes over iSCSI and also caching active data locally (D). Both gateways provide the local caching the requirement calls for.

opts.A: S3 can't be mounted as a file system with native tools, and third-party solutions provide neither caching nor file system semantics.
opts.C: Snowball Edge is meant for data transfer and temporary on-site compute, not for permanently expanding storage.
opts.E: The EFS file system can only be mounted from an on-premises network over private connectivity and has no local cache: latency is dictated by the link, and it doesn't replace block storage at all.

497.key: The cost here isn't for storage — it's that every gigabyte to and from S3 passes through the NAT gateway: both the gateway's hourly charge and the volume of data processed are billed. A gateway VPC endpoint removes NAT from this path entirely — a route to the S3 prefix is added to the private subnet's route table, traffic travels over the AWS network, and there's no charge for the endpoint or for the data that passes through it. This is the only option that actually reduces cost rather than shifting it around. Related questions: {{q:42,91,612}}.

opts.A: A NAT instance replaces a managed service with your own machine: you pay for the instance and its traffic, you're responsible for its fault tolerance, and you're limited by a single node's throughput.
opts.B: This setup isn't possible: NAT must sit in the public subnet, while the route table that needs changing belongs to the private subnet. The option describes a configuration that won't work.
opts.D: A second NAT gateway doubles the hourly charge and does nothing to reduce the volume of gigabytes processed.

498.key: The bucket has versioning enabled, and old (noncurrent) versions of the pictures are what's driving up cost. S3 Lifecycle rules have exactly the pair of settings needed for this: NoncurrentVersionExpiration deletes noncurrent versions, and NewerNoncurrentVersions specifies how many of the most recent ones to keep. Set it to 2, and cleanup happens automatically without a single line of code. The application keeps working with the current version of the object exactly as before.

opts.B: A Lambda function solves this with code you have to write, schedule, handle errors for, and paginate through version listings for. A Lifecycle rule does the same thing through configuration.
opts.C: S3 Batch Operations is a one-time job driven by an S3 Inventory report. You'd have to run it again and again, whereas Lifecycle runs continuously on its own.
opts.D: Deactivating versioning doesn't delete the old versions that have already accumulated — the bill stays the same. And the requirement to keep the two most recent versions becomes impossible to satisfy, since no new versions will ever be created.

499.key: The connection is used at under a tenth of its capacity, so a lower port speed is what's needed. Dedicated connections can only be ordered at 1, 10, or 100 Gbps, while lower speeds — from 50 Mbps to 500 Mbps — exist only as hosted connections, which an AWS Direct Connect Partner provisions. Ordering a 200 Mbps hosted connection into the existing account lowers the port charge without changing the privacy of the path or its security.

opts.A: A second connection at the same 1 Gbps doubles the port charge; sharing it with another account doesn't reduce the company's costs.
opts.B: The console doesn't let you order a dedicated connection at 200 Mbps — only 1 Gbps and above are available there.
opts.C: A gigabit connection through a partner costs about the same as now. The savings come from lowering the port speed, not from changing how the connection is ordered.

500.key: Windows file permissions have to be preserved, so the migration tool needs to understand ACLs — that's AWS DataSync: it carries access control lists and ownership along with the files and can write directly into the FSx for Windows File Server file system. The agent can be deployed as a virtual machine in the data center (A), or, if the network link is weak, run directly on an AWS Snowcone device connected to the local network (D). Both paths deliver the same result.

opts.B: Copying to S3 first using the CLI loses the Windows access control lists: the files become objects, and the ACLs never make it to FSx.
opts.C: Importing the drives into S3 turns the data into objects and loses the permissions the same way, and physically shipping drives gives no control over data integrity.
opts.E: Copying to a Snowball device with the CLI into S3 again turns the files into objects and loses the ACLs. Snowball is only useful here as a platform to run the agent on, not as an S3 waypoint.

501.key: Data arrives on average once a minute and needs to be analyzed on the fly, then stored in the data lake. Kinesis Data Firehose is a fully managed delivery service: it buffers, transforms, and writes to S3 on its own, and it scales without you managing shards. Real-time analysis on top of that stream is handled by Kinesis Data Analytics with an ordinary SQL query. There is nothing left to operate — that is exactly what maximum operational efficiency looks like.

opts.A: Data Streams requires shard management, and analysis in Lambda functions requires custom code.
opts.B: AWS Glue is a batch ETL service; it is not designed to ingest a continuous stream.
opts.D: API Gateway with functions means hand-built ingestion and hand-built analysis instead of two purpose-built managed services.

502.key: There are two weak points: a single instance, and images on a local volume. Moving the images to Amazon EFS and mounting it on every instance means any instance sees the full set of files (C). The site itself becomes an Auto Scaling group of at least two instances behind an Application Load Balancer, built from an AMI, with CloudFront placed in front to cache the images at edge locations and noticeably speed up delivery (E).

opts.A: There is no standard way to mount an S3 bucket as a file system on instances; the application would have to be rewritten to work through the API.
opts.B: Serving files over NFS from the "primary" instance turns it into a single point of failure — resilience gets worse, not better.
opts.D: Fault tolerance improves, but Global Accelerator optimizes the traffic path and does not cache static content. For a site serving images, the real gain comes from CloudFront's cache.

503.key: This is the classic pattern for a third-party service accessing customer accounts: the customer creates a role with minimal permissions themselves (here, read-only EC2 and CloudWatch access) and specifies the provider's account in the trust policy. The service calls AssumeRole and operates on temporary credentials. You never store anyone else's keys, and the customer can revoke access at any time simply by deleting the role. One essential addition from real-world practice: use an external ID in the trust policy to protect against the confused deputy attack.

opts.B: Issuing your own temporary credentials does not solve the underlying problem: to issue them you still need permissions in the customer's account, which again means a role with a trust relationship.
opts.C: Storing IAM user keys for thousands of customers in your own store is the worst option: long-lived secrets, responsibility for keeping them safe, and manual revocation.
opts.D: Cognito is meant for application end users, not cross-account access to AWS APIs. A password in a secrets store is again a long-lived secret.

504.key: Hundreds of accounts and many VPCs in a single Region are exactly the case Transit Gateway was built for. It is deployed in the networking team's account, shared with other accounts through AWS RAM, and each VPC connects with a single attachment. Routing management stays centralized with the networking team — operationally this is the most efficient option.

opts.A: A full mesh of peering connections across hundreds of VPCs means thousands of connections and edits to every route table. That is practically unmanageable.
opts.B: Connecting internal networks over the internet means losing privacy, paying for outbound data transfer, and getting worse latency.
opts.D: A transit VPC built on your own VPN gateways is the legacy pattern that Transit Gateway replaced: it requires its own appliances, is limited by tunnel throughput, and has to be maintained manually.

505.key: The jobs run six hours a day and tolerate interruption: if an instance is lost, another instance reprocesses the job. That profile is the textbook use case for Spot Instances — up to 90 percent savings, and the application's own retry logic already absorbs capacity reclamation.

opts.A: A Savings Plan pays off under round-the-clock load; running only six hours a day would leave the commitment underused.
opts.B: A Reserved Instance is billed continuously, but the instance only runs a quarter of the day.
opts.D: Larger On-Demand instances would only raise the bill further: the billing model itself has not changed.

506.key: The bottleneck is files passing through the application servers. A presigned URL removes it entirely: the application only issues a signed link, and the browser uploads the file straight into S3. The servers take no part in the data transfer, so a traffic spike during major events is bounded only by S3's own scalability, which is effectively unlimited.

opts.A: Files pass through the application servers, and those servers are exactly what becomes the bottleneck during a spike, requiring you to scale out the fleet and its bandwidth.
opts.B: A file gateway is a hybrid gateway for an on-premises location; it has nothing to do with uploads from users' browsers.
opts.D: An EFS file system is mounted on instances inside a VPC; you cannot upload to it directly from a browser.

507.key: The requirement calls for a single, globally consistent reservation store with update latency under one second, deployed across multiple Regions. DynamoDB global tables let you write in any Region with replication to the others typically completing in under a second, and each deployment talks to its own Regional endpoint.

opts.B: Aurora Read Replicas only accept reads: reservation writes would still go to the single writer Region, and latency for remote users would exceed one second.
opts.C: RDS read replicas have the same write problem, and their replication lag is noticeably higher than Aurora's.
opts.D: Separate independent databases with hand-built synchronization through Lambda functions guarantee conflicts and no single consistent state.

508.key: The requirement is automated backups plus a ready-made copy in another Region with no more than 24 hours of data loss. Both working options schedule backups twice a day and copy them automatically to us-west-2: an EC2-backed AMI lifecycle policy driven by tags with copy to the other Region configured (B), and an AWS Backup plan driven by tags with the copy destination specified (D). In both cases, once set up, no further intervention is needed.

opts.A: Copying the image manually on demand is exactly the manual effort the requirement says to avoid, and it gives no guarantee of staying within a day's worth of data.
opts.C: A custom function to move copies around is unnecessary code where AWS Backup already provides built-in cross-Region copy.
opts.E: The schedule is automatic, but the copy to the other Region is still done manually.

509.key: The immediate need is to block specific IP addresses. Explicit deny rules only exist on network ACLs, and they need to be applied to the web-tier subnets, where the load balancer sits and where the attacker's traffic arrives.

opts.A: Security groups have no deny rules: they only allow traffic.
opts.C: Same security group limitation, plus the application tier is the wrong tier to target.
opts.D: The network ACL is the right tool, but it's applied to the application-tier subnets — the malicious traffic never reaches them directly and will keep loading the web tier.

510.key: The application in eu-west-1 needs to reach databases in ap-southeast-2 — this calls for inter-Region VPC peering, updated route tables in both networks, and an inbound rule on the database's security group. One important detail: you cannot reference a security group from another Region — inter-Region peering doesn't support that. So the rule has to specify the application servers' IP addresses or range instead.

opts.A: The rule is added in the wrong place: the inbound allow rule needs to sit on the database side, not the application side. The direction described is also reversed.
opts.B: Referencing a security group ID over inter-Region peering isn't supported — the rule simply won't be created.
opts.D: Transit Gateway peering has the same limitation: security group references don't work across Regions, and the gateway itself is overkill for connecting just two networks.

511.key: The environment is used for only four hours out of an eight-hour workday, so whatever avoids paying for idle time wins. The key reads option C as pay-per-use pricing (an Aurora database billed by consumption), and under that reading it is cheaper than any instance that runs around the clock. The wording of the option itself is disputable: "Aurora On-Demand" literally describes ordinary hourly provisioning, in which case B — a small RDS Single-AZ instance that is stopped overnight — turns out cheaper. The question is worded carelessly; remember the underlying principle: irregular, partial utilization means paying for consumption rather than keeping an instance running.

opts.A: The same Aurora option, but without the pay-per-use qualifier: a provisioned cluster is billed for the entire time it exists, including the four idle hours every day.
opts.B: A strong alternative: RDS Single-AZ is the cheapest managed PostgreSQL option, and stopping it saves on compute. Its weakness is that RDS automatically restarts a stopped instance after 7 days, requiring a process that stops it again.
opts.D: S3 with S3 Select is not a PostgreSQL database at all: there is no schema, no transactions, no indexes, and no PostgreSQL protocol connectivity. The requirement is not met in principle.

512.key: AWS Backup selects resources by tag, so an untagged resource simply never enters the backup plan. The task boils down to finding such resources and tagging them: AWS Config sees the inventory of all resources across every account in the organization and can identify the ones missing the required tag (the required-tags rule), and remediation can then be automated. From that point on, the backup plan keeps working off tags, and newly created resources are picked up automatically.

opts.B: "Not running" is the wrong criterion — everything needs to be backed up regardless of state. And manually adding resources to a backup vault does not scale.
opts.C: A manual audit by account owners is the maximum possible operational overhead and guarantees gaps.
opts.D: Amazon Inspector looks for workload vulnerabilities and knows nothing about tags or backup plans.

513.key: Traffic is unpredictable, so the solution needs services that scale themselves and cost nothing while idle. A static website sits in S3; an image upload triggers a Lambda function that creates the required sizes and writes the results back to the bucket. There are no servers to plan capacity for, and availability is handled by the services themselves.

opts.B: CloudFront is a content delivery network, not a hosting platform that "invokes" Step Functions, and storing images in a relational database is inappropriate.
opts.C: A single EC2 instance is a single point of failure that cannot scale to handle traffic spikes.
opts.D: An ECS cluster plus a handler running on a separate EC2 instance is infrastructure that still needs to be maintained, and the instance again becomes the bottleneck.

514.key: When the EKS control plane's public endpoint is disabled, nodes reach it over its private address inside the VPC — that part works. But the nodes also need access to other services that expose public APIs: ECR (images), S3 (image layers), CloudWatch Logs, STS, EC2. In private subnets with no NAT, the only way to reach those is through a set of interface VPC endpoints (plus a gateway endpoint for S3). Without them, a node cannot pull images or register with the cluster — which is exactly why it fails to join.

opts.A: The node role's permissions do matter, but their absence would produce a different error, and the scenario specifically describes network isolation in a private cluster. In addition, the AmazonEKSNodeRole role typically already carries the required policies.
opts.C: Moving the nodes into a public subnet violates the requirement to keep the data plane in private subnets.
opts.D: Outbound traffic is allowed by security groups by default, and without an endpoint or a NAT gateway it still has nowhere to go.

515.key: The dump key has been corrected here: the correct set of three is A, B, C. Amazon Redshift does provide a Data API that traditional, containerized, and event-driven applications can use to access data (A); it supports both client-side and server-side encryption (B); and it is well suited to analytics workloads that run during set hours when the primary application is idle, since the cluster can be paused during that time (C).

opts.D: Caching to reduce load on a backend database is a job for ElastiCache or DAX; Redshift is an analytics data warehouse, not a cache.
opts.E: The description of global scaling to petabytes of data and tens of millions of requests per minute describes DynamoDB: a Redshift cluster is regional and is not built for that request rate. This is exactly why the dump key was corrected.
opts.F: Redshift has no concept of a secondary cluster replica: fault tolerance is built on snapshots and cross-region snapshot copies, not on a console-created replica.

516.key: The requirements are consistently low latency at peak load and minimal operational overhead. API Gateway paired with Lambda functions removes server management entirely, and provisioned concurrency keeps a set number of pre-initialized execution environments ready, so there are no cold starts and response time stays flat even under a sudden surge in requests.

opts.A: An ECS cluster behind a load balancer requires configuring scaling and maintaining the services.
opts.C: EKS adds Kubernetes cluster management on top — the most operationally heavy option.
opts.D: Reserved concurrency only reserves and caps a portion of concurrency for a function; it does not pre-warm execution environments, so cold starts remain.

517.key: Session Manager has built-in session log recording to S3: just point it at a bucket in the settings, and the data flows there on its own. No agent, no intermediate services, and no custom code are required.

opts.B: An agent plus exporting from a log group is an unnecessary middleman and a manual export where a direct setting already exists.
opts.C: A Systems Manager document run daily collects server logs, not session logs, and adds custom code and a schedule of its own.
opts.D: The combination of an agent, a log subscription, and a delivery stream solves the same problem with three unnecessary extra components.

518.key: RDS storage autoscaling grows the volume automatically as soon as free space runs low, and it does so with no downtime. You only need to turn the setting on once and set an upper limit.

opts.B: Instance size determines CPU and memory, not disk capacity.
opts.C: Provisioned IOPS changes I/O performance, not available storage space.
opts.D: Taking a backup, increasing storage, and restoring means both downtime and the maximum amount of manual work, whereas an RDS volume can be resized on the fly.

519.key: What's needed is a catalog of ready-made solutions that customers deploy themselves while the company manages them centrally. That is exactly what AWS Service Catalog provides: versioned products with launch constraints and access controls, available to users for self-service.

opts.A: CloudFormation templates are the raw material that catalog products are built from, but on their own they provide neither a self-service storefront nor centralized version and access management.
opts.C: Systems Manager documents automate operations on managed resources; they do not publish solutions for customers to deploy.
opts.D: Config items are entries in a resource's configuration history; they have nothing to do with distributing solutions.

520.key: The key detail is unpredictable traffic. In on-demand mode, DynamoDB instantly adapts to any spike, and you pay only for the requests actually made: with a load profile that can't be predicted in advance, this ends up cheaper than keeping provisioned capacity with headroom to spare.

opts.A: Provisioned capacity with auto scaling pays off under predictable load; with sudden spikes it either can't scale up fast enough or ends up paying for unused capacity.
opts.C: The same problem is compounded by the Standard-IA table class, whose requests cost more — and the read/write load here is moderate to high.
opts.D: The Standard-IA table class lowers storage cost at the expense of more expensive requests and is meant for infrequently accessed data, not an active web application.

521.key: Cross-account access within an organization is built on roles and STS, not on handing out long-lived keys. In each business unit's account, a role is created with a policy granting read access to that account's DynamoDB table and a trust policy allowing a specific role in the reporting account to assume it. The application runs under its own role and calls AssumeRole for the target account, obtaining temporary credentials for the duration of the session. There are no keys to rotate, and revoking access is a single edit to the trust policy.

opts.A: Access to DynamoDB is authorized through IAM, not through a password or connection string. There is simply nothing to store in Secrets Manager.
opts.B: Programmatic IAM users in every account mean long-lived keys that have to be stored somewhere, distributed, and manually rotated every month. That is exactly what the "MOST securely" requirement is asking you to avoid.
opts.D: DynamoDB does not authenticate clients using ACM certificates. No such mechanism exists.

522.key: Scaling needs to happen at two levels. Inside the cluster, horizontal pod autoscaling controls the number of pods, and it needs metrics from the Kubernetes Metrics Server (B). When pods run out of room, the Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler grows the number of nodes (C). Both are standard components and require no custom code.

opts.A: A custom function that resizes the cluster means code to write and maintain instead of using a built-in mechanism.
opts.D: API Gateway handles incoming requests and has nothing to do with cluster scaling.
opts.E: App Mesh provides observability and traffic management between services, but it does not manage capacity.

523.key: This is a disputed question. The dump key is option B: the fetching logic is pushed out to CloudFront edge locations, so the baseline application is never touched at all, and responses can be cached closer to the user. A strong alternative is option A: AppSync pipeline resolvers exist precisely to reach multiple data sources — including several DynamoDB tables — in sequence within a single request, and they require neither custom edge code nor managing its replication. By the operational-efficiency criterion, A looks like the more natural fit; by the "don't touch the existing application" criterion, it's B.

opts.A: Technically this is the most direct way to gather data from several tables in one request, which is why the question is flagged as disputed: the only objection is that it introduces a new API layer in front of the application.
opts.C: An edge-optimized API Gateway only brings the entry point closer to users; gathering data from multiple tables would still have to be done in the function's own code, so efficiency is no better.
opts.D: Athena Federated Query is built for analytical queries and runs with latency measured in seconds, which makes it unsuitable for serving data to the application in real time.

524.key: CloudTrail logs sit in S3 as compressed JSON files, and the simplest way to search them is Amazon Athena: the CloudTrail console has a built-in "Create Athena table" action, after which you can search for errors with ordinary SQL over the errorCode and errorMessage fields (AccessDenied, UnauthorizedOperation), filtered by user and time. No cluster and no code — you pay only for the data scanned, and partitioning by date limits how much gets scanned.

opts.A: AWS Glue with custom scripts means building an ETL pipeline where a SQL query against a ready-made table would do.
opts.B: AWS Batch runs containerized jobs. For parsing logs, that's unnecessary infrastructure and unnecessary code.
opts.D: QuickSight builds visualizations, but it still needs a table as its source (typically that same Athena table). For a one-off error search, a dashboard is overkill.

525.key: The key phrase is "programmatically": the cost data is needed by an application that builds a dashboard. Cost Explorer has an API (GetCostAndUsage for actual spend and GetCostForecast for forecasts), with results returned in pages via NextPageToken. Cost Explorer can also generate a 12-month forecast on its own. There is nothing to deploy, hence the minimal operational overhead.

opts.B: Downloadable CSV files mean a manual process: someone has to export them and load them into the dashboard. That is not programmatic access.
opts.C: AWS Budgets actions apply policies and send notifications, but they don't export data and don't work over FTP.
opts.D: Budgets reports are sent as emails and contain budget status, not the full cost and forecast data needed for programmatic processing.

526.key: The three minutes of downtime happened because, after the failover, the application kept holding connections to the old writer instance and had to re-establish them manually. RDS Proxy maintains a connection pool and routes it to the current writer instance itself, so the failover becomes nearly invisible to the application. The change amounts to swapping in the proxy endpoint.

opts.A: Additional read replicas have no effect on how long the writer instance failover takes.
opts.B: A second cluster with manual application failover means extra cost, more operations to manage, and no speed improvement.
opts.C: Memcached caches reads and does nothing to speed up a writer instance failover.

527.key: Maximum fault tolerance comes from a full second site: the web tier and application tier are deployed in a second Region, the database uses an Aurora global database with storage-level replication (typically under one second of lag), and Route 53 health checks with a failover routing policy shift traffic, after which the secondary cluster is promoted to primary.

opts.A: An Auto Scaling group exists within a single Region and cannot launch instances in Availability Zones belonging to a different Region. This option is technically impossible.
opts.B: A cross-Region Aurora replica created the standard way replicates data at the logical layer and is slower than a global database, while the requirement specifically calls for maximum fault tolerance.
opts.C: AWS DMS is a migration tool, not a built-in mechanism for ongoing cross-Region Aurora replication. It's an extra moving part that can become a point of failure itself.

528.key: The FTP clients can't be changed, and processing must start immediately and takes three to eight minutes. AWS Transfer Family provides a managed FTP server that writes files directly to S3; an object-created event notification triggers a Lambda function that processes the file and then deletes it. Eight minutes fits comfortably within Lambda's fifteen-minute execution limit, and there are no servers in the solution at all.

opts.A: The Glacier Flexible Retrieval class requires a retrieval step, and a nightly run contradicts the requirement to process files right away.
opts.B: A self-managed FTP server on an instance plus a nightly run means both extra operational burden and a violation of the immediate-processing requirement.
opts.C: AWS Transfer Family cannot write to an EBS volume: only S3 and EFS are supported as storage targets. And S3 event notifications don't apply to files on a volume.

529.key: There are two requirements: increase security and reduce operational load on the databases, while keeping the transactional workload. Managed Amazon RDS addresses both: the service handles patching, backups, Multi-AZ, and monitoring, and encryption at rest is enabled with a KMS key and covers storage, snapshots, backups, and replicas. The connection to the database also uses TLS in transit. Self-managing a database engine on EC2 gets you the same level of security only if you build it yourself.

opts.A: A database on EC2 leaves patching, backups, fault tolerance, and monitoring on you. Operational load goes up, not down.
opts.C: S3 with Macie is object storage plus data classification, not a transactional database. There's nowhere for the application to run queries and transactions.
opts.D: CloudWatch Logs collects logs. It provides neither encryption at rest nor data protection.

530.key: The traffic is gaming traffic over TCP and UDP, the load balancers already sit in multiple Regions, and the goal is to improve latency. Global Accelerator ingests packets at the edge location closest to the player, routes them over the AWS backbone to the right Region, and operates at layer 4, meaning it supports both TCP and UDP. To set this up, its listeners are configured on the same ports as the NLBs.

opts.A: CloudFront is built for HTTP and caching static content; it doesn't handle the game's UDP traffic, and the max-age parameter doesn't apply to dynamic game sessions.
opts.B: An Application Load Balancer only handles HTTP and HTTPS — replacing the NLBs with it would drop UDP support.
opts.D: API Gateway is a front end for HTTP APIs; it isn't deployed "behind" load balancers and has nothing to do with game traffic.

531.key: The third party just needs an ordinary HTTPS address it can call to invoke the function. A function URL provides exactly that directly on the Lambda function, along with authentication and CORS configuration, and requires neither a load balancer nor a gateway — the minimum possible operational overhead.

opts.B: A load balancer runs and is billed around the clock and adds a target group and rules where a single function setting would suffice.
opts.C: An SNS topic has no public hostname for incoming calls: it delivers messages outward, it doesn't accept arbitrary web requests.
opts.D: An SQS queue is invoked through the signed AWS API; you can't send an arbitrary webhook to it.

532.key: The most operationally efficient way to give every customer an individual, secure URL is a wildcard subdomain pattern. Register the domain, create a record like *.example.com in the Route 53 hosted zone pointing to the API Gateway endpoint (A); request a wildcard certificate in ACM in the same Region, since a Regional API's certificate must live in the API's own Region (D); and create a custom domain name in API Gateway for the REST API, importing that certificate (F). From there, every new customer gets their own subdomain with no infrastructure changes at all.

opts.B: Region matters here: a Regional API needs its certificate in the same Region, and a certificate in us-east-1 is required only for edge-optimized APIs.
opts.C: A separate hosted zone per customer means hundreds of zones, each billed and manually maintained — the opposite of operational efficiency.
opts.E: A separate API endpoint per customer duplicates the same configuration over and over and makes rolling out changes painful.

533.key: Detecting personal data in S3 is Macie's job, and delivering the notification to people is SNS's job. It's the standard pattern: Macie publishes findings to EventBridge, a rule filters events by the SensitiveData type and sends a message to an SNS topic that the security team is subscribed to. Note the key difference between the options: SQS puts a message on a queue that someone still has to read, while an SNS topic delivers the notification straight away, e.g. by email.

opts.B: GuardDuty looks for signs of compromise, not personal data inside objects. The wrong finding type is selected.
opts.C: The service choice is correct and the filter is even more precise, but an SQS queue doesn't notify people — it needs a consumer. SNS is what's used to alert the team.
opts.D: Both the service and the notification delivery method are wrong.

534.key: The logs need to be accessed frequently for the first 30 days, are kept as backup for the next 60, and are deleted on day 90. That means they can already move to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval on day 30 — the cheapest suitable storage class. Even accounting for the 90-day minimum storage duration charge, this is cheaper than keeping the data in Standard-Infrequent Access for all 60 remaining days.

opts.A: Transitioning to the same Standard class the objects are already in changes nothing and saves nothing.
opts.B: Standard-IA costs more per gigabyte than the archive class, and moving to Glacier on day 90 at the same time as deletion is pointless — the rule contradicts itself.
opts.D: The One Zone-IA class stores data in a single Availability Zone, which contradicts the high-availability requirement, and it has the same self-contradictory pair of rules on day 90.

535.key: The requirement is very specific: Kubernetes secrets must be encrypted specifically inside the EKS cluster's etcd store. There's a dedicated feature for exactly this — envelope encryption of secrets using a KMS key: it's enabled on the cluster with a customer managed key specified, after which EKS encrypts Secret objects before writing them to etcd. Don't confuse this with storing application secrets: AWS Secrets Manager stores them outside Kubernetes and has no effect on what's in etcd.

opts.A: Secrets Manager stores secrets in its own service and does not encrypt what's stored in the cluster's etcd. The requirement is specifically about etcd.
opts.C: The EBS CSI driver attaches volumes to pods. It has nothing to do with encrypting Secret objects in the control plane's store.
opts.D: Default EBS volume encryption protects node disks, not the control plane's etcd, which EKS manages itself.

536.key: Three things are needed at once: high availability, a separate place for heavy queries, and minimum cost. The key answer is C: a Multi-AZ instance deployment covers availability, and two read replicas serve the analysts — four instances total. This is disputable because option D solves the same problem with three instances: a Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment with two readable standby instances provides both automatic failover and a reader endpoint for the analysts. Per current documentation, D is cheaper and simpler, and most of the community picks it. Keep the two flavors of Multi-AZ straight: instance deployment has an unreadable standby, cluster deployment has readable standbys.

opts.A: Scaling up a single instance provides no high availability at all, and the analysts' heavy queries still hit the production database — exactly what the requirement says to avoid.
opts.B: In a Multi-AZ instance deployment, the standby is not readable: you cannot connect to it for queries. This option describes something that doesn't exist in this deployment type.
opts.D: A strong alternative, and arguably the better answer: three instances instead of four, HA, and a built-in reader endpoint. The dump key predates the introduction of the Multi-AZ DB cluster with readable standbys, which is why it picks C.

537.key: Both scaling and high availability across all three Availability Zones are required. The database moves to RDS for MySQL in a Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment, the web tier moves to an Auto Scaling group spanning three Availability Zones, and session state is moved out of the instances into ElastiCache for Redis: Redis is the one that supports replication and automatic failover, so losing a node doesn't mean losing sessions.

opts.B: Memcached does not replicate data and has no high-availability mode: a node failure means the sessions stored on it are gone.
opts.C: Moving MySQL to DynamoDB means reworking the data model and queries, which the requirement doesn't call for.
opts.D: A database in a single Availability Zone directly contradicts the high-availability requirement.

538.key: CloudFront can restrict access based on the requester's country: the distribution is configured with a list of allowed countries, and users from anywhere else get a denial with a customizable error page. Rolling content out to countries in phases just means editing that list over time.

opts.B: Signed URLs and cookies restrict access for specific users, but they can't determine country.
opts.C: Encryption protects the data but doesn't stop viewing by anyone who already has access through the application — it provides no geographic restriction.
opts.D: A time-limited link controls how long access lasts, not where the viewer is located.

539.key: A 30-second recovery point objective rules out nightly backups, while a one-hour recovery time objective means an active-active setup isn't necessary. A warm standby in the form of RDS for SQL Server, kept current through continuous change data capture replication via AWS DMS, gives a lag measured in seconds and lets you fail over within minutes. This also lets you keep the Standard edition, and you only pay for one small instance.

opts.A: Always On availability groups require the Enterprise edition — a licensing change — and an active-active setup is the most expensive option of all.
opts.C: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates disks and is a workable approach, but a pilot light configuration means a longer recovery time, and you'd still need to bring your own SQL Server license; the key distinction is that transaction-level replication is more reliable for a database than block-level replication.
opts.D: Nightly backups give a recovery point measured in a full day — that misses the 30-second requirement by four orders of magnitude.

540.key: There are three requirements: higher availability, better application performance, and offloading reporting from the primary database. Deploying RDS as a Multi-AZ cluster covers both: two standbys in different Availability Zones with synchronous replication, plus readable instances that reporting can be pointed at. Note that the question is worded imprecisely — Multi-AZ DB cluster deployments exist only for MySQL and PostgreSQL, not for Oracle; see the audit log for details. Even so, among the options given, C is still the only one that satisfies both requirements at once.

opts.A: Different Regions address disaster recovery, not availability within a Region, and require ongoing maintenance of DMS tasks.
opts.B: A single Availability Zone means no high availability, and a replica in that same zone doesn't help if the zone itself fails.
opts.D: Aurora isn't compatible with Oracle: migrating would require schema conversion and code rewrites, and the phrase "Multi-AZ instance deployment for Aurora" describes a deployment mode that doesn't exist.

541.key: Load is unpredictable and can be idle for long stretches, so the company should pay only for actual requests. The backend is a Lambda function behind API Gateway that reads data from DynamoDB (A). Authenticating subscribers requires an Amazon Cognito user pool, which stores accounts and issues tokens (C). The frontend is a static site deployed through AWS Amplify with built-in CloudFront integration (E).

opts.B: The ECS service behind a load balancer and the RDS database are billed around the clock, even when there is no traffic; the option is also self-contradictory, since it still mentions a Lambda function.
opts.D: An identity pool issues temporary AWS credentials to already-authenticated users; authentication itself is handled by a user pool.
opts.F: PHP is a server-side language, and S3 static website hosting cannot execute it: the site would not work.

542.key: Content is served through CloudFront, so access must be restricted at CloudFront, not at S3. There are two mechanisms: a signed URL grants access to a single specific file for a limited time, and signed cookies grant access to a group of files without changing the URL. The scenario describes granting rights to an individual piece of content "for a specific purpose, such as movie rentals or music downloads" — that is, to a specific object for a specific period — which is a signed URL. Rule of thumb: a single file or a streaming link to one specific resource calls for a signed URL; an entire library or whole site calls for signed cookies.

opts.A: "S3 signed cookies" doesn't exist: S3 has presigned URLs, while cookies are signed by CloudFront. And even an S3 presigned URL would bypass the distribution, going around the CDN.
opts.C: Origin access control blocks access to the bucket for everyone except the CloudFront distribution itself. It doesn't distinguish a premium customer from a random viewer — both reach the content through CloudFront.
opts.D: Field-level encryption encrypts specific fields in users' POST requests (such as a card number) so that intermediate services can't see them. It has nothing to do with restricting access to content.

543.key: Savings Plans discounts are shared across accounts only within a single organization with consolidated billing. Right now the accounts are billed separately, so the company must first create an organization — specifically in the account that already owns the plan and runs the instances (E), otherwise the commitment stays outside the sharing boundary — and invite the other accounts. After that, discount sharing is turned on in the management account (A), and the unused commitment starts covering the other accounts' usage. Compare with {{q:467}}.

opts.B: The discount-sharing toggle is available only in the organization's management account, not in the account that purchased the Savings Plan.
opts.C: AWS RAM shares resources such as subnets, prefix lists, and Transit Gateway. Savings Plans are not shared through it.
opts.D: A new payer account is possible, but then the account with the purchased plan would need to join the organization as a member account; option E is simpler and keeps the commitment inside the sharing boundary from day one.

544.key: The task is to release a new API version with minimal impact on customers and minimal data loss. API Gateway has a built-in mechanism for this: a canary release deployment on the same stage, which receives a set percentage of traffic, has separate metrics and logs, and is promoted to the production stage after verification. Neither the domain name nor the Route 53 record changes, and rollback is instant.

opts.B: Importing in merge mode updates the live API in place, all at once, for everyone: there's no gradual traffic shift, and rollback is complicated.
opts.C: Overwrite mode is even riskier — it replaces the entire API definition, so a mistake affects one hundred percent of customers immediately.
opts.D: A new endpoint with a new domain name and a Route 53 record switch runs into DNS caching: some clients keep hitting the old version for a while, the cutover is uncontrolled, and there's no way to shift a percentage of traffic.

545.key: The company needs a fallback error page when the primary site is unavailable, with minimal changes and no new infrastructure. This is exactly what a standard active-passive failover in Route 53 provides: the primary record points to the load balancer and is tied to a health check, while the secondary record points to a static site in an S3 bucket. As long as the health check passes, the primary record answers; once the load balancer is deemed unhealthy, Route 53 starts returning the bucket's address.

opts.A: Latency-based routing picks the fastest endpoint, not the working one. Some users would land on the error page even while the site is healthy.
opts.C: An EC2 instance just for a static page is unnecessary infrastructure to maintain, and an active-active configuration conflicts with the requirement to fail over "only when health checks fail."
opts.D: Multivalue answer returns several records at once and gives no priority to the primary: users could randomly land on the error page even when the site is healthy.

546.key: The key requirement is to keep the existing on-premises backup applications and workflows while eliminating physical tapes. That's exactly what Tape Gateway is for: it presents the backup software with a virtual tape library over the iSCSI protocol, while storing the virtual tapes in S3 and then in archival storage classes. The software and processes stay the same; the physical tapes disappear.

opts.A: NFS access through Storage Gateway is file-based, but the backup applications are configured to work with a tape library: the workflows would need to be redesigned.
opts.B: EFS over NFS means the same rework of procedures, and file storage costs noticeably more than S3's archival storage classes.
opts.C: EFS has no iSCSI interface at all: it's a file system that uses the NFS protocol.

547.key: A high-volume data stream needs to be ingested and landed in S3 with the least operational effort. Kinesis Data Firehose does exactly that: a fully managed delivery stream that scales itself, buffers records by time or size, optionally compresses and transforms them, and writes them to a bucket. No clusters, no shards, no code.

opts.B: AWS Glue is an ETL service for batch processing and cataloging, not a receiver for streaming data from sensors.
opts.C: Lambda functions would have to be written and wired together by hand, including buffering and retries, whereas Firehose provides this out of the box.
opts.D: DMS migrates data from databases; it doesn't ingest a stream from sensors.

548.key: The requirement is to centrally restrict which services each department's account can use, without building anything. In AWS Organizations this is done with an OU structure and SCPs: department accounts are grouped into organizational units, and a policy with an allow or deny list of services is attached to each unit. SCPs apply to every principal in the account, including root, and can't be bypassed with local IAM policies. Remember: an SCP restricts but never grants permissions — the effective permissions are the intersection of the SCP and the IAM policies.

opts.A: Systems Manager templates automate operations, but they don't prevent the use of services that aren't in the template.
opts.C: CloudFormation describes and provisions resources. It doesn't stop someone from creating something manually outside the template.
opts.D: Service Catalog is convenient for offering pre-built configurations, but it requires maintaining a product catalog in every account and doesn't restrict direct access to the services' APIs.

549.key: The database cluster in the private subnets needs outbound access to an external catalog provider, while inbound connections from outside must remain blocked and operational overhead must not increase. A NAT gateway in the public subnets, with a default route from the private subnets, delivers exactly that: a managed service where connections can only be initiated from inside.

opts.A: A NAT instance is a regular machine that has to be patched, scaled, and made redundant: operational overhead goes up.
opts.C: Routing to an internet gateway from a private subnet makes it effectively public and requires public addresses — security goes down.
opts.D: A virtual private gateway is for connecting a VPN or Direct Connect to your site, and it doesn't provide internet access.

550.key: Access to a KMS key in AWS is always two-sided: the principal needs permission in its IAM policy, and it must also be allowed in the key's own policy. For Lambda environment variables this means two settings: kms:Decrypt permission in the function's execution role (B), and an explicit allow for that role in the key's key policy (D). Missing either half causes an access error when the function runs. Don't confuse the execution role with the function's resource-based policy: the former describes what the function can do, the latter describes who can invoke it.

opts.A: A Lambda function's resource policy defines which services and accounts are allowed to invoke it. It doesn't grant permissions to use a KMS key.
opts.C: Function policy is just another name for the same resource-based policy governing who can invoke the function. It has nothing to do with decrypting environment variables.
opts.E: In a key policy, permission is granted to a principal — a role or an account — not to a "function policy." No such construct exists in KMS.

551.key: Notice the size: 50 KB reports. S3 Standard-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval both have a 128 KB minimum billable object size, so a 50 KB file is billed as if it were 128 KB, which shrinks the savings from a "cheap" tier by nearly two-thirds. The retrieval requirement is lenient — 6 hours — while the data must be kept for years. So the cheapest path is Standard for the first week, then Glacier Flexible Retrieval: its standard retrieval time of 3–5 hours fits within the 6-hour window, and storage costs roughly six times less than Standard-IA.

opts.B: Standard-IA provides millisecond access that isn't needed here, and it costs noticeably more than Glacier. On 50 KB objects, its 128 KB minimum billable size further erodes the savings.
opts.C: Intelligent-Tiering charges a monitoring fee per object, and it never moves objects smaller than 128 KB to the cheaper tiers at all. Across millions of small reports, that's cost with no benefit.
opts.D: Deep Archive delivers an object in 12 hours for standard retrieval and up to 48 hours for bulk retrieval. That doesn't meet the 6-hour requirement.

552.key: The instance type and family change every two to three months, so the commitment must not be tied to them. A Compute Savings Plan gives a discount regardless of instance family, size, Region, or even service, and the no-upfront, 1-year option is the most flexible choice compatible with such frequent changes.

opts.A: Reserved Instances for a 3-year term lock in a specific family and type: with changes every two to three months, the discount would go unused.
opts.C: Paying all upfront for Reserved Instances makes the same problem worse — the money is committed to a specific instance type.
opts.D: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan is tied to an instance family in a specific Region, and it's exactly the family that keeps changing here.

553.key: Discovering PII across buckets is a job for Amazon Macie. The detail being tested here is that Macie is Regional, so it must be turned on in every Region where the data resides, with a discovery job created in each one. Using a delegated administrator in an organization, this can be managed centrally, but the Regions still have to be listed explicitly.

opts.B: Security Hub aggregates findings from other services, and AWS Config rules check resource configuration, not object content.
opts.C: Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities and doesn't analyze data in S3.
opts.D: GuardDuty watches for suspicious activity, including around S3 data, but it doesn't classify personal data inside objects.

554.key: On-premises performance data shows high memory utilization for both the SAP application and the database. So both tiers should move to memory-optimized instances — this is also AWS's recommended choice for SAP.

opts.A: Compute-optimized instances provide little memory per core and aren't a fit for a memory-hungry SAP application.
opts.B: Storage-optimized instances are meant for heavy local I/O, but the bottleneck here is memory.
opts.D: HPC-optimized instances are designed for tightly coupled, network-intensive compute workloads, not for SAP applications.

555.key: SQS is a service with a public API, so instances in private subnets reach it either through NAT or privately through an interface VPC endpoint (PrivateLink). The correct option places the endpoint in the same private subnets where the instances run and protects it with a security group that has an inbound rule for those instances — that's exactly how access to an interface endpoint is controlled. An endpoint policy can additionally be attached to restrict which queues are reachable.

opts.B: Placing the endpoint in public subnets makes no sense: interfaces need to sit where the clients are — in the private subnets.
opts.C: Same mistake with public subnets, plus a queue access policy is attached to the queue, not to the endpoint.
opts.D: A gateway endpoint exists only for S3 and DynamoDB — there is no gateway endpoint for SQS. And a NAT gateway would send the traffic back out to the internet, which is what needs to be avoided.

556.key: The instances need to read from and write to DynamoDB without any credentials appearing in the template. The standard approach: an IAM role with the required permissions, an instance profile carrying that role, and a reference to the profile on the instances. The application then gets temporary credentials from instance metadata. Note the difference from the neighboring option: there the role grants read-only access, but the application also stores user data, so write access is needed too.

opts.A: A read-only role wouldn't let the application store user data, and the requirement calls for storing and retrieving it.
opts.C: Entering access keys as a template parameter is exactly what the requirement asks to avoid: the secret ends up in the stack's parameters and in the hands of whoever deploys it.
opts.D: The GetAtt function can indeed return a created user's access key, but passing the secret through user data leaves it in plaintext in the instance's metadata.

557.key: Semi-structured data lives in S3 and needs to be processed in parallel: Amazon Athena runs queries against S3 in a distributed, serverless way. Enriching the data with information from Redshift is handled by AWS Glue, which has connectors to both S3 and Redshift, so the join happens within a single ETL job.

opts.B: EMR would work, but it's a cluster that has to be provisioned, configured, and maintained, whereas both steps here are covered by serverless services.
opts.C: Kinesis Data Streams is meant for streaming data; using it to move files that already sit in S3 into Redshift doesn't fit.
opts.D: Lake Formation manages access and the data lake catalog — it doesn't enrich data.

558.key: Two networks in the same Region and the same account, with about 500 GB of monthly data transfer — the cheapest way to connect them is VPC peering. There's no charge for the connection itself, only for the data transferred, and there are no hourly fees. It's set up in one step, plus routes in both route tables.

opts.A: Transit Gateway charges an hourly fee per attachment plus a per-GB data processing charge. For two VPCs, that's noticeably more expensive than peering.
opts.B: A VPN between two VPCs adds an hourly connection charge, encryption overhead, and a tunnel bandwidth limit — unnecessary when private connectivity is already available within the Region.
opts.D: Direct Connect is for connecting your own site to AWS. It can't be used to connect two VPCs within the same Region, and it costs disproportionately more.

559.key: Tags that teams apply only affect billing once they're activated as cost allocation tags. They're activated in the Billing console (B — select the desired user-defined tag), specifically in the organization's management account (E); after that, Cost Explorer and consolidated billing reports can group costs by that tag across all accounts and Regions. Keep the distinction in mind: AWS-generated tags start with the aws: prefix and are created by the platform, while user-defined tags are ones you create yourself. Related question: {{q:459}}.

opts.A: AWS-generated tags are the platform's own internal labels. The product lines here are tagged with the company's own tags — that is, user-defined ones.
