opts.C: Resource Groups helps group resources for operations, but activating cost allocation tags is done in the Billing console.
opts.D: Member accounts have no such activation option: cost allocation tags are turned on centrally, in the management account.

560.key: Changes to the organization's OU structure need to be detected and reported to the operations team, without building a custom system for it. AWS Control Tower maintains a baseline of the landscape and reports drift itself — including accounts moving between OUs, hierarchy changes, and guardrail edits. Notifications are published to an SNS topic that the operations team subscribes to. No custom code or rules are required.

opts.B: AWS Config rules work with resource configuration inside accounts. They don't track the organization's OU hierarchy.
opts.C: An organization trail in CloudTrail would show API calls like MoveAccount, but the filtering, metrics, and notifications would all have to be built from scratch — more work than the ready-made drift notifications.
opts.D: CloudFormation drift detection compares a stack's resources against its template. It has nothing to do with an organization's OU structure.

561.key: The goal is to reduce read latency from DynamoDB with the least operational overhead. DAX was built exactly for this: a managed cache sitting directly in front of the table, compatible with the same API, so no loading or invalidation logic needs to be written — it's built in.

opts.B: Redis would deliver low latency, but caching, expiration, and consistency would have to be managed in application code.
opts.C: Same issue with Memcached, plus no data replication.
opts.D: Populating a cache through a stream and a function is the most complex of the proposed designs and the most to maintain.

562.key: A gateway endpoint for DynamoDB (B) provides private access, and adding a route table entry with the service prefix (A) routes traffic through it. These two steps are enough: calls to the tables stop leaving the internet.

opts.C: An interface endpoint for EC2 gives private access to the instance-management API, not to DynamoDB.
opts.D: Elastic network interfaces are created for interface endpoints; a gateway endpoint works through routes and has no interfaces.
opts.E: Security groups apply to interface endpoints. A gateway endpoint has none — access is restricted through an endpoint policy instead.

563.key: Kubernetes clusters run both in AWS and on premises, and they need to be viewed from one place. Amazon EKS Connector registers external clusters in the EKS console, after which those clusters and their workloads appear alongside the managed ones. An agent is installed; no other infrastructure is required.

opts.A: Container Insights collects metrics and logs, but it doesn't provide a unified list of clusters and their workloads.
opts.C: Systems Manager manages nodes, not Kubernetes objects: it won't show cluster information in the needed form.
opts.D: EKS Anywhere is a way to run clusters on your own site, not a tool for observing other people's clusters.

564.key: The discriminator is "even from database administrators." Any transparent storage-level encryption (EBS, RDS, S3 SSE) decrypts data automatically for anyone with access to the service, so a database administrator would see the content as usual. The only way to protect data from a privileged operator is client-side encryption: the application encrypts the field with a KMS key before writing it, and the table stores ciphertext that's useless without access to the key. Control over the key is kept separate from control over the database — that's the whole point of the separation of duties.

opts.A: EBS volume encryption is transparent to the operating system and to anyone who gains access to the instance. It doesn't protect against an administrator.
opts.C: S3 server-side encryption decrypts the object for anyone allowed access to the bucket and the key. Plus, S3 isn't a transactional store for purchases.
opts.D: Windows file system permissions are bypassed by the server administrator, and there's no data encryption here at all.

565.key: The applications must keep working without changes, so the target needs an engine compatible with MySQL that also scales automatically. Aurora MySQL is compatible at the protocol and query level, its storage grows on its own, and Aurora Auto Scaling adds and removes read replicas based on load. AWS DMS migrates the data while letting the source database keep running during the migration.

opts.A: RDS for MySQL is compatible, but storage scaling is about space, not performance: compute capacity still has to be scaled manually.
opts.B: Redshift is an analytics warehouse; it doesn't suit transactional workloads and isn't compatible with the application.
opts.D: DynamoDB is a non-relational store: every SQL query would have to be rewritten.

566.key: The requirements are a hierarchical directory structure and fast, concurrent writes from instances in two Availability Zones. That's the profile of Amazon EFS: a file system using the NFS protocol, mountable on every instance, with mount targets in each zone and consistency under concurrent writes.

opts.A: S3 is object storage: it has no real directory hierarchy or file operations, and the application is built specifically around those.
opts.C: An io2 volume attaches within a single Availability Zone, so instances in the second zone can't reach it, and a regular file system isn't designed for concurrent writes from multiple machines.
opts.D: Synchronizing separate volumes between instances causes data drift and lag: it doesn't provide concurrent writes.

567.key: Sensors send readings over HTTP, the volume is small and uneven, and the solution needs managed services plus the ability to add components easily. API Gateway receives the requests, a Lambda function processes and totals the readings, and DynamoDB stores the result. There are no servers to operate, scaling is automatic, and new independent components can be added just by subscribing to events.

opts.B: A fleet of instances behind a load balancer needs patching, monitoring, and scaling, and storing aggregates in S3 is awkward for frequently updated per-tenant counters.
opts.C: The first half is right, but SQL Server Express on an EC2 instance means a machine and a database that have to be managed by hand, and a single point of failure.
opts.D: Again a self-managed fleet of instances, and a shared file system is the wrong storage model for consumption counters.

568.key: The requirements are petabytes of storage and caching so drawings load quickly. S3 stores an unlimited amount of data without capacity planning, and CloudFront caches it at edge locations close to users. The pairing is standard and requires no servers or capacity tuning.

opts.B: Glacier is an archive with retrieval times measured in minutes to hours, and ElastiCache caches in memory within a Region — not built for large files.
opts.C: EBS volumes are capacity-limited, tied to a single Availability Zone, and don't scale to petabytes.
opts.D: Storage Gateway is a hybrid gateway for an on-premises site, while every component of this application is stated to run in AWS.

569.key: EventBridge publishes its own metrics to CloudWatch under the AWS/Events namespace: TriggeredRules shows whether the rule fired at all, while Invocations and FailedInvocations show whether the target was actually called. Those are exactly the two questions that need to be told apart.

opts.B: The dead-letter queue only holds failed invocations and stays empty if the rule never fired in the first place.
opts.C: CloudWatch Logs stores logs, not rule-invocation statistics; logging for EventBridge events has to be set up separately.
opts.D: CloudTrail records management API calls, not whether the rule fired and invoked its target.

570.key: The spike repeats on a known schedule — every Friday evening. An Auto Scaling group's scheduled actions change the desired and minimum capacity at a set time and then revert it. It's configured once and runs itself.

opts.A: A reminder just means someone will scale the group by hand every week.
opts.C: Manual scaling is the same thing: weekly human intervention.
opts.D: A metric-based automatic policy would only react after the load appears and requires tuning thresholds, whereas the timing of the spike is already known in advance.

571.key: ACM does not issue certificates signed by a third-party public CA: it either issues its own or accepts an imported one. So the only workable path is to obtain the certificate from the required CA outside of ACM, import it into ACM, and attach it to a custom domain in API Gateway (A).

opts.B: Creating a certificate in ACM that is signed by a third-party CA is not technically possible: ACM only signs certificates with its own certificate authority.
opts.C: Same impossible premise about issuing the certificate in ACM, plus a Lambda function URL does not support a custom domain or certificate.
opts.D: Repeats the same mistake: ACM cannot create a certificate from a third-party CA, and a function URL cannot be configured with a custom certificate.

572.key: The workload is inconsistent, the database is MySQL-compatible, and the company needs auto scaling with minimal administration. Aurora Serverless v2 fits exactly: capacity is measured in Aurora capacity units (ACUs), and each ACU provides roughly 2 GiB of memory, so a minimum of 1 ACU covers the stated steady-state 2 GiB, while the cluster scales up smoothly with no interruption in service.

opts.A: DynamoDB is a non-relational data store: an application built for MySQL would have to be rewritten, and 'default capacity settings' means fixed provisioned capacity with no auto scaling.
opts.B: A standard provisioned Aurora cluster is sized by instance class, not ACUs: this option describes a configuration that doesn't exist, and provisioned Aurora has no automatic compute scaling.
opts.D: RDS for MySQL with a fixed memory size does not scale for sudden workload increases: changing the instance class requires a manual change and downtime.

573.key: This is about cold-start latency for Java functions, with no strict latency requirements and a need for the most cost-effective option. Lambda SnapStart takes a snapshot of the initialized execution environment and restores it at invocation, cutting cold-start time dramatically — and it is not billed as continuously maintained capacity.

opts.A: Provisioned concurrency solves the same problem, but you pay for the entire time the instances are reserved: without strict latency requirements, that's overpaying.
opts.B: The timeout setting limits the maximum execution duration and has no effect on startup.
opts.C: More memory speeds up initialization slightly, but it also raises the cost of every invocation and doesn't address the root cause of the cold start.

574.key: The database is needed for two hours a week — paying for the other 166 hours makes no sense. The answer key picks B: a provisioned Aurora cluster can be stopped, and a stopped cluster is not billed for compute (you pay only for storage). Two details make this debatable: AWS automatically restarts a stopped Aurora cluster after 7 days, and at the version of Aurora Serverless v2 this dump reflects, it scaled down but not to zero, so the minimum capacity was billed continuously. Today Serverless v2 can scale to zero, which makes option A the stronger answer on a current exam. The underlying principle stays the same: for rare, short-lived workloads, either pay only for what you consume or stop the cluster entirely.

opts.A: A strong alternative. At the service version this question reflects, Serverless v2 could not scale below its minimum ACU, meaning it was billed around the clock — so the answer key preferred a cluster that can be stopped entirely.
opts.C: A Reserved Instance is billed regardless of whether the machine is running — the worst choice for two hours a week of use. It also means self-managing MySQL instead of using a managed database.
opts.D: Running MySQL in ECS containers again means self-managing the database, plus you still need to solve persistent storage. There's no cost savings compared with a stopped managed cluster.

575.key: Both high availability and extra read capacity are required, with minimal operational effort. The RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment provides exactly that: a primary instance plus two standby instances in other Availability Zones, with the standbys available for read traffic through a dedicated reader endpoint. A single configuration covers both requirements.

opts.A: DynamoDB is not PostgreSQL: the application would have to be rewritten.
opts.B: A standard Multi-AZ deployment provides availability, but the standby instance doesn't serve read traffic, so it adds no read capacity.
opts.D: Cross-Region read replicas are meant for readers in other parts of the world and for disaster recovery; for availability within a single Region, they add unnecessary cost and latency.

576.key: Users are distributed worldwide, and API request latency needs to be reduced. An edge-optimized endpoint routes requests through the nearest CloudFront edge location, from which they travel to the Region over the AWS backbone: the TLS connection is established close to the user, and overall request latency drops significantly.

opts.A: A private endpoint is accessible only from within a VPC — it doesn't work for public users.
opts.B: A Regional endpoint receives requests directly in the Region: remote users would experience the full latency to reach it.
opts.C: An interface VPC endpoint is a way to reach a private API from within a network, not a way to speed things up for internet users.

577.key: Certificates for CloudFront are issued by AWS Certificate Manager, at no charge. The key detail is domain ownership validation via DNS: with DNS validation, ACM renews the certificate automatically as long as the CNAME record stays in the hosted zone. That's exactly the automated issuance and renewal the requirement calls for.

opts.A: A security policy sets the minimum TLS version and cipher suite; it doesn't issue certificates.
opts.B: Origin access control restricts access to an origin, such as an S3 bucket, and has nothing to do with certificates.
opts.D: Email validation requires manual confirmation at every renewal, so it doesn't provide automation.

578.key: The requirement to go 'from milliseconds to microseconds' and 'cache requests to the database' describes DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) almost word for word: a managed, API-compatible cache in front of the table, so the application only needs to change its endpoint.

opts.B: Redshift is an analytics warehouse for large-scale queries, not a fast database for an application.
opts.C: Migrating to RDS means reworking the data model, and it still doesn't deliver microsecond response times.
opts.D: Redis can deliver the needed speed, but it requires building custom caching and invalidation logic, meaning more operational overhead.

579.key: The database is needed only during business hours on weekdays, and the company doesn't want to spend effort building automation. The ready-made Instance Scheduler on AWS solution deploys from a template and automatically starts and stops RDS and EC2 instances on a schedule — no custom code required.

opts.B: Turning off automatic backups saves pennies while also giving up point-in-time recovery.
opts.C: A custom function means code that has to be written and maintained; on top of that, CPU utilization is a poor signal for deciding when to stop the database.
opts.D: All Upfront reserved pricing pays off with round-the-clock usage, but here the database is needed for only about a quarter of the week.

580.key: A lift-and-shift migration with no architecture changes means the locally attached storage is replaced with a block volume on the instance. Among general purpose volumes, gp3 is the cheapest: for the same size it costs roughly 20% less than gp2 while providing baseline performance of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s regardless of volume size, whereas gp2 performance scales with volume size.

opts.A: FSx for Lustre is an expensive file system built for high-performance computing, while the application was designed for a local disk, not a shared resource.
opts.B: A gp2 volume solves the problem technically, but it costs more than gp3 at the same capacity, and cost is the deciding requirement here.
opts.C: FSx for OpenZFS is also a shared file system and also costs more than a block volume; it would require changing the architecture as well.

581.key: The requirement is for at least two instances to always be running, and for the architecture to survive an Availability Zone failure. That means each of the two zones needs two instances, with the group's minimum capacity set to four: if an entire zone is lost, exactly two instances remain running, as required.

opts.A: One instance per zone: the failure of either zone leaves only one instance running, but the requirement is at least two.
opts.C: All four instances in a single Availability Zone would not survive that zone's failure, and Spot capacity can be reclaimed at any time — unacceptable for a stateful production application.
opts.D: Spot Instances in the second zone can be reclaimed at any time, so there's no guarantee that two instances remain running.

582.key: There are two locations: the company's own data center near us-west-1 and the website in eu-central-1. Route 53 can route based on the requester's geographic location — a geolocation routing policy sends users in North America to the data center and users in Europe to eu-central-1. Each visitor lands on the nearest location, minimizing load time. It's also worth keeping geoproximity routing in mind, covered in the walkthrough for {{q:120,142}}.

opts.B: A simple routing policy returns records without regard to the client's location: it simply doesn't provide the behavior described in this option.
opts.C: A single record with a latency-based policy tied to us-west-1 keeps all traffic going to one location. The second location doesn't participate at all.
opts.D: A weighted routing policy splits traffic evenly regardless of geography: half of the European users would be routed across the ocean to the U.S. data center.

583.key: Do the math: 5 PB over a 1 Gbps link works out to roughly 10 TB a day, or about 485 days even at full uplink utilization — against a 6-month deadline. That rules out any online transfer option on arithmetic alone. Snowball with Tape Gateway is built exactly for this case: physical tapes are read into virtual tapes right on the device, the devices are shipped to AWS, and a lifecycle policy then moves the virtual tapes into S3 Glacier Deep Archive — the cheapest storage class, matching the ten-year compliance retention requirement.

opts.A: DataSync would transfer over the same link, so the six-month deadline still can't be met. It would also require an intermediate 5 PB NFS staging store, which the company doesn't have.
opts.B: Writing directly to Deep Archive still goes over the same uplink: about 485 days versus the six months available.
opts.D: An on-premises Tape Gateway creates virtual tapes in the cloud, but the data still travels over the internet link — the same math, and the same timeline failure.

584.key: The requirement is that groups of nodes must not end up on the same underlying hardware. That's exactly what a spread placement group does: each instance is placed on separate hardware with its own power and networking, so a single hardware failure affects only one node.

opts.B: Separate accounts have no effect on physical placement: the instances could still end up on the same host.
opts.C: Dedicated tenancy only guarantees that no other customer's instances share the host — your own nodes can still end up on the same hardware.
opts.D: Shared tenancy is the default mode and provides no placement guarantees at all.

585.key: The requirement is framed as a guarantee of capacity in the failover Region. Only a Capacity Reservation reserves the actual compute capacity in a specific Availability Zone: instances are guaranteed to launch at the moment of failover.

opts.A: On-Demand Instances aren't reserved in advance: at the moment of a regional outage, the needed capacity might simply not be available.
opts.B: A Savings Plan is a financial commitment made for a discount; it doesn't guarantee capacity.
opts.C: Regional Reserved Instances provide a discount and flexibility across zones, but they don't reserve capacity; only zonal Reserved Instances or a Capacity Reservation do that.

586.key: The key rule: an AWS account can belong to only one organization at a time. So the sequence has to be strict — the R&D account first leaves the prior organization (which requires it to have valid billing information and contact details on file, or it can't leave), and only then does the new organization's management account send it an invitation, which the account accepts. The resources themselves stay in place: only the account's organization membership changes.

opts.A: Simultaneous membership in two organizations is not technically possible.
opts.C: Creating a new account and migrating resources is a project involving downtime and risk, when simply moving the existing account is enough.
opts.D: The new organization's management account cannot be a member of another organization: it too is subject to the one-organization rule.

587.key: Traffic is unpredictable and can spike suddenly, integration with multiple web applications is needed, and an authorization step is required. API Gateway provides a single entry point, and a Lambda authorizer — a built-in mechanism of the gateway itself — handles authorization. From there, data flows into Kinesis Data Firehose, which buffers it and delivers it into S3 for analytics with no administration required.

opts.A: A Gateway Load Balancer is designed to route traffic to inspection appliances and doesn't perform request authorization, and containers backed by EFS require ongoing operations.
opts.B: A Kinesis Data Stream doesn't write to S3 on its own — it needs a consumer to do that, and using a separate authorization function instead of API Gateway's built-in authorizer adds unnecessary complexity.
opts.D: This repeats the same mistake of using a Gateway Load Balancer as the entry point for client requests, plus unnecessary container infrastructure.

588.key: The recovery targets are lenient: up to 24 hours of data loss and downtime are both acceptable. That makes copying automated snapshots to another Region once a day the cheapest option — you pay only for snapshot storage, with no running database copy in the second Region.

opts.A: A cross-Region read replica is a continuously running instance billed around the clock, delivering far tighter RPO/RTO than what's actually required.
opts.B: DMS requires a replication instance and a target database running continuously — again, unnecessary expense.
opts.C: Native engine backups copied to a bucket with cross-Region replication add an extra layer of automation and storage for the same outcome that built-in snapshot copying already provides.

589.key: Session state currently lives on the web servers themselves, so a server failure loses user sessions. The right fix is to move it to an external store: ElastiCache for Redis supports replication, automatic failover to a replica node, and data persistence, so sessions survive the failure of either a cache node or a web server.

opts.A: Memcached supports neither replication nor data persistence: sessions are lost if a node fails.
opts.C: Storage Gateway is a hybrid gateway for on-premises environments; it isn't designed for storing web application session state.
opts.D: A relational database can technically store sessions, but it's slower than an in-memory cache and more expensive; the standard choice for session storage is Redis.

590.key: Heavy reporting queries run once a month and interfere with the everyday workload. A read replica absorbs these queries, leaving the primary instance free to handle the daily workload it was sized for.

opts.B: Restoring from a backup gives a point-in-time snapshot of the data and requires a manual operation every month.
opts.C: Exporting to S3 and querying through Athena means building a separate export pipeline and working with stale data.
opts.D: Resizing the instance for just one day a month means paying the higher cost for all thirty days, and it doesn't separate the workloads.

591.key: The task is to route incoming requests to different microservices within EKS — that is, choose a backend based on path or host. That's a job for a layer 7 load balancer. The standard approach in EKS is an Ingress resource, which the AWS Load Balancer Controller provisions as an Application Load Balancer: a single ALB serves every service in the cluster, billed hourly plus LCU usage. The dump's answer key points to D (API Gateway), and that's debatable: API Gateway is billed per request and adds a separate component in front of the cluster. The rule of thumb: reach for API Gateway when you actually need its features — API keys, throttling, authorizers, request transformation; otherwise, ALB is the standard choice for EKS.

opts.A: A Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4 and distinguishes only ports and protocols. It cannot route requests to microservices based on URL.
opts.B: A strong alternative and the canonical solution for EKS: the same controller, but provisioning an ALB, which supports path- and host-based routing and is typically cheaper than API Gateway for steady traffic.
opts.C: Putting Lambda in front of EKS means building a custom proxy: per-invocation billing, extra latency, and hand-written routing logic instead of the load balancer's built-in rules.

592.key: There are three requirements: fast delivery to a global audience, blocking access from specific countries, and minimizing cost. CloudFront covers all three: content is served from edge locations (faster and cheaper than serving data-transfer-out directly from S3), geographic restrictions block requests from the listed countries, and signed URLs restrict access to a specific customer for a limited time. The bucket itself is locked down to direct access via origin access control (OAC), so the restrictions can't be bypassed.

opts.A: A public bucket serves images to everyone with no country restrictions, and MFA has nothing to do with anonymous read access. For paid content, this means lost revenue.
opts.B: An IAM user for every customer is an administrative nightmare at a global customer scale, and it still provides neither faster delivery nor country-level blocking.
opts.C: A fleet of instances behind load balancers in every country is the most expensive and labor-intensive option, and separate links per country are easily circumvented.

593.key: Fault tolerance is required at both the node level and within the Region, with no data loss. That calls for Redis replication groups with Multi-AZ enabled, where each shard consists of a primary node and replicas spread across different Availability Zones: a node failure triggers automatic failover to a replica, and the data is preserved.

opts.B: Append-only files (AOF) protect data on a single node, but if that node or its Availability Zone fails, access to the cluster is lost.
opts.C: This option sounds close, but it describes a cluster with read replicas without explicitly spreading shards across multiple nodes; the correct construct is specifically Multi-AZ replication groups with multi-node shards.
opts.D: Auto scaling adjusts capacity to match load and has nothing to do with fault tolerance.

594.key: It's not the instance launch that's slow, but the application reaching a fully productive state — it needs to warm up memory. Hibernation saves the in-memory state to disk, and an Auto Scaling warm pool keeps already-initialized instances on standby, which resume in seconds instead of going through a full application load.

opts.A: Auto scaling will add more instances, but each new one still has to go through the same slow warm-up.
opts.B: Spot Instances only change the price; initialization time stays the same.
opts.D: A Capacity Reservation guarantees instance availability but doesn't speed up loading the application into memory.

595.key: The traffic spikes happen on random days, so neither a fixed schedule nor a history-based forecast will work. Dynamic scaling reacts to an actual metric and adds instances only when the load has actually increased — delivering the needed performance without paying for idle capacity.

opts.A: Manually resizing the group requires someone to be on standby waiting for a random spike.
opts.B: Predictive scaling relies on recurring patterns, but the spikes here are random.
opts.D: Scheduled scaling doesn't apply for the same reason: there's no known time for the spike in advance.

596.key: The problem is connection exhaustion during an unpredictable monthly spike. Aurora Serverless v2 adjusts capacity to match load within seconds and scales back down during quiet periods, so there's no need to pay for peak-sized capacity year-round. The engine is PostgreSQL-compatible, so the application doesn't need to be rewritten.

opts.B: There's no such thing as auto scaling for a database running on an EC2 instance: only the instance itself can be resized, and only manually, with downtime.
opts.C: A larger RDS instance is billed around the clock for a peak that occurs only once a month: this is more expensive.
opts.D: Redshift is an analytics warehouse; it isn't suited to the transactional workload of an ecommerce application.

597.key: The latency appears specifically at the start of the workday — a classic cold-start pattern, since employees arrive at roughly the same time. Provisioned concurrency keeps function instances initialized, and scheduled scaling turns it on shortly before the workday begins, so the company isn't paying for the reserved capacity around the clock.

opts.A: The API Gateway throttling limit protects against overload and has no effect on function initialization time.
opts.C: Periodically invoking the function on a timer would warm up only a single instance, while employees generate dozens of concurrent requests.
opts.D: More memory speeds up computation, but the latency spike at the start of the day is caused by the creation of new execution environments.

598.key: The devices can only write to an SMB share, so an on-premises Storage Gateway is deployed in Amazon S3 File Gateway mode: the CSV files land directly as objects in the bucket (A). From there, an AWS Glue crawler determines the schema and creates a table in the data catalog (C), and analysts run SQL queries through Amazon Athena, paying only for the bytes scanned (F). No continuously running cluster is involved — for periodic queries, this is the most cost-effective path.

opts.B: FSx File Gateway caches access to FSx file systems, and the data doesn't end up in S3 where Glue and Athena could read it.
opts.D: An EMR cluster is billed for node run time, but queries are run only a few times a day: the money goes toward idle capacity.
opts.E: A Redshift cluster is also billed continuously; for periodic queries, it's noticeably more expensive than Athena's pay-per-scan pricing.

599.key: AWS Outposts sits in the customer's own facility, so the line of responsibility runs along the rack. It's the customer's job to provide the rack with resilient power and network connectivity (A), physical security and access control for the facility itself (C), and extra capacity in the ECS clusters so that a server failure or maintenance event doesn't take down the application (F): Outposts is a fixed pool of capacity that doesn't expand automatically.

opts.B: AWS itself manages the virtualization hypervisor, storage systems, and the AWS services running on Outposts — the customer has no access to that layer.
opts.D: AWS is responsible for the availability of the Outposts infrastructure, including the power supplies, servers, and networking equipment inside the rack.
opts.E: Physical maintenance of Outposts components is performed by AWS technicians who come on-site. The dump's answer key attributed this item to the customer — that's an error noted in the audit log.

600.key: The application runs over TCP on a nonstandard port and must handle millions of requests per second with low latency. That's a Network Load Balancer's profile: it operates at layer 4, handles millions of connections per second, adds minimal latency, and can listen on any port.

opts.B: An Application Load Balancer understands only HTTP and HTTPS: it doesn't handle an arbitrary TCP protocol.
opts.C: CloudFront works only with HTTP and HTTPS and cannot listen on an arbitrary TCP port.
opts.D: API Gateway handles HTTP and WebSocket, not arbitrary TCP, and it can't deliver that level of throughput.

601.key: The standard path from RDS for PostgreSQL to Aurora PostgreSQL is an Aurora read replica: it is created from the running instance, catches up, and stays in sync, after which it is promoted to a standalone cluster. Downtime is reduced to the minutes it takes to switch over, there is no data loss, and the whole process uses built-in console tools.

opts.A: Restoring from a snapshot gives you a point-in-time copy: changes made after the snapshot are lost, and the downtime is noticeably longer.
opts.C: Importing from S3 requires exporting the data beforehand and a lengthy write freeze.
opts.D: Dumping with pg_dump and restoring is the slowest path, with a large downtime window and manual steps.

602.key: There are hundreds of instances, and minimal effort is required. AWS Backup lets a single backup plan cover the entire fleet of instances, automatically backing up both the configuration and the attached volumes, and bulk restores can be kicked off through the API or CLI. There is no need to write any custom scripts or templates.

opts.A: Volume snapshots do not preserve instance configuration, and a CloudFormation template for hundreds of machines would have to be written and maintained by hand.
opts.B: Elastic Beanstalk deploys applications from code and is not designed to restore arbitrary instances from snapshots.
opts.D: Two custom Lambda functions handling snapshots and AMIs mean code, schedules, and error handling - that is the most effort, not the least.

603.key: The requirement is a serverless solution that processes thousands of items in an S3 dataset in parallel. The Step Functions Map state in Distributed mode is built exactly for this: it reads the list of objects from the bucket itself and launches up to ten thousand parallel child executions, with no cluster and no custom distribution code required.

opts.A: Inline mode for the Map state is limited to forty concurrent branches and keeps all the data in the execution state - it cannot handle thousands of items.
opts.C: AWS Glue can do the job, but it is Spark-based ETL with its own jobs and configuration - more operational overhead than the built-in Distributed Map.
opts.D: Multiple Lambda functions would require manually partitioning the work, tracking concurrency, and collecting results - you would have to build the entire orchestrator yourself.

604.key: This again comes down to unforgiving arithmetic: 80% of 500 Mbps is 400 Mbps, or roughly 4.3 TB per day. At that rate, ten petabytes would take thousands of days, but the deadline is six weeks. No amount of online transfer optimization helps here - this calls for physical shipping: multiple Snowball devices loaded in parallel. Rule of thumb: divide the data volume using "1 Gbps ≈ 10 TB per day," and if that exceeds the allotted time, the answer is an offline transfer.

opts.A: DataSync speeds up and verifies the transfer, but it still runs over the same 400 Mbps uplink. The timeline is off by two orders of magnitude.
opts.B: rsync also does not work with S3 directly as a file system, and either way it is limited by the same bandwidth.
opts.C: Multiple parallel CLI copy processes share the same link: the combined throughput will not exceed 400 Mbps.

605.key: The requirements are fewer servers, low-latency access to frequently used data, and minimal infrastructure changes. A Volume Gateway configured with cached volumes presents volumes over the same iSCSI protocol, so clients notice no difference, while the bulk of the data is stored in S3 and only the active portion stays in the local cache. This is exactly how dependency on on-premises storage servers is reduced.

opts.A: S3 File Gateway presents shares over NFS and SMB: the protocol would change, and the requirement calls for minimal changes.
opts.B: EBS volumes live inside AWS and attach to instances, not to the company's on-premises servers.
opts.C: Stored volumes keep the entire dataset on local disks, so the number and capacity of on-premises storage servers are not reduced.

606.key: "Maximize object durability" and "readily available at any time" set the frame: the storage class must keep copies across three Availability Zones and return objects instantly. That leaves S3 Standard and Standard-IA in play. The access pattern is known and tied to object age - heavy access for the first 30 days, then infrequent - so an explicit Lifecycle rule into Standard-IA is cheaper than automated tiering with its monitoring fee.

opts.A: S3 Glacier retrieval takes minutes to hours. That violates the "readily available at any time" requirement.
opts.C: One Zone-IA keeps a single copy in a single Availability Zone. That directly contradicts the requirement to maximize object durability.
opts.D: This combination does not make sense: Intelligent-Tiering already moves objects between tiers on its own, and layering a Lifecycle rule on top pushes them into IA anyway - after you have already paid for the monitoring. With a known access pattern, a plain transition straight to Standard-IA is cheaper.

607.key: The core problem is that 6 MB documents are stored in the database as binary large objects: the database bloats, performance drops, and RDS storage gets expensive. The right fix is to split the data: store the documents themselves in S3 and keep only metadata and references in the database. This sharply shrinks the database size, improves performance, costs far less to store in S3, and keeps the Multi-AZ configuration intact.

opts.A: Magnetic storage is slower, and doubling the capacity just raises the cost - performance would get worse, not better.
opts.B: A larger instance and Provisioned IOPS would speed things up, but it is the most expensive path, and the root cause - binary objects in the database - remains unaddressed.
opts.D: Moving to DynamoDB means rewriting the application, and the 400 KB item size limit makes storing six-megabyte documents impossible.

608.key: Only registered store IP addresses need to be allowed through, there are thousands of them, and the list keeps changing. AWS WAF with IP sets is built for exactly this: the set of addresses is maintained separately from the rule, supports tens of thousands of entries, and can be updated through the API without touching the web ACL itself. The web ACL is associated with the load balancer, and anything not in the set is blocked before it reaches the application.

opts.B: Firewall Manager centrally distributes WAF policies across accounts, but it does not do the filtering itself - WAF remains the underlying service either way.
opts.C: The Application Load Balancer has no Lambda-based authorization mechanism: it routes requests, and building custom validation would require code inside the application.
opts.D: Network ACLs are limited to roughly twenty rules per list (the maximum can be raised only slightly) - twenty thousand addresses will not fit.

609.key: What needs hiding is not entire tables but parts of them, and it must be done without rewriting the data. Lake Formation provides a built-in mechanism for this - data filters: they define which columns are visible (column-level security), which rows are returned based on a condition (row-level security), and, as a result, which individual cells a given principal can access. The filter is enforced at the service level, so it works the same way for Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR. The underlying data stays untouched, and no copies are created.

opts.A: A role with permissions on tables grants access on an all-or-nothing basis. The requirement is to hide parts of the data within a table.
opts.C: Stripping sensitive data before ingestion means losing information that other teams might need, plus building and maintaining a custom processing pipeline.
opts.D: Periodically purging tables with a function both destroys data and leaves a window during which the sensitive information is still exposed.

610.key: There are two requirements here, and they are met by two different mechanisms. Traffic from the instances to S3 must not go over the internet - that calls for a gateway VPC endpoint for S3, with a route added to the subnet route table. The company's on-premises servers must receive the application's output - that calls for a Direct Connect connection between the on-premises location and the VPC, a private link that bypasses the internet.

opts.A: An interface endpoint for EC2 gives private access to the EC2 management API, not to S3. Uploading data to the bucket would still go over the internet.
opts.C: Transit Gateway connects networks to each other, not a network to the S3 service. There is no way to attach a bucket to it.
opts.D: A NAT gateway is itself a path out to the public internet: that directly violates the requirement, and the proxy instances add extra work and cost.

611.key: The 503 errors mean data ingestion is bottlenecked by compute capacity. Kinesis Data Streams ingests the stream independently of processing speed and retains records, while Lambda functions process them in parallel and scale automatically. Spikes stop causing failures because ingestion and processing are decoupled.

opts.B: A usage plan with a quota throttles the vendor, meaning it drops part of the data instead of accepting it.
opts.C: SNS delivers messages immediately and does not buffer them: during a spike, the instances would still get hit with the same storm of requests.
opts.D: Containers on EC2 instances scale over minutes and still require managing capacity: peak spikes would still get dropped.

612.key: The application in the private subnet needs to reach S3 without going out to the internet. A VPC endpoint is the only mechanism that provides such a path: traffic to S3 travels over the AWS network, with no public addresses or NAT required. The bucket policy can additionally be tightened with an aws:SourceVpce condition, so the bucket holding sensitive data will not respond to requests that do not come through this endpoint. For S3, a gateway endpoint is typically used since it is free; an interface endpoint is needed when access must also come from an on-premises network over Direct Connect.

opts.A: An internet gateway exists to send traffic out to the internet, and a bucket policy has no way to describe such a source in the first place. This directly violates the requirement.
opts.B: A VPN connects the VPC to an external network, not the VPC to S3. Requests to S3 would still go through the public endpoint.
opts.C: A NAT gateway is an internet egress path with address translation. It violates the requirement, and on top of that it is billed per gigabyte processed.

613.key: This is about a built-in EKS feature: secrets encryption with a KMS key. The cluster is configured once, after which Secret objects are encrypted using envelope encryption before being written to etcd - handled by the control plane, not the application. No code and no extra services are needed, hence "least operational overhead." The same mechanism is covered in {{q:535}}; do not confuse it with storing application secrets in Secrets Manager or Parameter Store.

opts.A: Encrypting inside the application means every container has to work with KMS directly, and other cluster components would still read the secrets from etcd in plaintext.
opts.C: A separate Lambda function for encryption means your own code and an extra hop in the chain, whereas EKS can do the same thing through configuration alone.
opts.D: Parameter Store stores parameters outside of Kubernetes. The Secret objects in etcd would remain unencrypted, and the requirement is specifically about those.

614.key: An Application Load Balancer is placed between the web tier and the application tier, with a target group containing the application servers' Auto Scaling group, and access is restricted using security groups: the inbound rule on the load balancer and on the application servers allows traffic only from the web servers' security group. This rule keeps working no matter how the number or addresses of instances change, because it references a security group rather than specific addresses.

opts.A: PrivateLink is for publishing a service to other VPCs or accounts, not for separating tiers within a single network. A network ACL also operates on subnets and address ranges and has no concept of a dynamic Auto Scaling group.
opts.B: A VPC endpoint provides access to AWS services or to services published through PrivateLink; you cannot place one "in front of" your own instances within the same VPC.
opts.C: The load balancer setup itself is sound, but the rule is expressed through a network ACL - which operates on address ranges and subnets and cannot reference the web servers' security group, so it stops being accurate whenever the fleet's composition changes.

615.key: What is needed is collecting, aggregating, and summarizing the cluster's metrics and logs in one place. Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights does this natively for EKS: it collects metrics at the cluster, node, pod, and container level, pulls in logs, and builds ready-made dashboards in the CloudWatch console.

opts.A: The CloudWatch agent collects node-level metrics and logs, but it does not aggregate them by Kubernetes object and does not provide ready-made summaries.
opts.B: App Mesh manages traffic between services; it does not perform centralized collection of cluster metrics and logs.
opts.C: CloudTrail records AWS API calls, not what is happening inside the application within the cluster.

616.key: The requirement is continuous monitoring for suspicious activity across the account, workloads, and access to the bucket, with findings surfaced on a dashboard. That is GuardDuty: it analyzes CloudTrail, S3 data event logs, DNS logs, and VPC Flow Logs to detect anomalies and known malicious patterns. Findings are natively sent to AWS Security Hub, which serves as the unified dashboard. The distinction: GuardDuty detects, Security Hub aggregates and evaluates compliance.

opts.A: Macie looks for sensitive data, and AWS Config tracks resource configuration: neither one is a malicious-activity monitor.
opts.B: Inspector looks for vulnerabilities, and CloudTrail is an API call log, not a findings dashboard.
opts.D: AWS Config tracks configuration compliance and does not detect attacks or anomalous access.

617.key: The target storage needs to serve data over NFS to multiple AWS resources - that is Amazon EFS (B). Migrating without interrupting existing services is what AWS DataSync does: an agent is deployed in the data center and transfers the data incrementally while verifying integrity, without disrupting operations on the source server (E). Two hundred gigabytes moves quickly over any reasonable connection.

opts.A: FSx for Lustre is built for high-performance computing, costs significantly more, and uses a different protocol.
opts.C: S3 does not serve data over the NFS protocol: the requirement explicitly names the protocol.
opts.D: Manually copying with an operating system command gives you no integrity verification, no incremental transfer, and no protection against interruption.

618.key: A five-minute RPO for both planned maintenance and unplanned disruptions is achieved with a Multi-AZ deployment: FSx synchronously replicates data to a second Availability Zone and fails over automatically. Cross-region copies are produced by a scheduled AWS Backup plan, and five-year immutability comes from Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode - in that mode, no one, including the account owner, can shorten or remove the retention period.

opts.A: A Single-AZ configuration does not deliver a five-minute RPO if the Availability Zone fails.
opts.B: Governance mode lets users with sufficient permissions remove the lock and delete copies, and the requirement states that no one should be able to delete the data.
opts.D: This option has both problems at once: a single Availability Zone instead of two, and a lock mode that can be overridden.

619.key: Developers get root-user access in their own accounts, which means they can bypass or change any IAM policy within the account. The only mechanism that also constrains the root user of a member account is a service control policy attached to the accounts or their OUs: it denies actions like cloudtrail:StopLogging, DeleteTrail, UpdateTrail, and similar. This is typically combined with an organization trail created from the management account, which member accounts cannot modify.

opts.A: An IAM policy cannot be attached to the root user, and IAM policies do not apply to it anyway. That is exactly why SCPs exist.
opts.B: An organization trail is created in the management account, not "from within the developer accounts." And the mere presence of a trail does not prevent someone from disabling it without an SCP in place.
opts.D: A service-linked role lets a service take action on your behalf. It cannot restrict what the root user does.

620.key: The requirements are durable storage with consistently low latency. A Provisioned IOPS EBS volume delivers a guaranteed number of operations per second with predictable latency, and the data is replicated within the Availability Zone and survives an instance stop.

opts.A: Instance store is ephemeral: data disappears when the instance stops, and durability is explicitly required.
opts.B: Memcached is an in-memory cache with no data persistence: it does not qualify as durable storage.
opts.D: Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) volumes are optimized for high sequential throughput, not for consistently low latency on random operations.

621.key: The task is to keep a copy of every new object in another region with the least effort. That is exactly what S3 Cross-Region Replication exists for: it is turned on with a rule on the source bucket (versioning is required), copies new objects asynchronously, retries automatically on failures, and can replicate metadata, tags, and encryption status. There is no code and no monitoring to build - the service manages the state. Keep in mind the limitation: replication applies only to objects created after it is enabled; existing objects have to be copied separately with S3 Batch Replication.

opts.B: CORS controls which websites a browser is allowed to let access the bucket from JavaScript. It does not copy any data between regions.
opts.C: A Lifecycle rule can change storage class and delete objects within a single bucket. It cannot copy objects to another bucket.
opts.D: The "S3 event plus Lambda" combination technically works, but it is your own code: error handling, retries, concurrency limits, and invocation costs. By the LEAST operational effort criterion, it loses to built-in replication.

622.key: There are two requirements here, met by two different picks. For the static page, it is S3 plus CloudFront (D): serving from edge locations scales without any effort on your part. For the database, "rapidly evolve their schema" means no rigid schema, which points to DynamoDB rather than the relational Aurora. What is left is picking a capacity mode: the answer key goes with C (provisioned with auto scaling), while the community debates in favor of A (on-demand). The case for A: millions of users arrive in a wave, and provisioned auto scaling raises capacity in steps that can lag behind a sharp spike. The case for C: the load is predictable - the same window every morning - and provisioning against a known profile is cheaper.

opts.A: A strong alternative: on-demand absorbs the spike instantly and needs no configuration. The key favored provisioned because the load pattern in the question repeats predictably, making it cheaper to plan capacity for.
opts.B: Aurora is a relational database with a fixed schema. The requirement to "rapidly evolve their schema" points in exactly the opposite direction.
opts.E: A fleet of EC2 instances that periodically pulls static content from EFS is the heaviest to operate and the least scalable way to serve a single static page. S3 with CloudFront achieves the same thing with no servers at all.

623.key: SQL injection and XSS are filtered by AWS WAF, and API Gateway is supported directly: a regional web ACL is associated with the API stage. No additional components are needed - hence "most operationally efficient." The options involving CloudFront add an unnecessary layer (useful when the API is edge-optimized or needs caching and global distribution), and Shield handles DDoS, not injection attacks.

opts.A: AWS Shield protects against availability attacks and does not inspect request content for injections.
opts.C: CloudFront is added without a need for it, and Shield again is not the right service for SQL injection.
opts.D: This would work, but CloudFront is an unnecessary component here: WAF attaches directly to API Gateway, which is simpler to operate.

624.key: Fifteen hundred employees already live in Active Directory, and they cannot be given a second set of credentials. The standard answer is SAML 2.0 federation: the corporate directory (via ADFS or IAM Identity Center) acts as the identity provider, roles with the appropriate policies are created in AWS, and Active Directory groups are mapped to those roles. The user signs in with their corporate password, receives temporary role credentials, and keeps access to on-premises resources at the same time.

opts.A: Fifteen hundred IAM users means a second set of credentials and manual upkeep - exactly what needs to be avoided.
opts.B: Cognito is meant for application end users, not for employee access to the AWS console and APIs. And an "Active Directory-based user pool" is not the right mechanism.
opts.C: Cross-account roles address access between AWS accounts, but they do not let employees sign in with their corporate credentials: an identity provider is needed.

625.key: Distribution rights are tied to countries, so users need to be routed to different content based on their location. In Route 53 that is a geolocation routing policy: records are mapped to a continent, country, or US state, and the request goes to the load balancer authorized to serve that region. Do not confuse this with geoproximity: that policy routes based on geographic distance with a configurable bias and does not guarantee alignment with legal boundaries.

opts.A: CloudFront with WAF can block countries, but the task is not to block - it is to serve different content to different countries, and routing does that more precisely.
opts.B: WAF on the load balancers again blocks rather than distributes users to the right destinations.
opts.D: Geoproximity is based on distance to the resource, not the user's country: a user near a border could easily land on the wrong load balancer.

626.key: There are two requirements: an online transfer, and automatic integrity verification after the transfer. DataSync does both: the on-premises agent reads the source storage, transfers the data to S3 over multiple TLS-encrypted threads, and on completion compares source and destination checksums, reporting any discrepancies in the task report. Neither File Gateway nor Transfer Acceleration performs this kind of verification. Keep the distinction clear: DataSync is transfer with verification, Storage Gateway is ongoing hybrid access, and the Snow Family is offline shipping for when the network link is not enough.

opts.A: Snowball Edge is an offline device that is physically shipped to AWS; you cannot "perform an online transfer" with it. The option contradicts itself.
opts.C: S3 File Gateway is built for ongoing file-based access to S3 objects with a local cache, not for a one-time migration with integrity verification.
opts.D: Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads through edge locations. It does not perform any automatic checksum verification after the transfer.

627.key: The task is hosting DNS zones, not administering servers. Route 53 is a managed service with a 100% availability SLA, so the 200 zones are simply created in it and populated by importing zone files. There is no more patching, scaling, or monitoring of your own servers to do, and a million requests a day is a perfectly ordinary load for it.

opts.B: A single EC2 instance is the same single point of failure as before, just now in the cloud. Downtime alerts do not substitute for actual availability.
opts.C: AWS SMS migrates virtual machines as-is: the DNS servers would still exist, along with all the operational burden that comes with them.
opts.D: An Auto Scaling group of DNS servers requires synchronizing zones across instances and scales based on CPU utilization, which has little to do with DNS load. Complexity goes up with no gain over a managed service.

628.key: What is needed is a report on incomplete multipart uploads across many buckets, accounts, and regions at once. S3 Storage Lens does this natively: it aggregates metrics organization-wide (when connected to AWS Organizations), and among its metrics are the count and size of incomplete multipart uploads, along with a breakdown by their age. From there, what is found gets addressed with a Lifecycle rule using AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload - see {{q:326,725}}.

opts.A: AWS Config tracks resource configuration, not bucket contents. It does not count incomplete uploads.
opts.B: An SCP denies actions. Reporting is not its function.
opts.D: A Multi-Region Access Point routes requests to buckets across regions and does not produce any upload statistics.

629.key: The requirement is to upgrade the version, verify functionality, and lose no data, with minimal effort. RDS Blue/Green Deployments creates a full copy of the database on the new version, keeps it in sync through replication, and lets you test it. The switchover takes about a minute and is done with a single command, and rollback stays available because the old environment remains in place.

opts.A: A snapshot is just a safety net: an in-place upgrade still means downtime and no way to test the new version under load beforehand.
opts.B: Native backup and restore requires manual steps, causes noticeable downtime, and does not let you validate functionality ahead of time.
opts.C: A DMS task would have to be configured and maintained manually - the same end result, but with significantly more effort.

630.key: The job runs once a day, can take up to two hours, and cannot tolerate interruption. That rules out interruptible capacity, and Lambda's fifteen-minute limit does not fit either. An ECS task on Fargate, triggered by an EventBridge scheduled event, is billed only for the actual two hours and requires no continuously running instance.

opts.A: A Reserved Instance is billed around the clock, even though it only runs two hours a day.
opts.B: The Lambda function execution limit is fifteen minutes, and the job runs up to two hours.
opts.D: The EC2 launch type means an instance that runs - and is billed - outside the job's execution window.

631.key: Profiles, relationships, and interactions are graph data, which points to Amazon Neptune. Its built-in Neptune Streams capability can track changes in the database: the change log is published by the database itself, with no need for additional services or ingestion code.

opts.A: The database choice is correct, but Kinesis Data Streams would have to be populated manually — an extra pipeline instead of a built-in stream.
opts.C: QLDB is a ledger with an immutable transaction history; it isn't designed to analyze relationships between entities.
opts.D: Both the database choice is wrong, and Neptune Streams doesn't apply to QLDB.

632.key: The data is modified by several Linux instances across multiple Availability Zones, and the storage need will keep growing over months. Amazon EFS solves all of this at once: it mounts over NFS on every instance in every zone, supports concurrent writes, and grows automatically with no capacity planning.

opts.A: Glacier is an archive with retrieval times measured in minutes to hours; you can't modify data stored there.
opts.B: An EBS volume lives in a single Availability Zone and attaches to one instance, and you'd have to resize it manually.
opts.D: Even a Provisioned IOPS volume in Multi-Attach mode is limited to a single Availability Zone and requires a cluster-aware file system: instances in another zone can't attach to it.

633.key: Read queries are slow, so they need to be offloaded from the primary instance. An RDS read replica is created from the source instance and takes all the read traffic, leaving writes to the primary.

opts.A: The standby instance in a Multi-AZ deployment doesn't serve requests: it exists only for failover.
opts.B: Transfer Acceleration is an Amazon S3 feature; it has nothing to do with RDS.
opts.D: Firehose delivers streaming data to storage destinations and doesn't increase the concurrency of database requests.

634.key: The data must stay in the source account while several external agencies get read access to it. The standard mechanism is cross-account access: a bucket policy (or a role that the agencies' accounts assume) grants the needed accounts s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket permissions on the relevant prefix. No copies are made, the accounts stay on the agencies' side, and access can be revoked with a single policy edit. That's both maximum security and minimum operational effort.

opts.A: "S3 global tables" doesn't exist — global tables are a DynamoDB feature. Even replication would mean copies of the data outside your control.
opts.B: A public bucket exposes the data to the entire internet, not just the agencies. "For a limited time" changes nothing: during that window anyone, including crawlers, can download the data.
opts.D: An IAM user per analyst in your own account means outside people holding long-lived credentials inside your perimeter, plus ongoing work provisioning and revoking accounts.

635.key: Data must be accessible in the secondary Region using the same CIFS and NFS protocols as the primary Region, so the secondary Region needs an FSx for ONTAP file system too. The standard, lowest-effort replication between them is NetApp SnapMirror: it's built into ONTAP, runs on a snapshot-based schedule, transfers only changes, and lets you quickly promote the target volume to read-write during a disaster.

opts.A: A custom copy function to S3 is code you have to write and maintain, and more importantly, S3 doesn't serve data over CIFS or NFS.
opts.B: Backups via AWS Backup give a much longer recovery time: during a disaster you'd have to create the file system from a backup instead of failing over to one that's already running.
opts.D: EFS doesn't support the CIFS protocol, so the requirement for identical access isn't met.

636.key: An SNS topic delivers events immediately and, if the handler fails, drops them after a few retries. To make processing scalable and lossless, an SQS queue sits between SNS and the function: it absorbs bursts, holds messages, provides retries and a dead-letter queue, and the function reads from it in batches.

opts.A: Intermediate processing in ECS adds infrastructure and doesn't solve the problem of buffering events.
opts.B: Same issue with EKS: an extra cluster instead of a simple queue.
opts.D: AWS SMS is a server migration service; it can't act as an event target.

637.key: Load swings from zero to over 500 requests per second, the dataset is under a gigabyte and grows unpredictably, and access is by key. That calls for services that scale instantly and from zero: AWS Lambda as the compute behind API Gateway (B) and Amazon DynamoDB as the key-value store (C). Neither capacity nor servers need to be planned.

opts.A: Fargate scales, but tasks take seconds to start and are billed for runtime: for a workload that swings between zero and 500 requests, Lambda fits better.
opts.D: An EC2 Auto Scaling group reacts on the order of minutes, and it still keeps a minimum number of instances running when idle.
opts.E: Aurora requires choosing an instance class and is billed continuously, whereas the access pattern needed here is simple key-value.

638.key: Files need to be distributed to employees worldwide without creating an AWS account for each one or standing up infrastructure. A presigned URL solves this: the application (here, a Lambda function) signs the link with its own permissions, the link is valid for a limited time, and it grants access to exactly one object. Employees need only a browser. Useful limit to remember: a URL signed with long-term credentials is valid for at most 7 days, while one signed with temporary credentials is valid no longer than those credentials themselves.

opts.B: An IAM user and a separate policy for every employee worldwide is ongoing administrative work: provisioning, revoking, rotating keys, and untangling permissions.
opts.C: S3 File Gateway is a component you have to deploy and maintain, and employees would have to mount network shares. That's overkill for distributing files to remote users.
opts.D: Transfer Family with a custom identity provider adds both an hourly endpoint charge and integration work to build. For simply handing out files, that's unnecessary complexity.

639.key: Traffic skewing toward a single target with an otherwise healthy load balancer is usually explained by session affinity: a client that lands on one instance keeps returning to it via a cookie, so distribution stops being even. Disabling sticky sessions restores the standard round-robin algorithm and evens out the load.

opts.B: A Network Load Balancer distributes by flow and doesn't fix the affinity problem, while giving up HTTP-layer features.
opts.C: More instances won't help if traffic keeps going to the same target anyway.
opts.D: Health check frequency affects how fast a failure is detected, not how requests are distributed.

640.key: Access to a KMS key is always checked on two sides, and that's exactly what this question is testing. On the principal side: the function's execution role must have kms:Decrypt — the policy is attached to the role, and the role is assigned to the function (E). On the resource side: that same role must be explicitly allowed in the key policy (B). Remove either half and the function gets an AccessDeniedException when it tries to decrypt the object. Compare with {{q:550}} — the same pairing applies there for Lambda environment variables.

opts.A: A function's resource policy controls who can invoke it. It doesn't grant permissions to work with a KMS key.
opts.C: In a key policy, permissions are granted to a principal — a role or an account. "Allow the function's resource policy" is a construct that doesn't exist in KMS.
opts.D: An IAM policy can't be attached to a function: it's attached to the execution role, and the role is then assigned to the function. The option describes an operation that doesn't exist.

641.key: The Cost and Usage Report is a highly detailed cost export, and it must be enabled in the organization's management account, since only there can you see usage across all member accounts. Reports are delivered to S3 in Parquet format partitioned by month, and running SQL queries against them once a month is a natural fit for Athena: you pay only for bytes scanned and maintain no infrastructure. That makes it both the most scalable and the cheapest option for a monthly review.

opts.A: Kinesis is meant for streaming data, while the CUR is delivered as files in S3. An EMR cluster for a monthly report is unnecessary expense.
opts.C: Enabling reports in each member account produces scattered exports instead of one unified view, and a persistent Redshift cluster costs more than Athena for once-a-month queries.
opts.D: Again, per-account reports, and again Kinesis used for the wrong purpose. QuickSight also builds visualizations on top of a data source rather than replacing one.

642.key: The key word is UDP. Of the AWS load balancers, only the Network Load Balancer works with UDP: it operates at layer 4, supports TCP, UDP, and TLS, and attaches to the Auto Scaling group as a target group. The group scales freely in both directions, and the load balancer distributes packets across healthy instances.

opts.B: An Application Load Balancer only understands HTTP and HTTPS: it can't handle the game's UDP packets.
opts.C: A Route 53 weighted policy hands out addresses via DNS without checking load or instantly removing failed instances. That's name distribution, not load balancing.
opts.D: A NAT instance with port forwarding is a homegrown setup, a single point of failure, and manual upkeep every time the group's membership changes.

643.key: The logs sit in S3 at tens of gigabytes per day, and they're analyzed once a week. Athena runs standard SQL queries directly against the objects in the bucket and is billed by the amount of data scanned: nothing is charged between queries, and there's no infrastructure at all.

opts.B: Loading the logs into RDS means a continuously running instance and growing storage — expensive for analysis done once a week.
opts.C: OpenSearch Service keeps a cluster running around the clock and is built for search and observability, not one-off SQL queries.
opts.D: An EMR cluster also runs and is billed continuously, and requires administration.

644.key: Certificates are needed for the domain itself and all its country subdomains, along with proof of ownership. A public certificate requested in ACM for example.com and the wildcard *.example.com covers both the apex and all subdomains (A). Domain ownership is validated by adding the required DNS records at the DNS provider — a method that also supports automatic certificate renewal (E).

opts.B: A private certificate is issued by your own certificate authority and isn't trusted by public visitors' browsers.
opts.C: A certificate for the apex domain alone doesn't cover country1.example.com and similar subdomains.
opts.D: Validating by email and then switching to DNS validation is an unnecessary extra step; going straight to DNS validation is enough.

645.key: The requirement is rare and very specific: keys must physically stay in the company's own key manager outside AWS, and multiple vendors must be supported. That describes an AWS KMS external key store (XKS): KMS acts as a facade while the external key manager performs the cryptographic operations through the XKS proxy, and the key material never enters AWS. Distinguish the three options: the default KMS key store keeps keys in AWS; a custom key store backed by CloudHSM keeps keys in your own CloudHSM cluster but still inside AWS; an external key store keeps keys outside the cloud entirely.

opts.A: CloudHSM runs inside AWS: the cluster is deployed in your VPC, but that's still the cloud, and the requirement is to keep keys outside it.
opts.C: The default KMS key store means keys live inside the AWS service. That directly contradicts the requirement.
opts.D: A custom key store backed by CloudHSM still keeps keys in the cloud and additionally requires deploying and maintaining an HSM cluster — maximum operational overhead.

646.key: Hundreds of instances, parallel access to a shared dataset, and sub-millisecond latency point to Amazon FSx for Lustre. The file system links to an S3 bucket, so source data is loaded from there and results are exported back, letting engineers work through postprocessing at their own pace after the compute cluster has been shut down.

opts.A: EFS provides neither sub-millisecond latency nor the throughput hundreds of compute nodes need.
opts.B: S3 doesn't mount as a file system through standard means and doesn't provide the latency required for parallel access.
opts.D: AWS RAM shares resources between accounts and does nothing to turn a bucket into a mountable file system.

647.key: VoIP means UDP, and the requirement to avoid relying on IP address caching on client devices rules out DNS-based solutions. Global Accelerator (A) provides two static anycast IP addresses, works with UDP, routes traffic over the AWS backbone, and fails over between Regions within seconds based on health checks.

opts.B: Route 53 is DNS: the client caches the response, and if a Region fails it keeps sending traffic to the dead address until the TTL expires. Geolocation routing also picks a Region by geography rather than actual latency.
opts.C: CloudFront only serves HTTP and HTTPS. Voice traffic over UDP can't pass through it.
opts.D: An ALB operates within a single Region and only handles HTTP/HTTPS — no cross-Region failover and no UDP.

648.key: The requirements are sub-millisecond latency, sustained high throughput, high availability, and simultaneous access from thousands of compute nodes. That's Amazon FSx for Lustre in persistent mode: it replicates data within the Availability Zone and automatically replaces failed components, which scratch mode does not do.

opts.A: Scratch file systems don't replicate data and don't recover from a server failure, so the high-availability requirement isn't met.
opts.C: EFS in Bursting Throughput mode provides neither that level of sustained throughput nor sub-millisecond latency.
opts.D: EFS Provisioned Throughput solves the throughput-stability issue, but an NFS file system's latency is still measured in milliseconds, not fractions of one.

649.key: Same requirement as in {{q:425}}: provision performance independently of capacity, with a daily peak up to 15,000 IOPS. A gp3 volume lets you set IOPS independently of size, up to 16,000, so 15,000 fits comfortably, and its per-gigabyte cost is lower than gp2's and notably lower than Provisioned IOPS volumes.

opts.A: gp2 ties performance to size at a ratio of three IOPS per gigabyte: reaching 15,000 IOPS would require provisioning — and paying for — 5 TB.
opts.B: io1 covers the requirement but costs significantly more than gp3 and is overkill at 15,000 IOPS.
opts.D: Magnetic volumes deliver on the order of hundreds of IOPS: the requirement can't be met at all.

650.key: The company wants to move to managed services while keeping SQL Server, and to offload reporting from the production database. Amazon RDS for SQL Server supports read replicas that analytics can be pointed at, while AWS handles patching, backups, and fault tolerance. The application and its queries stay unchanged.

opts.B: SQL Server on EC2 instances remains entirely the company's responsibility to operate: operational overhead isn't reduced.
opts.C: DynamoDB is a non-relational store: migrating means rewriting all the application logic, and it has no such thing as "on-demand replicas."
opts.D: Aurora MySQL is incompatible with SQL Server: this would require schema conversion and rewriting queries.

651.key: Read the requirements as a timeline and pick a storage class for each segment. The first 180 days: Standard. The next 180 days, access is infrequent, but the data "cannot be lost," so Standard-IA, not One Zone-IA. After 360 days, it's archived but "available instantly upon request" — that's exactly the definition of Glacier Instant Retrieval. After 5 years, only auditors need access with a 12-hour window — that matches Glacier Deep Archive's standard retrieval. Remember the difference between the three Glacier tiers: Instant Retrieval is milliseconds, Flexible Retrieval is minutes to hours, and Deep Archive is 12 hours and the cheapest of the three.

opts.A: One Zone-IA keeps a single copy in one Availability Zone, and the requirement explicitly forbids losing the images.
opts.B: Same single-zone problem, plus Glacier Flexible Retrieval doesn't return the object instantly after 360 days.
opts.D: The storage classes for durability are chosen correctly, but Glacier Flexible Retrieval on the segment after 360 days returns the object in minutes to hours, while instant access is required.

652.key: The workload runs six hours a day, so the cluster should exist only for that window — a transient cluster terminates as soon as its jobs finish and isn't billed for the other eighteen hours. Data can't be lost, so the primary node and the core nodes, which hold HDFS data, run on On-Demand Instances, while the task nodes, which store nothing, run on Spot Instances, delivering the savings.

opts.A: A long-running cluster is billed around the clock, even though the workload only runs a quarter of the day.
opts.C: Spot core nodes hold HDFS data: their reclamation means data loss, which the requirement explicitly forbids.
opts.D: This combines both drawbacks — a cluster that keeps running plus data sitting on Spot nodes.

653.key: A tag value needs to be set based on who created the resource, and that value lives in an external database. No declarative policy can do this: an SCP or tag policy can require a tag to be present or restrict its allowed values, but neither can compute a value by looking up the creator. This calls for an event-driven handler: an EventBridge rule catches CloudTrail events for resource creation, and a Lambda function looks up the creator's cost center in the RDS database and applies the tag.

opts.A: An SCP can require a tag to be present at creation time (using the aws:RequestTag condition), but it can't populate a value from an external database. And a policy can't require a tag on resources that already exist, either.
opts.C: A CloudFormation stack is a way to deploy the function, not a way to schedule its execution. And running on a schedule is too late anyway: the resource is already created without a tag.
opts.D: A default tag value doesn't solve the problem: what's needed is the actual cost center of the creating user, otherwise cost allocation is meaningless.

654.key: Each component is replaced with a managed equivalent. Static content moves into an S3 bucket and is served through CloudFront. The PHP application becomes Fargate tasks running in ECS behind an Application Load Balancer, so no servers remain. Sessions move into an ElastiCache for Redis cluster deployed across multiple Availability Zones, so they now survive the failure of any single node.

opts.A: Elastic Beanstalk manages the deployment, but a single machine in a public subnet with a public IP address is neither highly available nor secure.
opts.B: Serving static content through a Lambda function and API Gateway is inefficient and costly, and the PHP application would need to be rewritten to run on Lambda.
opts.C: The code stays on a single EC2 instance — the single point of failure remains, so the high-availability requirement isn't met.

655.key: Two requirements both point to the same load balancer type. Sticky sessions via cookies are supported by the Application Load Balancer (C) — it operates at the HTTP layer and can issue a cookie that binds a client to a target.
