AWS WAF also attaches to an ALB, not to an NLB, so a web ACL is created and associated with this public load balancer (E). One solution satisfies both requirements.

opts.A: A Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4: it doesn't issue cookies, and WAF can't attach to it.
opts.B: A Gateway Load Balancer is designed for inserting traffic-inspection appliances, not for publishing a web application.
opts.D: A second target group and Elastic IP addresses on the instances provide neither session affinity nor a way to attach WAF.

656.key: Each image is requested only once or twice a year, but access still needs to be instant and reliable. The S3 Standard-Infrequent Access class is built exactly for this: storage costs roughly half of Standard, availability and latency are the same, and only a small retrieval fee applies. The site can be served straight from the bucket as a static website, with no server at all.

opts.A: EBS volumes plus a continuously running instance is the most expensive setup, and it's also limited to a single Availability Zone.
opts.B: EFS with a web server on an instance costs more for both storage and compute, with no benefit over a static website.
opts.C: Standard works, but with such infrequent access the storage overpay is significant, and cost is named as the deciding requirement.

657.key: Office CIDR ranges change, and rewriting rules across every security group in every account is too costly. A customer-managed prefix list is a named list of CIDRs that's referenced in a security group rule instead of listing addresses directly; when the list changes, the rules update automatically. AWS RAM lets you share that list across the organization, so it's maintained in one place and used everywhere. There's no charge for the list itself, hence the most cost-effective option.

opts.A: Security groups don't work across accounts and VPCs: ones created in the management account won't apply to resources in other accounts.
opts.C: AWS managed prefix lists are maintained by AWS itself (for its own service ranges) — you can't add office networks to them. Security Hub also doesn't apply changes; it assesses compliance.
opts.D: Firewall Manager can propagate common security groups, but it's a paid service that requires Security Hub and policy setup. For simply changing a list of addresses, a prefix list is simpler and cheaper.

658.key: There are two separate requirements, solved at two different levels. Multi-protocol access over NFS and SMB from a single file system is provided only by Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP (E). Minimum network latency between compute nodes comes from a cluster placement group: instances are packed into a single rack in one Availability Zone for maximum throughput and minimum latency between them (A).

opts.B: A partition placement group deliberately spreads instances across different hardware sets for fault tolerance — that increases, not decreases, latency between nodes.
opts.C: FSx for Lustre is very fast, but it uses the Lustre protocol and serves data over neither NFS nor SMB.
opts.D: FSx for OpenZFS supports NFS but not SMB, so the multi-protocol access requirement isn't met.

659.key: The link is already 90 percent utilized, and 50 TB needs to move in two weeks — the remaining bandwidth is nowhere near enough, and pushing it would also hurt production traffic. So the data has to travel physically: Snowball Edge Storage Optimized carries tens of terabytes, encrypts its contents with AWS KMS keys, and uses none of the company's network at all.

opts.A: DataSync is still limited by the same congested VPN link: it can't speed up the transfer.
opts.B: A dedicated Direct Connect connection typically takes weeks to provision and costs as much as permanent infrastructure, while this is a one-time job on a two-week deadline.
opts.D: Storage Gateway is built for ongoing hybrid access to data in the cloud, not a one-time bulk migration, and it runs over that same congested link.

660.key: Peak hours arrive at the same time every day, but metric-based dynamic scaling reacts after the fact — which is exactly why the application only recovers two to three hours into the peak. A scheduled scaling policy adds capacity ahead of time, before the peak begins, and the problem goes away.

opts.A: A load balancer distributes traffic but doesn't add the capacity that's missing.
opts.B: Reacting to a memory metric is still a reaction after the fact, with the same lag.
opts.C: Same issue with a CPU metric: scaling only starts after performance has already degraded.

661.key: The applications scale in bursts, and each new instance opens its own connections to the database. RDS Proxy is a managed connection pool: it reuses connections and smooths out spikes, and the applications only need to point to its endpoint instead of the database endpoint.

opts.A: DynamoDB is a different database; it doesn't provide connection pooling for RDS, and switching to it would mean rewriting the application.
opts.C: A custom proxy on EC2 is infrastructure you have to provision for high availability, patch, and scale yourself.
opts.D: A Lambda function acting as a proxy adds another moving part and custom code instead of a ready-made managed service.

662.key: The symptom is that snapshot costs grow month over month even though no new volumes are being purchased: old snapshots are piling up because nothing is removing them. The solution has two steps: a one-time cleanup of unneeded snapshots, plus a process — Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager creates snapshots on a schedule and deletes them automatically according to a retention policy. After that, the snapshot volume stops growing without anyone having to intervene, unlike a one-time cleanup.

opts.A: Monitoring volume utilization and shrinking volumes solves a different problem; besides, Elastic Volumes can only increase a volume's size, not decrease it.
opts.B: A custom script adds development work and still doesn't address the snapshot problem — snapshots are what's growing.
opts.C: A one-time cleanup removes the symptom, but the situation repeats next month: there's still no policy governing snapshot creation and retention.

663.key: The requirement is that only the ECS cluster can access the data in the database and the bucket, meaning what needs restricting is the network and authorization path, not encryption. For the database, that's a security group that allows connections only from the subnets the ECS tasks run in. For the bucket, it's a VPC endpoint plus a bucket policy with a condition that requests come only through that endpoint (aws:SourceVpce). Encryption doesn't help with this requirement: it protects data from outsiders, but it doesn't stop anyone with network access and valid credentials from connecting.

opts.A: Encrypting with a KMS key doesn't restrict database connections: any client that reaches RDS with the correct password gets the decrypted data. This is an access problem, not a storage problem.
opts.B: An AWS managed key's policy can't be edited, and 'specify the role as a user' doesn't describe any working access-restriction mechanism.
opts.C: Restricting the bucket to the ECS task execution role misses the target: that role is used by the ECS agent to pull images and send logs, while the application in the container runs under the task role. A policy written this way would end up blocking the application itself.

664.key: Baseline load is low, but the spike drives CPU to ten times normal and happens irregularly. A burstable instance in unlimited mode immediately supplies the CPU needed and doesn't throttle (A), and reacting to an unpredictable spike needs to happen based on actual demand — request count.

opts.B: Scaling on requests is correct here, but compute optimized instances keep expensive, constant CPU capacity on standby for a spike that happens only twice a month. For a workload that's 'almost always quiet, occasionally sharp,' burstable unlimited delivers the same result more cheaply.
opts.C: Scheduled scaling requires knowing the timing of the spike in advance. Here only the frequency is known — twice a month, with no fixed schedule.
opts.D: Predictive scaling learns from recurring daily and weekly patterns. An event that happens twice a month isn't such a pattern, so the forecast won't catch it — which is exactly the mistake in the original answer key.

665.key: Two requirements: infrastructure is provisioned through automation, and every change to it can be tracked and audited. The first is CloudFormation: infrastructure is defined as code, deployed repeatably, and templates are versioned. The second is AWS Config: it maintains a configuration history for every resource, shows what changed and when, and can check compliance against rules. Don't confuse Config with CloudTrail: Config answers 'what did the resource look like and how did it change,' while CloudTrail answers 'who called which API.'

opts.A: AWS Organizations manages accounts and policies, but it doesn't provision infrastructure within accounts.
opts.C: Service Catalog distributes approved products for deployment, but it doesn't track a history of resource configuration changes.
opts.D: The infrastructure part is correct, but Service Catalog still isn't a change-auditing tool — that role belongs to AWS Config.

666.key: There are two weak points, and both need to be addressed. The database moves to an RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ instance: the engine stays the same, so no code changes are needed, and a synchronous replica in another Availability Zone provides fault tolerance (B). The application is stateless, so it's enough to put it in an Auto Scaling group spread across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer (E).

opts.A: A VPC has a single internet gateway that works across all Availability Zones: you can't create one per zone, and it has nothing to do with availability anyway.
opts.C: DynamoDB is a non-relational data store: an application built for MySQL would have to be rewritten, which the requirement rules out.
opts.D: DataSync copies files between storage locations and can't keep a live database consistent across multiple instances.

667.key: The key requirement is accessing S3 both from the company's Region and from its on-premises location over Direct Connect, without traversing the internet. The distinction that matters is between the two endpoint types: a gateway endpoint works only through VPC route tables and isn't reachable from an on-premises network, while an interface endpoint is a network interface with a private IP in your subnet that you can reach over Direct Connect or VPN. So the hybrid scenario calls specifically for an interface endpoint (PrivateLink). The trade-off is an hourly charge per endpoint per Availability Zone plus a per-GB processing charge, which the free gateway endpoint doesn't have.

opts.A: A gateway endpoint is reachable only by resources inside the VPC: it works as a route in the route table, and a request coming from on-premises over Direct Connect never reaches it.
opts.B: Transit Gateway connects VPCs and on-premises networks to each other, but it isn't an access point for S3.
opts.D: A KMS key encrypts data and has no effect on the network path: without an endpoint, the request still goes to the service's public endpoint.

668.key: The requirement is that resources can only be created with a tag value from an approved list. AWS Organizations has a dedicated tool for exactly this: a tag policy. It defines the allowed tag keys and values and applies across every account in the organization, and with enforcement turned on it blocks resource-creation operations that use a noncompliant tag. This is a declarative setting with no code and no per-account policy edits.

opts.A: An IAM group with a tag condition could require the tag to be present, but it can't restrict the allowed values organization-wide, and here users sign in through Identity Center rather than belonging to IAM groups.
opts.B: Denying everything tagged with the application name is the opposite of the goal: the requirement is to allow creation when the correct value is used.
opts.C: Resource Groups groups together resources that already exist for bulk operations. It can't validate or restrict anything.

669.key: RDS has built-in integration with Secrets Manager for the master user password: once enabled, RDS creates the secret itself, encrypts it with a KMS key, and sets up rotation on a schedule — for example, every 30 days. No function, no schedule, and no code to write, which is exactly what LEAST operational overhead calls for. Applications retrieve the password from the secret via a role rather than from configuration.

opts.A: A custom scheduled function means code, permissions, error handling, and monitoring — exactly the work the built-in integration removes.
opts.B: The CLI command changes the password manually, meaning a person has to do it every 30 days, and it doesn't address securely storing the new password.
opts.D: Parameter Store has no built-in rotation and no integration with RDS for changing the master password.

670.key: The company already knows the number of read and write operations per second the application performs, and the table is only needed four hours a week. Provisioned mode lets you set capacity units to exactly what the tests require and lower them afterward — with known load, that's cheaper than paying per request.

opts.A: On-demand mode doesn't use capacity units at all, so that configuration isn't possible.
opts.C: A one-year reserved capacity commitment assumes continuous use, while the table only runs a few hours a week.
opts.D: A three-year commitment makes the same problem worse: the paid-for capacity would sit idle almost all the time.

671.key: The requirement is to catch unusual spending, not just cross a fixed threshold. AWS Cost Anomaly Detection builds a model of normal spending by service, account, and tag, and reports deviations along with an estimated size and likely cause; recipients are configured through a subscription (email or an SNS topic). That's what sets it apart from AWS Budgets, where a person sets the threshold and there's no assessment of what's 'unusual.'

opts.A: A zero-spend budget alerts on any spending at all. For a running production environment it turns into constant noise.
opts.C: Pricing Calculator estimates the future cost of a configuration during planning and performs no monitoring at all.
opts.D: CloudWatch exposes an estimated-charges metric, but it doesn't detect anomalies or explain them — it isn't a cost-analysis tool.

672.key: The data already sits in S3, and the goal is to take a quick look at it to decide whether a further pipeline is worth building. An AWS Glue crawler determines the schema itself and populates the catalog, after which Athena runs standard SQL queries with no server to manage — minimal effort and no infrastructure.

opts.A: External tables in a Spark catalog with Glue jobs mean writing jobs instead of just running a query.
opts.C: A Hive metastore and an EMR cluster mean deploying and maintaining a cluster just for a one-time look at the data.
opts.D: Kinesis Data Analytics analyzes streams, and the data here has already landed in a bucket.

673.key: Recent files need to stay quickly accessible, while anything older than seven days only needs to be retrievable within 24 hours — that points directly at S3 Glacier Deep Archive, where standard retrieval takes about twelve hours and costs less than any other storage class. S3 File Gateway gives on-premises applications the familiar SMB share they expect, caching recent files locally, while a lifecycle rule moves objects to the archive after seven days.

opts.A: DataSync copies data but doesn't give on-premises clients transparent access to what's been moved, and it doesn't manage a lifecycle.
opts.C: FSx File Gateway caches access to FSx file systems; the data doesn't become S3 objects, so S3 lifecycle rules don't apply to it.
opts.D: Giving users direct access to S3 changes the familiar workflow, and Glacier Flexible Retrieval costs more than Deep Archive even though the 24-hour window allows the cheapest class to be chosen.

674.key: The database is suffering specifically from read load, so it needs to be addressed on two fronts at once. A read replica takes all of the read traffic off the primary instance (B), while an ElastiCache cluster eliminates repeated round trips to the database for the same results entirely (D). Together they remove the bottleneck during traffic spikes.

opts.A: RDS Storage Auto Scaling applies to storage capacity, not compute power.
opts.C: A Multi-AZ standby instance doesn't serve queries — you can't read from it.
opts.E: Placing the instances in the same Availability Zone as the database saves milliseconds of network latency but reduces fault tolerance and doesn't solve the heavy-read problem.

675.key: The requirement includes an unusual constraint: the storage administrator's permissions can't change. That rules out deny policies, so the protection has to live on the resource itself. EBS snapshots support a lock: a snapshot is placed in governance or compliance mode for a set period, and it can't be deleted even by someone with full permissions. This is configured as a property of the snapshot, which is also why it takes the least administrative effort.

opts.A: A separate instance and CLI access don't prohibit anything: the administrator can still delete the snapshot with their existing permissions.
opts.B: A deny policy changes the storage administrator's permissions, which the requirement explicitly forbids.
opts.C: Recycle Bin lets you recover a deleted snapshot within a retention window, but it doesn't prevent the deletion in the first place. The requirement is specifically about prevention.

676.key: VPC Flow Logs are written to a CloudWatch Logs log group, and the simplest way to deliver them from there to OpenSearch Service in near real time is a subscription to Kinesis Data Firehose: it's a managed delivery stream with a built-in OpenSearch destination, buffering, and retries. There's no consumer code to write.

opts.A: Kinesis Data Streams is just transport; writing to OpenSearch from it requires your own consumer application, which you'd have to build and operate.
opts.C: CloudTrail records API calls and can't serve as a destination for VPC flow logs.
opts.D: Same mistake, with CloudTrail again cast as the destination for flow logs.

677.key: The cluster is for infrequent resiliency testing, EKS itself needs to manage the nodes, and above all cost matters. A managed node group made up entirely of Spot Instances gives up to a 90 percent discount, and EKS provisions and replaces the nodes itself, including when spot capacity is reclaimed. For resiliency testing, interruptions are even a bonus.

opts.B: Adding an On-Demand node group increases cost unnecessarily: the environment is for testing and used infrequently.
opts.C: A self-managed Auto Scaling group that adds nodes via user data means self-managed nodes, while the requirement is for EKS to manage the nodes.
opts.D: On-Demand Instances only is the most expensive option, even though interruptions are acceptable here.

678.key: The requirement is full control over creating, rotating, and disabling encryption keys with minimal effort. That's an exact description of a customer managed key in KMS: you create the key, write its key policy, turn on automatic annual rotation or rotate on demand, can disable the key or schedule it for deletion, and every use is visible in CloudTrail. From there the bucket is configured for SSE-KMS with that key, and encryption happens automatically.

opts.A: SSE-S3 gives you no ability to create, disable, or manage rotation: the service fully owns the keys, and you never even see them.
opts.C: An AWS managed key can't be disabled, deleted, or have its key policy edited. And 'creating' an AWS managed key isn't even possible — services create them automatically.
opts.D: Manually downloading objects, encrypting them on an instance, and re-uploading them is the most effort possible, and it has to be repeated for every new object.

679.key: There are two requirements pulling in opposite directions: copies must be retained for exactly 30 days (i.e., they can't be deleted early), and they must be deleted automatically once that period passes. S3 Object Lock handles the first: the bucket is created with Object Lock enabled (A), and objects get a default retention period of 30 days (C). An S3 Lifecycle rule handles the second, expiring objects after 30 days (E): once the retention period ends, the objects become deletable, and the rule removes them. One key detail: Object Lock can only be enabled when the bucket is created, and it automatically turns on versioning.

opts.B: Versioning by itself protects nothing: an object version can still be deleted. Object Lock also turns on versioning automatically, so enabling it separately isn't needed.
opts.D: A Lifecycle rule can transition and delete objects, but it can't protect them from deletion. Protection is Object Lock's job.
opts.F: A tag noting a retention period is just metadata. On its own it doesn't prevent or trigger anything.

680.key: Files need to be copied continuously, only changed files should be re-copied, and operational overhead needs to be minimal. AWS DataSync supports both S3 and EFS as destinations, tasks can run on a schedule, and the 'transfer only data that has changed' mode compares metadata and only rewrites an object when the source has actually changed. No custom code is needed at all.

opts.B: A Lambda function with the file system mounted means custom code, error handling, retries, and execution-time limits for large files.
opts.C: Transferring all data every run rewrites the entire dataset each time: the requirement is to overwrite a file only when the source has changed.
opts.D: An instance running its own script is maximum operational overhead: the machine has to be maintained and the script kept up.

681.key: The phrase "must be able to control rotation of the encryption keys" rules out everything except a customer managed key: only with it can you enable automatic annual rotation, trigger on-demand rotation, disable the key, and edit its policy. EBS volumes are encrypted with this key at creation, and everything after that is transparent to the instances. It helps to keep the hierarchy in mind: AWS owned keys are invisible and unmanageable, AWS managed keys are visible but their policy and rotation are outside your control, and customer managed keys give you full control.

opts.B: AWS managed keys rotate automatically once a year, and this cannot be configured. The requirement to control rotation is not met.
opts.C: Imported key material does not support automatic rotation: you would have to import new material yourself. That's maximum operational overhead.
opts.D: An AWS owned key doesn't even appear in your account: no policy, no usage log, no rotation control. EBS volumes cannot be encrypted with this type of key.

682.key: The requirement isn't just to turn on encryption but to put a process in place: block the creation of unencrypted resources and find any that already exist. The first part is handled by an IAM policy with an ec2:Encrypted condition that denies creating unencrypted volumes. The second part is handled by the AWS Config managed rule encrypted-volumes, which continuously evaluates resources, combined with automatic remediation through a Systems Manager Automation document. Both services are fully managed with no custom code to maintain — hence the LEAST administrative overhead. General pattern: "detect noncompliant resources and remediate" on the exam almost always means AWS Config plus SSM Automation.

opts.B: KMS manages access to keys but doesn't search for noncompliant resources. Pairing Lambda with EventBridge means writing your own code where a ready-made Config rule already exists.
opts.C: Macie classifies sensitive data in S3. It doesn't inspect EBS volumes at all.
opts.D: Inspector looks for vulnerabilities and insecure configurations in workloads, not whether a volume is encrypted. Also, an existing volume can't be encrypted "in place" — you need a snapshot and a new volume.

683.key: Application changes must be minimal, while resiliency needs to improve. The web tier moves as-is onto EC2 instances, but now in an Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer: the code doesn't change, and a node or Availability Zone failure stops being a problem (A). The MySQL database moves to an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployment — same engine, same protocol, but with automatic failover (C).

opts.B: A database behind a Network Load Balancer in an Auto Scaling group doesn't work: MySQL nodes don't scale by adding copies without replication.
opts.D: Moving the web tier to Lambda functions means rewriting the application, which the requirement says to avoid.
opts.E: Switching to DynamoDB means changing the data model and rewriting queries.

684.key: Some applications can't run in the region itself, but users near eu-central-1 need single-digit millisecond latency. AWS Local Zones are AWS sites in major cities that you extend your existing VPC into: compute runs physically closer to users while remaining part of your network.

opts.A: You can't extend a VPC to a CloudFront edge location: there's no compute of yours there.
opts.C: CloudFront regional edge caches are part of the content delivery network, not a place to run applications.
opts.D: Wavelength Zones sit inside mobile network operators' networks and are meant for 5G device traffic, not regular corporate users.

685.key: The database is private, and the number of concurrent functions spikes with traffic — connections run out quickly. RDS Proxy maintains a connection pool and reuses connections, so database performance stays predictable. To reach the private database, the functions are deployed inside the VPC.

opts.A: A custom endpoint only routes requests to selected instances and doesn't manage a connection pool.
opts.C: Here both the endpoint is wrong and the functions are outside the VPC, so they can't reach the private database.
opts.D: The proxy is chosen correctly, but functions outside the VPC still can't reach the private endpoint.

686.key: The key phrases are "the number of accounts and VPCs will increase" and "simplify connecting new ones." A transit gateway is built as a hub-and-spoke: each new VPC is added with a single attachment, each new site with a VPN attachment, and routing is configured centrally in the gateway's route tables. Nothing needs to be reconfigured in the networks that are already connected.

opts.A: VPC peering connections grow quadratically and provide no transit: connecting a new site to all the networks through them requires editing every route table.
opts.B: A homegrown VPN on an EC2 instance means your own software, your own patching, limited throughput, and a single point of failure.
opts.D: A central VPC with peering connections runs into the same limitation: transit routing through peering doesn't work, so the other VPCs won't be able to see the company's sites.

687.key: The company has no ML experience, so it needs a service that both trains and predicts on its own. Amazon Forecast trains on the historical data in S3 (E), and a Lambda function with a function URL calls the ready-made predictor to return a forecast (D). The pair is consistent: training and inference happen in the same service.

opts.A: Deploying a SageMaker model and an inference endpoint is ML engineer work: choosing an algorithm, features, tuning. That directly contradicts the "no ML experience" condition.
opts.B: Training in SageMaker requires the same expertise. In the dump key, this option was also paired with calling a Forecast predictor — an inconsistent pair: train in one service, predict in another.
opts.C: A Lambda function calling a SageMaker endpoint inherits the same problem: the endpoint first has to be obtained by training a model manually.

688.key: In IAM Identity Center, permissions aren't granted to individual users but through a permission set assigned to a group on an account. The pattern is: create groups (developers and administrators), create a permission set with the needed policies for each group, and assign the groups to the relevant accounts. A new hire is simply added to a group and immediately gets access to all the required accounts with the right permissions. That's the minimum operational overhead as the team grows.

opts.A: There's no need to create users "for each account": in Identity Center there's one user, and access to accounts is granted through assignments. A custom policy per group isn't the right mechanism either — permissions are described in a permission set.
opts.B: Same mistake with per-account users, plus attaching policies to individual users instead of a permission set adds more manual work with each hire.
opts.D: Assigning a permission set to each user individually and handing out extra permissions inside accounts breaks consistency and requires manual action for every new hire.

689.key: Checking "is this volume encrypted" is exactly what AWS Config managed rules exist for. The encrypted-volumes rule evaluates every EBS volume on creation and change, flags noncompliant ones, and keeps a history — and you pay for configuration evaluations, not for infrastructure running around the clock. No code, no schedule. This can be extended with automatic remediation via SSM Automation and a preventive deny in an SCP — see {{q:682,419}}.

opts.A: Custom API calls in a scheduled function mean code, permissions, handling paginated results, and gaps between runs. Config does the same thing as a service.
opts.B: A Fargate task adds a container image on top of that, which has to be built and updated. Even more work for the same check.
opts.C: Tags have nothing to do with encryption, and Cost Explorer shows spending, not the encryption state of volumes.

690.key: Throughput needs to increase in both directions, and S3 has two standard techniques for that. On upload — multipart upload (C): the file is split into parts, the parts go to S3 in parallel, and total speed stops being limited by a single TCP connection (AWS recommends it for files over 100 MB and requires it above 5 GB). On download — parallel byte-range requests using the Range header (D): the object is pulled by multiple threads at once. Both techniques also improve robustness: a failed part is retried instead of the whole file.

opts.A: An access point is a named entry point with its own policy, useful for splitting permissions between teams. It doesn't affect throughput.
opts.B: Spreading files across multiple buckets doesn't increase speed: S3 scales by prefix within a bucket automatically, and extra buckets only add management overhead.
opts.E: A random prefix is outdated advice from when S3 performance depended on key distribution. Today S3 supports at least 3,500 write and 5,500 read requests per second per prefix and scales automatically, and for a single large file the technique is useless anyway.

691.key: The requirement is shared access from multiple Availability Zones with strong consistency — new content must be visible immediately. Amazon EFS, mounted on all instances in the group, meets this (B). The second working option is to store content in S3 and serve it through CloudFront, setting the Cache-Control header to no-cache so edge locations check back with the origin every time (E); S3 itself provides strong read-after-write consistency.

opts.A: Volume Gateway is meant for hybrid access from an on-premises site and serves block volumes over iSCSI: it doesn't provide shared access for instances across different Availability Zones.
opts.C: A shared EBS volume is limited to a single Availability Zone and requires a cluster file system; that doesn't work for an Auto Scaling group spanning multiple zones.
opts.D: DataSync runs periodic copy tasks, not continuous synchronization between nodes, so it won't provide strong consistency.

692.key: The discriminating phrase is MOST high-performing, meaning the lowest actual latency for the user. In Route 53, that's what latency-based routing does: the service measures latency to the regions and sends the client to wherever the response is actually fastest. The dump key points to geolocation, and that's its weak point: geolocation routes by the user's country or continent, not by measured latency; the geographically closest region isn't always the fastest one. On the real exam, when the wording is about performance, pick the latency policy; geolocation is the right choice when the question is about content localization or country-based legal restrictions.

opts.A: This is the answer that matches the question's wording: latency-based routing sends the request to the region with the lowest measured latency. This is exactly where the dispute with the dump key lies.
opts.C: Failover is for disaster recovery switching, not performance, and it serves a "primary — secondary" pair, not three equal regions. Also, a CNAME can't be created at the zone apex.
opts.D: Geoproximity routes by geographic distance with an adjustable bias — that's still not measured latency, and it requires a traffic flow policy. Also, an ALB at the zone apex needs an alias A record, not a CNAME.

693.key: There are two weak points: a single Availability Zone and a database embedded in the instances. The Auto Scaling group is stretched across three Availability Zones, and the embedded NoSQL database is migrated to DynamoDB using AWS DMS. DynamoDB is fully managed, replicates across zones, and provides eventual consistency by default — exactly what the requirement calls for — while the operational burden of self-managed replication disappears.

opts.A: Swapping the load balancer changes nothing: the instances are still in a single zone, and the database's own replication still has to be maintained manually.
opts.B: The load balancer is swapped for no reason (the application is web-based, so an ALB is appropriate), and the main problem — a single Availability Zone — remains.
opts.C: The zones are fixed, but the embedded database's own replication on the instances is still entirely on the team's shoulders: maximum operational overhead.

694.key: The requirements are minimal latency and cart data that survives even when the connection drops. ElastiCache for Redis solves both: the catalog, which changes once a month, is cached in memory and served in sub-millisecond time, while cart and session data live outside the web servers, so a user reconnecting loses nothing. Redis also supports replication and data persistence.

opts.A: Sticky sessions tie a user to a specific server: if it fails, the cart is lost, and database latency stays the same.
opts.C: OpenSearch is a search engine, not a session cache: latency is higher, and it isn't designed for storing shopping carts.
opts.D: A single instance with an EBS volume is a single point of failure, and snapshots only restore data to the moment they were taken.

695.key: Observability for microservices comes from metrics plus tracing. Container Insights collects metrics and logs from the EKS cluster, while AWS X-Ray traces each request's path through all the microservices, showing exactly where time is being lost. Together they give the full picture.

opts.A: A cache reduces the number of requests but doesn't solve the problem of finding bottlenecks: it doesn't add any observability.
opts.C: CloudTrail records calls to AWS APIs, not interactions between the microservices themselves.
opts.D: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations about account configuration and doesn't analyze application performance.

696.key: The key idea: access to decryption is controlled by the KMS key policy, not the bucket policy. If each customer has their own key, and that key's policy allows only the customer's role to use it, then neither another customer nor a company employee can decrypt the objects — even with permission to read the bucket, they'd get AccessDenied on kms:Decrypt. That's exactly the separation required: the company stores and processes the data but can't read it. A separate key per customer also gives you cryptographic erasure: destroy the key, and the customer's data can no longer be recovered.

opts.A: ACM certificates are for TLS, not for encrypting data at rest, and there's no "certificate policy" that denies access to principals.
opts.B: A bucket policy governs S3 API calls but not KMS operations: you can't deny decryption there. An employee with permission to read the object and access to the key would still get the plaintext data.
opts.D: The same mistake with certificates as in option A, plus a public certificate doesn't contain any secret material for encrypting customer data at all.

697.key: Instances must stay in private subnets, and internet traffic still has to reach them somehow. The standard approach is an internet-facing Application Load Balancer in the public subnets: it accepts requests and forwards them to the instances over the internal network. The site's DNS name points to the load balancer.

opts.A: An Auto Scaling group has no address or name that a DNS record can point to.
opts.C: A NAT gateway handles outbound connections and must sit in a public subnet; inbound traffic doesn't pass through it.
opts.D: An instance in a private subnet has no public address, and giving it one would violate the security requirement.

698.key: Fargate does not provide access to the underlying nodes, so the storage must be network-attached and shared between containers. Amazon EFS is the only solution that fits: it is natively supported by Fargate, stores data across multiple Availability Zones, can be mounted by all tasks simultaneously, and is registered in the cluster as a StorageClass.

opts.A: EBS volumes are not supported by Fargate tasks, and Multi-Attach is limited to a single Availability Zone and requires a cluster-aware file system.
opts.C: A single EBS volume cannot be shared by containers across different Availability Zones, and it does not work with Fargate.
opts.D: Multiple file systems with custom synchronization through Lambda means extra code and a risk of data divergence; EFS is already accessible from every zone.

699.key: The company wants to manage neither servers nor storage. That points to ECS on Fargate for compute, which has no nodes at all, and Amazon EFS for persistent storage: it is supported by Fargate as a volume, mounts into the containers, and is fully managed by AWS. Data survives task restarts and is shared between containers.

opts.A: Self-managed EKS nodes and EBS volumes on instances are exactly the servers and storage the company wants to move away from.
opts.C: An S3 bucket cannot be mounted into an ECS task as a persistent storage volume: containers can only reach it through the API.
opts.D: The EC2 launch type means the company would still have to manage the underlying instance fleet itself — the requirement is not met.

700.key: The TCP and UDP protocols immediately rule out the Application Load Balancer: this calls for a Network Load Balancer in each Region (A). Global availability and minimal latency come from Global Accelerator (C): it issues a pair of static anycast IP addresses, ingests traffic at the nearest edge location, routes it over the AWS global network, and shifts away from a failed Region within seconds, without depending on DNS caching. The load balancers themselves can be internal, since the accelerator is what faces the internet.

opts.B: ALB only works with HTTP and HTTPS, so it cannot handle the UDP part of the application.
opts.D: Route 53 geolocation routing selects a Region based on the client's country, not actual latency, and failover is bounded by the DNS records' TTL.
opts.E: CloudFront does not serve UDP traffic, and its strength is caching HTTP content, which is not a requirement here.

701.key: The requirement is minimal configuration changes plus an audit trail of the DDoS sources. AWS Shield Advanced is subscribed onto the existing load balancer without any architecture rework, provides automatic mitigations and detailed attack telemetry (console-level diagnostics and reports), and gives access to the DDoS Response Team (DRT), who help tune the protections. It is specifically the ability to engage the DRT and get detailed attack reports that distinguishes Advanced from the free Standard tier.

opts.A: WAF rules based on 'unknown sources' do not work against random IP addresses: block lists cannot keep up with the attack, and this approach provides no audit trail of the attack sources.
opts.B: Inspector looks for vulnerabilities and has nothing to do with DDoS, and the DRT team operates only under a Shield Advanced subscription.
opts.D: Adding CloudFront in front of the application is a significant architecture change, and filtering on unknown sources still does not solve the problem when the source addresses keep changing.

702.key: Data from Snow Family devices lands only in Amazon S3 — that is the only destination an import job supports. From there, an FSx for Lustre file system is created and linked to that bucket as a data repository: the objects appear as files, load lazily on first access, and the compute cluster gets sub-millisecond latency and high throughput. The dump key pointed to importing directly into FSx for Lustre, but no such capability exists — see the audit log for details.

opts.A: File gateway is a hybrid gateway for an on-premises location, and its latency is nowhere near the required sub-millisecond figures.
opts.C: EFS does not deliver sub-millisecond latency or the throughput the compute cluster needs.
opts.D: Data from Snow Family devices cannot be imported directly into an FSx for Lustre file system: the import job only unloads it into an S3 bucket.

703.key: The source is NFS servers, the volumes are small, the copying is periodic, and cost matters. AWS DataSync is deployed as an agent on-premises, can mount the NFS export, and syncs changes to S3 on a schedule while verifying data integrity. You pay only for the data transferred, with no persistent infrastructure to stand up.

opts.A: AWS Glue is an ETL service for cataloging and transforming data, not a tool for copying files from on-premises NFS servers.
opts.C: AWS Transfer Family charges an hourly fee for the enabled endpoint regardless of volume, which works out more expensive for infrequent small copies.
opts.D: A dedicated Direct Connect link is permanent, expensive infrastructure, out of proportion to the task of periodically copying small volumes of data.

704.key: The key requirements are UDP, millions of requests per second, and ultra-low latency. Among AWS load balancers, only the Network Load Balancer supports the UDP protocol, and it operates at Layer 4 with minimal overhead, scaling to millions of requests per second.

opts.A: The Application Load Balancer works with HTTP and HTTPS: it does not handle UDP.
opts.B: Gateway Load Balancer is designed for routing traffic through virtual network appliances, not for exposing game servers.
opts.D: Duplicating the servers in another Region does not solve UDP load balancing and doubles the cost.

705.key: Moving from MySQL to PostgreSQL is an engine change, so the database objects are converted using AWS DMS Schema Conversion (A). The data itself is migrated by a DMS task running in change data capture mode: a full load first, then continuous application of changes from the transaction log, so everything that happens to the source database during the migration ends up in Aurora PostgreSQL (D).

opts.B: You cannot create an Aurora PostgreSQL read replica on an RDS for MySQL instance: read replicas only work within the same engine.
opts.C: An Aurora MySQL replica is possible, but the target database needs to be PostgreSQL — that is not the right path.
opts.E: Promoting a replica applies to a same-engine migration from MySQL to Aurora MySQL; no such replica exists for a cross-engine migration.

706.key: The reporting script is interfering with the critical application, so it needs to be moved off the primary instance. A read replica absorbs these queries: it is set up in a single operation, requires no extra code, and the application keeps working against the primary database.

opts.A: Picking an instance by connection count is custom logic you would have to build into the script, and reading from the standby instance of a Multi-AZ deployment is not possible at all.
opts.C: A manual export done by the development team is the maximum possible operational effort, plus human error.
opts.D: The script is looking for specifically new entries, so the cache would constantly miss and provide no benefit.

707.key: What is needed is visibility into requests reaching the application. That is exactly what ALB access logs provide: enabled with a single setting and written directly to S3, and the most convenient way to analyze those files is a table in Athena — standard SQL, no infrastructure to run.

opts.A: CloudTrail records calls to AWS management APIs, not end-user requests to the application.
opts.C: Reviewing files by hand in a text editor does not scale and is not really a solution.
opts.D: Querying the load balancer from EMR is not possible: access logs are only delivered through S3, and a cluster is unnecessary overhead here.

708.key: A NAT gateway sends traffic out to the internet, so it must itself sit in a public subnet with a route to an internet gateway, while remaining in the same VPC as the instances. The public type of gateway is the only one that provides internet access.

opts.A: A NAT gateway in a private subnet has no route to an internet gateway, so it cannot send traffic out.
opts.B: A private NAT gateway is meant for connectivity to other networks and on-premises locations; it does not provide internet access.
opts.D: A private gateway does not provide internet access, no matter which subnet it is placed in.

709.key: This question is about where to attach the SCP. The restriction needs to apply only to the nonproduction accounts, so the policy is attached either directly to those three accounts (B) or to a separate OU that they are moved into (E) — the second approach is preferable in practice, since new accounts only need to be placed into the same OU. Two important facts: an SCP attached at the root applies to every account, including the production one, and SCPs never apply to the organization's management account.

opts.A: A policy on the organization root would also apply to the production account, where launching these instance types is allowed.
opts.C: SCPs do not apply to the organization's management account — that is a quirk that is frequently tested on the exam.
opts.D: Attaching the restriction to the OU containing the production account means denying it exactly where the restriction is not needed.

710.key: A 'private and secure connection' between EC2 and S3 means a VPC endpoint: traffic travels over the AWS network, bypassing the internet. But an endpoint alone is not enough for 'secure' — to keep a bucket holding classified data from accepting requests that arrive by any other path, its bucket policy needs an aws:SourceVpce (or aws:SourceVpc) condition that permits access only through the intended endpoint. That is exactly the combination the correct option describes. Related questions — {{q:480,208,612}}.

opts.B: An IAM policy grants permissions but does not change the network path: the request would still go to S3's public endpoint over the internet.
opts.C: A NAT gateway is itself a path out to the internet. It violates the requirement for a private connection.
opts.D: Access keys are just a means of authentication, and a long-lived secret at that. They add nothing to the privacy of the channel.

711.key: There are two problems: insufficient read capacity, and connections running out under a traffic spike. Adding reader instances to the Aurora cluster relieves the read load and also serves as failover targets, while RDS Proxy maintains a connection pool, eliminating timeouts when the number of clients spikes. Both can be added to the running cluster with virtually no downtime.

opts.A: An EventBridge rule with a Lambda function only logs the cluster's state changes: it has no effect on scalability.
opts.B: Zero-downtime restart shortens the interruption during a restart, and Database Activity Streams is for auditing. Neither one increases throughput.
opts.D: A cache does relieve read load, but DMS is not designed for continuous replication into Redis, and a 'write-around' approach would require reworking the application.

712.key: Requests originate inside the VPC and go out to the on-premises data center's DNS. That direction calls for a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint plus a forwarding rule: the rule says 'send queries for this domain to these DNS addresses in the data center,' and associating the rule with the VPC turns it on for that network. Traffic travels over the VPN, and the private names are never published externally.

opts.B: An inbound endpoint is for the opposite direction — when servers in the data center need to resolve AWS resource names. Here it is the VPC doing the querying, not the data center.
opts.C: A private hosted zone stores records inside Route 53 and would require manually duplicating every data center name into it and then keeping them in sync. That is not name resolution for the on-premises service, it is a copy of it.
opts.D: A public hosted zone exposes internal names and addresses on the open internet — a direct violation of the requirement for maximum security.

713.key: The access pattern for the photos is not known in advance: some get viewed for months, others for less than a week. The S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class automatically moves objects between tiers based on actual access, with no retrieval fees and no lifecycle rules to manage. The metadata used to select which photos to display fits neatly into DynamoDB alongside a reference to the S3 object.

opts.A: DynamoDB is not meant for storing files: the item size limit is 400 KB, and photos can be up to 20 MB.
opts.C: An age-based rule does not reflect actual popularity: photos that stay popular for months would move into the infrequent-access class, and every access to them would start costing more.
opts.D: Glacier and Deep Archive require retrieval time and charge early-deletion fees — unacceptable for a photo hosting service — and OpenSearch is overkill for storing metadata.

714.key: The requirement is to stop routing new requests to overloaded targets. The least outstanding requests algorithm routes each request to the target with the fewest in-flight requests, and the RequestCountPerTarget and ActiveConnectionCount CloudWatch metrics — both measured per target — let you monitor that imbalance.

opts.A: Round robin distributes requests evenly and would keep loading up the already-overloaded instances.
opts.C: Same problem with round robin, and the chosen metrics are load-balancer-wide, not per-target.
opts.D: The algorithm is right, but RequestCount and TargetResponseTime are load-balancer-level metrics and do not show the distribution across individual targets.

715.key: The company needs to know when Savings Plans coverage drops, meaning when a growing share of usage stops being covered by the purchased commitment. AWS Budgets has a dedicated budget type for exactly this — a Savings Plans coverage budget with a coverage threshold and email notifications. It is configured once and runs without any code. Worth remembering alongside it is the related utilization budget type, which tracks whether the purchased commitment is being fully used.

opts.B: A custom function and email reports mean code to write and maintain where a ready-made budget type already exists.
opts.C: An AWS Budgets report delivers budget status on a schedule, but by itself it is not a coverage threshold with a drop notification.
opts.D: A Savings Plans alert subscription reports on events of the plan itself (expiration, purchase), not on a drop in usage coverage.

716.key: The MSK cluster needs to become reachable from the internet with encrypted traffic and minimal effort. Public access for MSK is a built-in capability: public subnets are created in the existing VPC, the cluster is deployed into them, and mutual TLS authentication is enabled in the security settings — it provides both in-transit encryption and client authentication. There is no need to create a new VPC.

opts.B: The result is the same, but with extra work: creating a separate VPC and moving the cluster is noticeably more effort.
opts.C: An Application Load Balancer works with HTTP, not the Kafka protocol, and private subnets do not make the cluster reachable from the internet.
opts.D: A load balancer in private subnets is not reachable from the internet, and there is no such thing as an HTTPS listener for the Kafka protocol.

717.key: The requirements are: process orders as soon as they arrive, stay secure and resilient, and integrate with the on-premises system over the connectivity that already exists. An AWS Transfer Family SFTP server is created as an internal server (reachable only from the VPC and the connected network) across two Availability Zones, S3 serves as storage, and a Transfer Family managed workflow invokes the Lambda function immediately after a file is uploaded — no scheduled polling at all.

opts.A: An internet-facing server is unnecessary: connectivity to the company network already exists, and a public endpoint only widens the attack surface.
opts.B: A single Availability Zone provides no resilience, and the endpoint is public again.
opts.C: Periodically polling the file system on a schedule contradicts the requirement to process orders immediately.

718.key: The constraint is strict: data processing must stay on the company's premises. The only way to still get a managed AWS service under that constraint is AWS Outposts: the rack sits in the customer's data center but is managed like an AWS Region. EMR clusters are deployed on Outposts, Hadoop and Spark are migrated there, scaling and maintenance work the same way they would in the cloud, and the data physically never leaves the site.

opts.A: Here processing runs on a cloud-based EMR cluster while HDFS data travels over the VPN link: this violates the data-locality requirement and hurts performance.
opts.B: DataSync copies the data to the cloud, meaning the data leaves the premises — a direct violation of the requirement.
opts.D: Snowball moves the data into S3, after which processing happens in the cloud. The requirement calls for the opposite.

719.key: Windows, Mac, and Linux clients read the data over SMB and NFS, some of the data is accessed infrequently, and operational overhead must be minimized. S3 File Gateway serves both protocols and stores files as objects in a bucket, and the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class automatically moves infrequently read objects to cheaper tiers with no rules to manage and no risk of retrieval latency.

opts.A: EFS works only over the NFS protocol: Windows and Mac clients that need SMB would be left without access.
opts.B: FSx for ONTAP supports both protocols, but it costs noticeably more than S3 and requires more configuration, including tiering policies.
opts.D: FSx for OpenZFS serves data over NFS and does not support SMB, and it has no automatic cost reduction for infrequently accessed data.

720.key: The monolith needs to be broken into microservices so that updating individual modules does not stop the whole application, and scaling can be flexible. ECS with service auto scaling lets each microservice be updated independently through a rolling deployment, so there is no downtime during a rollout, and a report that takes twenty minutes to generate is not interrupted.

opts.A: A single Lambda function is still the same monolith, and the fifteen-minute execution limit is shorter than the time it takes to generate the report.
opts.B: Spot Instances can be reclaimed at any moment, and the report restarts from the beginning whenever it is interrupted.
opts.D: A single application environment with an all-at-once deployment strategy means the monolith stays intact and downtime occurs with every update.

721.key: The requirements are Python support, automatic scaling, and minimal infrastructure and operational support. A Lambda function satisfies all of it at once: Python code runs without managing a single server, concurrency scales up under a load of hundreds of requests per second, and billing applies only to actual execution time.

opts.A: A Spot Fleet is still instances that need to be prepared and maintained, and interruptions make testing the component harder.
opts.B: Elastic Beanstalk manages the deployment, but underneath it there are still EC2 instances with all their upkeep.
opts.C: Self-managed EC2 instances in an EKS cluster represent the most infrastructure and operational support of all the options: nodes must be provisioned, patched, and scaled. This was the option marked as the key in the dump, and it contradicts the serverless requirement — see the audit log walkthrough.

722.key: Thirty VPCs, each with its own private virtual interface, means thirty objects to configure and no connectivity between the networks themselves. A transit gateway solves both problems at once: the Direct Connect connection attaches to it through a single transit VIF via a Direct Connect gateway, every VPC attaches as an attachment, and turning on route propagation removes the need to maintain route tables by hand. The networks can then reach both each other and the company's on-premises site.

opts.B: A Direct Connect gateway gives the on-premises site connectivity to all the VPCs, but it does not connect the VPCs to each other: the requirement that "each VPC communicates with all the others" is not met.
opts.C: A transit VPC with a full mesh of peering connections is an outdated and labor-intensive pattern — exactly the operational burden the requirement asks to avoid.
opts.D: Thirty VPN connections in place of the existing dedicated connection: worse latency, limited by tunnel bandwidth, and VPC-to-VPC connectivity is still missing.

723.key: An instance can only have one role, so "attaching a second role" is not possible — but there is also no need to remove the existing policies. The correct action is to take the existing role and attach the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore managed policy to it, keeping the existing permissions for RDS access. The option is worded awkwardly, but in meaning it describes exactly that: the instance keeps its existing permissions plus the Systems Manager agent's permissions, so the applications are not interrupted.

opts.B: Systems Manager manages instances through the instance role and the agent, not "on behalf of an IAM user." That configuration does not exist.
opts.C: Default Host Configuration Management does automatically assign a role to instances, but it replaces the existing one with its own and does not preserve the RDS access permissions already granted to the application.
opts.D: Removing the existing policies would cut off the applications' access to the databases — a direct violation of the requirement not to interrupt operation.

724.key: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler increases the number of pods, but when the nodes are full, new pods have nowhere to run. That is exactly the gap the Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler closes: it watches for pods stuck in a pending state and adds nodes to the group, then removes them when idle. It is a standard component and requires no custom code.

opts.A: Scaling based on memory usage applies to pods and does not solve the problem of the nodes themselves running out of capacity.
opts.C: A custom function that resizes the EKS cluster is code to write and maintain in place of a ready-made component.
opts.D: An EC2 Auto Scaling group has no awareness of unscheduled pods on its own: without the Cluster Autoscaler, it does not know when to add nodes.

725.key: The trap is in the premise itself: "number and size of S3 objects remain constant," yet the bill keeps growing. That means the company is paying for something invisible in the object listing — incomplete multipart uploads. Every aborted multipart upload of a 50 GB object leaves behind the parts already received; they are billed as storage and do not show up among the bucket's objects. The fix is a Lifecycle rule with the AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload action, for example seven days after the upload starts. A useful diagnostic pattern: a mismatch between the sum of object sizes and the storage bill almost always points to exactly this.

opts.A: Transfer Acceleration speeds up transfers and costs extra money. The rising bill is not caused by upload speed but by leftover parts from aborted uploads.
opts.C: S3 Inventory is a report on a bucket's contents. It does not prevent anything and has no effect on the bill.
opts.D: CloudFront caches responses and reduces outbound data transfer costs, but it does not change how much data is stored in S3. The problem is in storage, not delivery.

726.key: The game needs frequent real-time updates and lookups of player coordinates. ElastiCache for Redis keeps data in memory, supports geospatial data structures and radius-search commands, so it can take over both writing and reading positions, offloading the database.

opts.A: A Multi-AZ configuration improves availability but adds nothing to performance.
opts.B: OpenSearch Service is a search and analytics engine, not a store for frequent point updates of coordinates.
opts.C: DAX works exclusively with DynamoDB and cannot sit in front of a PostgreSQL instance.

727.key: The problem is not data loss as such, but the ability to delete the entire table. Deletion protection is turned on with a single switch on the table and simply blocks the operation until it is explicitly turned off — no code, no backup-and-restore plan required.

opts.A: A combination of a trail, a rule, and a restore function is the most complex construction of all, and it only reacts after the deletion has already happened.
opts.B: A backup plan with manual recovery means both downtime and manual work, whereas deletion can simply be blocked outright.
opts.D: Point-in-time recovery saves the data inside a table, but if the table itself is deleted, recovery still has to be done manually and with an interruption in service.

728.key: There are two constraining requirements: minimize bandwidth cost and provide instant access to data at no extra charge. Storage Gateway in stored volumes mode keeps the full data set locally on the company's own disks, while only point-in-time snapshots asynchronously flow to S3. That means reads come from the local copy with instant response and no calls to the cloud, and only the changes travel over the link.

opts.A: Glacier storage is meant for archives: expedited retrieval costs money, which directly contradicts the "at no additional cost" wording.
opts.B: Cached volumes mode keeps only a frequently used subset locally, so requests for the rest of the data go to S3 — that means both latency and network traffic.
opts.D: A dedicated connection adds a constant and fairly high recurring cost, whereas the requirement was to minimize bandwidth spend, not to build out a bigger link.

729.key: Two things are needed at once: analysis of daily and weekly historical usage patterns with capacity raised ahead of time, and a response to actual changes in utilization. Predictive scaling builds a forecast from history and raises capacity ahead of demand, while a target tracking policy simultaneously adjusts capacity to match real load. Together they cover both requirements.

opts.A: Step scaling reacts after the fact and builds no forecast from history at all.
opts.C: A schedule does not automatically analyze history and does not react to deviations from the usual pattern.
opts.D: A simple policy with a longer cooldown period reacts even more slowly and provides no forecasting.

730.key: The scenario states the cause directly: repeated, identical read queries. An in-memory cache answers them without reaching the database, so load on the cluster drops immediately and stays down. ElastiCache for Redis costs substantially less than additional Aurora reader instances and actually solves this problem instead of just masking it.

opts.B: One more read replica only postpones the problem briefly: the queries keep repeating, load rises again, and you end up paying for a permanent instance.
opts.C: Auto scaling of read replicas just means adding more billable instances while the underlying source of load remains unaddressed.
opts.D: Multiple writer instances (multi-master) increase write capacity, but the problem is with reads, and that configuration costs more anyway.

731.key: Some requests returning data that is not the latest is a sign of eventually consistent reads, which is DynamoDB's default. Strongly consistent reads return a result that reflects all successful prior writes and solves exactly this problem; latency stays within an acceptable range, as the scenario states directly.

opts.A: There is no such thing as read replicas for DynamoDB tables.
opts.B: A global secondary index is always only eventually consistent, so it would make data freshness worse, not better.
opts.D: Eventual consistency is the current behavior, and it is exactly what is causing the problem.

732.key: SQL injection and other web-based attacks arrive through the application, so they need to be filtered at the application layer — AWS WAF with managed rule groups in front of the application. Security groups and network firewalls do not help here: the attack travels over the allowed port 443 inside an otherwise legitimate request. The second half of the answer — RDS parameter group settings (for example, requiring TLS and configuring logging parameters) — adds defense on the database side, but the key part of the answer is WAF.

opts.A: Security groups and network ACLs filter by address and port. They cannot see malicious SQL embedded inside an allowed HTTPS request.
opts.C: Network Firewall filters VPC network traffic and does not parse HTTP request parameters for injection patterns.
opts.D: Separating database accounts limits the damage but does not prevent the attack itself. The company is also already applying least privilege.

733.key: The company needs to detect abnormal and failed login attempts to its databases across many accounts, without building its own analytics. Amazon GuardDuty does this out of the box with its RDS Protection feature: it analyzes Aurora login events, looks for suspicious patterns (brute-force attempts, logins from unusual addresses, anomalous users), and surfaces findings. It is enabled at the organization level through a delegated administrator, so it covers every account at once with no filters or storage to build.

opts.A: An SCP denies actions; it does not analyze database login attempts.
opts.C: Aurora general logs in CloudWatch give raw records, but anomaly detection would have to be built from scratch: filters, thresholds, correlation. That is far more work.
opts.D: CloudTrail records calls to the RDS management API, not authentication attempts inside the database itself.

734.key: After the acquisition there are two Direct Connect connections in different Regions and many VPCs. A Direct Connect gateway is a global object that lets a single connection reach the virtual private gateway of any VPC in any Region, provided the CIDR blocks don't overlap — which the scenario confirms. Adding a new VPC afterward is just one association; no separate interfaces or tunnels are needed.

opts.A: Inter-Region peering connects VPCs to each other, but it doesn't provide access to the data centers, and the number of peering connections would grow quadratically.
opts.B: A private virtual interface attaches to a virtual private gateway in the same Region as the point of presence. It cannot directly reach a VPC in another Region — that's exactly what the Direct Connect gateway exists for.
opts.C: A mesh of self-managed VPN appliances on EC2 instances is the heaviest possible operational load, and VPN CloudHub connects sites through a virtual private gateway, which has nothing to do with the scenario described.

735.key: The requirements are absorbing large traffic spikes, processing updates strictly in the order received, storing the processed updates in a highly available database, and minimizing management overhead. Kinesis Data Streams preserves record order within a shard and absorbs peak traffic, Lambda functions read the stream without any servers to manage, and DynamoDB provides a highly available store for the leaderboard.

opts.B: Order is preserved, but the fleet of EC2 instances needs to be maintained, and Redshift is an analytics warehouse, not a database for a leaderboard.
opts.C: SNS does not guarantee delivery order, and a SQL database on EC2 means both administration and a weak point for availability.
opts.D: A standard SQS queue does not preserve message order, and the processing instances again require upkeep.

736.key: The logs sit in buckets across different accounts and need to be collected into one bucket without leaving us-west-2 and without manual effort. S3 Same-Region Replication does exactly this: a rule on each source bucket asynchronously copies new objects to the destination bucket, even across accounts, preserving metadata and letting the destination account take ownership of the objects. There's no code, no schedule — you pay only for replication operations and storage. Worth noting: like CRR, replication requires versioning and only applies to objects created after it's enabled.

opts.A: A Lifecycle rule doesn't copy objects between buckets — it changes storage class and deletes objects within its own bucket.
opts.C: A daily script that copies the entire bucket contents re-transfers the same data over and over: costly in requests, requires its own infrastructure to run, and introduces a day's worth of delay.
opts.D: A Lambda function triggered on object creation works, but it's code in every account: error handling, retries, concurrency limits, and per-invocation charges at log volume. That's more operational overhead than built-in replication.

737.key: Latency needs to drop both for people uploading and for people streaming, so both operations must go to the nearest Region. An entry point that itself picks the nearest bucket is an S3 Multi-Region Access Point, and the application should go through its ARN for both reads and writes (E). But if a write can land in any of the three buckets, one-way replication from us-east-2 alone no longer works: bidirectional replication between all three Regions is needed (C), otherwise a video uploaded in Europe would never show up in Asia. "Fewest changes to the application" is only the tiebreaker here — the solution first has to satisfy both latency requirements.

opts.A: One-way replication from us-east-2 only carries over what was written in us-east-2. Developer uploads gain nothing from this — they still travel across the ocean.
opts.B: The chain "us-east-2 → eu-west-2 → ap-southeast-1" doesn't work by default: a replica doesn't get replicated further unless replica modification sync is explicitly enabled. Plus, upload latency is still unresolved.
opts.D: The Multi-Region Access Point is only used for viewing, while uploads still go to us-east-2. Half of the latency requirement goes unmet — just to save one code change in the application.

738.key: What needs optimizing is specifically the upload, and content is consumed mostly in the same Region where it was uploaded. S3 Transfer Acceleration accepts the file at the edge location nearest the uploader and then carries it to the bucket over the AWS backbone, cutting latency and transfer time — exactly the scenario this feature was built for.

opts.A: CloudFront is optimized for delivery; uploads through it don't speed up the way they do with Transfer Acceleration.
opts.C: Intermediate EC2 instances in every Region add an extra layer, extra cost, and extra operations, with no latency benefit.
opts.D: Multiple CloudFront distributions relate to content delivery and have no effect on upload speed.

739.key: A single message needs to reach multiple recipients, with each recipient getting only what it needs. That is exactly the SNS topic model with subscription filter policies: the topic fans the message out, the filter drops what's irrelevant, and SQS queues in front of the functions add buffering and retries on failure.

opts.B: EventBridge can also filter and invoke multiple targets, but this scenario is about fanning out application messages, for which SNS with filters is simpler and cheaper, and EventBridge doesn't provide a buffer in front of the functions.
opts.C: Amazon MSK is a Kafka cluster that needs to be configured and operated, and it cannot publish messages directly into functions on its own.
opts.D: Separate queues per recipient mean the filtering and fan-out logic has to be built by hand at the source.

740.key: The task splits in two: encrypt the millions of objects already uploaded, and ensure future objects are encrypted too. For the existing objects, the standard path is an S3 Inventory report, which shows the encryption status of every object, combined with an S3 Batch Operations job that copies the listed objects with the required encryption. The requirement for a "customer-provided key" points to SSE-C, where the client supplies the key with every request and S3 never stores it. A fair caveat about the question itself: SSE-C cannot actually be selected in the default encryption setting (only SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, and DSSE-KMS are available there), so the second half of the option is technically imprecise — but none of the other options solve the task at all.

opts.B: Storage Lens shows aggregate bucket statistics, not a list of unencrypted objects, and it doesn't touch objects already uploaded. Also, SSE-KMS is not a "customer-provided key."
opts.C: AWS Batch is a service for containerized batch computing, not a mechanism for bulk operations on S3 objects — that's what S3 Batch Operations is for. And again, it's not the key type required.
opts.D: The default encryption setting only affects new objects. Millions of already-uploaded files would remain unencrypted.

741.key: A managed, resilient DNS service is needed, and quickly. A Route 53 public hosted zone plus importing the previous provider's zone file migrates all records in one step; the only thing left is switching the NS records at the registrar. Route 53 runs on an anycast network and carries a 100 percent availability SLA.

opts.B: A private hosted zone only resolves inside the specified VPCs. Public users would not be able to resolve the site's name at all.
opts.C: Simple AD and AWS Managed Microsoft AD are directory services for Windows domains, not public DNS zone hosting.
opts.D: A Resolver inbound endpoint handles queries from the on-premises network to VPC resources. It does not make Route 53 authoritative for the public domain and still leaves the company dependent on the previous provider.

742.key: There are two distinct tasks: application configuration and secrets. AWS AppConfig stores and rolls out configuration with validation and gradual deployment, while Secrets Manager stores credentials encrypted, hands them out based on role, and can automatically rotate them for RDS. Each tool is used for what it's built for, with nothing to code. A useful distinction: Parameter Store is fine for parameters and simple secrets and is cheaper, but it has no built-in rotation.

opts.B: Lambda is a code execution environment, not a configuration store. And Parameter Store can't automatically rotate a database password.
opts.C: Files in a bucket mean manual updates, manual rotation, and access control you build yourself. Maximum administrative work.
opts.D: Storing database credentials inside the database itself is circular: you need to connect to the database to read the password, but you need the password to connect.

743.key: Encryption at rest is already on; what's left is securing the channel. RDS provides a TLS connection by default, but the client has to trust the server's certificate: that means downloading the AWS root certificate bundle (the global-bundle package) and referencing it in the connection string with verification turned on (for MySQL, that's VERIFY_CA or VERIFY_IDENTITY mode). On top of that, the parameter group can require TLS for all connections — for MySQL that's require_secure_transport.

opts.A: IAM database authentication changes how you log into the database, not whether application traffic is encrypted. It does not address the in-transit requirement.
opts.B: Self-signed certificates are useless here: the server presents its own certificate, issued by an AWS certificate authority, and the client needs to trust exactly that one.
opts.C: A snapshot and restore with encryption enabled is an operation for data at rest, which the scenario says is already enabled.

744.key: Clients only allow traffic to addresses authorized on their firewalls, so the load balancer needs a fixed IP address. An Elastic IP address can only be assigned to a Network Load Balancer (A) — one per Availability Zone.

opts.B: ALB does not support Elastic IP addresses: it only has a DNS name, behind which the addresses change. Such a load balancer cannot be added to an allowlist.
opts.C: An A record pointing to an Elastic IP address does not by itself describe a working setup: the address still needs something to attach to, and it cannot be attached to an ALB.
opts.D: A proxy on EC2 in front of the load balancer provides a static address, but it adds a self-managed node and a new point of failure exactly where an NLB solves the problem natively.

745.key: Basic hygiene for a new account: stop using root for day-to-day work and protect it with multi-factor authentication. IAM users are created for daily tasks (or, better, access through roles or IAM Identity Center), and root is reserved for the handful of actions available nowhere else — closing the account, changing the support plan, account recovery. Access keys are never created for root, and if any exist, they should be deleted.

opts.A: The root user cannot be disabled or deleted: it exists for as long as the account exists. It can only be protected.
opts.C: Creating access keys for root and using them is the exact opposite of the recommendation: such a key cannot be restricted with policies.
opts.D: Handing root credentials to a specific person does not make the account more secure: actions become unattributable to an individual, and permissions remain unrestricted.

746.key: Minimum latency between nodes is achieved at two levels. A cluster placement group packs instances as physically close together as possible within a single Availability Zone, giving the highest throughput and lowest latency between them (C). Enhanced networking (an ENA adapter with SR-IOV support) removes network virtualization overhead and reduces jitter (A).

opts.B: Spreading instances across separate accounts has no effect on network latency and only complicates management.
opts.D: Multiple network interfaces on an instance add addresses and traffic separation but do not reduce latency.
opts.E: EBS optimization allocates a separate bandwidth path for disk operations and has nothing to do with node-to-node traffic.
