747.key: The defining details are the SMB protocol and the requirement not to change the applications. That means the target storage has to stay file-based and speak SMB — Amazon FSx for Windows File Server. AWS DataSync handles the migration: it copes with millions of small files and deeply nested directories, preserves structure and permissions, verifies integrity, and runs incrementally.

opts.A: S3 is object storage with no SMB protocol: the applications would have to be rewritten, and Direct Connect by itself doesn't migrate data.
opts.B: FSx for Lustre is built for high-performance computing and speaks the Lustre protocol, not SMB.
opts.D: A volume gateway serves block volumes over iSCSI, not file shares over SMB: the way applications access data would change.

748.key: Collecting metrics, logs, and traces from many accounts into one place is a built-in CloudWatch capability — cross-account observability. It's enabled as a monitoring account in the observer account, while a small template is deployed in the source accounts to allow sharing data. After that, dashboards and queries in the monitoring account see data from every connected account, with no copying and no per-query roles.

opts.B: SCPs only restrict permissions. They don't grant access to another account's data.
opts.C: An IAM user with policies in each account means long-lived credentials and manual setup per account, and the data would still have to be viewed one account at a time.
opts.D: The same scheme with a user and cross-account policies: it works, but it requires roles, switching between them, and gives no unified view in the CloudWatch console.

749.key: The entry point is CloudFront, and WAF is already attached, so it is enough to add an IP match rule for the offending address to the existing web ACL. The request is dropped at the edge location, before it ever reaches the load balancer or the instances. Network ACLs and security groups are useless here: by the time traffic reaches the instances, it already comes from CloudFront and the ALB, not from the client's original address.

opts.A: The CloudFront distribution has no network ACL: it is a global service, not a resource inside your VPC.
opts.C: The instances see the load balancer's address, not the client's, so blocking an address at the subnet level accomplishes nothing.
opts.D: Same reason: the instances' security group filters the source, which is the ALB.

750.key: Thousands of employees, ten accounts, and an existing identity provider already in place — this is exactly the IAM Identity Center scenario. It connects to the external IdP over SAML, users and groups are synchronized through SCIM, and account access is granted by assigning a permission set to a group. Employees sign in with their corporate credentials and receive temporary roles. Not a single IAM user needs to be created.

opts.A: IAM users in every account for thousands of employees is exactly the manual work that Identity Center eliminates. Federation, moreover, is not configured "for IAM users" — it is configured through roles.
opts.B: An account has a single root user, and it is not meant for employees. Synchronizing it with a directory is neither possible nor safe.
opts.D: AWS RAM shares resources between accounts; it does not grant people access to accounts.

751.key: Five employees need full access, and the simplest approach is to grant it once, to a group. Full access is described by the AdministratorAccess managed policy, and it is identity-based: it attaches to a user, group, or role. Resource-based policies belong to resources (a bucket, a queue, a KMS key) and cannot be attached to an IAM group — that distinction is exactly what the wrong options are built on.

opts.A: AdministratorAccess is a policy attached to a principal, i.e., identity-based. It is not a resource-based policy.
opts.B: SystemAdministrator grants broad but not full access: a number of actions, including IAM and billing management, are excluded. The requirement calls for full access.
opts.D: Both the policy type is named incorrectly, and the policy itself does not grant full access.

752.key: Exactly-once delivery and minimal infrastructure management are both required. In AWS, only an SQS FIFO queue guarantees exactly-once processing — it also preserves message order (D). Serverless compute is provided by AWS Lambda, which natively reads from such queues (A).

opts.B: EC2 instances require full-time upkeep — that contradicts the requirement for minimal management.
opts.C: SNS guarantees at-least-once delivery and can deliver a message more than once: that is unacceptable for payments.
opts.E: An EKS cluster means managing both the nodes and the Kubernetes platform itself.

753.key: Minimal operational effort is achieved by not running a self-managed SFTP server: AWS Transfer Family is a managed, highly available service, and S3 provides storage with eleven nines of durability. The nightly batch job is run by an instance that a scheduled Auto Scaling group brings up — it pulls the files from the bucket, processes them, and shuts down.

opts.A: The service and the compute are chosen correctly, but EFS as storage costs more than S3 and is not needed: files are simply written once and read once a night.
opts.B: A self-managed SFTP server on an instance has to be patched and maintained, and the EBS volume is tied to a single Availability Zone — less resilient, more work.
opts.C: The same self-managed SFTP server with all its operational overhead: swapping EBS for EFS does not change that.

754.key: The question states three requirements, and the third one is decisive: "Static IP addresses are required." Only AWS Global Accelerator provides static anycast addresses — CloudFront has no fixed IP addresses; its addresses change. The second requirement, protection against common web exploits, is AWS WAF, and WAF attaches to ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway, AppSync, and Cognito, but not to an NLB. The intersection of both conditions points to option B: ALB in each Region, WAF on the ALB, Global Accelerator on top. The dump key points to D, where WAF is placed correctly but there are no static addresses — so this question is flagged as disputed.

opts.A: AWS WAF cannot be attached to a Network Load Balancer: NLB operates at Layer 4 and is not among WAF's supported resource types.
opts.B: This is the option that satisfies all three requirements at once, including static IPs from Global Accelerator. This is exactly where it diverges from the dump key.
opts.C: The same WAF-on-NLB mistake, plus CloudFront does not provide the static IP addresses the requirement calls for.

755.key: The "too many connections" symptom and the goal of speeding up failover are solved by the same tool. RDS Proxy maintains and reuses a connection pool to the cluster, relieving the exhaustion, and when a replica is promoted to the writer instance, it redirects connections to the new writer itself — according to AWS, this cuts failover time by more than 60 percent, which comfortably exceeds the required 20.

opts.A: Switching from Aurora to RDS is a step backward for failover speed: Aurora's failover is already faster.
opts.C: DynamoDB and DAX would mean rewriting the application, and they have nothing to do with the failover speed of an Aurora cluster.
opts.D: Redshift is an analytics warehouse; it does not serve transactional workloads.

756.key: The data must be handed over already stripped of personal information, always reflecting the latest conversations, and without duplicating files. S3 Object Lambda inserts a function directly into the object read path: the provider accesses the access point, the function redacts the personal data on the fly, the source bucket stays untouched, and scaling happens automatically.

opts.B: Batch processing on an instance creates a second copy of every file, lags behind the most recent conversations, and requires maintaining a machine.
opts.C: A web application on an instance is even more custom code and infrastructure for the same task.
opts.D: Moving part of the data into a table changes the output format and still requires a processing pipeline for every new file.

757.key: The application cannot be modified and cannot run on more than one instance, so horizontal scaling is off the table — the only lever left is faster recovery. A CloudWatch alarm on the StatusCheckFailed_System metric with a recovery action restarts the instance on healthy hardware, preserving its instance ID, private IP address, and attached volumes.

opts.A: Termination protection prevents accidental deletion, but it does not recover anything when the hardware fails.
opts.B: There is no such thing as Multi-AZ configuration for an EC2 instance: that is a property of managed databases.
opts.D: RAID across volumes protects against a single disk failure, but not against failure of the instance itself or its underlying host.

758.key: Containers, three Availability Zones, minimal changes to the application, and minimal operations — this is Amazon ECS. Service Auto Scaling with target tracking maintains the required number of tasks, a minimum of three tasks guarantees presence in every zone, and a spread placement strategy on the Availability Zone attribute distributes them evenly across the zones.

opts.B: Self-managed EKS nodes mean the company operates both the Kubernetes cluster and its nodes: noticeably more operational work.
opts.C: EC2 instances in a placement group abandon container orchestration and go back to managing machines.
opts.D: Turning a containerized application into Lambda functions requires rewriting it, and the requirement calls for minimal changes.

759.key: The demand split is stated explicitly: newer movies are watched often and unpredictably, older ones rarely. For newer movies, use Intelligent-Tiering so there is no need to guess and no retrieval charges; for older movies, use Glacier Flexible Retrieval, the cheapest class from which a file can still be pulled quickly. The "within 5 minutes of a user purchase" requirement is met by expedited retrieval, which returns an archive in 1-5 minutes. Worth noting for real life: expedited retrieval is designed for archives up to roughly 250 MB, so promising five minutes for a 10 GB movie is optimistic — but on the exam, expedited is treated as the answer to "minutes."

opts.A: "Move it once demand drops" is not something a Lifecycle rule can do: it acts on object age, not on demand. Plus a single IA class does not give two different price points for two different groups of movies.
opts.B: Standard-IA returns the file instantly, so the time requirement is met, but storing older movies costs roughly three times as much as Glacier. Costs are not minimized.
opts.D: Bulk retrieval from Glacier Flexible Retrieval takes 5-12 hours. A user who just paid for a movie will not wait that long.

760.key: The infrastructure must be serverless, and the container needs 50 GB of space for temporary files. ECS on Fargate runs the ready-made image without a single instance, and an EFS volume attaches to the task and provides as much space as needed with no capacity planning. There is nothing to manage: no nodes, no disks.

opts.A: An S3 bucket cannot be mounted as a volume for a Lambda function, and the function's ephemeral storage is capped at 10 GB.
opts.B: EBS volumes cannot be attached to Lambda functions at all: that capability does not exist.
opts.D: The EC2 launch type means running your own fleet of instances, so the infrastructure stops being serverless.

761.key: The directory does not support SAML, so standard federation is impossible. What remains is the classic identity broker pattern: a custom application authenticates the user against LDAP, then calls AWS STS (AssumeRole or GetFederationToken) and hands the user temporary credentials along with a console sign-in URL. The key idea: access to AWS is always obtained through temporary STS credentials, while the identity-verification method before that can be anything.

opts.A: IAM Identity Center connects external providers over SAML or through AD. A directory that does not support SAML cannot be integrated this way.
opts.B: An IAM policy is not "embedded into LDAP": it describes permissions in AWS, not an authentication mechanism.
opts.C: Rotating IAM keys in step with LDAP passwords leaves long-lived credentials in place and does not provide single sign-on. It is a homegrown synchronization scheme, not federation.

762.key: The task is to quickly restore an accidentally deleted AMI with minimal operations. AWS provides Recycle Bin for exactly this: a retention rule is set once, after which deleted images and snapshots are placed in the bin for the configured period and can be restored with a single action. No copies, no accounts, no scripts.

opts.A: Snapshots in a separate account mean building your own copy automation and manually restoring the image from a snapshot.
opts.B: Periodically copying images to another account requires scripts, schedules, and extra storage.
opts.D: AMIs cannot simply be uploaded to an S3 bucket: they are not files, they are EC2 service entities.

763.key: Do the math: 150 TB at 100 Mbps, uploading only at night, works out to roughly a year of transfer, and the deadline is a month. The network connection is ruled out by arithmetic alone, so the data has to travel physically. Multiple Snowball devices can be ordered in parallel, filled, and shipped to AWS; the only costs are rental and shipping.

opts.A: Snowmobile is a truck sized for tens of petabytes: for 150 TB it is disproportionately expensive and slow to arrange.
opts.C: Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads, but it is still bottlenecked by the company's same 100 Mbps connection: the deadline will not be met.
opts.D: An endpoint and a VPN do not increase the connection's bandwidth: the arithmetic stays the same.

764.key: The task is to migrate all three tiers with minimal changes and to get point-in-time restore. The virtual machines move to EC2 instances, and the database moves to Amazon RDS for MySQL: the same engine, with point-in-time restore included in the service. Both application tiers sit in private subnets, just as in the on-premises data center where the servers were not exposed directly to the internet; only the load balancer faces outward.

opts.B: Aurora MySQL is a different cluster engine, meaning a bigger architectural change than necessary, and the web tier is moved into public subnets.
opts.C: The database choice is correct, but web instances with public addresses is an unnecessary change to the network model compared with the original.
opts.D: A database in public subnets is a serious security mistake, and the engine changes again without any need.

765.key: The partner needs to read a queue in someone else's account while staying under its own credentials. That is exactly what a resource-based policy on the queue itself provides — an SQS access policy: it names a principal from the partner's account and grants sqs:ReceiveMessage and sqs:DeleteMessage on the specific queue. The partner accesses the queue with its own roles, neither assuming nor handing over anything. General rule: cross-account access to a resource that supports resource-based policies can be granted directly, without AssumeRole.

opts.A: An instance profile attaches a role to an EC2 instance in your own account. It has nothing to do with granting permissions to another account.
opts.B: An IAM policy in your account describes the permissions of your own principals. It grants nothing to another account's principals without permission on the resource side.
opts.D: An SNS topic policy controls access to a topic, not to an SQS queue.

766.key: The developers work both from the office and remotely, the instances sit in a private subnet, and the company needs the cheapest way to give them access. Session Manager solves this without a single additional resource: the agent on the instance opens an outbound connection to the service, so no bastion, open ports, VPN, or SSH keys are needed. The instance is given a role with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy, developer access is described by IAM policies, and sessions are logged. The service itself is free — you only pay for the instances.

opts.A: A bastion host in the same private subnet is unreachable from outside, and the ec2:CreateVpnConnection permission has nothing to do with EC2 Instance Connect. The scheme does not work.
opts.B: Two separate VPN setups — one for the office and one for remote work — mean both an ongoing charge and configuration on every device.
opts.C: A bastion host in the public subnet means an extra instance, an open SSH port, and key and address-list management. It costs more and is less secure than Session Manager.

767.key: The company wants to cut capital expenses on its on-premises arrays, but researchers need instant access to a working subset of the data, while the full dataset is not needed on a daily basis. A volume gateway in cached volumes mode does exactly that: the full dataset is stored in S3, while the frequently used portion stays in the local cache, so latency for the working subset stays minimal and the on-premises arrays no longer need to grow.

opts.A: DataSync moves data to S3 on a schedule, but it does not leave local applications with fast access to the working subset or the familiar way of accessing it.
opts.B: A file gateway would solve the problem for file shares, but the data lives in block storage arrays, not on a file server.
opts.D: Accessing EFS through a VPN tunnel means link latency on every access: the requirement for instant access to the working subset is not met.

768.key: Reverting a table to any point within the last 24 hours is a textbook description of point-in-time recovery in DynamoDB. It is turned on with a single switch, gives second-level precision, and retains history for 35 days — no code or schedules required.

opts.B: AWS Backup makes copies on a schedule: you cannot roll back to an arbitrary minute between them.
opts.C: Hourly backups via a function mean both custom code and up to an hour of potential data loss.
opts.D: A stream of changes gives you a log, but you would have to write the recovery logic yourself.

769.key: Processing takes less than 5 seconds, and the load swings from a few files an hour to hundreds of concurrent uploads. An S3 object-created event notification that invokes a Lambda function directly does the job: you pay only for actual invocations, scaling happens automatically, and there are no intermediate services.

opts.A: CloudTrail logs API calls with a delay and is not meant to trigger processing, and AppSync is a GraphQL API service.
opts.C: Kinesis Data Streams adds a billed stream and shard management where a standard bucket notification is already enough.
opts.D: An SNS topic does not process the files itself and in this design is just an unnecessary link between the bucket and the function.

770.key: The two workloads have different usage profiles, so they call for different pricing models. The production instances run around the clock — for those, a Compute Savings Plan gives a discount without tying you to an instance family. The nonproduction instances are only needed during business hours on weekdays: it's cheaper to pay for them On-Demand and shut them down when not in use — then you pay nothing at all for the idle time.

opts.A: Dedicated Hosts cost more than regular instances and give no discount for a test environment.
opts.B: Reserved Instances for the nonproduction environment are billed continuously, so shutting the machines down saves nothing.
opts.D: Dedicated Hosts for the production environment are the most expensive option, and a Savings Plan for an environment that only runs a quarter of the week would go largely unused.

771.key: Switching engines from Oracle to PostgreSQL requires converting the schema and stored code — that's what the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) does. AWS DMS migrates the data with a full-load task plus change data capture: it moves the existing records first, then continuously replicates the changes happening to the source database during the migration. The connection already exists — the Site-to-Site VPN.

opts.A: A full-load-only task migrates a snapshot and does not capture changes, and the requirement explicitly calls for capturing them.
opts.B: DataSync moves files, not the contents of a relational database, and provides no change capture at all.
opts.D: Snowball is a one-time physical data transfer; it does not carry over changes made during the migration, and the VPN connection is already sufficient here anyway.

772.key: The application is already containerized, and the company needs managed hosting that scales individual services with no infrastructure to maintain. Both orchestrators running on Fargate qualify: ECS with Fargate (A) and EKS with Fargate (B) run tasks and pods without a single server to manage, and scaling is configured at the service or pod level.

opts.C: Lambda functions don't run arbitrary container services as long-running applications; there, the image is just a packaging format for the function code.
opts.D: EC2 worker nodes in ECS still need to be patched and scaled by you.
opts.E: EKS with EC2 nodes has the same problem: it brings back infrastructure that needs to be maintained.

773.key: The traffic spike is sudden but not permanent: what's needed is capacity that appears as traffic grows and disappears after the sale ends. An Auto Scaling group with a scale-out policy and a launch template built from a preconfigured AMI delivers exactly that — new instances start quickly because the image already contains the configured application, and there are no extra machines running outside the peak.

opts.A: Stopped instances are not used by an Auto Scaling group as reserve capacity: it launches new instances from a template rather than starting existing ones.
opts.B: Keeping the group's minimum size sized for peak load means paying for peak capacity around the clock.
opts.C: Caching dynamic content in CloudFront and ElastiCache and then shrinking the fleet is a complex, unreliable design: traffic patterns shift, and a reduced fleet won't hold up against cache misses.

774.key: The task is to quickly and without custom development find out about security groups where SSH is open to the entire internet. AWS Config has the restricted-ssh managed rule for exactly this: it checks inbound rules for port 22 with a source of 0.0.0.0/0 and flags noncompliant security groups. The notification is built with standard services: compliance changes are published to EventBridge, which forwards them to an SNS topic. Not a single line of code — hence "as soon as possible" with minimal effort.

opts.A: A custom script means development, a schedule, pagination handling, and ongoing maintenance. Config delivers the same result with a ready-made rule.
opts.C: A role with permissions to open up security groups, plus a notification when it's assumed, does not detect violations that already exist and does nothing to prevent groups from being changed directly.
opts.D: Blocking non-administrators from changing security groups breaks workflows and still doesn't surface rules that are already open.

775.key: The microservices live in separate accounts, run on Lambda and EKS, and need HTTPS communication plus a service registry — that is exactly what Amazon VPC Lattice is for. You create a service network, register each microservice in it with an HTTPS listener and targets (functions, pods, or instances), and associate the VPCs that need access with the network. Service discovery, routing, and authorization are all built in, with no peering connections or endpoints to create by hand.

opts.A: An inspection VPC with a firewall is about traffic filtering. It provides no service registry or discovery, and the design is more complex.
opts.C: PrivateLink works, but it requires an endpoint service and an interface endpoint for every service-consumer pair. As the number of teams grows, that's a lot of objects and no unified registry at all.
opts.D: Peering connections and prefix lists grow quadratically, there's no service discovery whatsoever, and route tables would need editing with every change.

776.key: The key requirements are sub-millisecond response time plus snapshot and replication capabilities. That description matches ElastiCache for Redis: an in-memory cache responds in fractions of a millisecond, supports replication with automatic failover, and can save snapshots of the data. The metrics already showed that simply scaling the database doesn't help, so what's needed is a caching layer.

opts.A: Aurora with replicas would speed up reads, but that's still scaling the database, which the scenario already says doesn't help, and it doesn't give sub-millisecond response times.
opts.B: DynamoDB global tables solve multi-Region write availability, not sub-millisecond response time, and would require rewriting the application.
opts.D: Memcached is fast but supports neither snapshots nor replication — two of the three stated requirements go unmet.

777.key: Sharing an encrypted AMI is again two operations, but within an organization they can be done at the organizational unit level. First: add the target OU's ARN to the AMI's launch permission list — since 2021, AMIs can be shared with an entire organization or with individual OUs, not just with individual accounts. Second: allow that same OU to use the KMS key that encrypts the snapshots, by updating the key policy (typically with an aws:PrincipalOrgPaths condition). Without the second half, developers would see the image but be unable to launch an instance from it. The same mechanism for a single account is covered in {{q:80}}.

opts.B: The organization root ARN opens the image to every account in the company, but sharing is only needed with the development OU. That's broader than required.
opts.D: A single account's ARN shuts out the rest of the development OU's accounts, whereas the requirement is to share with the whole OU.
opts.E: Recreating the key would make the already-encrypted snapshots unreadable, and granting the permission to the organization root is again broader than required.

778.key: Do the math: 1 PB per office at 2 Gbps takes roughly a month and a half of continuous transfer for a single office alone, and the deadline is four weeks across eighty offices. Network links are ruled out by arithmetic. That leaves physical devices: batches of Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices are ordered in parallel to all offices, filled on-site, and shipped back to AWS. You pay only for device rental and shipping.

opts.A: Eighty new 10 Gbps connections mean months of provisioning and enormous ongoing cost for a one-time migration.
opts.C: Snowmobile is a single truck for tens of petabytes; it isn't available in every country and physically can't visit eighty offices worldwide in four weeks.
opts.D: A volume gateway transfers data over the same office internet connection and is meant for ongoing hybrid storage, not a one-time petabyte-scale migration.

779.key: The requirement is specific — restrict access using IAM specifically, not mount-time settings. EFS has a resource-based policy for the file system, and it can deny the elasticfilesystem:ClientWrite action to the instance roles while leaving ClientMount and ClientRootAccess intact as needed. Such a deny applies at the service level, so the application cannot write even when mounted in regular read-write mode.

opts.A: A read-only mount is a client-side setting: anyone with root on the instance can remount the volume as writable. And that's not "IAM access control," which the requirement calls for.
opts.C: An identity policy attaches to a principal, not "to a file system." The wording describes a construct that doesn't exist.
opts.D: EFS access points with POSIX permissions restrict access at the file-system level, but that's again not an IAM mechanism, and root on the instance can bypass the restriction.

780.key: This is a near-verbatim repeat of {{q:222}}: an external vendor works from its own AWS account. The correct design is a role in your account with policies for the required actions and a trust policy that allows a principal from the vendor's account to assume it. The vendor calls AssumeRole and gets temporary credentials, and you can revoke access at any time just by editing the trust policy. In practice, an external ID is added on top.

opts.B: An IAM user with a password means long-lived credentials handed out externally, plus manual revocation. Less secure in every respect.
opts.C: You cannot add a user from another account to your own IAM group: groups only work within a single account.
opts.D: A permission boundary caps the maximum permissions of a principal, but it does not let another account act in yours. That's the wrong mechanism.

781.key: There are two requirements: understand whose spending it is, and get notified when it reaches 60% of the budget. The first is handled by cost allocation tags: resources are tagged with an owner or department, the tag is activated in the management account, and after that spending is broken down by those tags. The second is a budget in AWS Budgets with a 60% alert threshold. Note that Cost Explorer forecasts cannot be used to identify owners: a forecast shows future amounts, not who's responsible.

opts.B: Forecasts don't identify resource owners, and Cost Anomaly Detection looks for anomalies, not a percentage of a given budget.
opts.C: Trusted Advisor gives optimization recommendations, not threshold notifications tied to a department's budget.
opts.D: Half of this is right (a budget with a threshold), but Cost Explorer forecasts can't establish who owns the spending — that's what tags are for.

782.key: The application must be reachable only from the company's office, yet it still needs outbound access to download updates. The instances go in private subnets behind an internal load balancer whose inbound rule allows only the office network's address block, arriving over the already-configured tunnel. NAT gateways in the public subnets provide the outbound access needed for patches.

opts.A: A public load balancer with a source of 0.0.0.0/0 exposes the internal application to the entire internet.
opts.C: Instances in public subnets are exposed externally, a NAT gateway in a private subnet doesn't work, and the rule is set on outbound traffic instead of inbound.
opts.D: A public load balancer again makes the application reachable from the internet, and an outbound rule does nothing to restrict access from outside.

783.key: The requirement is for immutable, cryptographically verifiable records of data changes — that's a word-for-word description of Amazon QLDB: the ledger's journal is protected by hashing, the history cannot be rewritten, and the service itself is fully managed.

opts.A: Redshift is an analytics warehouse; it does not provide immutability or cryptographic verification of history.
opts.B: Neptune stores graphs and is built for relationship queries, not for a verifiable change log.
opts.C: Timestream is optimized for time-series data and likewise offers no cryptographic verification of history.

784.key: Error handling, retries, and state management need to be taken off the company's plate. AWS Glue DataBrew handles the data preparation with no code, while a Step Functions state machine orchestrates running the jobs — some in parallel, some strictly in order — with retries, branching, and state built in.

opts.A: A collection of Lambda functions means retries, ordering, and state all have to be implemented by hand.
opts.B: Athena runs queries, but it does not orchestrate a chain of jobs or manage their state.
opts.D: AWS Data Pipeline is a legacy service, and a single midnight run contradicts the requirement for regular, parallel jobs.

785.key: The core requirement is that no payment gets processed twice. An SQS FIFO queue provides exactly-once processing: duplicates within the deduplication window are dropped, and a message isn't handed to another consumer until it's acknowledged. It's the only option with that guarantee.

opts.A: S3 event notifications are delivered at-least-once, so a duplicate invocation — and a duplicate payment — is possible.
opts.B: A standard SQS queue also only guarantees at-least-once delivery and allows duplicates.
opts.D: A DynamoDB stream can likewise invoke the handler more than once and provides no protection against a duplicate payment.

786.key: The task is to gather usage and configuration data about on-premises servers before a migration. That's exactly what AWS Application Discovery Service exists for: an agent-based or agentless collector captures CPU load, memory, disks, and network connections, and the results feed into AWS Migration Hub, where the home Region is set up beforehand.

opts.A: Systems Manager manages nodes that are already connected and isn't built for pre-migration inventory with dependency mapping.
opts.C: The Schema Conversion Tool converts database schemas, and Trusted Advisor analyzes resources inside AWS, not on-premises servers.
opts.D: Both tools are for database migration and don't collect any data about server load.

787.key: An organization-wide managed landscape is needed: auditing every API call and login across existing and new accounts, plus compliance monitoring against the FSBP standard. AWS Control Tower is deployed in the organization's management account, automatically enables an organization-wide CloudTrail trail and aggregates the logs, and Account Factory creates new accounts already configured this way. Security Hub with the Foundational Security Best Practices standard gives continuous compliance evaluation across all accounts.

opts.B: Control Tower is specifically deployed in the organization's management account: the landscape can't be set up from a member account.
opts.C: AMS Accelerate is a paid managed service with an RFC request process, which is more expensive and slower. GuardDuty also looks for threats rather than checking FSBP compliance.
opts.D: Security Hub is the right pick, but going through AMS Accelerate and RFC requests can't compete with ready-made Control Tower on cost or speed.

788.key: The data already sits in S3 in the columnar Parquet format, and queries run only occasionally. The cheapest path is to avoid standing up any cluster at all: an AWS Glue crawler discovers the structure and creates a table in the data catalog, and Amazon Athena runs queries directly against the objects, billed by bytes scanned. The Parquet format also cuts the amount of data scanned considerably.

opts.A: Moving ten terabytes into Aurora means paying for storage and a continuously running instance just to serve occasional queries.
opts.B: Redshift Spectrum can read from S3, but it requires a running Redshift cluster, which is billed continuously.
opts.D: An EMR cluster is also billed for node uptime: for occasional queries, that's more expensive than paying for data scanned.

789.key: The dump's key (option D) was corrected during the audit. The requirement is to block deployment, and the conditions are expressed in terms of the template's content: an inline policy, a wildcard in the Statement, a public IP on an instance. An SCP operates on API calls and request conditions and cannot see the contents of a CloudFormation template, so it can't check "does this contain an inline policy with a wildcard." That's the job of AWS Control Tower proactive controls: they're implemented through CloudFormation Hooks and validate the template before resources are created, blocking a noncompliant stack. Keep the three kinds of controls straight: preventive (SCPs, restrict actions), detective (AWS Config, find issues after the fact), and proactive (validate the template before deployment).

opts.B: Detective controls find noncompliance in resources that already exist and report on it. They cannot block a deployment.
opts.C: AWS Config also reacts after the fact, and automatically deleting created resources is a risky, blunt way to achieve compliance.
opts.D: This was the original dump key. An SCP can deny ec2:RunInstances with a public IP based on a condition, but it can't parse the contents of an IAM resource inside a template to find an inline policy with a wildcard. Half the requirement stays unmet.

790.key: The application can't be rewritten, so scalability and availability have to be built around it as-is. The instances move into an Auto Scaling group across private subnets in multiple Availability Zones (B), while an Application Load Balancer in a public subnet accepts public traffic and spreads it across the instances (E). The application itself doesn't change.

opts.A: A larger instance is still a single machine: no availability gain and no horizontal scaling.
opts.C: A NAT gateway lets traffic out; it can't accept inbound requests.
opts.D: Same problem as option A: a single point of failure remains.

791.key: Lambda environment variables are already encrypted at rest with an AWS managed key by default, but their values are visible in plaintext in the console and API to anyone with permission to read the function's configuration. To keep developers from seeing the values, encryption helpers are enabled: the variable is encrypted with a customer managed KMS key right in the console, only ciphertext is stored in the configuration, and the function decrypts it in code with a Decrypt call. Permission on the key is granted to the execution role, as covered in {{q:550,640}}.

opts.A: Switching to EC2 has nothing to do with the task: secrets in an instance's configuration are just as visible to anyone with access.
opts.B: There's no such thing as "SSL encryption for a Lambda function via CloudHSM": CloudHSM isn't integrated with environment variables, and SSL protects the channel, not stored values.
opts.C: ACM certificates are issued for TLS on load balancers, CloudFront, and API Gateway. They can't be used to encrypt environment variables.

792.key: Millions of end users with identity verification before accessing REST APIs is the Cognito user pool plus API Gateway with a Cognito authorizer combination. The user pool handles sign-up, sign-in, password recovery, and MFA, and issues a JWT; API Gateway validates that token with a built-in authorizer, with no code required. Keep the two Cognito concepts distinct: a user pool is a user directory and authentication, while an identity pool exchanges a token for temporary AWS credentials.

opts.B: An identity pool doesn't authenticate users: it issues AWS credentials to users who are already authenticated. Verifying login requires a user pool.
opts.C: A custom Lambda authorizer is code that has to be written and maintained, whereas the built-in Cognito authorizer works out of the box.
opts.D: An IAM user can't serve as the login mechanism for millions of clients: IAM is designed for principals within an account, not for an application's end users.

793.key: Deleting a KMS key doesn't happen instantly: scheduled deletion waits 7 to 30 days, and during that whole window it can be cancelled with a CancelKeyDeletion call. The solution is built on exactly that: an EventBridge rule catches the ScheduleKeyDeletion event from CloudTrail, triggers a Systems Manager Automation runbook that cancels the deletion, and simultaneously publishes a message to an SNS topic for the administrators. Every component is managed, with no custom code.

opts.A: An AWS Config rule evaluates resource compliance and can't be the target of an EventBridge rule that cancels something. The mechanics of this option don't work.
opts.B: A custom Lambda function with cancellation logic plus an extra CloudWatch alarm is code and more moving parts where a ready-made runbook already suffices.
opts.D: The CloudTrail-plus-metric-filter-plus-alarm setup only notifies the administrators. It doesn't cancel the deletion itself, and the requirement is to prevent losing the key.

794.key: Reports take under ten minutes to generate and are almost always requested in a single week of the month. A Lambda function starts instantly on an EventBridge rule, fits comfortably within the fifteen-minute limit, and is billed only for actual run time — outside the reporting period there's no cost at all.

opts.A: Instances running the entire last week of the month are billed around the clock, even though they're only busy for minutes at a time.
opts.C: An ECS task is cheaper than an instance, but it starts more slowly than a function and is billed in coarser intervals, which is a meaningful overpayment for ten-minute jobs.
opts.D: Spot Instances are cheaper, but they still run for a week straight, and capacity reclamation could interrupt a report mid-generation.

795.key: A tightly coupled HPC workload comes down to two things: the network between nodes and the file storage. Elastic Fabric Adapter gives instances OS-kernel bypass and low latency for MPI libraries (D). For storage, FSx for Lustre in scratch mode delivers maximum throughput at the lowest price, and the lack of replication is not a concern for intermediate computation data (B).

opts.A: Global Accelerator optimizes the path from users' traffic to an application and has no effect on communication between compute nodes.
opts.C: CloudFront delivers content over HTTP to end users and has nothing to do with high-performance computing.
opts.E: Elastic Beanstalk deploys web applications; it has no networking or storage optimization features for computation.

796.key: Training a model is off the table, so a ready-made service is needed. Amazon Rekognition has built-in unwanted-content detection for images (content moderation) and requires no training. It's called from a Lambda function that the application invokes when a photo is uploaded.

opts.A: SageMaker Autopilot trains a model — a direct violation of the requirement.
opts.C: Comprehend analyzes text, not images, and CloudFront Functions are too limited to call out to external services.
opts.D: Rekognition Video is built for video streams and recordings, but photos are being uploaded here: ordinary image analysis is what's needed.

797.key: AWS lets you register multiple MFA devices for a single root user (up to eight), and that's the standard way to avoid losing access if one device is lost. The second device is kept somewhere separate — for example, a hardware key in a safe. Also keep in mind the procedure for total loss: recovering root access requires confirmation through the account's email address and phone number, so those contacts must stay current, and the root email address should be a distribution list, not a personal inbox.

opts.A: No other account can substitute for root: some operations (closing the account, changing the support plan, account recovery) are available only to it.
opts.C: Creating a new administrator once access is already lost isn't possible — and it doesn't restore root access anyway.
opts.D: Attaching an administrator policy to another user doesn't grant root privileges and doesn't solve the problem of a lost MFA device.

798.key: There are hundreds of partners a day, and each one needs notifications delivered to its own HTTP endpoint. An SNS topic supports HTTP and HTTPS subscription protocols: adding a partner comes down to creating a subscription, and the fan-out is scaled by the service itself. The publishing application doesn't care how many subscribers there are.

opts.A: Timestream is a time-series database, and the fan-out delivery would have to be written and scaled by hand.
opts.C: A task per partner in a state machine means reworking the state machine every time a new partner is added.
opts.D: Kinesis Data Streams requires custom producer and consumer applications and doesn't deliver data to HTTP endpoints.

799.key: There's no in-house machine learning expertise, so a ready-made service is needed. Amazon Comprehend extracts entities from text with no model training, and it's invoked from a Lambda function triggered by the bucket's upload notification — billed only for actual processing.

opts.B: Amazon Forecast predicts time series and doesn't work with text.
opts.C: Amazon Polly synthesizes speech: it doesn't extract ingredient names from text.
opts.D: SageMaker means building and training a custom model — exactly what the company lacks the expertise for, and it's noticeably more expensive.

800.key: A Lambda function mounts an EFS file system through an access point while sitting inside a VPC, and network access to a VPC in another account comes from peering. That lets the function reach the mount target in the owning account directly: no data copy is created, there's no second storage system to pay for, and growth in volume doesn't change anything — EFS scales on its own.

opts.A: A second copy of the file system means paying for storage twice and running continuous synchronization, which will also lag behind.
opts.C: An intermediate function in the second account is an extra hop, extra code, and paying for another function on every call.
opts.D: Lambda layers are size-limited and meant for libraries, not for a growing set of user files.

801.key: The discriminator is "must manage the encryption keys outside the AWS Cloud." Any SSE scheme (with an AWS key, a customer key in KMS, or the default key) means the key lives inside AWS. The only way to keep the keys entirely on your own side is to encrypt the data locally before sending it, and put only ciphertext into S3. TLS covers encryption in transit. Note the related question {{q:965}}: it uses the same logic with the phrasing "encrypt the data before storing."

opts.A: A customer managed key is a key you control, but it's stored and used inside AWS KMS. The requirement to keep keys outside the cloud isn't met.
opts.B: An AWS managed key gives you even less control: both storage and key policy sit on AWS's side.
opts.C: Default encryption is SSE-S3, where the service fully manages the keys. That directly contradicts the requirement.

802.key: Notifications arrive from mobile devices over HTTP, so a managed entry point is needed — API Gateway with a Lambda function for basic validation. Backend processing runs long and needs adjustable CPU and memory: that's a job for ECS on Fargate, where resources are set in the task definition and there's no infrastructure to maintain.

opts.A: An SQS queue can't be the event source for an EventBridge rule the way it's described, and EKS Anywhere runs on the company's own premises — the infrastructure would still need maintaining.
opts.B: Self-managed EKS nodes mean manual patching, scaling, and monitoring.
opts.C: Spot Instances can be reclaimed in the middle of processing a long-running payment, and a Spot Fleet requires configuration and upkeep.

803.key: A second factor should be requested not always, but when a login looks suspicious: a new country, an unfamiliar device, an unusual address. That's a built-in Amazon Cognito user pools feature — adaptive authentication (advanced security): it scores the risk of each login attempt and, based on a configured threshold, requires MFA, blocks, or allows the attempt through. The service scales to millions of users without any infrastructure of your own.

opts.B: An identity pool doesn't perform user login and can't assess risk: it only exchanges a token for temporary AWS credentials.
opts.C: IAM users aren't meant for an application's end users and don't scale to millions, and IAM has no adaptive authentication.
opts.D: IAM Identity Center is built for employees and access to AWS accounts, not for application customers. It also has no risk scoring based on geolocation or device.

804.key: The requirements are a massively parallel warehouse, model training via SQL commands, and serverless services wherever possible. AWS Glue runs the daily transformation with no clusters to manage, Redshift Serverless provides an MPP architecture billed for actual usage, and Redshift ML lets you create and train models directly with SQL commands.

opts.A: An EMR cluster isn't a serverless service: nodes have to be chosen and are billed for uptime.
opts.B: Aurora is not a massively parallel processing warehouse, and the scenario names MPP as an explicit requirement.
opts.D: Athena is a query engine over data in S3, not a data warehouse, and there's no such thing as "Athena ML."

805.key: The requirement is strict: data must physically stay in the company's data center, while EKS and other AWS managed services are still needed. That's exactly the AWS Outposts scenario: an AWS rack is installed on the customer's premises, managed from the console as part of a Region, and workloads and their data never leave the site.

opts.A: Local Zones are AWS-owned facilities in major cities; they can't be deployed inside a company's own data center.
opts.B: Snowmobile is transport for a one-time bulk transfer of huge amounts of data into the cloud — the opposite of keeping data on premises.
opts.D: Snowball Edge provides some local compute and storage for the duration of a task, but it's not a platform for running EKS and other managed services on an ongoing basis.

806.key: The data sits on NFS file storage, the volume is growing, and the main requirement is cost. S3 File Gateway keeps the file access applications are used to, but under the hood everything is stored as objects in S3, where a gigabyte costs a fraction of any file system, and a lifecycle rule moves infrequently read data to even cheaper storage classes.

opts.A: A volume gateway serves block volumes over iSCSI, while the applications use NFS: the access method would change.
opts.C: EFS Standard-IA costs more per gigabyte than S3, and the problem of runaway cost growth remains.
opts.D: One Zone-IA is cheaper, but the data is stored in only one Availability Zone, and it still loses to S3 on cost per gigabyte.

807.key: The code is CPU-bound, and Lambda's CPU share grows with the memory allocated: raising the memory per Compute Optimizer's recommendation lets the function run noticeably faster, and the total cost per invocation drops. Provisioned concurrency, meanwhile, keeps latency low under high concurrency and is billed at a reduced rate for duration.

opts.A: Reducing memory also takes away CPU time: the function runs longer, and latency increases.
opts.B: Reserved concurrency only caps the number of concurrent instances — with a growing stream of messages, that's a direct hit to latency.
opts.C: Correct concurrency management paired with reduced memory means, for CPU-heavy code, longer duration and higher cost.

808.key: The requirement is to scan images for known vulnerabilities with the fewest changes to the workloads. If images are stored in Amazon ECR, scanning is turned on through repository settings: basic scan on push checks OS packages against the CVE database, while enhanced scanning, built on Amazon Inspector, additionally covers programming-language dependencies and continuous rescanning. Neither the ECS task definition nor the application changes at all.

opts.B: Container images aren't stored in S3, and Macie looks for sensitive data, not vulnerabilities. This setup doesn't work.
opts.C: Moving from ECS to EKS is about the largest possible change to the workloads, and the requirement explicitly asks for minimal changes.
opts.D: A homegrown pipeline with a bucket, events, and a function is code and extra components where ECR already scans images natively.

809.key: An EventBridge rule catches the Batch job's completion event, and an API destination is what can call an external HTTP API with a username and password: credentials are stored in the connection, retries are built in, and there's no custom code (A).

opts.B: EventBridge Scheduler invokes targets on a schedule and does not match incoming events. The phrase "Scheduler matches the SUCCEEDED event" describes behavior that doesn't exist.
opts.C: AWS Batch does not publish events to API Gateway. Job state changes go to EventBridge — that's the only place to catch them.
opts.D: Same false premise about publishing to API Gateway, plus an unnecessary Lambda function where an API destination already handles authentication to the third-party API on its own.

810.key: The company has no internet gateway, no dedicated connection, and no VPN — so access has to be purely private and one-directional. The vendor puts a Network Load Balancer in front of its database and publishes it as an endpoint service; the company creates an interface endpoint in its own VPC. The connection is initiated only from the company's side, only the one published service is visible, and overlapping address spaces don't matter.

opts.A: The Hosted Connection program is about ordering a Direct Connect link through a partner and is unrelated to this task, and peering between two different companies' accounts would open up both networks entirely.
opts.B: Client VPN connects individual users to a VPC; it doesn't link two networks together.
opts.D: Transit gateway and peering are listed together as mutually exclusive solutions, and both give broad network connectivity instead of access to a single service.

811.key: The requirement is access to the RDS database without going out to the internet. Amazon Managed Grafana connects to data sources in private networks through AWS PrivateLink: a private connection is created between the Grafana workspace and the resource in the VPC, after which the database is registered as a data source. The database needs no public endpoint at all.

opts.A: A public endpoint on the database is exactly what the requirement forbids: the data becomes reachable from the internet.
opts.B: An Amazon Managed Grafana workspace isn't created inside the customer's VPC: it's a managed service, and privacy is provided through PrivateLink specifically.
opts.D: This has two mistakes at once: the workspace isn't placed in a VPC, and the database is still exposed through a public endpoint.

812.key: A ready-made, no-code solution is needed, with data lineage, profiling, and the ability to share the transformation steps. That's AWS Glue DataBrew: visual transformations are assembled into recipes, which are published and reused by other employees.

opts.A: The Glue Studio visual editor generates Spark jobs, and sharing happens at the job level rather than as reusable recipes; it also provides no data profiling.
opts.B: EMR Serverless requires writing job code — a direct violation of the requirement.
opts.D: Athena queries are also code, and on top of that they provide no profiling or data lineage.

813.key: The requirement "keeps working even after the development instance is replaced" rules out anything tied to a specific address. The right approach is an alias A record pointing to the same load balancer, plus a listener rule that, based on the Host header for the development address, forwards the request to the target group containing the development instance. Replacing the instance only changes target registration in the group; the DNS record and the rule stay the same.

opts.B: An instance's public IP address changes when it's recreated, and the A record would need manual updates. The automatic-resilience requirement isn't met.
opts.C: An ALB listener rule can redirect to a URL, but tying it to the instance's public address breaks in exactly the same way when the machine is replaced.
opts.D: Putting all the instances in one target group would make the load balancer spread developer requests across the whole fleet: reliably reaching the development instance specifically becomes impossible.

814.key: The application runs on Kubernetes and communicates over AMQP — so changes should be kept to a minimum. EKS keeps the familiar manifests and tooling, and Amazon MQ is a managed broker that supports AMQP, so the messaging code stays the same. Operational overhead is minimal.

opts.A: SQS uses its own API, not AMQP: the code would need rewriting. ECS is also a different orchestration system.
opts.C: Self-managed EC2 instances still need to be maintained, and Kubernetes orchestration is lost in the process.
opts.D: Moving a containerized application to Lambda means reworking it, and SQS still doesn't support AMQP.

815.key: The load balancers are already spread across Regions; what needs to change is the path traffic takes from the player to the Region. A standard accelerator in AWS Global Accelerator provides fixed anycast addresses, accepts connections at the nearest edge location, and carries them over the AWS backbone instead of the public internet, while the existing NLBs are simply registered as its endpoints. End-to-end load time drops without reworking a single piece of the architecture.

opts.A: Replacing NLBs with ALBs changes the load-balancing layer but does nothing to shorten the path over the public internet from the player to the Region.
opts.B: Equal weighting in Route 53 sends half the users to a Region that is decidedly far away: average latency would go up, not down.
opts.C: New Regions take a long time and a lot of money, and traffic would still travel to them over the public internet.

816.key: Some vendors can only speak SFTP, and the company wants a managed service with minimal operations. AWS Transfer Family creates an SFTP endpoint that drops files straight into the same S3 bucket the rest of the application writes to. No servers, no scaling, no patching — the service itself provides availability.

opts.A: DMS migrates database data and isn't a mechanism for receiving files from partners over SFTP.
opts.C: A self-run SFTP server on an instance is a machine you have to patch, back up, and scale yourself.
opts.D: S3 File Gateway serves SMB shares and is meant for a local network, whereas the vendors specifically need SFTP.

817.key: Textract extracts text from PDF documents but doesn't deal with meaning or tone. Analyzing content and assessing sentiment is Amazon Comprehend's job — a ready-made service that needs no training or custom model; the results are saved to S3.

opts.A: Athena runs SQL queries against data and doesn't determine sentiment.
opts.B: SageMaker means building and training a custom model — the most work possible where a ready-made service already exists.
opts.D: QuickSight builds dashboards from already-prepared data, but it doesn't extract meaning or sentiment from text itself.

818.key: Data arrives in real time from third-party applications and needs to land in S3 in raw form. The standard combination is a Kinesis Data Streams stream as the ingestion point and Firehose as the consumer, which buffers records and writes them to the bucket. Both services are managed, scale with load, and require no instances or custom delivery code.

opts.B: DMS migrates databases: EC2 instances can't be its source, and it isn't built for streaming event ingestion.
opts.C: DataSync copies files on a schedule from file systems and storage, not a real-time event stream.
opts.D: Direct Connect is a link to the company's own premises, while the data comes from third-party applications over the internet. Direct writes to Firehose are possible without it anyway.

819.key: DynamoDB's item size limit is 400 KB, and the data already reaches 700 KB and keeps growing. The standard pattern for this: store the object itself in S3, and keep an item in the table with an attribute pointing to it. This removes both the current limit and the future growth problem.

opts.A: Splitting data between two databases creates two storage models and a permanent filtering code path — maximum complexity.
opts.C: Splitting an object into items requires custom slicing and reassembly logic, and BatchWriteItem is limited to sixteen megabytes and twenty-five items.
opts.D: Compression only pushes the limit back: the data keeps growing, and there's no guarantee a compressed object will fit under 400 KB.

820.key: Hundreds of jobs running one to twenty minutes, almost no code changes allowed, and both a schedule and future event-driven triggering are needed. The jobs are packaged into containers and run as Fargate tasks, while Amazon EventBridge Scheduler sets both recurring schedules and one-time runs at a specified moment. Fargate removes the execution time limit.

opts.A: Some jobs run up to twenty minutes, which exceeds the Lambda function's fifteen-minute limit.
opts.B: AWS Batch is built for queues of batch jobs and doesn't provide a convenient scheduler with future-event triggering for hundreds of different schedules.
opts.D: A Wait state in Step Functions can be adapted, but building hundreds of workflows instead of schedules is noticeably more work.

821.key: The source is the Salesforce SaaS application, the destination is Redshift, traffic must not travel over the public internet, and development effort should be minimal. Amazon AppFlow has a ready-made Salesforce connector, handles both the initial load and picking up changes on a schedule or by event, and privacy is provided by the AWS PrivateLink option: the flow travels over the AWS internal network.

opts.A: You can't build a VPN connection to Salesforce the way you would to a regular network, and Glue DataBrew is a data-prep tool, not a SaaS integration mechanism.
opts.B: Direct Connect links AWS to the company's own premises; there's no way to extend it to someone else's SaaS service.
opts.D: VPC peering can only be created between VPCs within AWS. Salesforce is an external service and has no VPC of its own to peer with.

822.key: The scenario explicitly allows changing the application, so moving from a file system to object storage is on the table. S3 costs several times less per gigabyte than EFS, and Intelligent-Tiering itself moves objects between tiers based on actual access frequency — no rules, no retrieval charges, and no risk that an infrequently read file won't be available instantly.

opts.B: FSx for Windows File Server is also file storage, and it costs more than EFS: costs would rise, not fall.
opts.C: FSx for OpenZFS is again a file system priced at EFS level or higher; there's no savings.
opts.D: Glacier Flexible Retrieval is cheaper to store, but standard retrieval takes hours, while the application indexes and serves files: that delay is unacceptable.

823.key: The discriminator is routing based on the query string. Only an Application Load Balancer can parse an HTTP request and pick a target group by query string, header, path, or method — it's a layer-7 load balancer. Encryption is provided by a TLS listener with a certificate from ACM, which is free and auto-renewing. A Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4 and knows nothing about the request's content.

opts.A: An NLB doesn't parse HTTP: it has no query-parameter-based routing.
opts.B: A Gateway Load Balancer is built for inserting network security appliances into the traffic path and doesn't do HTTP routing.
opts.D: Same mistake with the NLB, plus importing a certificate into IAM is an outdated approach: ACM issues and manages certificates for load balancers.

824.key: There are two weak points: a single machine handling everything, and the database living inside it. The application moves into an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, and the database moves into an Aurora Serverless cluster compatible with MySQL: the same engine, capacity adjusts automatically as traffic grows, and data is stored across multiple Availability Zones.

opts.A: Redshift is an analytics warehouse, not a transactional database, and it has no such thing as "MySQL-compatible nodes."
opts.B: A target group without an Auto Scaling group doesn't provide automatic growth in instance count — the scalability requirement isn't met.
opts.D: Redis is a cache, not a database, and it has no "MySQL connector" at all: there's nowhere to store the data.

825.key: This is the same text as question {{q:202}}, but the dump's key is the opposite answer — which is why both questions are flagged as disputed. The case for SSE-S3: the service manages and rotates its own keys, there's nothing to configure or maintain, and that's literally "least operational overhead." The case against it: SSE-S3's annual rotation cadence isn't documented anywhere, whereas a KMS key's automatic rotation runs every 365 days and is verifiable through CloudTrail records. If the question mentions "compliance" or requires proving the rotation period to an auditor, choose KMS; if the emphasis is purely on minimal effort, choose SSE-S3.

opts.B: A strong alternative, and the key for question {{q:202}}: a customer managed key with automatic rotation gives a verifiable yearly cycle. It costs more and requires setting up a key policy — hence the dispute over "least operational overhead."
opts.C: Manual rotation means a yearly task for a human, whereas KMS achieves the exact same result by simply enabling automatic rotation.
opts.D: Imported key material is the most labor-intensive option, and automatic rotation isn't supported for it in KMS: new material has to be imported by hand.

826.key: Same scenario as question {{q:28}}: users stay in self-managed Active Directory, but sign-in must work across every account in the organization. The solution is IAM Identity Center together with AWS Managed Microsoft AD, with a two-way trust established between it and the on-premises forest. Identity Center uses the directory as its identity source, and account access is granted by assigning a permission set to AD groups.

opts.A: Creating another directory in the cloud and declaring it the source means standing up a second set of users: the requirement is to keep managing them in the on-premises Active Directory.
opts.C: Directory Service by itself doesn't provide single sign-on across the organization's accounts — that's Identity Center's job.
opts.D: A self-hosted identity provider on EC2 is infrastructure you'd have to build and maintain, whereas the Identity Center plus Managed AD combination is a standard pattern.

827.key: An Aurora cluster has exactly two storage configurations: Standard and I/O-Optimized. Under heavy, sustained I/O load, I/O-Optimized delivers predictable performance and pricing (D): I/O operations are included in the price.

opts.A: Standard is the default configuration, where every I/O operation is billed separately. Under growing load, that's exactly what you're trying to move away from.
opts.B: Provisioned IOPS is an EBS volume type that applies to RDS, not to an Aurora cluster. Aurora has no volumes for you to manage.
opts.C: General Purpose is also an EBS volume type from the RDS world. The concept doesn't apply to Aurora, and the trap here relies on conflating these terms.

828.key: The task is to continuously show the state of NIST and PCI DSS controls across hundreds of accounts and present that to auditors. That's exactly what AWS Security Hub exists for: it aggregates findings, ships ready-made check packs for industry standards, and produces a compliance score. A delegated Security Hub administrator is designated for the organization, after which the service is turned on automatically for all member accounts. Keep the distinction clear: Security Hub is for standards compliance, GuardDuty for threat detection, Inspector for vulnerabilities, and Config for configuration state.

opts.A: Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities and insecure network paths. It has no check packs for NIST or PCI DSS.
opts.B: GuardDuty looks for signs of compromise in logs and traffic. It doesn't evaluate compliance of controls against standards.
opts.C: CloudTrail records API calls. No "security standards" get enabled in it.

829.key: A data lake with hundreds of applications accessing objects randomly is the definition of an unpredictable access pattern. There's no way to guess the age at which an object goes cold, and paying a retrieval fee for every unexpected access is unwelcome. S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between the frequent and infrequent tiers on its own, based on actual access, charges no retrieval fee, and returns data instantly from both tiers. One Lifecycle rule on the bucket, and the service runs on its own after that.

opts.B: Glacier doesn't provide immediate availability, and S3 Select is no longer supported for queries against Glacier archives. Random access from hundreds of applications simply doesn't work on an archival tier.
opts.C: Storage class analysis produces a report that a person then turns into rules by hand, and with random access, moving to Standard-IA means paying a fee for every unexpected read. That's both more manual work and a risk of overpaying.
opts.D: A scheme with a Lambda function that moves objects back to Standard on access is a homemade copy of Intelligent-Tiering: custom code, a delay on first access, and a charge for every transition between classes.

830.key: A million profiles and ten million many-to-many connections, and the requirement is to find mutual connections up to five levels deep. That's a graph problem, and Amazon Neptune solves it: vertices and edges, graph traversal in predictable time, with no repeated table joins.

opts.A: A five-level traversal in Athena turns into five sequential joins over terabytes of data — slow and expensive.
opts.C: QuickSight visualizes data that's already been computed, but it doesn't perform the graph traversal itself.
opts.D: In a relational database, that kind of traversal needs recursive joins, and at ten million connections performance collapses.

831.key: No bandwidth needed, little traffic, and it has to go up fast and cheap — that's a description of AWS Site-to-Site VPN. An IPsec tunnel is configured in hours, encrypts traffic between the site and the VPC, is billed hourly, and costs far less than a dedicated connection.

opts.A: Client VPN connects individual users to a VPC and is billed per connection and per hour of endpoint uptime. The task here is to link network to network.
opts.B: Direct Connect takes weeks to provision and is expensive because of the port and cross-connect fees. For light traffic, that's overpaying.
opts.C: A bastion host gives administrative access to individual machines, not secure connectivity between networks.

832.key: Both the current Active Directory-based authentication and the SFTP access method need to be preserved, while files are stored in S3. An AWS Transfer Family server with an SFTP endpoint takes its identity provider from AWS Directory Service, and AD Connector provides the link to the on-premises domain — it proxies authentication requests to the existing directory without copying any accounts.

opts.A: S3 File Gateway serves resources over SMB, while employees work over SFTP: the access method would change.
opts.B: A self-managed fleet of instances running an SFTP server is exactly the operational burden the requirement asks to avoid.
opts.D: Picking AWS Directory Service as the identity provider isn't enough by itself: without AD Connector or a domain trust, there's no connection to the on-premises directory. That's the difference from the correct option.

833.key: Each handler needs its own slice of the order data, and coupling needs to stay loose. An EventBridge event bus provides a rule per validation step, and the input transformer rewrites the event before invoking the target, handing the function only the fields it needs. Adding a new step just means adding a new rule, with no change to the source.

opts.A: A queue per step plus a transformer function is custom routing code and an extra component.
opts.B: SNS filtering decides whether to deliver a message or not, but it can't strip out individual fields: a subscriber receives the whole event.
opts.D: A shared queue with a dispatcher function brings back tight coupling: the distribution logic ends up back in custom code.

834.key: The cause of the problem is stated directly: reports running during business hours interfere with creating new records. An Aurora MySQL cluster in a Multi-AZ configuration with multiple read replicas fixes this by splitting the load — reports go to the reader endpoint, which distributes them across the replicas, while writes stay on the primary instance.

opts.A: DynamoDB requires rewriting the application and is a poor fit for ad hoc reports, which are relational by nature.
opts.B: A more powerful machine speeds everything up at once, but the contention between reports and writes remains, and database maintenance still falls on the company.
opts.D: Aurora has no "backup instance" available for queries: reads are served specifically by the replicas through the reader endpoint.

835.key: The site has no internet access, only Direct Connect, and S3 access needs to be as cheap as possible. The key picks C: a VPC with an interface endpoint for S3 — traffic from the data center travels over a private VIF into the VPC and on to S3, never leaving the AWS network. The cost angle is disputable: an interface endpoint is billed hourly per Availability Zone plus per gigabyte processed, whereas a public VIF (option A) gives access to AWS public endpoints directly over Direct Connect with no internet involved and no hourly endpoint fee. By the MOST cost-effective criterion, A looks stronger; by the "nothing public in the network" criterion, C does.

opts.A: A strong, and by cost the better, alternative: a public VIF gives access to S3 through Direct Connect with no internet exposure and no hourly endpoint charge. The one objection is that it uses the service's public addresses, which doesn't fit every company's policy.
opts.B: A NAT gateway sends traffic to the internet, which the site doesn't have, and it charges per gigabyte processed. Routing through the internet directly contradicts the scenario.
opts.D: VPC peering connects two VPCs. There's no mechanism to peer a VPC with an on-premises network or with Direct Connect directly.

836.key: Two sites in different Regions, traffic needs to be split, and an unhealthy Region shouldn't get any of it. Route 53 multivalue answer returns several addresses at once, but each record is tied to its own health check, and unhealthy ones are excluded from the answer. That delivers both load distribution and protection against a Region going down.

opts.A: A simple routing policy doesn't support health checks: it would keep returning the address of a failed Region right alongside the working one.
opts.C: A target group registers targets by instance ID only within its own VPC — instances from another Region can't be added to it.
opts.D: Registering by IP address does allow addresses outside the VPC, but that traffic would travel over inter-Region peering or the internet, with a single point of failure in the first Region's load balancer. If that Region goes down, everything goes down with it.

837.key: Files must be available to many instances across different Availability Zones, without copying between machines and without reworking the access method. Amazon EFS mounts over NFS on all the instances at once, stores data across multiple zones, and has no limit on individual file size — large files of 25 GB or more are handled natively.

opts.A: S3 is object storage accessed through an API: employees and applications would have to change how they work with files.
opts.B: A snapshot is restored as a separate volume, which attaches to a single instance in a single Availability Zone. There's no shared access, and copies immediately diverge.
opts.D: Instance store is ephemeral and local to each machine: data isn't shared and is lost when the instance stops.

838.key: The dump's key (option C) was corrected during the audit: it proposes "SSL encryption with KMS keys for the database volumes," but SSL protects data in transit, while the requirement is specifically about encryption at rest. The data lives in two places: the EBS volumes of the EC2 instances and RDS storage. So encryption is enabled for both EBS and RDS, both with KMS keys. The infrastructure changes are minimal: for EBS it's enough to create volumes encrypted (or turn on default encryption at the account level), and for RDS it means restoring the instance from an encrypted snapshot copy, as covered in {{q:121}}.

opts.A: ACM issues TLS certificates for securing connections. They can't be used to encrypt database volumes.
opts.B: CloudHSM gives you full control over encryption, but it requires deploying and maintaining an HSM cluster. That's disproportionate for a "least amount of changes" requirement when KMS achieves the same result through configuration.
opts.C: This was the original dump key: SSL protects data in transit, while the question is about data at rest. The phrase "SSL encryption with KMS keys for the volumes" conflates two different mechanisms.

839.key: The problem is that all traffic to S3 goes through the NAT and runs into its bandwidth limit. The right fix is a gateway endpoint for S3 with a route added to the private subnets' route tables: traffic to the buckets stops going through the NAT and never reaches the internet at all, the bandwidth constraint disappears, and there's no charge for the endpoint itself.

opts.A: A managed NAT gateway scales better than an instance, but traffic still travels over the internet and is still billed by gigabytes processed. The requirement to avoid the internet isn't met.
opts.B: A larger NAT instance only pushes the saturation point back and doesn't change the route through the internet.
opts.D: A transit gateway connects networks to each other; S3 can't be attached to it, and it has no effect on the route to the bucket.

840.key: What needs accelerating is specifically the TCP connections from reporters worldwide to the broadcast system. Global Accelerator accepts the connection at the nearest edge location and carries it onward over the AWS backbone: a shorter path, less loss and jitter, and fixed addresses. For RTMP streams, which run over TCP, that's exactly what's needed.

opts.A: CloudFront is optimized for delivering and caching content to viewers, not for ingesting incoming streams from sources.
opts.C: Client VPN gives secure network access but doesn't accelerate the network path and provides no fixed anycast addresses.
opts.D: Instances with Elastic IP addresses receive traffic over the ordinary internet: no path acceleration appears.

841.key: Daily snapshots are already working correctly — they're incremental and kept for a month. For seven-year retention of the monthly copies, there's a standard tier called EBS Snapshots Archive: a snapshot is moved into the archive and costs roughly three-quarters less than standard storage. It's managed through a lifecycle policy, meaning no manual work.

opts.A: EBS snapshots can't be directly copied into Glacier Deep Archive: these are different services, and no such operation exists.
opts.C: Keeping monthly snapshots in the standard tier for seven years would cost several times more than the archive tier.
opts.D: The EBS direct APIs allow reading snapshot blocks, but exporting 350 TB every month with your own tooling means both huge cost and maximum manual effort.

842.key: Cross-Region replication of EFS data is needed, using a managed service. AWS Backup (D) handles the schedule, retention, and cross-Region copy of the backup, and the file system is simply assigned to the plan.

opts.A: "EFS-to-EFS backup" is a legacy AWS Solutions CloudFormation deployment — a set of resources you deploy and maintain yourself. It isn't a managed service.
opts.B: A nightly script into S3 plus CRR means custom code, a schedule, and monitoring on your side, plus a change in data model: files become objects.
