opts.C: rsync over VPC peering is an entirely self-built solution: your own instance, your own retries, your own integrity checks.

843.key: Availability, scalability, and minimal administration are all required. The web tier moves into an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer — it can absorb the promotional surge — and the SQL Server database moves into managed RDS in a Multi-AZ configuration with automatic failover.

opts.A: Two fixed instances don't scale for a surge, and read replicas aren't a substitute for a Multi-AZ configuration when it comes to fault tolerance.
opts.B: A database on EC2 instances across separate Regions means self-managed replication and maximum administration.
opts.D: Three static instances and a database spread across three EC2 machines give neither automatic scaling nor a managed database.

844.key: The application can't be rewritten, it writes to an SMB share and needs low latency, and connectivity to AWS already exists. AWS Storage Gateway in file gateway mode is installed on premises, presents the application with the familiar SMB share it expects, and at the same time stores every file as an object in S3: the company policy is satisfied, the code doesn't change, and latency is governed by the local cache.

opts.A: EFS uses the NFS protocol and lives in the cloud: wrong protocol, and latency over the VPN would be noticeable.
opts.B: FSx for Windows File Server speaks SMB, but it lives in the cloud: every operation would cross the tunnel, and the low-latency requirement isn't met.
opts.C: Snowball is a device for a one-time bulk transfer, while files are generated daily and need continuous copying.

845.key: The task is tiny and runs once a day. A scheduled Lambda function scans a fifteen-row table and sends emails through SNS, which has a built-in email delivery protocol. No servers, no scheduler of your own.

opts.A: A cron script on an EC2 instance means a machine running around the clock for a couple of seconds of work a day.
opts.B: Same unnecessary machine, and on top of that SQS doesn't send emails: it's a message queue.
opts.D: The schedule is right, but you can't send an email through an SQS queue — that needs SNS or SES.

846.key: The date of the spike is known in advance — the holiday recurs every year. A recurring scheduled action increases the Auto Scaling group's capacity ahead of the expected peak, so the instances are already in place before the users arrive. That's exactly the proactive scaling the scenario calls for.

opts.A: A CPU-utilization alarm only fires after users have already felt the slowdown — that's a reaction, not preparation.
opts.C: Manually adjusting the limits for the peak period requires someone to do it by hand every year.
opts.D: Notifications about instance launches only inform the administrator and add no capacity.

847.key: Rotating a database password is exactly what Secrets Manager does with no code: the secret is stored encrypted with a KMS key, and for RDS PostgreSQL AWS provides a ready-made rotation function that just needs to be turned on with a period set. The application reads the password via GetSecretValue through its role, so the password change is invisible to it. Keep the service boundaries straight: Secrets Manager is for secrets with rotation, Parameter Store for parameters and simple secrets without rotation, and KMS for encryption keys, not passwords.

opts.B: Parameter Store has no built-in automatic rotation: there's no way to "enable it on the parameter."
opts.C: A custom rotation function means code, permissions, testing, and maintenance. Secrets Manager achieves the same thing through configuration.
opts.D: KMS rotates cryptographic keys, not database user passwords. It doesn't solve the task.

848.key: The application uses Oracle features that require privileged access — and standard RDS for Oracle provides no SYS-level privileges or operating system access. Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle was built specifically for cases like this: it's a managed service that still gives access to the underlying operating system and database settings, and it supports the Bring Your Own License model.

opts.A: Standard RDS for Oracle doesn't offer privileged access, and replacing third-party vendor features with Lambda functions means rewriting the application.
opts.C: DynamoDB is a non-relational store: migrating from Oracle would mean completely rewriting the data model and queries.
opts.D: Moving to PostgreSQL with a code rewrite contradicts both the requirement to use the existing license and the requirement for lowest cost.

849.key: Backups need to be centralized and automated using AWS-native tools. AWS Backup was built exactly for this: it supports EC2, RDS, DynamoDB, and many other services, defines plans with schedules and retention periods, manages the backup vaults, shows the status of every job in one place, and replaces custom scripts.

opts.A: Third-party software and a virtual tape library aren't AWS-native tools or centralization — they're just carrying the old approach over.
opts.C: AWS Config tracks configuration compliance and doesn't take scheduled snapshots.
opts.D: State Manager maintains a desired configuration state on nodes, but it isn't a backup service.

850.key: An infrastructure map is resources and the relationships between them — a graph. Amazon Neptune stores this kind of data as vertices and edges and lets you query it with graph query languages, including SPARQL, so questions like "which resources are connected to this vulnerable node" are answered with a single query and no infrastructure of your own.

opts.A: In a relational database, relationships are unwound through repeated table joins: queries become unwieldy and slow.
opts.C: Redshift is built for analytics over large datasets, not for traversing relationships between objects.
opts.D: DynamoDB stores items by key; PartiQL doesn't turn it into a graph database, and it can't traverse relationships.

851.key: The key phrases are "only when they are actively working" and "limited size." The cheapest solution is one that isn't billed while idle and still keeps developers from spinning up an arbitrarily large cluster. The key picks B: a Service Catalog product with size restrictions baked in — size stays under control, and developers launch it themselves. The weak point of the key is that a provisioned Aurora instance keeps billing overnight too, and the developers are spread across time zones. Option C adds Aurora Serverless on top of the same Service Catalog approach, and since it scales down on its own when idle, it actually matches the "only needed while working" requirement more precisely.

opts.A: A manual start/stop schedule doesn't work for developers spread across time zones and puts the whole burden on operations. There's also no size restriction here — anyone can launch a large instance.
opts.C: A strong alternative: Serverless scales down when idle, so billing tracks actual usage. The objection against it is that "default capacity settings" don't satisfy the requirement to limit the database size.
opts.D: Trusted Advisor finds idle databases after the fact, and automatic deletion destroys the developer's data instead of just pausing it. That's a reaction to the problem, not a solution.

852.key: All instances need to see the same site content with minimal lag, and users are constantly changing it. A shared Amazon EFS file system mounts on every instance, and a write made on one machine is immediately visible to the others: no synchronization and no lag.

opts.A: Copying content from the "most recently launched" instance at boot means lag and complete chaos when changes happen concurrently, and the load balancer has no way to route changes to a specific machine.
opts.C: Syncing once an hour means up to an hour of lag, while the requirement calls for the least possible lag.
opts.D: An EBS snapshot gives each machine its own copy frozen at the moment the snapshot was taken: changes on one instance are never visible to the others at all.

853.key: WAF is already in place and filters known attack patterns. The next layer is detecting anomalous behavior across the account and the network, and that's Amazon GuardDuty: it analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and data events to surface reconnaissance, calls to known malicious addresses, and unusual API activity. Automated response is built from standard building blocks: findings flow into EventBridge, and a Lambda function adds the offending IP address to an IP set in the web ACL.

opts.B: Firewall Manager rolls out WAF, Shield, and Network Firewall policies across accounts. It doesn't do threat detection and doesn't produce findings.
opts.C: Inspector looks for vulnerabilities in images and instances, not suspicious behavior, and it doesn't update WAF rules.
opts.D: Macie classifies sensitive data in S3. It has nothing to do with detecting threats in the environment.

854.key: The requirement is not to maintain static database credentials. IAM database authentication solves this: IAM authentication is enabled on the Aurora cluster, a database user is created with the rds_iam grant, and the application on the instance calls generate-db-auth-token and connects with that temporary token (valid for 15 minutes). Permission for rds-db:connect comes from the role attached to the instance — so identity comes from the role, and no password ever exists.

opts.A: Passing a user name and password as template parameters is still static credentials, and they end up in the stack parameters and in the instance configuration.
opts.B: Parameter Store just stores that same static password, and it still has to be rotated manually. The requirement not to maintain static credentials isn't met.
opts.D: An IAM user can't be "associated with instances": an instance runs under a role. And with IAM authentication, the database user name isn't required to match the IAM user name.

855.key: A custom domain name on CloudFront requires a public certificate, and a public certificate issued by ACM is free. Important detail: the certificate for CloudFront must be located in the us-east-1 Region regardless of where the origins are located.

opts.A: Private certificates are issued by AWS Private CA, which is a paid service; browsers also don't trust them by default.
opts.B: Here the certificate is both private and in the wrong Region.
opts.D: The certificate is public and free, but the Region is wrong: CloudFront only accepts certificates from us-east-1.

856.key: The need is to grant one external person access to a single object for a limited time without creating an account for them. That's exactly what a presigned URL is: the link is signed with your permissions and carries an expiration, and the recipient just downloads the file over HTTPS. Nothing needs to be created and later revoked — the link expires on its own. A useful number: a presigned URL signed with long-lived credentials can live for up to 7 days (604,800 seconds), which matches the required duration exactly; a URL signed with a role's temporary credentials stops working as soon as those credentials do.

opts.A: Moving the operations data into a publicly accessible website bucket exposes the entire dataset to the whole internet for the sake of one report. Maximum risk for minimal benefit.
opts.B: Public access to the whole bucket for a week is the same mistake: the consultant needs one report, but all of the company's data is exposed.
opts.C: An IAM user and access keys for an outside person are long-lived credentials that have to be created, delivered over a secure channel, and remembered to be revoked. More work and more risk.

857.key: Tightly coupled computation requires minimal latency and high throughput between nodes. A cluster placement group packs instances as close together as possible within a single Availability Zone, delivering low-latency, full-bandwidth networking — the standard solution for high performance computing.

opts.B: Dedicated tenancy affects which hardware you share, not network latency between nodes.
opts.C: Spot Instances change the pricing model and can be reclaimed — that has nothing to do with network characteristics.
opts.D: A capacity reservation guarantees that instances can launch, but not that they're placed close together.

858.key: AWS's recommended maximum resiliency is achieved when every single point of failure is eliminated: two connections from each data center, terminating at two different Direct Connect locations, ending on different equipment. Then a failure of a router, a Direct Connect location, a cable, or an entire data center doesn't cut off connectivity to the VPC.

opts.A: The connections only originate from the primary data center: its failure breaks connectivity entirely, and the secondary site is never connected at all.
opts.B: A single location and a single device is two shared points of failure for both connections at once.
opts.D: The devices are different, but there's only one location, and only one connection runs from each data center: resiliency falls short of maximum.

859.key: This answer has two parts. Where to look: Trusted Advisor in the organization's management account shows checks across all member accounts at once, so the finance team doesn't need to go through accounts one by one (A). What to look at: the instances are heavily utilized and run continuously, so savings come from purchasing a commitment — the RDS Reserved Instance Optimization check shows where switching from On-Demand to Reserved Instances will pay off (C).

opts.B: Going through each member account individually is unnecessary work: the organizational view in Trusted Advisor already aggregates the checks.
opts.D: The idle DB instances check looks for instances with low utilization, and the scenario explicitly states utilization is high. It won't produce any recommendations here.
opts.E: Compute Optimizer and the compute optimization checks apply to EC2, Lambda, and other compute resources, while this scenario is about RDS.

860.key: The goal is specifically to reduce data transfer cost when frequently accessing large files in S3. A gateway endpoint for S3 isn't billed at all: no hourly charge and no per-gigabyte processing charge, and traffic stays on the AWS internal network. All that's needed is adding a route in the private subnets' route tables.

opts.B: A single NAT gateway means paying per gigabyte processed plus cross-AZ traffic from instances in other zones. For large files this is the most expensive option.
opts.C: An interface endpoint for S3 exists, but it's billed hourly and per gigabyte processed, whereas a gateway endpoint is free. It also works through an address and a DNS record rather than a route table entry.
opts.D: A NAT gateway in each zone removes the cross-AZ component, but the per-gigabyte processing charge remains and scales with the volume of large files.

861.key: The problem is stated directly: a high volume of write operations and a suspected shortage of I/O performance. A managed RDS for MySQL instance with Provisioned IOPS SSD storage provides guaranteed, adjustable IOPS, and CloudWatch metrics show the real picture and let you raise the value if needed without changing the architecture.

opts.B: An ElastiCache cache speeds up reads, but the load here is on writes: the bottleneck remains. Queries also can't simply be redirected to the cache instead of the database.
opts.C: DocumentDB is compatible with MongoDB, not MySQL: the application and the data model would have to be rewritten.
opts.D: EFS is a file system, not a relational database. Storing a MySQL database on it under heavy write load is a poor choice for both performance and integrity.

862.key: The key phrase is "third parties do not have access to the data before the data is encrypted and sent to AWS." All server-side encryption happens inside AWS, after the object is received, so neither SSE-KMS nor dual-layer DSSE-KMS qualifies. The application itself must encrypt the data before sending it — that's client-side encryption. It's convenient to keep the key in KMS: the application requests a data key from KMS, uses it to encrypt the file locally, and sends the ciphertext to S3 along with the encrypted copy of the data key (an envelope encryption scheme).

opts.A: "Client-side encryption with a key managed by S3" isn't a real configuration: SSE-S3 keys never leave the service, and client-side encryption is configured in the application, not on the bucket.
opts.B: SSE-KMS encrypts the object after S3 has already received it. Before that point the data is unprotected — exactly what needs to be avoided.
opts.C: DSSE-KMS adds a second layer of encryption, but both operations still happen on the service side after the object is received.

863.key: RDS already takes automated backups — all that's needed is to change their retention period to 30 days. The backup is taken daily by the service itself, the retention period can be set up to 35 days, and no additional actions or code are required.

opts.A: A custom function for daily snapshots duplicates a built-in capability and requires ongoing maintenance.
opts.C: Systems Manager Maintenance Windows schedule operations on managed resources, while the RDS backup retention period is configured on the instance itself.
opts.D: Manual snapshots every day via the CLI is the maximum possible operational effort.

864.key: Reads are interfering with writes, so they need to be separated. An Aurora read replica within the same cluster reads from the shared storage, lags by milliseconds, and is added in a single step: the application sends reads to the reader endpoint and writes to the cluster endpoint. This is the cheapest approach — one extra instance with no data replication of its own.

opts.A: A second cluster with a copy job means doubling the storage cost, data lag, and ongoing maintenance.
opts.B: DAX is a cache for DynamoDB — it doesn't work with Aurora at all.
opts.D: Redshift is an analytics warehouse that also requires a separate load pipeline: expensive and not suited to the application's operational queries.

865.key: Ingesting the stream with the least operational effort calls for Kinesis Data Firehose: it scales itself and buffers and delivers data with no shard management (A). Processing takes thirty minutes, which is twice the Lambda function execution limit, so the serverless option that remains is AWS Fargate running on ECS — the task runs for as long as it needs to, with no servers to manage (E).

opts.B: The Lambda function execution limit is fifteen minutes, and the job needs thirty. Even splitting the work with Step Functions would mean reworking the logic.
opts.C: DMS migrates database data — it doesn't ingest streaming data.
opts.D: A group of EC2 instances is infrastructure that has to be maintained, while a serverless solution is required.

866.key: The requirement is that data must not travel over the public internet. A gateway endpoint for S3 adds a route to the service's prefix in the VPC route table, and calls to the bucket stay inside the AWS network. The bucket can additionally be restricted with an aws:SourceVpce condition so it only accepts requests through this endpoint.

opts.B: An S3 bucket can't be registered as a load balancer target: it's a service, not a network resource with an address inside the VPC.
opts.C: Placing a bucket inside a VPC isn't possible — S3 is a regional service outside your network.
opts.D: Direct Connect connects the company's own on-premises site to AWS, but the instances are already inside AWS.

867.key: Recommendations on EBS volume size, type, and cost, complete with estimated monthly savings, come from AWS Compute Optimizer: it analyzes CloudWatch metrics from recent weeks and suggests, for example, moving from gp2 to gp3 or lowering provisioned IOPS, showing the estimated savings. Besides EBS, it also covers EC2 instances, Auto Scaling groups, Lambda functions, and ECS tasks on Fargate.

opts.A: Inspector looks for vulnerabilities and gives no storage cost recommendations at all.
opts.B: Systems Manager manages the fleet: inventory, patching, access. It doesn't handle volume cost optimization.
opts.C: CloudWatch shows metrics, but it doesn't turn them into recommendations with estimated savings — that's what Compute Optimizer does on top of those same metrics.

868.key: This is an inventory task: find, among many buckets across regions, the ones that don't have versioning enabled. S3 Storage Lens is the only service among the options that builds a summary across all of an organization's buckets across every region and account at once, and one of its metrics is the share of buckets with versioning enabled. From there the report shows exactly which buckets fall short. In practice, AWS Config with the s3-bucket-versioning-enabled rule solves the same task — option A is missing from the source PDF, and it was most likely that.

opts.C: IAM Access Analyzer for S3 looks for buckets that are accessible from outside the account or organization. It doesn't check versioning status.
opts.D: A Multi-Region Access Point is an entry point for routing requests to buckets in different regions. It doesn't build configuration reports.

869.key: The requirements are strictly-once processing of every order and resilience to unpredictable traffic surges. An SQS FIFO queue gives exactly-once processing by dropping duplicates, and the queue's buffer smooths out surges: a Lambda function works through orders at its own pace, and the customer never notices.

opts.B: A standard SNS topic delivers a message at least once and doesn't buffer surges — an order could be processed twice or lost during a failure.
opts.C: AppFlow moves data between SaaS services and AWS; it doesn't process orders.
opts.D: X-Ray traces requests; "pulling orders from CloudWatch" isn't a processing mechanism at all.

870.key: A role is always created where the resources live: in the Production account, and its trust policy points to the Development account (C). Developers assume the role via STS, and in the beta phase access is expanded by adding people in the source account — the role itself doesn't need to change.

opts.A: Two policies written by hand in each account don't create trust between accounts: without a trust policy, assuming the role isn't possible. And this doesn't scale well either.
opts.B: A role in the Development account can't grant permissions on Production resources: permissions are granted by the account that owns the resources.
opts.D: An IAM group can't be a principal in a trust policy, and the Production account trusting itself gives Development developers nothing.

871.key: The same scenario as in {{q:345}}: serverless authentication, global delivery, and minimal login latency. Cognito handles users and issues tokens, CloudFront serves the application from edge locations, and token validation runs in a Lambda@Edge function right at the edge location, so the user doesn't need to reach the origin region just to authorize. The design scales linearly as the user base grows.

opts.B: Managed Microsoft AD is a paid directory service, overkill for an application with a small user base, and an ALB doesn't serve content globally.
opts.C: A plain Lambda function runs in a single region and adds authorization latency, and S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads into a bucket, not serving the site.
opts.D: The AD directory is again overkill, and Elastic Beanstalk means servers instead of a serverless architecture.

872.key: The restriction has to apply across all accounts, can't be bypassed locally, and needs to be maintained from a single point. That's a service control policy: the organization creates a policy with a Deny on ec2:RunInstances conditioned on the instance type not being in the allowed list (ec2:InstanceType), and attaches it to the relevant accounts or OUs. An SCP applies to every principal in an account, including root, so a developer can't work around it with their own policy. The same technique appears in {{q:492}}.

opts.A: IAM policies would have to be maintained separately in each account, and an account administrator could change them. They also have no effect on root at all.
opts.B: AWS RAM shares resources between accounts. It can't deny instance types.
opts.C: A role by itself denies nothing: a developer could act without going through it. Plus the role would still have to be created and maintained in every account.

873.key: There are two requirements: automate inventory and OS updates across a diverse fleet, and get a monthly summary of vulnerabilities. The first is covered by Systems Manager: Inventory collects the list of installed software, and Patch Manager applies updates to both Windows and Linux against patch baselines and shows compliance status. The second is Amazon Inspector: continuous package scanning against the CVE database, with reports that are convenient to review monthly.

opts.A: Security Hub aggregates findings from other services, but doesn't find vulnerabilities itself: without Inspector there's nothing to build the reports from.
opts.C: Shield Advanced protects against DDoS, and AWS Config records configuration and doesn't install updates.
opts.D: GuardDuty detects suspicious activity, not vulnerabilities, and AWS Config again isn't a patching tool.

874.key: The least downtime requirement calls for warm standby: an ASG and load balancer are already running in the DR Region, DynamoDB operates as a global table, and the switch is done by DNS failover (A). There's no waiting for infrastructure to be created.

opts.B: Creating instances, load balancers, and tables from CloudFormation at the moment of a disaster is pilot light: deployment takes minutes — exactly the downtime the requirement asks to avoid.
opts.C: The same pilot light pattern: the global table exists, but the compute layer is only born once a disaster actually happens.
opts.D: The infrastructure here is ready, but the switchover is handed to a CloudWatch alarm with a 10-minute evaluation period and a Lambda function. That adds at least those same ten minutes to the downtime, versus the seconds a Route 53 health check takes.

875.key: Traffic to S3 must not go over the public internet, and the solution needs to be cheap. A gateway endpoint for S3 adds a route to the service's prefix in the private subnets' route table and isn't billed at all: no hourly charge and no per-gigabyte processing charge.

opts.A: A NAT gateway sends traffic out to the internet, which violates the requirement, and it also charges per gigabyte processed.
opts.B: Storage Gateway is designed for hybrid access from an on-premises site, but the instances are already inside the VPC.
opts.C: An interface endpoint solves the privacy requirement, but it's billed hourly and per gigabyte processed, while a gateway endpoint is free.

876.key: "The transport layer of the OSI model" is layer 4, meaning TCP or UDP, which calls for a Network Load Balancer (B). High availability comes from an Auto Scaling group spread across multiple Availability Zones and using application health checks: the failure of a zone or of a single instance is compensated for automatically (D). Together this is the cheapest option — no extra services and no manual steps.

opts.A: Route 53 hands out addresses, but it doesn't instantly remove a failed instance or restore capacity. Manually adding instances isn't high availability.
opts.C: A second load balancer for HTTP isn't needed: the scenario specifies the transport layer, and an extra ALB is just extra cost.
opts.E: A CloudWatch alarm that restarts an instance doesn't save you from the failure of an entire Availability Zone and provides no load balancing.

877.key: Fewer than 100 visits a month means there's no reason to pay for a server running around the clock. The form is served and processed by Lambda functions behind API Gateway, and the company is notified by publishing to an SNS topic with an email subscription. The setup costs nothing while idle. A similar walkthrough appears in {{q:285}}.

opts.A: ECS tasks are billed for time running around the clock, even though there's almost no traffic.
opts.C: Amplify Hosting serves static content and functions, but an SQS queue doesn't send emails on its own: notification would need another component.
opts.D: Windows instances running continuously is the most expensive and labor-intensive setup, and client-side scripts can't send email on their own.

878.key: The requirement is MOST securely, so every notification must reach only the people it's addressed to. The correct AWS mechanics: keep the root address on a company-managed distribution list (not a personal employee mailbox), and assign alternate contacts by category — billing, operations, and security — so bills go to finance and security incidents go to the security team. The dump key gives A, and that's its weak point: it proposes one shared mailbox that every account owner can access, a direct violation of least privilege. The alternate contacts mechanism in A is described correctly; the dispute is only about where the root address points.

opts.B: By the security criterion this is the strongest option: each business unit has its own distribution list for root and separate alternate contacts by category. No one reads another account's mail.
opts.C: Tying root to one specific person's individual address is a well-known mistake: the employee goes on leave or leaves the company, and account-recovery access is lost. AWS specifically recommends a distribution list, not a personal mailbox.
opts.D: A centralized mailbox with aliases is more convenient for bookkeeping, but it again means one shared mailbox sees root notifications for every account. That's broader than necessary and falls short of separate lists per business unit.

879.key: Timeouts during peak load are solved with two independent techniques. Purchase requests go into an SQS queue, and instances in an Auto Scaling group that scales on queue length process them: the peak is smoothed out and no order is lost (C). Read load on the database is taken off by an ElastiCache cache in front of the Aurora cluster (B). Both steps are cheaper than scaling the database up.

opts.A: Retries with no buffer just amplify the storm of requests against an already overloaded database, and RDS Proxy solves a connection-pooling problem, not peak processing load.
opts.D: Retries in a Lambda function have the same drawback: there's no queue, so the load isn't smoothed out.
opts.E: A usage plan in API Gateway throttles clients, meaning it drops some purchases instead of processing them.

880.key: The Cost and Usage Report sits in S3 as files, so the dashboard is built through the chain "Athena reads the files, QuickSight visualizes them." Athena turns the export into a SQL table partitioned by month, and QuickSight connects to it as a data source and lets you share the dashboard with leadership. For the requested slice, it's enough to filter rows by the NAT gateway service and group by day for the current month.

opts.A: DataSync moves files between storage systems and isn't a data source for QuickSight.
opts.C: CloudWatch builds dashboards from metrics, not from report files in S3, and it can't query them.
opts.D: Athena is the right choice, but CloudWatch can't use it as a source for a dashboard — that's what QuickSight does.

881.key: The TTL is currently zero, meaning CloudFront goes back to S3 on every request. Caching needs to be turned on, but in a way that keeps stale content alive for no more than a few minutes after a deployment. The direct fix is option A: a default TTL of 2 minutes, so an object expires on its own two minutes after being published. The second half of the key is debatable: a Cache-Control: private directive forbids caching in shared caches, including CloudFront, which undoes the very thing this whole exercise is for. The logical pairing with A is option E: a long max-age plus an invalidation on deploy. Remember the distinction: TTL limits how long something can go stale on its own, while an invalidation removes an object from the cache on an event.

opts.B: An S3 bucket has no TTL setting. Cache lifetime is set either by the CloudFront distribution's cache behavior or by Cache-Control headers on the objects.
opts.D: Lambda@Edge on viewer response changes the header in the response to the end client after it has already passed through the CloudFront cache, and it doesn't affect how long the object is kept at the edge location. It's also extra code and extra cost.
opts.E: A strong alternative: a 24-hour max-age maximizes cache hits, and an invalidation on every deploy guarantees new content propagates to every location right away. The key preferred the short TTL because it protects against staleness even if an invalidation is forgotten.

882.key: The same task as in {{q:417}}: the discount needs to cover both the instances and a growing number of functions, and the functions need direct access to the instances. A Compute Savings Plan applies to EC2, Lambda, and Fargate under one commitment, and connecting the functions to those same private subnets gives direct network connectivity inside the VPC.

opts.A: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan covers only instances, and the cost of the functions will keep growing at full rate.
opts.B: The same limited plan, and public subnets don't bring the functions any closer to the instances.
opts.D: Staying in the Lambda service VPC means the functions get no network access to the instances in the private subnet.

883.key: Developers need to be warned about spending and new resource creation needs to stop automatically once the limit is used up. That's exactly what AWS Budgets does: a budget per account, alerts on actual and forecast values, and a budget action that applies a deny policy to the developer's IAM role once a threshold is reached. No code, no custom function of any kind. A related question about how budget actions work mechanically is {{q:455}}.

opts.A: The scheme with tags, a Config rule, and a deletion function is custom development, risks deleting something needed, and reacts only after the fact.
opts.C: Cost Explorer and anomaly detection only show data and send notifications. They don't stop new resources from being created.
opts.D: Service Catalog plus custom start/stop functions means both a product catalog and code in every account. More work, and the spending limit still isn't enforced automatically.

884.key: The rule is simple: each tier accepts traffic only from the tier before it and only on the port it needs, with the source specified by referencing a security group rather than by IP address. The web tier accepts HTTPS from the ALB's security group (A), the application tier accepts HTTPS from the web tier's security group (E), and the database accepts SQL Server traffic from the application tier's security group (C).

opts.B: Outbound rules already allow all traffic by default; opening internet egress for the web tier isn't a stated requirement and only widens the attack surface.
opts.D: The direction is reversed: the database shouldn't be initiating connections to the web tier, let alone over the SQL Server protocol.
opts.F: The application tier has no reason to open outbound SQL Server traffic to the web tier: the database sits in the other direction.

885.key: The requirement is to cover the most services with the fewest savings plans. A Compute Savings Plan covers EC2, Lambda, and Fargate under a single commitment (D), while SageMaker isn't covered by it and needs a separate SageMaker Savings Plan (C). That's two plans covering four services.

opts.A: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan applies only to EC2 instances and doesn't extend to SageMaker.
opts.B: A Compute Savings Plan doesn't cover SageMaker: the wording describes a scope that doesn't exist.
opts.E: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan doesn't extend to Fargate.

886.key: The goal is to move from SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL with minimal changes to the application code. Babelfish on Aurora PostgreSQL accepts connections over the TDS protocol and understands the T-SQL dialect, so the applications keep sending the same queries (B). The schema and data themselves are migrated with AWS SCT and AWS DMS (C).

opts.A: The Schema Conversion Tool converts database objects — it doesn't rewrite queries inside application code.
opts.D: RDS Proxy manages a connection pool and does nothing to help with T-SQL dialect incompatibility.
opts.E: DMS migrates data and doesn't rewrite application code.

887.key: There are two requirements: encrypt all new volumes and prevent an unencrypted volume from being created at all. The EC2 account attribute "encryption by default" (A) works preventively — an attempt to create an unencrypted volume in that region simply fails.

opts.B: AWS Config flags a violation after the fact and can trigger remediation, but it doesn't stop the volume from being created. It doesn't satisfy the "prevent the creation" requirement.
opts.C: Systems Manager creating encrypted copies is manually fixing volumes that already exist, not blocking new ones.
opts.D: Creating a KMS key and configuring Migration Hub blocks nothing: a key on its own doesn't force encryption to happen.

888.key: The clickstream needs to be ingested in real time under traffic that fluctuates through the day. Kinesis Data Streams in on-demand mode adjusts its capacity to traffic automatically — no shard management needed — and Lambda functions read the stream and process records as they arrive.

opts.B: Firehose delivers data into storage with buffering, and AWS Glue is batch ETL: that pair doesn't provide real-time analysis.
opts.C: Kinesis Video Streams is built for video streams, not click events.
opts.D: Managed Service for Apache Flink processes streams but doesn't ingest them itself: it needs a source such as Kinesis Data Streams.

889.key: A verbatim repeat of question {{q:868}}: find buckets without versioning enabled across all regions. S3 Storage Lens builds a summary across every bucket in an account or organization at once, one of its metrics is the share of buckets with versioning enabled, and the report shows exactly which ones fall short. A real-world alternative is the AWS Config rule s3-bucket-versioning-enabled, but it isn't among the options here.

opts.A: CloudTrail records API calls. It doesn't show the current state of bucket settings and doesn't build an inventory.
opts.C: IAM Access Analyzer for S3 finds buckets accessible from outside the account or organization — it doesn't check versioning.
opts.D: A Multi-Region Access Point routes requests to buckets. It doesn't produce configuration reports.

890.key: The same requirements as in question {{q:66}}: instant access, files that can't be recreated, active for 30 days, kept for 4 years, then deleted. The difference here is the set of options: this one includes S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, which returns an object in milliseconds just like Standard-IA, but costs roughly a third as much to store. For data that's rarely accessed after 30 days, that's the cheapest class with instant access. The tradeoff is a 90-day minimum storage duration and a higher retrieval charge — neither of which conflicts with this scenario.

opts.B: One Zone-IA keeps a single copy in one Availability Zone, and the files in the scenario can't be recreated. That risk isn't worth a roughly 20% saving over Standard-IA.
opts.C: A correct but not the cheapest option: for infrequent access, Glacier Instant Retrieval costs roughly a third of Standard-IA's storage price for the same instant retrieval.
opts.D: The rule doesn't delete the files after 4 years — it moves them to Glacier, even though the policy allows deletion. You'd pay for storage indefinitely, and on top of that the data sits in the pricier Standard-IA for the first 4 years.

891.key: There are three requirements: write to the nearest bucket, avoid the congested public internet, and get failover with the least management overhead for S3. An S3 Multi-Region Access Point gives a single global entry point: a request enters the AWS network at the nearest edge location and then travels over the AWS backbone to the nearest bucket, and if a region becomes unavailable, traffic automatically shifts to the other one. To keep the same objects in both buckets, Cross-Region Replication is layered on top. An active-active setup with a single global endpoint is exactly the "least amount of management" here.

opts.A: Hitting the regional endpoints directly goes over the public internet, which the scenario asks to avoid, and failover on a region outage would have to be coded into the application.
opts.B: A Multi-Region Access Point has a single global endpoint — "create one endpoint per region" isn't possible with it. An active-passive setup also doesn't route the user to the nearest bucket.
opts.C: Cross-account replication is about a different account, not a different region. Choosing the nearest endpoint and handling failure would again fall on the application.

892.key: The applications can't be changed, but they need to survive an Availability Zone failure. An AMI is captured from each instance, two copies are launched from it in separate Availability Zones, and a load balancer sits in front, distributing traffic and excluding an unhealthy target. The application itself stays exactly as it was.

opts.A: A group of exactly one instance recovers the machine after a failure, but the application is unavailable while it's launching: that isn't fault tolerance.
opts.B: Hourly copies are backup, not fault tolerance: recovery takes time and manual action.
opts.D: Breaking the application into components is exactly the kind of architecture change the scenario forbids.

893.key: Two properties are needed at once: accounts with automatic guardrails and centrally managed networking. The first comes from Control Tower with Account Factory, the second from a networking account holding a VPC whose subnets are shared with the workload accounts through AWS RAM (A).

opts.B: AWS Organizations by itself doesn't create accounts with automatic guardrails: preventive and detective controls are configured by Control Tower.
opts.C: Control Tower is right here, but a VPC in each workload account routing through an inspection VPC is about traffic inspection, not centralized management of networking components, and it takes considerably more configuration.
opts.D: This combines both mistakes: Organizations without guardrails, and separate VPCs instead of shared subnets.

894.key: The site serves static content, so a compute fleet and a load balancer aren't needed at all. The content moves into an S3 bucket and is served through CloudFront: you only pay for storage and transfer, edge caching lowers outbound transfer cost, and growing traffic doesn't require a single additional server.

opts.B: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache within a region; it doesn't serve bucket content to users and doesn't form this kind of setup.
opts.C: Amplify already serves the site through its own content delivery network; putting a load balancer in front of it is pointless and more expensive.
opts.D: EC2 instances acting as a cache in front of Amplify brings back the servers this solution is meant to get rid of.

895.key: Clients need the SMB protocol, everything lives in AWS, and administration needs to be minimal. Amazon FSx for Windows File Server speaks SMB natively, supports Windows ACLs and Active Directory, and AWS handles maintenance, backups, and fault tolerance. Connecting is just mounting the share. A similar walkthrough appears in {{q:249}}.

opts.A: Volume Gateway presents block volumes over iSCSI and is built for hybrid scenarios, not for file access by applications in the cloud.
opts.B: Tape Gateway emulates a tape library for backup systems.
opts.C: A self-managed Windows server with a file server role has to be patched, backed up, and scaled by you — maximum administration.

896.key: The requirements are a 5-minute recovery point, a 20-minute recovery time, and minimal configuration changes. An Aurora global database replicates at the storage layer with typically sub-second lag, and managed failover promotes the secondary region to primary in a single operation while preserving the topology. The application keeps using the same cluster endpoints.

opts.A: A cross-Region Aurora read replica replicates through the logical layer and lags more, and failover is a manual process with many steps.
opts.C: A separate cluster with replication configured by hand is a manual construction, and the failover onto it is manual too: hitting a 20-minute RTO is doubtful.
opts.D: DMS needs a replication instance and ongoing upkeep, and it isn't designed to be Aurora's standard disaster recovery mechanism.

897.key: The job runs at least an hour, is stateful, and can't tolerate interruption. That rules out both Lambda with its fifteen-minute limit and interruptible instances. AWS Fargate running on ECS runs a container for as long as needed with no servers to manage, and EventBridge Scheduler puts it on a weekly schedule.

opts.B: The Lambda function execution limit is fifteen minutes, and the job needs at least an hour.
opts.C: AWS can reclaim Spot Instances at any moment, and the job can't tolerate interruption.
opts.D: DataSync moves data between storage systems and isn't a tool for running arbitrary jobs.

898.key: Amazon Security Lake was built exactly for this: it collects security data from AWS services, on-premises sources, and partner solutions on its own, normalizes it into the open OCSF format, and stores it in an S3 bucket in your account. There's essentially no development involved — just enable the service and point it at the sources.

opts.A: Lake Formation with Glue crawlers is a general-purpose data lake builder: normalizing formats and pulling together security sources would have to be built by hand.
opts.B: A custom function exporting data to CSV means code, schemas, and ongoing maintenance — the maximum amount of development.
opts.D: DMS migrates database data and isn't built for collecting security events.

899.key: Five applications now and more than a hundred eventually, all needing access to a shared VPC and connectivity with each other, with minimal administration. A transit gateway works as a hub: a new VPC connects with a single attachment and immediately gets connectivity to everything else through the gateway's route tables. The number of objects grows linearly, not quadratically.

opts.A: Software VPN tunnels on your own devices mean licenses, maintenance, limited bandwidth, and many points of failure.
opts.B: Peering isn't transitive: for a hundred VPCs to see each other you'd need thousands of connections and edits to every route table.
opts.C: Direct Connect connects the company's own site to AWS, not VPCs to each other: it doesn't apply to this task.

900.key: A single container platform is needed for both cloud and on-premises. ECS covers both cases: cloud containers launch with the Fargate launch type, and on-premises ones register through Amazon ECS Anywhere with the external launch type (A). An Application Load Balancer sits in front of the cloud services for HTTP traffic (B).

opts.C: A Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4, while the scenario explicitly calls out HTTP traffic, which needs application-layer capabilities.
opts.D: Fargate is AWS compute capacity: you can't run containers on it inside the company's own data center.
opts.E: ECS Anywhere works with the external launch type, not Fargate: the combination described doesn't exist.

901.key: There are two requirements: increase security and reduce operational overhead for the databases. A managed Multi-AZ Amazon RDS for SQL Server instance takes patching, backups, and failover off your hands (Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby copy in another Availability Zone), and encryption at rest is turned on with a KMS key and covers disks, snapshots, and backups. Running SQL Server yourself on EC2 gets the same encryption but leaves all the operations to you. A related question is {{q:529}}.

opts.A: SQL Server on EC2 still means your patches, your backups, and your own fault tolerance. Operational overhead doesn't go down.
opts.C: S3 with Macie is object storage plus data classification. There's nowhere to run relational transactional queries there.
opts.D: DynamoDB is a non-relational database with a different data model: moving SQL Server there means rewriting the application. CloudWatch Logs just collects logs and doesn't protect data.

902.key: There are two requirements, and each is met by its own piece. Availability is improved by an Auto Scaling group spread across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer: a zone or instance failure doesn't take the application down. AWS WAF attaches specifically to the load balancer — that's the resource type it supports; a web ACL can't be attached to an Auto Scaling group or a placement group. That leaves this as the only option where both conditions are met correctly.

opts.B: A cluster placement group packs instances close together within a single Availability Zone for low latency — that actually hurts availability, and WAF can't attach to a placement group.
opts.C: Two fixed instances give cross-zone fault tolerance but don't scale or get replaced automatically: availability improves less than with an Auto Scaling group.
opts.D: The error is in the last step: a web ACL can't be linked to an Auto Scaling group — it attaches to the load balancer.

903.key: There are many applications, each with its own prefix, and granular control is required. That's exactly what S3 access points were designed for (A): each application gets its own entry point with its own policy, and the bucket policy never balloons into something unreadable.

opts.B: Setting ACLs on every object with Batch Operations doesn't scale, requires re-running for new objects, and ACLs themselves are now disabled by default and not recommended by AWS.
opts.C: Replicating into a separate bucket per application doubles the storage and its cost and still doesn't provide granular control within a prefix.
opts.D: The same unnecessary data copy: access points don't require splitting objects across buckets — they work on top of a single one.

904.key: Processing takes two minutes and needs 512 MB of memory — ideal for a Lambda function. The S3 notification puts a message on an SQS queue, the function reads it and processes the image right after upload. You only pay for the actual two minutes per file, and the instance fleet disappears entirely.

opts.B: A Reserved Instance is billed around the clock, even though the work only shows up sporadically.
opts.C: An instance in an ECS cluster runs and is billed continuously, and SNS without a queue also doesn't provide a reliable buffer.
opts.D: An Elastic Beanstalk application again means continuously running instances with all their cost and maintenance.

905.key: The catch is that there are two workloads and neither is HTTP. A Network Load Balancer in each Region serves both the TCP EC2 instances and the on-premises UDP workload — the latter through a target group registered by IP address, reachable over VPN or Direct Connect (D). Global Accelerator sits on top: it provides static anycast addresses, entry at the nearest edge location, a path over the AWS backbone, and fast failover if a Region goes down (A). TCP connection state is preserved because the accelerator consistently picks the same target.

opts.B: CloudFront works with HTTP and caching; it serves neither the stateful TCP workload nor UDP.
opts.C: An Application Load Balancer only understands HTTP and HTTPS, so it doesn't fit either of the two described workloads.
opts.E: The mistake is in the second half: the on-premises UDP workload can't be served through an ALB — it doesn't support that protocol.

906.key: The snapshots were deleted by a script running with legitimate permissions, so deny policies and copies to another Region are poor fixes: the script would delete the copies too, and a deny would break the routine cleanup. Recycle Bin for EBS snapshots exists exactly for this: a retention rule intercepts the deletion and holds the snapshot for a set period (7 days here), after which it disappears on its own. Recovery is a single console action, with no development at all.

opts.A: A deny on deletion would break the routine cleanup of expired snapshots that the company needs, and it wouldn't protect against deletion by other principals.
opts.B: A copy in another Region doesn't help if the same script also runs there, and it doubles storage cost.
opts.D: EBS snapshots can't just be "copied to S3" like files: they're managed objects of the service. An export would require separate development.

907.key: The bucket is closed to public access, and access to the template is needed just once, on a specific user request. A presigned URL provides a temporary link with a limited lifetime, whose permissions are inherited from whoever signed it: CloudFormation reads the template through it, and no bucket settings need to change at all.

opts.A: A gateway endpoint gives a private route to S3 from inside a VPC, but CloudFormation accesses the template as an AWS service, not from your network.
opts.B: API Gateway in front of the bucket is an extra layer that has to be built and secured, while the built-in presigned URL already solves the problem.
opts.D: Temporarily opening public access violates the security requirement: during that window the template is available to everyone.

908.key: The external engineers need both console access and OS-level access to instances in private subnets, as securely as possible. Console access is granted through IAM Identity Center: temporary credentials, sign-in through a corporate identity provider, no handing out IAM users across accounts. OS access goes through Session Manager: an agent on the instance, a role in the instance profile, no open ports, no SSH keys, no bastion — and every session is logged and constrained by IAM policy.

opts.B: Local IAM users in every account means long-lived credentials for outside people and manual upkeep. Session Manager is the right choice here, but the way console access is granted isn't.
opts.C: Open SSH filtered by IP address plus handing out keys to external engineers is the weakest option: keys can't be revoked centrally, and the address list has to be maintained.
opts.D: A bastion adds an extra server with an open port and again requires handing out keys and local IAM users.

909.key: Reports and the workload share a single instance, which is why performance sags during business hours. A read replica in the same Region takes the reporting load off the primary database and is the cheapest of all the options: there's no cross-Region traffic, and you only pay for the replica instance itself.

opts.A: A cross-Region replica solves the same problem but adds cross-Region data transfer charges with no benefit, since reports are generated in the same place.
opts.B: The standby instance in a Multi-AZ setup isn't readable: reports can't be pointed at it.
opts.C: Logical replication through DMS needs a replication instance and a target database plus ongoing upkeep — more expensive and more complex than a standard read replica.

910.key: A granularity no coarser than two minutes is required. Basic EC2 monitoring publishes metrics every five minutes, while detailed monitoring publishes every minute. It's enough to turn on detailed monitoring on the instances and work with the standard CloudWatch metrics.

opts.A: Logs in Redshift with dashboards means analyzing text records rather than performance metrics, and it doesn't improve the granularity.
opts.C: Fetching logs with a function doesn't turn them into metrics and doesn't change how often they're published.
opts.D: A pipeline of S3, Redshift, and QuickSight is a heavy layer on top of logs, while the needed metric frequency is just a single setting.

911.key: A hundred and fifty photos a day is rare, short bursts of processing. A bucket notification invokes a Lambda function the moment a photo is uploaded: you only pay for those hundred and fifty invocations, there's no infrastructure running continuously, and the thumbnail appears right away.

opts.A: An EMR cluster running continuously for a few seconds of work a day is a wildly disproportionate cost.
opts.B: An always-on instance polling every minute is also billed around the clock and adds maintenance.
opts.D: S3 Storage Lens is a storage-usage analytics tool — it can't invoke functions on an event.

912.key: There are millions of objects, they're in Deep Archive, and the solution needs to be serverless. An S3 Inventory report lists the objects along with their dates, a Lambda function picks out the ones to delete while honoring the retained-data list, and S3 Batch Operations applies it at scale across millions of objects — with no servers involved anywhere.

opts.A: A script on an EC2 instance is both a server and manual upkeep — not a serverless solution.
opts.B: AWS Batch runs jobs on a compute environment that you have to define and pay for; the built-in mechanism for bulk operations on objects fits better.
opts.C: A Glue crawler builds a catalog for analytics, not a list of objects to delete, and it doesn't perform deletions.

913.key: The principle of least privilege in AWS services is implemented through separate roles: each Lambda function gets its own execution role, and its policy allows only the actions it actually needs against the relevant bucket prefix. That way a compromise or bug in one function doesn't open access for the others, and permissions can be adjusted function by function. The bucket can additionally be locked down with a policy that lists only these roles.

opts.A: A shared role with full bucket access is the direct opposite of least privilege: every function gets everything.
opts.B: Tying access to the endpoint's IP addresses is fragile and doesn't identify the function: any resource on the same network would get the same permissions.
opts.D: A function's ARN isn't a principal in a bucket policy: authorization is evaluated against the role the function assumes when it calls the API.

914.key: Each layer is swapped for a managed service. The static frontend becomes an S3 bucket behind CloudFront, giving both global reach and HTTPS. The microservices become Lambda functions behind API Gateway, which comes with authorization, throttling, and scaling built in. The database becomes Amazon RDS for MySQL instead of a self-managed instance. Almost nowhere is left to operate manually.

opts.A: A database on a Reserved EC2 instance stays on the company's own upkeep: patches, backups, fault tolerance — all manual.
opts.C: Lambda functions can't be registered as Network Load Balancer targets: that target type is only supported by an Application Load Balancer.
opts.D: Without CloudFront there's no global delivery, and the database again stays on an EC2 instance with all the operational burden.

915.key: Near-real-time access to rankings is required, along with data persisting on disk across an application restart. ElastiCache for Redis satisfies both: it's in-memory with sub-millisecond latency, it offers durability (RDB and AOF), replicas, and sorted sets — practically built for leaderboards. As a managed service, operational overhead is minimal.

opts.A: S3 with CloudFront is built for static files and caching, not counters updated near real time.
opts.B: Self-managed EC2 instances across multiple Regions with manual data synchronization is the maximum operational load with the worst reliability.
opts.D: Memcached can neither persist data to disk nor replicate it: rankings would disappear after a restart, which the requirement explicitly forbids.

916.key: The requirement "the data for each customer must be encrypted separately" means a separate key per customer — that way a compromised or revoked key doesn't affect the others, and cryptographically deleting a customer's data is as simple as deleting their key. "Secure, centralized key management" points to KMS, and "LEAST operational overhead" means nothing custom needs to be deployed. Put together: one KMS key per customer, with a key policy restricting access and CloudTrail logging enabled for key usage.

opts.A: Storing encryption keys in an S3 bucket is an anti-pattern: the keys sit right next to the data and are protected only by access permissions, not by a hardware module. There's no centralized management and no logging of key usage.
opts.B: A custom hardware module in the cloud is the maximum operational cost: the cluster has to be deployed, maintained, and made redundant. CloudHSM exists for this, but the requirement calls for minimal effort.
opts.C: A single key for every customer violates the core requirement: different customers' data ends up protected by the same secret, and access can't be revoked for just one customer.

917.key: Every requirement is addressed at once: an Application Load Balancer accepts and distributes web traffic, an Auto Scaling group grows processing capacity with load, an SQS queue holds orders that haven't been processed yet so none are lost during a surge, and an RDS database in a Multi-AZ configuration survives an Availability Zone failure.

opts.A: A NAT gateway doesn't accept inbound traffic, and "storing unprocessed orders in a function" provides neither a buffer nor a durability guarantee.
opts.B: A Network Load Balancer in front of an Application Load Balancer is redundant, and Redshift is an analytics warehouse, not built for ingesting orders.
opts.C: A Gateway Load Balancer passes traffic through network appliances and can't store orders.

918.key: The key detail is the file size: 10 KB on average across millions of files. IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval have a minimum billable object size of 128 KB, and the archive classes also carry per-object metadata overhead, so small files in an archive end up costing many times their actual size. Hence the first step: pack the files into larger objects before migrating. From there, follow the access pattern: a year of rare but instant access calls for Glacier Instant Retrieval, then seven years of pure archive calls for Glacier Deep Archive.

opts.B: The packing step is correct, but the storage classes chosen cost more than necessary: Standard-IA is pricier than Glacier Instant Retrieval for access once or twice a year, and storing seven years of archive in Glacier Instant Retrieval instead of Deep Archive is roughly a fourfold overpay.
opts.C: The files aren't grouped, so millions of 10 KB objects get billed at the 128 KB minimum size. Plus Glacier Flexible Retrieval for seven years costs more than Deep Archive and isn't needed here since urgent access isn't required.
opts.D: Again no grouping — the same overpay for the minimum object size — and Standard-IA in the first year costs more than Glacier Instant Retrieval for access once or twice.

919.key: A single io1 volume's limit is 64,000 IOPS, and it's already fully provisioned, so the number of operations on that volume can't be raised any further. The fix is to attach additional io1 volumes and stripe them together with LVM: operations spread across the volumes, and total throughput scales roughly with their count.

opts.B: An io1 volume can't be set above 64,000 IOPS: that's a hard limit per volume.
opts.C: Increasing the size to 2 TB doesn't raise the IOPS limit: io1 performance is provisioned separately and is already maxed out.
opts.D: A storage-optimized instance gives fast local disks, but the EBS volume stays the same with the same limit, and database data can't be kept on ephemeral storage.

920.key: A publish/subscribe model is required, which means an SNS topic. The cheapest way to front it is an HTTP API in API Gateway: it costs roughly 70 percent less than a REST API for the same request handling, and the extra REST capabilities aren't needed here.

opts.A: An SQS queue is a one-consumer-per-message model, not publish/subscribe.
opts.B: The design is correct, but a REST API costs noticeably more than an HTTP API for functionality that's identical for this task.
opts.C: A WebSocket API with an enhanced fan-out stream is the most expensive setup and overkill for simply notifying subscribers.

921.key: The application is monolithic and only runs on a single instance, so it can't scale horizontally: the option left is to size up the instance and pin the Auto Scaling group to one machine so it recovers automatically. The sagging reads on the database are fixed with a read replica that read traffic is redirected to.

opts.B: Writes can't be pointed at the replica: a read replica is read-only.
opts.C: A max group size of two conflicts with the application's own restriction, and sizing up the database instance doesn't separate reads from writes.
opts.D: Sizing up the database instance raises the overall ceiling, but reads would still compete with writes for the same resources.

922.key: The correct access model in AWS is roles with fine-grained permissions: a developer signs in through federation or Identity Center, assumes a role, and gets temporary credentials with exactly the permissions their task needs. No long-lived keys are created, access is revoked by changing the role assignment, and actions are attributed to individuals in CloudTrail. That's exactly what the correct option describes.

opts.A: Shared credentials make it impossible to tell who did what, and turn one person leaving into a password reset for everyone. A blatant violation of security practice.
opts.C: Access keys are a long-lived secret that has to be stored and rotated. For people, the standard path is temporary role credentials.
opts.D: Cognito is meant for application end users, not for employee access to AWS resources.

923.key: A single instance is pegged at 100 percent CPU, which calls for horizontal growth along with better availability. An AMI is captured from the running server and referenced in a new launch template (B), and then an Auto Scaling group with an Application Load Balancer is created that adds instances under load (E). The application itself isn't rewritten.

opts.A: Sizing the instance up vertically doesn't provide availability: the single machine remains a point of failure.
opts.C: An Auto Scaling group with a load balancer scales horizontally, not vertically — the wording describes a mode that doesn't exist.
opts.D: Compute Optimizer recommends an instance type, which helps with vertical scaling; it doesn't address horizontal growth.

924.key: IAM Access Analyzer helps find excessive permissions: beyond finding resources with external access, it analyzes CloudTrail activity history and generates policies based on actions actually used, and its unused access findings surface unused permissions, roles, and keys. It's a managed service that operates at the organization level through a delegated administrator, so there's no need to go through accounts by hand.

opts.A: Network Access Analyzer analyzes network paths to resources, not IAM permissions.
opts.B: An alarm on resource creation doesn't answer the question of who has more permissions than needed, and it requires manually reviewing every event.
opts.D: Amazon Inspector looks for vulnerabilities in workloads. It doesn't analyze IAM policies.

925.key: The regulatory requirement "protected from deletion or modification for a fixed period of time" means a mode nobody can bypass. S3 Object Lock in compliance mode forbids deleting or overwriting an object version until the retention period expires, and neither an administrator nor the root user can shorten or remove that period — only wait it out. Governance mode works differently: it protects against accidents, but any user with the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission can routinely bypass it. Compare this with {{q:446}}, which adds the requirement to also cover objects that already exist.

opts.A: Governance mode can be lifted by a user with bypass permission. That's not a sufficient guarantee for a regulatory requirement.
opts.C: Versioning makes deletion reversible but doesn't forbid it, and a Lifecycle rule that deletes after a set period doesn't protect anything at all — it only deletes.
opts.D: Moving to Glacier changes cost and access speed. The object can still be deleted or overwritten afterward.

926.key: The application runs around the clock, but the load consists of a flat baseline plus short bursts. An ECS capacity provider lets you mix: the steady portion runs on regular Fargate, which guarantees availability, and the bursts are covered by Fargate Spot at up to a 70 percent discount. Interruption of the spot task only affects the extra, burst portion of the load.

opts.A: Right-sizing tasks is useful but doesn't save money on bursts and requires manual load testing.
opts.C: Keeping the steady baseline on spot capacity is risky: its reclamation would hit the baseline availability, and the requirement is uninterrupted operation.
opts.D: Compute Optimizer helps with task sizing but doesn't provide a mixed capacity model or savings on bursts.

927.key: The key phrase is "managed solution with proactive engagement." Proactive engagement from the AWS Shield Response Team is only available with a Shield Advanced subscription: it monitors protected resources and reaches out to you when an attack is detected. Both the load balancer and the Route 53 hosted zones get added to the subscription, covering the application and the DNS. Shield Standard works automatically but offers no proactive support.

opts.A: There's no AWS Config managed rule that detects DDoS attacks: Config evaluates resource configurations.
opts.B: WAF helps against application-layer attacks, but it doesn't protect against volumetric attacks and doesn't provide proactive engagement from the AWS team.
opts.C: GuardDuty analyzes logs and produces findings, but it doesn't provide automatic DDoS protection or proactive support.

928.key: TCP traffic is handled by the Network Load Balancer, and WAF can't attach to it — so filtering has to be done at the network layer. Since 2023, NLBs support security groups, but they can only be assigned when the load balancer is created: you can't add a security group to an existing NLB. Hence the answer's wording — recreate the load balancer with a security group that allows only trusted addresses. That's the smallest possible architectural change.

opts.A: AWS WAF doesn't support Network Load Balancer: it works with HTTP resources like CloudFront, ALB, and API Gateway.
opts.C: A second load balancer alongside the first doesn't stop anyone from still reaching the old one, and it doubles cost instead of solving the problem.
opts.D: Shield Advanced protects against availability attacks, but it doesn't restrict access by address and doesn't stop unauthorized connection attempts.

929.key: For the function to publish a message to an encrypted topic, three permissions are needed, and all three are listed in the answer. First, the SNS topic's own resource policy allows the function's role to publish (A). Second, the KMS key's policy allows that same role to perform key operations — for publishing, that's kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt (C). Third, the function's execution role has the corresponding permissions in its own IAM policy (F). The general rule this question is built around: access to a KMS key is checked from two sides — the key's policy and the principal's policy — and access to a topic is checked by its own policy on top of that.

opts.B: Switching to an AWS managed key contradicts the scenario (the company uses customer managed keys) and doesn't solve the permissions problem: without the right grants, publishing still fails.
opts.D: The principal in a resource policy is a role (or an account), not a Lambda function's ARN. Naming the function's ARN as the principal won't work.
opts.E: API Gateway in front of the SNS topic is an unnecessary layer that grants the function neither publish rights nor KMS key permissions.

930.key: The dump key here is corrected to A. The scenario explicitly limits changes: touch the portal minimally, and don't change any code at all. So the existing portal stays as-is but moves into an Auto Scaling group with On-Demand instances, which delivers the required 100 percent uptime. The new text-extraction program runs infrequently, so it becomes a Lambda function invoked when a document is uploaded: you pay only for the actual seconds it runs.

opts.B: Spot Instances can be reclaimed at any time, which conflicts with the requirement of 100 percent portal uptime.
opts.C: A Savings Plan for a rarely-running extraction program means paying for a commitment that's barely used.
opts.D: This is exactly the option the dump used as its key. It moves the portal to static hosting on S3 and proposes reimplementing existing functionality through API Gateway and Lambda — i.e., rewriting the application, which the scenario forbids twice over.

931.key: A cross-account invocation is authorized from both sides. The function needs a resource policy that lets SNS invoke it (A), and the topic needs a policy that lets that function subscribe (C). Without either half, the subscription either can't be created or won't work.

opts.B: An SQS queue in the administrator account changes what invokes the function: the queue becomes the trigger instead of the topic. That's incompatible with option A and adds a component the task doesn't need.
opts.D: Using EventBridge to relay SNS notifications is an extra service in a place where SNS can already invoke a Lambda function in another account directly.
opts.E: S3 and Athena instead of invoking the function change the architecture entirely: processing stops being event-driven and analysis becomes on-demand.

932.key: The Amazon VPC CNI plugin is what manages pod networking in EKS: it assigns pods addresses straight from the VPC's subnets. Custom networking mode lets you specify exactly which subnets those addresses come from, which is what the scenario requires, and because the pods get real VPC addresses, regular security groups apply to them — giving controlled, secure communication within the network.

opts.A: A transit gateway routes traffic between networks and has nothing to do with assigning subnets to Kubernetes pods.
opts.B: Direct Connect connects the company's own site to AWS. It has nothing to do with choosing pod subnets or how pods communicate with each other.
opts.D: Anti-affinity rules control which nodes pods get placed on, not which subnet a pod gets its address from.

933.key: The database is already managed; the single point of failure is the lack of a standby in another zone. The least effort is to modify the instance itself to turn on Multi-AZ: AWS creates the standby instance in another zone and sets up synchronous replication itself, the endpoint doesn't change, and the application isn't touched. Applying it during the maintenance window also takes care of the downtime question.

opts.B: Moving to DynamoDB is a change of data model and a rewrite of the application's queries. That's maximum effort, not minimum.
opts.C: A new instance restored from a snapshot means downtime, loss of the most recent data, and a changed endpoint, while the same goal is reached just by flipping a setting.
opts.D: RDS doesn't fit into an EC2 Auto Scaling group, and spreading write requests across several independent databases through Route 53 would cause data to diverge.

934.key: The requirements line up so that only one service fits: managed storage supporting both NFS and SMB, with shared access to the same data from both protocols, plus redundancy at the Availability Zone level. That's Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP with multi-protocol access enabled in a Multi-AZ configuration.

opts.B: Self-managed servers on EC2 instances aren't a managed service, the data between them isn't shared, and redundancy would have to be built by hand.
opts.C: FSx for Lustre doesn't serve data over NFS, and two separate storage systems don't give shared access to the same files.
opts.D: S3 File Gateway serves both protocols, but it's a hybrid gateway with a local virtual appliance, not consolidated managed storage with zonal redundancy.

935.key: Three requirements are met with two steps. Scalability and availability for the web layer: an Auto Scaling group with instances in private subnets across multiple Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer (B). Lower MySQL read latency: moving to an Aurora MySQL cluster with the primary instance and a reader instance in separate Availability Zones — read queries go to the replica with millisecond replication lag (C). As a bonus, the database also leaves the public subnet.

opts.A: A single instance in a second Region with a failover policy provides neither scalability nor lower read latency, and it's still a single machine.
opts.D: An Auto Scaling group and a load balancer's target group exist within a single Region: instances from other Regions can't be added to them.
opts.E: Cross-Region replicas are for readers in other parts of the world or for disaster recovery. The scenario is about read latency for one application, and this kind of replication would only add latency and cost.

936.key: Of the options listed, only Secrets Manager can automatically rotate secrets (C), and with thousands of functions you need a single way to retrieve the secret without copy-pasting code — that's a Lambda layer (B).

opts.A: Lambda@Edge and security headers have nothing to do with storing secrets: that's about processing HTTP requests at the edge.
opts.D: Parameter Store stores parameters cheaply, but it has no built-in automatic rotation of its own — and that's exactly what's required.
opts.E: "Consumer with dedicated throughput" is Kinesis terminology, and environment variables created that way aren't rotated.

937.key: AWS Compute Optimizer analyzes usage metrics and produces recommendations for all three resource types named in the scenario at once: EC2 instances, Auto Scaling groups, and EBS volumes. Just turning the service on is enough — reports are generated automatically, with no manual exports or bill parsing.

opts.A: The Cost and Usage Report is a detailed cost breakdown, not resource right-sizing recommendations.
opts.B: Billing alarms warn when a spending threshold is crossed and contain no recommendations at all.
opts.D: There's no need to split the task across two tools: Compute Optimizer already covers both Auto Scaling groups and EBS volumes.

938.key: Shared storage for instances across different Availability Zones, high performance, and a requirement to stay inside the VPC — that's Amazon EFS. The file system mounts over NFS on each instance, mount targets are created in the VPC's subnets, so traffic stays inside the network.

opts.A: Accessing S3 through its API means rewriting the application, and without a VPC endpoint the traffic would also leave the network.
opts.B: Mounting an S3 bucket as a volume with standard tools isn't possible: no such capability exists.
opts.C: An EBS volume lives in a single Availability Zone and, in general, attaches to a single instance: the requirement of shared access across zones isn't met.
