939.key: After year-end reporting wraps up, the replica is only a quarter loaded while the primary instance is still at sixty percent. That means the replica should be sized down while the primary is left alone: it's under a reasonable load and has headroom for growth.

opts.A: Deleting the replica sends the reporting queries back to the primary instance and overloads it again.
opts.C: Sizing the replica up at twenty-five percent utilization wastes money, and sizing the primary down at sixty percent removes its headroom for growth.
opts.D: Deleting the replica and sizing the primary up is the most expensive path and loses the separation of reads from writes.

940.key: The workload is long-running and steady, and the goal is minimum cost. The biggest discount comes from the longest commitments with full upfront payment: three-year Reserved Instances for RDS and a three-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan with All Upfront for the instances.

opts.A: On-Demand pricing for RDS is the most expensive mode for a steady workload.
opts.B: A one-year commitment with no upfront payment gives the smallest discount of all the commitment-based options.
opts.C: A one-year term with partial upfront saves less than three years with full upfront.

941.key: IRSA is built from two halves. First: the EKS cluster has an OIDC provider, and the IAM role must trust exactly that provider — the trust policy names the provider and a condition scoped to a specific service account (E). Second: the Kubernetes service account itself is annotated with that role's ARN, after which pods running under it get temporary credentials via web identity (D). This way permissions are granted precisely to an application, not to the whole node.

opts.A: Permissions granted to the node's role are available to every pod on that node — the opposite of the granular access IRSA exists to provide.
opts.B: Kubernetes network policies restrict traffic between pods. They neither grant nor take away AWS API permissions.
opts.C: The cluster has no single role that permissions for every service account can be folded into: the mapping is done through individual roles via OIDC and annotations.

942.key: The requirements are encryption at rest, automatic rotation exactly once a year, the ability to confirm rotation through CloudTrail, and minimum cost for the key. Rotation you can enable, verify, and see logged is only offered by a customer managed KMS key: it has an automatic rotation toggle (365 days), a history of key material, and CloudTrail entries for every use. The cost is one dollar a month per key plus request charges, which is the lowest price at which all three requirements are satisfied; the only further saving comes from turning on an S3 Bucket Key, as in {{q:1009}}.

opts.A: With SSE-C the customer manages the key: AWS doesn't store it, doesn't rotate it, and doesn't log its use. No automatic rotation and no CloudTrail trail.
opts.B: SSE-S3 is free, but the keys are invisible: the rotation period isn't documented, and there are no separate CloudTrail entries for key usage. The audit requirement isn't satisfied.
opts.C: Naming it without qualification means the AWS managed key (aws/s3): it's free and rotates on its own, but you control neither its policy nor its rotation and can't configure it. The control the scenario requires comes specifically from a customer managed key.

943.key: To see spending broken down by application, resources are tagged with the application's name, and that tag is activated as a cost allocation tag in the management account — billing ignores it until activation. After that, Cost Explorer builds a breakdown by tag value and can email a regular report. No extra services or storage needed, which also makes it the cheapest option.

opts.A: AWS Budgets doesn't export historical spend by application: it watches thresholds.
opts.B: Loading the CUR into an RDS instance means a continuously running database and writing your own queries — noticeably more expensive and complex than Cost Explorer.
opts.D: Downloading bills by hand every month is manual work, and without activating the tags no application breakdown appears in the bill at all.

944.key: Resiliency is built at all three layers at once. The web layer: an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones, so a zone failure doesn't stop the application. The database: RDS in a Multi-AZ configuration with automatic failover to the standby. Static content: S3 served through CloudFront, which takes load off the instances and brings content closer to users.

opts.A: A single Availability Zone for both the instances and the database: a zone failure stops the application entirely. Versioning protects against deletion, not downtime.
opts.C: The instances are still in one zone, and serving static content directly from them loads down the web layer and goes down along with it.
opts.D: The EFS One Zone-IA class lives in a single Availability Zone — the weakest link in a design that's supposed to be resilient.

945.key: The task is to pass traffic between accounts through a network security appliance transparently, without changing the applications. That's exactly what a Gateway Load Balancer was built for: it operates at layer 3, encapsulates traffic in GENEVE, and hands it off to a fleet of inspection appliances while preserving the original addresses. A GWLB endpoint (a flavor of PrivateLink) is created in the application accounts, and routes send traffic through it into the networking account. This is the standard pattern for centralized inspection.

opts.A: An NLB works at layer 4 and isn't built for transparent inspection: it terminates flows and changes the addressing scheme, while security appliances need the original traffic.
opts.B: An ALB is an HTTP request load balancer inside the application account. It doesn't provide centralized inspection of cross-account traffic.
opts.D: A plain interface endpoint publishes a specific service — it doesn't wrap arbitrary traffic for inspection. That specifically requires a GWLB endpoint.

946.key: Reporting queries need to be routed to three specific replicas with a distinct configuration. Aurora has a custom endpoint for exactly this: a defined set of instances is added to it, and requests are balanced only among those. The rest of the cluster never sees the reporting load.

opts.B: Cloning the cluster creates a separate copy of the data that stops receiving fresh writes: it won't be anywhere close to real time.
opts.C: A specific instance's endpoint points to exactly one machine: there's no automatic distribution across three replicas.
opts.D: The reader endpoint spreads requests across every replica in the cluster, including the other three, when only the three selected ones are wanted.

947.key: The connection string in the environment variable moves into Secrets Manager: the secret is stored encrypted with a KMS key, the Lambda function retrieves it with a GetSecretValue call under its execution role, and a ready-made AWS rotation function handles rotation for RDS PostgreSQL on a 30-day schedule. No custom code, and no redeploying the function whenever the password changes. A practical detail: the secret value is typically cached in the function's global scope or via the Parameters and Secrets Extension so the API isn't called on every invocation.

opts.A: Parameter Store stores the parameter encrypted, but it has no built-in automatic rotation — there's no way to "configure it in Parameter Store."
opts.C: An environment variable means the function has to be updated every time the password changes, and rotation has to be written by hand. That's the most operational effort of the options given.
opts.D: KMS stores encryption keys, not credentials: you can't retrieve a username and password from it, and rotating the key doesn't change the password in the database.

948.key: The volume of changes swings throughout the day, and exactly the needed capacity should be provisioned. That's a description of AWS DMS Serverless: the service assesses the load itself and picks compute units, scaling them up and down as it goes, so you never pay for idle capacity.

opts.A: A Multi-AZ configuration improves the replication instance's fault tolerance, but the capacity stays fixed.
opts.C: A DMS replication instance is a managed resource: it can't be placed into an EC2 Auto Scaling group.
opts.D: DMS can't be run in your own ECS containers: it's a managed service with its own way of provisioning capacity.

949.key: The SaaS provider hosts its application on AWS, so it can be reached through AWS PrivateLink: the provider publishes its service behind a Network Load Balancer, the company creates an interface endpoint in its own VPC, and calls go to a private address. Traffic never leaves the AWS network, nothing is opened to the outside, and connections are only ever initiated from the company's side.

opts.A: Site-to-Site VPN connects a VPC to the company's own network, not to a third party's SaaS application: there's no customer gateway on their end for you to connect to.
opts.B: A transit gateway routes traffic between your own VPCs and sites, but it doesn't provide access to someone else's published service.
opts.C: This wording describes the same idea as the correct option but cuts off partway through and doesn't describe a working configuration: PrivateLink has no mode of "outbound traffic only, with no service published by the provider."

950.key: The requirement of encryption "at the network and session layer" describes IPsec, i.e. AWS Site-to-Site VPN: the tunnel encrypts all traffic between the corporate network and the VPC. The second requirement, preventing unrestricted access, is met with network controls inside the VPC: routes send traffic through the virtual gateway, and security groups plus network ACLs allow only the necessary ports and subnets. Keep this key fact in mind: Direct Connect by itself doesn't encrypt traffic — VPN or MACsec has to be layered on top of it for encryption.

opts.A: Direct Connect is a dedicated link, but not an encrypted one: the encryption requirement isn't met. Route tables also aren't an access-control mechanism.
opts.B: IAM policies control access to the AWS API, while this is about a network connection between a data center and a VPC.
opts.D: A transit gateway connects networks to each other, but it doesn't by itself create an encrypted channel to the corporate network: VPN or Direct Connect is still needed for that.

951.key: The same task as {{q:339}}: remove hardcoded credentials and enable rotation without rewriting the application. Secrets Manager stores the username-password pair encrypted, the application reads it with a single call under its role, and rotation is handled by a ready-made function AWS provides as a template for RDS MySQL — it just needs to be turned on. The application never knows the password changed: it fetches the current secret value every time.

opts.A: KMS manages encryption keys and doesn't store logins and passwords. Rotating a key doesn't change the credentials in the database.
opts.B: Local storage plus a cron job means a copy of the secret on every server and hand-rolled synchronization with the database. That's more code and more risk than a managed service.
opts.D: Parameter Store has no mechanism for rotating database credentials: "configure a rotation schedule through Parameter Store" isn't possible.

952.key: A verbatim repeat of question {{q:134}} with the same answer, and a handy check of understanding. Serverless SQL over data in S3 is Athena, so the RDS options are out immediately. From there, pick an encryption scheme compatible with cross-Region replication: a multi-Region KMS key exists in both Regions with the same key material, so replicas can be read in place with no re-encryption and no second key policy to manage.

opts.B: Amazon RDS is a database server that data has to be loaded into, while the requirement is serverless analysis of data already sitting in S3.
opts.C: Athena is the right choice, but SSE-S3 means separate, invisible keys in each Region: there's no way to manage them or confirm the replica is protected. The "encryption plus cross-Region replication" combination on the exam is solved with multi-Region KMS keys.
opts.D: The encryption choice is right, but RDS still isn't a serverless way to run SQL over S3 objects.

953.key: There are three different datasets here with three different access patterns, and the winning solution treats each one differently. The original uploaded images are needed twice a year for model training, with no urgency — the cheapest class, Glacier Deep Archive. Premium users' generated images can be downloaded anytime — S3 Standard. Regular users' generated images are available once every six hours, meaning infrequent reads that still need to be served instantly — Standard-IA. The general lesson: don't pick one storage class for a whole bucket when the scenario lists several distinct data categories.

opts.B: All generated images go to Glacier Flexible Retrieval, where an object takes minutes to hours to come back. A premium user promised download at any time shouldn't have to wait that long.
opts.C: One Zone-IA for the source images is both pricier than Deep Archive and riskier: a single copy in one Availability Zone for data touched twice a year is a bad tradeoff.
opts.D: Two mistakes at once: the source images sit in the pricier, less durable One Zone-IA, and the generated images are in Glacier, from which they can't be served to a user quickly.

954.key: The same scenario as {{q:422}}: irregular load ranging from idle for weeks to thousands of requests at once, an asynchronous interface, and a gigabyte of model data in memory. An SQS queue accepts and holds requests, ECS services read from it, and auto scaling driven by queue length grows both the number of service copies and the cluster's capacity.

opts.A: A Network Load Balancer can't invoke Lambda functions as a target, and reloading a gigabyte of model data on every cold start is unacceptable.
opts.B: A load balancer in front of the models makes processing synchronous, whereas the interface is described as asynchronous, and a burst of thousands of requests would cause failures.
opts.C: The number of vCPUs for a Lambda function isn't something auto scaling adjusts, and a gigabyte-sized model doesn't fit the Lambda execution model well.

955.key: The acceptable recovery time is 30 minutes, and the standby site doesn't need to serve customers while the primary is healthy. That's the pilot light pattern: a load balancer and an Auto Scaling group at minimal capacity are pre-deployed in the second Region, the Aurora cluster is converted into a global database with continuous replication, and Route 53 is set up for active-passive failover based on health checks. During an outage the group scales up and the secondary cluster is promoted to primary — all within the time limit.

opts.B: An active-active setup serves traffic in the second Region continuously, which the scenario doesn't call for, and it costs noticeably more. An Auto Scaling group also can't span instances across Regions.
opts.C: Restoring the database from a backup gives an RPO measured in hours, whereas a global database keeps it at seconds. And an Auto Scaling group still can't be cross-Region.
opts.D: Desired capacity of zero means instances have to boot from scratch during a disaster along with application warm-up, and the infrastructure itself is only created from a configuration backup after the failure happens. Hitting 30 minutes is far from reliable.

956.key: The first requirement rules out half the options: jobs "cannot be disrupted," and AWS reclaims Spot Instances with only a two-minute warning. So compute has to be On-Demand (which, for short batch jobs, is also cheaper than a reservation since you only pay for actual runtime). Second, the data: 30 days of active access is Standard, then almost two years sitting untouched is Glacier Deep Archive, the cheapest class, plus expiration after 2 years so you stop paying.

opts.A: Spot Instances get interrupted, and the scenario explicitly forbids interrupting the jobs. Glacier Instant Retrieval for two years of untouched storage is also roughly four times pricier than Deep Archive.
opts.B: Compute is chosen correctly, but the data is actively read for the first 30 days, and Glacier Instant Retrieval charges per retrieval. It also has a 90-day minimum storage duration, so moving to Deep Archive on day 30 triggers an early-deletion penalty.
opts.C: The same mistake with Spot, plus Glacier Flexible Retrieval costs more than Deep Archive, and fast access to data older than 30 days isn't required by the scenario.

957.key: Single-digit-millisecond latency rules out the internet and VPN — a dedicated connection is needed. A Direct Connect connection is created with a transit virtual interface to a Direct Connect gateway (D), and that Direct Connect gateway is then associated with the existing transit gateway (B). That single pair of objects gives the site connectivity to every VPC attached to the transit gateway, and adding new networks changes nothing about this setup.

opts.A: A separate VPN per VPC runs over the internet: latency is unpredictable, and the single-digit-millisecond requirement isn't met.
opts.C: A VPN connection isn't established directly to a Direct Connect gateway — that construction doesn't exist. A VPN terminates on a virtual private gateway or a transit gateway.
opts.E: Associating a VPN with a transit gateway is possible, but it's again a path over the internet with unpredictable latency.

958.key: The timeouts happen right at the moment of the switch: the application is still holding connections to the old primary instance and doesn't learn about the change immediately. RDS Proxy maintains a connection pool and redirects it to the new primary itself, cutting the failover time the application experiences by more than half.

opts.B: A read replica takes load off the primary instance but has no effect on failover duration.
opts.C: Performance Insights helps find the bottleneck but doesn't speed anything up on its own.
opts.D: Copying snapshots to other Regions is a disaster recovery concern, not the speed of failover within a Multi-AZ configuration.

959.key: The instances are already tagged, and all that's needed is starting and stopping them on a schedule. State Manager associations in Systems Manager do this out of the box: the target is selected by tag, the action and schedule are set through configuration, and there's no custom code at all.

opts.A: A CloudWatch alarm tracks metrics, not the time of day, and would still require a custom function.
opts.B: Trusted Advisor gives optimization recommendations, not a list of instances to start and stop on a schedule.
opts.D: A schedule with functions works, but that's custom code that has to be written and maintained, while State Manager solves the task with configuration alone.

960.key: The same technique as in question {{q:88}}: outbound traffic from S3 is billed to the bucket owner by default, and Requester Pays flips that rule. The marketing firm accesses the bucket under its own account and pays for both the requests and the outbound transfer, while the company continues paying only for storage. The firm already has access — nothing about that needs to change, only the billing. Keep in mind: with Requester Pays every request must be signed and include acknowledgment of paying, and anonymous requests are rejected.

opts.B: Cross-Region Replication means the company itself pays for cross-Region transfer of every object plus storing the copy. That's a cost increase, not a decrease.
opts.C: AWS Resource Access Manager can't share S3 buckets — bucket access is granted through a bucket policy or a cross-account role. And even with access granted, the transfer bill would still land on the owner.
opts.D: The storage class has no effect on outbound transfer cost, and syncing to someone else's bucket is an export paid for by the company.

961.key: The dump key was corrected during the audit. Rate limiting is configured with an AWS WAF rule, but a web ACL can't be attached to Global Accelerator: the service isn't among the resource types WAF supports (CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync, Cognito, App Runner, Verified Access). So the rate-based rule is created on the Application Load Balancer that sits behind the accelerator and receives its traffic. The change is minimal — the architecture stays the same, only a web ACL is added to the existing load balancer.

opts.A: The original dump key. AWS Global Accelerator isn't a resource a WAF web ACL can attach to, so this configuration isn't possible.
opts.B: A custom function reading metrics and editing network ACLs means code, a delayed response, and the hard limit on rules in an ACL.
opts.D: Putting CloudFront in front of Global Accelerator is a significant architectural rework, while the requirement calls for minimal effort.

962.key: Calculating metrics shouldn't touch the table's provisioned capacity. The DynamoDB export connector in AWS Glue reads data not from the table itself but from an export to S3 produced by the backup mechanism, so no read capacity units are consumed at all.

opts.A: The Athena connector for DynamoDB scans the table itself and consumes its read capacity.
opts.C: Redshift's COPY command can't read a DynamoDB table without spending its capacity — it performs a scan.
opts.D: A Hive external table in EMR also reads the table directly, taking read capacity away from the customer-facing site.

963.key: Jobs need to be stored durably, processed in parallel, and stay loosely coupled. An SQS queue stores jobs durably and decouples the sender from the processors, while an Auto Scaling group grows and shrinks based on the number of messages in the queue — that is, on actual work volume rather than an indirect signal.

opts.A: SNS doesn't store messages: if there's no ready subscriber, the job is lost, and scaling on CPU doesn't reflect queue length.
opts.B: The queue choice is right, but scaling on network usage is an indirect signal that may not correlate with the number of jobs at all.
opts.D: An SNS topic again doesn't provide durable storage of jobs.

964.key: The requirements are a modular architecture instead of a monolith, keeping the structured database schema, storing images, and minimal operations. ECS on Fargate runs container services with no managed node to look after, RDS in a Multi-AZ configuration preserves the relational schema and provides fault tolerance, and images go into S3, which grows without limit.

opts.A: EC2 instances have to be patched and scaled by you, and storing images in a relational database is a bad practice that bloats it and drives up cost.
opts.B: A monolith wrapped inside Lambda functions doesn't become modular, and DynamoDB's 400 KB item size limit makes storing images impossible.
opts.C: EKS on EC2 instances requires managing nodes, and Glacier Deep Archive takes hours to retrieve an object — unacceptable for product images.

965.key: "The company must encrypt the data before storing the data in Amazon S3" means encryption has to happen on the application side, before it's sent. That's client-side encryption using a key the company controls (typically a customer managed KMS key via envelope encryption, or a key of its own). Every SSE-based option is out by definition: those are performed by the service after the object is received. Compare this with {{q:801}}, which additionally requires keeping the keys entirely outside AWS.

opts.B: SSE-KMS encrypts the object only after S3 has already received it. The "before storing" requirement isn't met.
opts.C: With SSE-C the client sends the key along with the request, but S3 is still the one doing the encryption after receiving the plaintext data. The key also travels over the network with every request.
opts.D: Client-side encryption with keys managed by S3 isn't possible: those keys never leave the service and aren't available to the application.

966.key: The task is to give each team its own permissions on a shared EMR cluster while keeping jobs from reaching the instance role's credentials through instance metadata. That's EMR runtime roles: a job is submitted specifying a role, EMR runs it as that role, and access to the instance profile from the job's code is blocked. That way the same infrastructure serves teams with different permissions.

opts.A: Interface endpoints control the traffic path, not what permissions a job has. They can't separate teams by permission.
opts.C: An instance profile grants the same permissions to every job on the cluster and stays reachable through instance metadata — exactly what needs to be avoided.
opts.D: Turning off application-scoped roles does the opposite: it reverts job execution back to the shared instance role instead of runtime roles.

967.key: Forms need to be processed exactly once with nothing lost. An SQS FIFO queue provides exactly that: the message is stored durably, duplicates within the deduplication window are dropped, and ordering and exactly-once processing are both guaranteed.

opts.B: An HTTP API forwards the request onward but stores nothing: if the processor is unavailable, the data is lost.
opts.C: A standard queue guarantees at-least-once delivery, so the same form could be processed twice.
opts.D: A synchronous workflow ties the tiers together tightly: if the processor is busy or down, the data is lost again.

968.key: The requirements are ingesting streaming data, near-real-time search, and visualization — using AWS-native services. Kinesis Data Streams ingests the streams from the producers, OpenSearch Service indexes them and provides search with real-time updates, and Amazon QuickSight builds the dashboards.

opts.A: Self-managed instances to ingest the stream is unnecessary operations, and Athena gives queries over data in S3 with a delay, not real-time search.
opts.B: EMR and Redshift are batch and analytical processing: they don't provide real-time updates.
opts.C: An EKS cluster for stream ingestion means managing infrastructure, and CloudWatch isn't a search engine for application data.

969.key: The application needs to be containerized and run without managing infrastructure. AWS App2Container analyzes the running application and produces an image along with deployment artifacts, including a CloudFormation template, and ECS on Fargate runs the containers with no node to manage, scaling based on CloudWatch metrics.

opts.B: The EC2 launch type brings node management back: operations don't decrease.
opts.C: App Runner isn't a tool for containerizing an existing application and doesn't deploy workloads onto ECS: it's a standalone run service.
opts.D: The same mistake about App Runner's role, and EC2 nodes in EKS again mean managing infrastructure.

970.key: What needs to be stored is specifically credentials — username-password pairs — using a managed service with minimal effort. That's Secrets Manager: secrets are encrypted with a KMS key, access is granted through a role, and there's a dedicated BatchGetSecretValue call for reading many secrets in a single request. The presence of that API in the scenario is itself the clue: Parameter Store has no such operation.

opts.A: Parameter Store has no BatchGetSecretValue call: that API belongs specifically to Secrets Manager. This option describes a combination that doesn't exist.
opts.B: AWS Batch is a service for running batch compute jobs on containers — it has nothing to do with reading secrets. An unnecessary component in the design.
opts.C: Two mistakes at once: the store is picked without the needed API, and AWS Batch is added for no reason.

971.key: Thousands of Outposts servers worldwide regularly download the same set of 100 files from a bucket in ap-northeast-1. Identical content, many remote consumers, repeated downloads — that's a textbook CDN problem: CloudFront caches the files at edge locations, so the second and every subsequent server in a region gets them locally. The dump key picks C (S3 Transfer Acceleration), and that's its weak point: Transfer Acceleration speeds up transfer over the AWS backbone, but it caches nothing, so each of the thousands of servers still pulls the file all the way from Tokyo. On the merits, option D is the stronger fit.

opts.A: The CachingDisabled policy turns off caching, removing the one reason to put CloudFront in front at all. Every request still goes all the way to the origin in ap-northeast-1.
opts.B: Replicating to a second bucket with origin failover solves a fault-tolerance problem, not latency. It's also doubled storage and extra configuration on top of a "LEAST operational overhead" requirement.
opts.D: This option addresses the problem on its merits: CloudFront caches the 100 files at edge locations near the servers, and repeat downloads happen locally. This is where the disagreement with the dump key lies.

972.key: A Windows Server cluster needs shared storage reachable by both nodes, and the nodes must sit in different Availability Zones. Amazon FSx for Windows File Server takes the least effort here: it supports continuously available shares for clustering, replicates synchronously between zones, and provides high availability on its own. Nothing needs to be written or configured by hand.

opts.B: Application-level replication between two gp3 volumes is hand-rolled logic, with a risk of divergence and the most implementation work of the options.
opts.C: An active/standby setup without a cluster provides no automatic failover, and iSCSI access to ONTAP takes more configuration than a ready-made shared folder.
opts.D: There's no such thing as service-level EBS volume replication across Availability Zones — that capability doesn't exist.

973.key: This is about the load balancer's own security group, so one inbound rule and two outbound rules are needed. Inbound HTTPS from 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443 is the public internet traffic (A). Outbound HTTPS to the instances on port 443 forwards requests to the application (C). Outbound HTTPS to the instances on port 8443 is the health check (E).

opts.B: Allowing outbound traffic to the whole internet is excessive: the load balancer only needs to reach its own targets.
opts.D: An inbound rule from the instances isn't needed: the load balancer initiates the connections to the targets, and the responses are permitted by connection state.
opts.F: The same applies to health checks: they're outbound, so no inbound rule is needed for them.

974.key: Two independent requirements. A certificate for a custom domain on CloudFront always comes from ACM in us-east-1 (A) — the bucket's Region doesn't matter. And the ability to write to the bucket through the distribution comes from origin access control (D): CloudFront supports uploads to S3 via OAC.

opts.B: A certificate issued in eu-west-1 simply won't be visible to CloudFront: the distribution only pulls certificates from us-east-1.
opts.C: S3 Transfer Acceleration is a separate endpoint for faster uploads straight to S3. It doesn't grant CloudFront write access and isn't needed alongside a distribution.
opts.E: An S3 website endpoint serves static content over HTTP, doesn't support uploads, and doesn't work with OAC.

975.key: The data already sits in S3 as Parquet, client-side encrypted with a KMS key (CSE-KMS), and queries are only needed occasionally. Amazon Athena reads such files directly: it supports client-side encryption with KMS keys, understands Parquet and prefix-based partitions, and you're billed only for the bytes scanned — a query for a single calendar day scans only that day's prefix. No cluster, no standing infrastructure. Cost tip: columnar format plus partitions plus a partition filter cut the Athena bill by a large factor.

opts.B: S3 Select works on one object per request and can't read data encrypted on the client side. A moving average across many files can't be computed this way.
opts.C: Redshift Spectrum requires a Redshift cluster, which is billed continuously, while queries here are only occasional. That's a noticeable overpay for sporadic lookups.
opts.D: EMR Serverless would work, but it's already the Spark framework with its own configuration and startup cost. For a handful of SQL queries, Athena is simpler and cheaper.

976.key: The requirement is to route each user to the geographically closest instances. In Route 53, geoproximity is what handles distance: it computes proximity to the coordinates given for each resource and lets you shift the boundaries of influence with the bias parameter. Within a Region, the load balancer already spreads requests across all Availability Zones.

opts.A: Geolocation routes by the requester's country or continent, not by distance: a user near a border can easily be sent to a far-away Region simply because that's what the rule says for their country.
opts.C: Multivalue answer returns a random set of healthy records and doesn't account for proximity to the user at all.
opts.D: A weighted policy splits traffic in set proportions regardless of where the request came from.

977.key: Both directions need to be covered with minimal effort. At rest: turn on RDS encryption with a KMS key — it covers disks, snapshots, backups, and replicas, and needs no application changes. In transit: TLS, and the public-facing part (the load balancer, the application's domain) is covered by a free ACM certificate with automatic renewal. A useful detail about the database connection itself: ACM doesn't issue a certificate for it — the client has to trust RDS's root certificate from the AWS bundle, as covered in {{q:743}}.

opts.B: IPsec tunnels to a database inside the VPC is an over-engineered construct that has to be deployed and maintained, while RDS already supports TLS natively.
opts.C: Third-party application-level encryption means custom development and managing your own keys. That violates the minimal-operational-overhead requirement.
opts.D: A VPN provides privacy for the channel between networks, but it doesn't encrypt application traffic to the database and doesn't replace TLS. It's also an extra component to operate.

978.key: There are two requirements: retain data for 90 days and be able to restore to any point within the last 14 days. RDS automated backups are capped at 35 days, so AWS Backup is needed: the plan sets a 90-day retention period, and continuous backup provides point-in-time restore. Everything is configured through a single plan.

opts.A: The maximum retention for RDS automated backups is 35 days: 90 days can't be set.
opts.B: Daily manual snapshots can be kept indefinitely, but they don't provide point-in-time restore, and deleting old ones would have to be automated yourself.
opts.C: The clone feature belongs to Aurora and doesn't work for RDS for Oracle, and it doesn't substitute for point-in-time restore.

979.key: The load is variable, mostly reads, with occasional writes; the database needs to be relational and managed; and cost is the priority. Aurora Serverless adjusts capacity to actual usage and scales down during lulls, so you don't pay for peak capacity around the clock, and growth in user count is handled automatically.

opts.A: Provisioned IOPS storage is billed continuously at peak values, even though the load is variable.
opts.C: DynamoDB isn't a relational database, and the scenario explicitly calls for a relational model.
opts.D: Magnetic storage is outdated and slow, and multiple read replicas are billed around the clock regardless of actual load.

980.key: There are many buckets and more are created continuously, so listing them in a policy is endless manual work. A gateway endpoint provides the private route, and the restriction "only our account's buckets" is best expressed not as a list but as a condition: Deny on S3 actions whenever aws:ResourceAccount doesn't match your account ID. That policy is written once and automatically covers every future bucket, while blocking access to buckets belonging to other accounts on the internet.

opts.A: Listing specific buckets in a policy works, but it needs an edit for every new customer. It loses on operational overhead compared to a condition on the account ID.
opts.B: A NAT gateway sends traffic out to the internet and is billed per gigabyte, and a security group can't distinguish your account's buckets from anyone else's.
opts.D: A policy on "all buckets" can't be applied to someone else's buckets the application might try to reach, and NAT again means the internet and transfer charges.

981.key: The company already uses IAM Identity Center, so team access should be granted through its native mechanism — a permission set assigned to a group for the relevant accounts. Permissions are defined once and reused, new employees get access by being added to a group, and credentials are always temporary. Setting up parallel IAM roles or users per team would duplicate the access model and require maintaining it by hand.

opts.A: Roles with fine-grained policies are the right idea, but done around the already-configured Identity Center: access assignment and rotation would have to be managed separately.
opts.C: Individual IAM users are long-lived credentials and manual upkeep, which conflicts with both minimal effort and the presence of Identity Center.
opts.D: A separate account per team is a heavy restructuring of the landscape just to separate access to two services.

982.key: The application runs outside AWS, so it has no instance role or task role, and long-lived keys shouldn't be issued. That's exactly what IAM Roles Anywhere exists for: the virtual machines present an X.509 certificate issued by a trusted certificate authority, exchange it for temporary role credentials, and use those to work with S3. No keys are stored anywhere, the lifetime is bounded, and revocation happens by revoking the certificate or the trust.

opts.A: Allowing a range of public IP addresses isn't authentication: anyone behind the same NAT would get access. Unacceptable for sensitive data.
opts.C: IAM user keys on a virtual machine are a long-lived secret that has to be distributed and rotated manually. That's exactly what the "temporary access" requirement is meant to avoid.
opts.D: Secrets Manager just stores those same long-lived keys more neatly: a compromised key stays valid until it's manually revoked.

983.key: Many new accounts are planned, and each needs access to the directory and DNS services in the data center. A transit gateway is set up once, shared with the accounts via AWS RAM, their VPCs attach to it, and the Direct Connect link is associated with it through a Direct Connect gateway. Each new account is added with a single attachment, giving fast, cheap, and consistent access for all of them.

opts.A: A separate Direct Connect link per account means months of provisioning and multiplying port costs.
opts.B: VPC endpoints provide private access to AWS services, not to the directory and DNS servers in the company's data center.
opts.C: A VPN connection per account means traffic over the internet with unpredictable latency and many constructs to maintain.

984.key: The content is dynamic, the audience is global, and cost specifically needs to be optimized. CloudFront with the existing load balancer as the origin solves both: TLS terminates at the nearest edge location, the request travels to the Region over the AWS backbone, and outbound traffic from CloudFront is cheaper than outbound traffic straight from the Region. Dynamic content doesn't even need to be cached — the win comes from the network itself and connection reuse.

opts.B: Geographic routing makes sense when multiple sites are deployed. There's only one Region here, and routing won't make it any closer to the user.
opts.C: S3 only serves static files: a dynamic application can't be moved there. Public read access is also a poor practice.
opts.D: Direct Connect is a dedicated link to one specific company site, not a way to deliver content to millions of users worldwide.

985.key: Three requirements at once: the highest durability, high availability, and a reasonable price under a pattern where part of the data goes untouched for months. Eleven nines of durability are shared by every class except One Zone (which has the same number but in a single zone — losing the zone loses the data), narrowing the choice to Standard, Standard-IA, and Intelligent-Tiering. Since the access pattern isn't known in advance and keeps changing, Intelligent-Tiering wins: tiering happens automatically, there's no retrieval fee, and availability and durability match Standard.

opts.A: S3 Standard meets the durability and availability requirements, but you pay the full rate for data that sits untouched for months. The scenario also demands cost-effectiveness.
opts.C: Deep Archive takes up to 12 hours to return an object, while the data is used continuously with a peak during business hours. That's a hard violation of the availability requirement.
opts.D: One Zone-IA keeps a single copy in one Availability Zone: both "highest level of durability" and high availability are out.

986.key: Data from the EBS volume needs to become available to every instance in the Auto Scaling group, without significant code changes and with resilience to failures. Amazon EFS solves this directly: the file system mounts over NFS on each instance, the application keeps using ordinary paths, and data is stored across multiple Availability Zones. General Purpose performance mode gives the lowest latency and suits most workloads.

opts.A: A self-managed NFS server on an instance with a single volume is a single point of failure and a machine that has to be maintained.
opts.B: The application runs on Linux, and SMB confined to a single Availability Zone gives neither the native protocol nor resilience to a zone failure.
opts.C: EBS volumes stay tied to a single instance and a single zone: no shared access results.

987.key: Clients communicate over TCP, so a Network Load Balancer is needed — an Application Load Balancer only understands HTTP and HTTPS (A). Automatic growth as user count rises comes from an Auto Scaling group, which adds instances as needed and removes surplus ones (B).

opts.C: An Application Load Balancer works at the HTTP layer and doesn't suit arbitrary TCP traffic.
opts.D: Manually adding instances contradicts the requirement for automatic scaling.
opts.E: A Gateway Load Balancer is built for passing traffic through virtual network appliances, not for publishing an application.

988.key: The requirements split into two, and each half is met by a different type of organization policy. Allowed tag values (sensitive and nonsensitive) are described by a tag policy with enforcement turned on for EC2 resources (A). Forbidding instance creation without the tag and forbidding tag deletion are API actions, which are governed by an SCP: Deny on ec2:RunInstances with a Null condition on aws:RequestTag, and Deny on ec2:DeleteTags (D). The key distinction: a tag policy governs tag values, an SCP governs which actions are allowed.

opts.B: An SCP can't describe the set of allowed tag values as such — that's what a tag policy is for. Conditions can check a specific value, but that doesn't replace managing the value dictionary.
opts.C: A tag policy doesn't forbid API calls: it can neither block launching an instance nor forbid deleting tags. That's what an SCP does.
opts.E: An AWS Config rule plus deleting resources with a function is a reaction after the fact and risks losing a needed resource. The requirement calls for prevention.

989.key: RDS automated backups delete themselves once their retention period expires, so it's enough to set that period to 30 days — no extra cost and no extra services needed. Manual snapshots stick around until deleted, so old ones have to be removed by hand.

opts.A: AWS Backup is an unnecessary layer here: automated backup retention is configured directly in RDS, and a backup service would add its own cost on top.
opts.B: Turning off automated backups and deleting everything that exists violates the requirement to keep backups younger than 30 days.
opts.D: CloudFormation deploys infrastructure, not deleting backups by age; existing backups would again be lost.

990.key: The application can only speak the NFS protocol and can't be changed. In AWS, the managed file system that speaks it is Amazon EFS: it mounts on instances as an ordinary network resource, grows automatically, and stores data across multiple Availability Zones.

opts.A: DataSync moves data between storage systems and isn't storage itself.
opts.B: EBS volumes provide a block device, not an NFS network resource: the application can't work with it the way it used to.
opts.D: EMRFS is an access layer to S3 for EMR clusters, not an NFS file system for general-purpose applications.

991.key: The application drowned in a burst of traffic and the data was lost for good. An SQS queue fixes both problems at once: it absorbs any burst, stores messages durably, and hands them to the application at whatever pace it can keep up with, so unprocessed events stay in the queue instead of disappearing.

opts.A: Scanning a bucket for new objects is polling with a delay and requires custom logic to track what's already been processed.
opts.B: A gateway with functions can absorb the burst, but that's reworking ingestion, and this design has no buffer with replay capability.
opts.D: A table polled for new records again requires custom query logic and provides no buffering for the burst.

992.key: Maximum security means the database shouldn't be reachable from the internet at all, and the channel should be encrypted. The cluster is placed in private subnets with no public address, and the office connects over Site-to-Site VPN with a customer gateway on its side: access is only possible from the office network, traffic is encrypted, and there's no public endpoint.

opts.A: A cluster in public subnets gets an internet-reachable endpoint, and having a VPN doesn't cancel that out: the database can still be attacked around the tunnel.
opts.C: Security groups scoped to the office's addresses restrict the source, but the traffic still travels over the open internet with no network-layer encryption, and office addresses can be spoofed under other network conditions.
opts.D: Public subnets plus database users is protection only at the account level, with fully open network access. The least secure option.

993.key: This is about the charge for data transfer between instances. Traffic between Availability Zones is billed, while traffic within a single zone over private addresses is not. So every instance that exchanges data needs to sit in the same Availability Zone.

opts.A: An Auto Scaling group manages the instance count and has no effect on transfer billing.
opts.B: A single Region is necessary but not sufficient: cross-zone traffic within a Region is still billed.
opts.D: Multiple Availability Zones is exactly what generates the transfer charge.

994.key: A verbatim repeat of question {{q:336}}: encrypt credentials and rotate them every 14 days with the least effort. Secrets Manager handles it all through configuration — the secret is encrypted with a KMS key, attached to the Aurora cluster, the rotation period is set to an arbitrary number of days, and AWS provides the rotation function for supported databases. The other options assemble the same result from custom code and homegrown ways of delivering the password to the instances.

opts.B: Parameter Store keeps the password encrypted, but rotation has to be written and maintained by hand.
opts.C: A file on a shared file system plus a custom rotation function adds development work, file permissions, and the risk of the database and the file drifting out of sync.
opts.D: Periodically downloading the password file leaves a window where the application works with a stale value, and again requires a custom rotation function.

995.key: Video processing takes up to twenty minutes, which exceeds Lambda's fifteen-minute execution limit. Containers are needed instead: ECS on Fargate scales with demand, is billed for the actual runtime of the tasks, and requires no node management. Metadata is stored in Aurora, and the video files themselves go into S3 with Intelligent-Tiering, which automatically cuts the cost of rarely-read content on its own.

opts.A: Twenty minutes doesn't fit within Lambda's fifteen-minute limit: the job would get cut off.
opts.C: An EC2 instance fleet has to be maintained and scaled, and a load balancer in front of video-processing tasks isn't needed at all.
opts.D: EKS on EC2 instances means managing nodes, a database in a single Availability Zone is fragile, and Glacier Deep Archive takes hours to retrieve files.

996.key: The cluster needs to stay Kubernetes, and the company doesn't want to manage the compute infrastructure. AWS Fargate on EKS solves this fully: a Fargate profile is created, and pods that match its rules run with no node behind them at all — no patching, no node scaling.

opts.A: Self-managed nodes are the most work: images, updates, scaling, all done by hand.
opts.B: Managed node groups simplify life, but EC2 nodes still exist and their lifecycle still needs attention.
opts.D: Karpenter automates node provisioning, but the nodes still exist — the infrastructure hasn't gone away.

997.key: The database needs to be structured, scale with traffic, have backups, and be cheap. Aurora Serverless checks every box: a relational model, capacity that adjusts automatically to actual load, and built-in automated backups to AWS storage. You pay almost nothing while idle.

opts.A: A self-managed database on interruptible instances risks losing the node at any moment, plus all the operations fall on the company.
opts.B: Amazon RDS has no on-demand capacity mode: the instance class is picked in advance and billed continuously.
opts.D: A non-relational database conflicts with the structured-schema requirement, and backing up straight to Glacier means slow recovery.

998.key: The requirement is to stop using the public S3 endpoint. A gateway endpoint adds a route to the service's prefix in the subnet's route table, traffic goes through the endpoint inside the AWS network, and the endpoint policy grants permissions on the needed bucket. The nightly upload doesn't need a single line of code changed.

opts.B: The bucket can't be moved inside the VPC: S3 is a regional service with no addresses in your network.
opts.C: An access point changes how addressing and access control work, but the call still goes over the public endpoint unless there's a matching VPC endpoint on the network.
opts.D: Direct Connect connects the company's own site to AWS. The instance is already inside the VPC, so building a dedicated link to it makes no sense.

999.key: The product catalog changes rarely, and searching it is what loads down the database's CPU. An ElastiCache for Redis cache with lazy loading keeps query results in memory: the first request goes to the database, later ones are served from the cache, and load on the instance drops.

opts.A: Redshift is built for analytics over large datasets, not fast catalog lookups in a live application.
opts.C: Adding web servers doesn't help: the bottleneck is the database, and more instances just pile on more pressure against it.
opts.D: Multi-AZ improves availability, not performance, and throttling queries makes the site worse, not better.

1000.key: The existing storage is block-based (iSCSI), space is running out, and hot data needs to be read with low latency. Volume Gateway in cached volumes mode was built for exactly this: the volume is presented to applications as an iSCSI device, the full dataset lives in S3, and a local disk holds a cache of recently used blocks. There's no need to grow local capacity, and the applications don't need to be rewritten. Compare with {{q:307}} — same logic, different wording.

opts.A: S3 File Gateway serves data over SMB and NFS, i.e. file protocols. The applications work with block volumes over iSCSI, and switching would mean reworking them.
opts.C: Stored volumes keep the full data copy locally and only snapshot it to AWS. The lack of on-site space is left unsolved.
opts.D: Tape Gateway emulates a tape library for backup and archiving. It isn't built for everyday low-latency access.

1001.key: Order collection is fast and fulfillment is slower, so the tiers need to be decoupled with buffers: one SQS queue per stage, so nothing is lost during a burst. The groups then need to scale based on the number of messages in the corresponding queue — a direct measure of the work that's piled up.

opts.A: Keeping minimum capacity at peak level means paying for peak instance count around the clock and still doesn't protect against data loss.
opts.B: Spinning up new Auto Scaling groups on a signal is an unworkable, unmanageable scheme with no buffer for the orders in it.
opts.C: The queues are chosen correctly, but SQS doesn't send notifications about its own state: scaling needs to be driven by the message-count metric.

1002.key: Continuous multi-Region availability is achieved with global tables: DynamoDB replicates the data across Regions itself and allows writes in any of them. The gaming service's load is predictable and steady, so provisioned capacity with auto scaling costs less than paying per request.

opts.A: Tables in a single Region and global tables at the same time is a contradiction: a global table by definition spans multiple Regions.
opts.B: A cache speeds up reads, but nobody maintains cross-Region replication by hand: that's exactly what global tables exist for.
opts.C: Homegrown replication built on change streams is code that has to be written and maintained, and on-demand mode is more expensive under steady load.

1003.key: The data has already moved to S3, but the local rendering application needs to read it with low latency and without being rewritten against an object API. S3 File Gateway is deployed on-site, presents the bucket as a shared folder over NFS or SMB, and keeps a local cache of hot files: the first read comes from S3, later ones from local disk. You're paying for S3 and a lightweight gateway, not a second full-fledged storage system — hence "most cost-effective."

opts.A: Mountpoint for Amazon S3 mounts the bucket as a file system, but every read still goes to S3 over the WAN, and it doesn't provide a real local cache of hot data or full POSIX semantics. Latency for on-site rendering would stay high.
opts.C: Copying data into FSx for Windows File Server means a second paid storage system on top of the S3 you're already paying for, plus a separate gateway. It meets the latency requirement but loses on cost.
opts.D: A homegrown file server calling the S3 API is development and operations you do yourself: caching, consistency, and fault tolerance would all have to be built by hand.

1004.key: The API is public, runs over HTTP, and the complaints about latency come from customers abroad. Putting CloudFront in front of the API solves it two ways: TLS terminates at the nearest edge location and the request continues over the AWS backbone from there, and cacheable responses are returned without touching the Region at all. The key differentiator here is cost: CloudFront has no fixed hourly charge, while Global Accelerator always does.

opts.A: A dedicated link to every customer's data center is the most expensive and slowest option available, and a public virtual interface doesn't even combine with a Direct Connect gateway.
opts.C: Global Accelerator would also speed things up and would be the right answer for non-HTTP traffic, but it costs more: a fixed accelerator fee plus a data transfer premium, with no caching at all.
opts.D: VPN tunnels to every customer's network don't scale, require configuration on each customer's side, and don't speed up a public API.

1005.key: Thousands of responses an hour call for a buffer, and sentiment analysis calls for a ready-made service. API Gateway accepts the results and drops them on an SQS queue, which absorbs the burst; a Lambda function drains the queue and calls Amazon Comprehend for the sentiment score, and the results are kept for the following twelve months.

opts.B: An API on an EC2 instance is a bottleneck that has to be scaled and maintained by hand.
opts.C: Amazon Rekognition analyzes images and video — it doesn't determine text sentiment.
opts.D: Amazon Lex builds conversational bots; it doesn't do sentiment analysis for surveys.

1006.key: The errors happen because instances get patched while still part of the target group. Systems Manager has a ready-made automation document, AWSEC2-PatchLoadBalancerInstance, that takes the instance out from behind the load balancer itself, installs the updates, and puts it back (C); this process is triggered by maintenance windows, which handle taking instances out of service and patching on a schedule (D).

opts.A: Switching the target type from IP address to instance doesn't fix the problem: the instance still stays in the target group during patching.
opts.B: It's precisely the current document that causes the errors, so leaving it unchanged isn't an option.
opts.E: State Manager maintains a desired configuration state, but it doesn't take instances out from behind a load balancer for the duration of patching.

1007.key: Two requirements shape the answer. "Least operational effort" points to AWS Glue: it's managed, serverless ETL, with no clusters to stand up and tear down, unlike EMR. "All data must be encrypted where it is processed" plus "customer-specific keys" points to client-side encryption with KMS keys (CSE-KMS): data is encrypted before it's written, with its own key per customer, and the job's intermediate results are protected too. This is set through a security configuration attached to the Glue job.

opts.A: SSE-S3 uses keys the service manages — they can't be "customer-specific." And encryption happens only at write time to S3, not during processing.
opts.B: An EMR cluster per customer means managing clusters instead of serverless jobs, and CSE-Custom requires implementing your own key provider. The most effort of the options.
opts.D: Again clusters instead of Glue, and SSE-KMS protects objects at rest in S3, not data during processing.

1008.key: The application is stateless and resilient to failures, so interruptible capacity is a fit. The cheapest setup: build an AMI, put it in a launch template, create an Auto Scaling group on top of a Spot Fleet, and attach an Application Load Balancer. Capacity scales itself, and Spot Instances cost up to 90 percent less than On-Demand; reclamation isn't a concern because there's no state to lose.

opts.A: Two On-Demand instances is fixed capacity: it still falls short at peak and the company pays for idle capacity during lulls. No real scaling.
opts.B: The same fixed-capacity drawback, and Route 53 weighted routing also doesn't remove a failed instance instantly the way a load balancer does.
opts.C: Changing the instance type requires stopping it, i.e. downtime, and still leaves a single machine as a point of failure. That's vertical scaling, not seamless scaling.

1009.key: Objects are read frequently, KMS encryption is mandated by policy, and the cost driver is calls to KMS rather than storage: under SSE-KMS every read or write means a Decrypt or GenerateDataKey call. An S3 Bucket Key solves exactly this: S3 requests one bucket-level key from KMS for a short period and derives per-object keys from it itself, cutting the number of KMS calls — and the bill for them — by roughly 99%. Encryption stays SSE-KMS, and key permissions and logging are preserved.

opts.A: SSE-S3 is indeed cheaper, but it drops KMS entirely, while the company has strict requirements and key management already built around KMS.
opts.C: Client-side encryption with KMS keys increases the number of KMS calls and requires reworking the application — the opposite of "without additional calls to KMS."
opts.D: This combination isn't possible: with SSE-C the client supplies the key with every request, and it's never stored in KMS. It also doesn't save on calls.

1010.key: A lift-and-shift move on a tight timeline means block-level replication of the virtual machines. The standard tool is AWS Application Migration Service: the Replication Agent is installed on the machines (B), initial replication completes and test instances are launched for acceptance testing (C), and at cutover, work on the source machines stops and the final instance is launched (D). Downtime comes down to minutes.

opts.A: The Schema Conversion Tool converts database schemas and doesn't collect information about virtual machines.
opts.E: App2Container packages applications into containers, i.e. changes how they run — that's no longer a lift-and-shift.
opts.F: DMS migrates database contents, not entire virtual machines.

1011.key: Two halves of the task. Permissions: the Cognito user pool confirms identity and issues a token, but that token can't be used to call S3 — an identity pool is needed to exchange it for temporary IAM role credentials scoped to the right bucket prefix (A). Path: the application runs in a private subnet, so calls to S3 go through a VPC endpoint without ever reaching the internet (C). Distinguishing the user pool from the identity pool is the most common source of confusion in Cognito questions.

opts.B: The user pool issues identity and access tokens for your own application, not AWS credentials. They can't be used to call S3.
opts.D: A NAT gateway sends traffic out to the internet, contradicting the idea of private access, and there's no such thing as a "request initiated by Cognito" condition in a bucket policy.
opts.E: Restricting by user IP address doesn't work for mobile or home users and isn't an authorization mechanism at all.

1012.key: The symptom is described precisely: the queue grows while the processing instances sit at 100 percent CPU, and the peaks are unpredictable. That means scaling has to track queue length. A target tracking policy driven by a metric based on ApproximateNumberOfMessages (typically messages per instance) adds processing capacity exactly when messages start piling up, regardless of any schedule.

opts.A: Scheduled scaling doesn't work with unpredictable peaks, and CPU is already at 100 percent by the time it would trigger — the signal arrives too late.
opts.B: A cache in front of DynamoDB won't help: the bottleneck is compute processing of the messages, not reading from the database.
opts.C: CloudFront caches responses at the web tier, but the delays occur at the order-processing tier reading from the queue.

1013.key: Interruptions aren't tolerable, so Spot Instances are ruled out entirely. For running continuously Monday through Saturday, Standard Reserved Instances are purchased, and for the twelve hours on Sunday, Scheduled Reserved Instances — reserved for exactly that recurring window. Worth noting: AWS no longer offers this reservation type to new customers, but within the logic of the question it remains the only interruption-free option for a recurring window.

opts.B: Convertible Reserved Instances are billed continuously: for twelve hours once a week, that's an almost entirely unused commitment.
opts.C: Spot Instances can be reclaimed, and the scenario explicitly forbids interruptions.
opts.D: The same Spot problem here, plus a smaller discount from Convertible Reserved Instances for the steady workload.

1014.key: Image processing is a stream of batch jobs, and the company doesn't want to manage infrastructure. AWS Batch itself provisions and runs the compute resources for the job queue (including on Fargate), AWS Step Functions describes the sequence of steps and removes manual handoffs, and the large result files land in S3, which grows without limit and costs less than file storage systems.

opts.A: An ECS cluster on interruptible instances still requires managing the compute environment, and SQS only provides a queue, not workflow orchestration.
opts.C: Lambda functions are limited in time and memory for heavy image processing, and interruptible instances again mean managing your own infrastructure.
opts.D: A group of EC2 instances is exactly the infrastructure the company doesn't want to manage, and an EBS volume isn't shared across machines and is limited in size.

1015.key: There are two problems — slow downloads and slow uploads — and they're solved with different tools, with minimal effort. CloudFront in front of the bucket speeds up downloads: images are cached at edge locations near the user. S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads: the file is accepted at the nearest edge location and travels to the bucket over the AWS backbone. Both are turned on with configuration, no architecture changes needed.

opts.B: Moving the site to instances across multiple Regions is a rewrite of the architecture with ongoing cost, while minimal implementation effort is required.
opts.C: Uploading through CloudFront is inefficient, and buckets in multiple Regions with replication and download redirection is a complex, expensive construction.
opts.D: Global Accelerator doesn't work with S3 as an endpoint: that configuration doesn't exist.

1016.key: Traffic to S3 must not travel over the internet, and the cheapest solution is needed. An S3 gateway endpoint adds a route to the service's prefix in the VPC route table, traffic stays inside the AWS network, and the endpoint itself carries no charge — neither hourly nor per data processed.

opts.A: An interface endpoint is also private, but it's billed hourly and per traffic processed, while a gateway endpoint is free.
opts.C: Allowing the NAT gateway's IP address doesn't change the route: traffic still goes over the internet.
opts.D: A second NAT gateway just doubles the cost and leaves the same path over the internet.

1017.key: Pods need distinct permissions rather than the shared node permissions, which calls for IRSA: separate Kubernetes service accounts are created for the UI and the data services, each annotated with its own IAM role's ARN, and the roles trust the cluster's OIDC provider with a condition scoped to a specific service account. That way the UI pod can reach only its DynamoDB table, and the data-services pod only its bucket. Note: the option's wording actually swaps the services (S3 is assigned to the UI, DynamoDB to data services) — that's a typo in the dump; the mechanism itself is described correctly. The same technique is covered in {{q:941,223}}.

opts.A: Policies on the instance profile grant permissions to every pod on the node at once, and Kubernetes RBAC controls access to the Kubernetes API itself, not to AWS services.
opts.B: An IAM policy can't be attached to a pod directly: the principal is the role a pod assumes via its service account.
opts.C: The mechanism is named almost correctly, but the FullAccess managed policies grant full access to the entire service, which conflicts with the requirement for scoped access.

1018.key: Users stay in the on-premises Active Directory, and access is needed across several accounts in the organization. The lightest path is AD Connector: it keeps no copy of the directory and instead proxies authentication requests to your own domain controllers, connecting as an identity source to IAM Identity Center. From there, permission sets are assigned to AD groups for the relevant accounts. No forest trust and no second directory in the cloud need to be stood up — hence the minimal operational overhead.

opts.A: Managed Microsoft AD with a trust relationship works, but it's an additional directory in the cloud that has to be paid for and maintained, plus setting up a forest trust. More effort than AD Connector.
opts.B: IAM users for a distributed team means manually managing permissions and long-lived credentials, conflicting with both the requirements and minimal effort.
opts.D: Cognito is built for application end users, not for employee access to AWS accounts.

1019.key: An API in API Gateway has its own access-restriction mechanism — a resource policy. It denies every address except the listed trusted ones, and the check is performed by the gateway itself before the backend is ever invoked.

opts.A: A private integration controls how the gateway reaches the backend inside the network — it doesn't restrict client access by IP address.
opts.C: API Gateway is a managed service; it can't be deployed into your own subnet, and network ACLs don't apply to it.
opts.D: A security group can't be attached to API Gateway: the service has no network interfaces of yours for inbound traffic to hit.
